story:
Amelia held a book about turtles. It had a shiny green cover. She opened it and saw little black marks on every page.

"What are these?" she asked. Her mother smiled. "Those are words. They say things."

Amelia squinted at the marks. "The turtle page says turtle things," she decided. She turned the pages from the front to the back. "This way," she said, nodding.

"I want to keep this book forever," Amelia said. She hugged it tight.

Her mother shook her head. "We borrow library books. Then we take them back. Other kids want to read about turtles too."

Amelia frowned at the turtle book. Then she frowned at the shelf. Another girl stood there, looking sad.

"Are you waiting for this book?" Amelia asked her.

The girl nodded. "Turtles are my favorite."

Amelia looked at the cover one more time. She opened the front page and pointed at the words. "The words tell turtle things," she said. "You read this way, front to back."

She gave the book to the girl. The girl waved goodbye. Amelia waved back.

"Can we come back next week?" Amelia asked her mother.

"Yes," said her mother. "And maybe the turtle book will be home again."

Scarlett wanted to help Mom make soup. Mom said, "You can watch from here." Scarlett stood on her stool.

The pot began to hiss. Steam rose up like a little cloud. Mom put in a spoon and lifted it out. "This is hot," Mom said. She blew on the spoon. She blew one time. She blew two times. Then she touched a tiny drop to her lip. "Now it is warm."

Scarlett wanted to touch the pot. Mom shook her head. "Hot things can hurt you," she said. "We look with our eyes."

Scarlett looked with her eyes. She saw the soup roll and bubble. Then Mom gave her a cool cup of water. Scarlett put her hand on it. "This one is cold!" she said. "The pot is hot. My cup is cold."

After lunch, Scarlett was tired. She climbed into her bed. Her teddy was waiting there. Mom tucked her in. "Stay close to me when you wake up," Mom said.

Scarlett nodded. "Hot pot, cold cup," she said softly. Her eyes closed. Mom smiled and turned out the light.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. A big bowl sat in the middle. It was too far away. "I want the peas," she said. Her tummy wanted food now. That was her problem.

"Pass the peas, please," said Daddy. Mommy passed the bowl. Then Daddy passed it to Aubrey. Lucky girl! She put her nose close. "I smell them," she said. Her nose did that. She looked at the peas. Her eyes saw little green balls. She counted them out loud. "One pea, two peas, three peas." She touched the peas with her fingers. Cold and smooth.

Then Aubrey ate one pea. Her tongue tasted it. Yum! She heard a funny sound. Crunch, crunch. Her ears heard it. "The peas go crunch," she said. "My ears heard that." She ate some more. "One pea, two peas, three peas." Mommy smiled. Aubrey smiled too. "More peas, please," she said.

Livia went to the art gallery with her dad. She saw a big red painting. "Red," she said. Dad smiled and nodded.

Then she saw a blue painting. "Blue," she said. Then a yellow one. "Yellow!" Dad clapped his hands.

At a little table there were paints. Livia wanted to make green like the grass. She painted with yellow. It was just yellow. She painted more yellow. Still just yellow. A boy next to her was sad. His brush fell down with a little noise. Livia picked it up for him. He said, "Thank you." He pointed at his paint. It was blue.

Livia had an idea. She put blue on her yellow. She mixed it with her brush. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said.

Dad said, "Let's try red and yellow." Livia mixed them. The paint turned orange. Then she mixed red and blue. It turned purple, not yucky at all.

A gallery lady came by. "What a pretty green," she said. Livia chased a drip of paint down the paper with her brush.

"We can hang it at home," said Dad. Livia held up her painting. "Look, green!" she said.

Thomas wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He stood on his little stool by the sink. He turned the tap. The water came out. It was cold. Thomas put his hands under it. "Too cold!" he said.

Then Thomas turned the other tap. Steam floated up. Thomas held his hand close, not touching. The air felt hot. He pulled his hand back fast. "Hot water can hurt me," Thomas said. He turned the hot tap back a little. Then he mixed the two waters. He felt it with one finger. Now it was warm and nice. Thomas rubbed the rough towel on his wet hands. He did not touch the pink soap with the sharp top, because that was Mama's.

Mama came to the door. "I will not forget you, Mama," Thomas said. He held out his hand. "Can we have a cookie now?" Mama laughed and took his warm, dry hand.

Nora wanted to go outside. The sheep on her coat needed to come too. But first she had to put it on. She pushed one arm in. She pushed the other arm in. "One, two," she said.

Now the zipper. She pulled it up. But the zipper did not move. Nora pulled again. "Oh no," she said. The zipper made a loud noise, click, click. Dad looked over. "Your coat is all bumpy," he said. Nora looked down. Yes, the coat was twisted. One side was up and one side was down.

Nora smoothed the coat. She made it flat. She made it straight. Then she held the zipper and pulled. Up it went! "Zip it all the way to the sheep," said Dad. Nora zipped it to the top. She patted the sheep. "Bumpy coat, no zip," Nora said. "Flat coat, yes zip!" She ran to the door. "Outside now!"

Miles went to the library with his dad. They rode the bus. The bus was not heavy to sit on, but the doors were heavy to push.

Miles wanted to draw on the library tablet. He pushed the button on top. The screen stayed dark. He held the button down and counted. One, two, three. The screen lit up. "It comes on when I hold it," said Miles. He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. He drew a big red cat.

Then it was time to go. Miles did not just set the tablet down. He tapped the app closed. He held the button again and the screen went dark. He hung his picture on the fridge later. "Hold the button, draw, then put it away," said Miles. His dad smiled and held his hand.

Cooper wanted the red car. His big sister Mia wanted it too. She grabbed one end. He grabbed the other end. The car did not go anywhere.

Then Mia said, "You go first. Then me." She let go. Cooper zoomed the car on the floor. One turn. Two turns. Then he gave the car to Mia. She zoomed it too. It was fair.

Outside, rain fell on the street. The road was wet. Cooper watched from the window. He saw a man slip on the wet street. The man got up slow. He walked on, more careful now.

"The floor is wet too," Cooper said. He walked with small steps. The car was safe in his hands. Mia held out her hand. Cooper put the car in it.

"Your turn," he said.

Sara went to the library with her Mama. The library sat next to the bread store. Sara could smell the warm bread. She felt happy.

Sara wanted the big red book about wild bears. She ran to the shelf. Her heart went fast. She was so excited. Then a shelf fell over. CRASH! Sara jumped. Her tummy felt tight. She was scared.

Mama knelt down next to her. "Take a big breath," Mama said. "Breathe in slow." Sara breathed in slow. Then she breathed out. Her tummy felt loose again. "The loud noise made me scared," Sara said. "The slow breath made me feel better." Then Sara saw a little boy crying by the fallen shelf. His book was under it. He looked sad. Sara picked up the book and gave it to him. He stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Sara smiled too. "Mama," she said, "I helped him." Mama hugged her tight.

Declan ran to the paint table. He wanted the red brush. But the red brush was all wet. It sat in a cup of water. "Why is it wet?" Declan asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Yesterday you painted with it. We wash the brushes later. Now they dry." Declan touched the cup. The water felt cool. He could smell the old paint, sweet and sticky on his fingers. That was the problem. The red brush was not ready now. Declan picked a different brush. This one was blue and dry. The blue paint felt smooth on his hand. He drew a big sun. Later, after snack time, Declan looked again. The red brush was dry! "It dried because we waited," he said. He dipped it in red paint. He drew a red apple next to his sun. "Today the sun is yellow," he said. "Tomorrow I will paint a red cat."

Charlie wanted toast with butter all by herself. She took the butter out of the fridge. The butter was cold and hard. She pushed it on the bread. The bread tore. "Oh no," said Charlie.

Then the butter sat on the counter while she got her cup. The butter got warm and soft. She tried again. The soft butter made the toast smooth. It went on thin, like a little blanket. "Why did it work now?" Charlie asked herself. "The butter got warm. Warm butter is soft!" She put a small pat on top. It looked like a little yellow flower.

Next came the milk. Charlie set the cup on the table. She held the jug with two hands. She poured slowly, slowly. One step, two steps, three steps, pour. The milk went up, up, up. Not one drop spilled.

"Look, Mama!" said Charlie. "I made breakfast all by myself." She took a big bite of toast and a big sip of milk. "Can we do it again tomorrow?"

Madeline was at Grandma's house. It was her birthday. Big balloons sat on the chair. The cake came out. It had three little candles on top. The candles were lit. They made little flames.

Madeline wanted to eat the cake. She reached for it. "Wait," said Grandma. "The candles are still on." Madeline looked at the flames. They were warm. She could feel the heat on her nose.

Grandpa leaned down. "Make a wish," he said. "Then blow." Madeline took a big breath. She blew hard. Out went the candles. One, two, three. Little smoke curls went up. They looked like gray ribbons.

"Now we can eat," said Grandma. The cake was cool and sweet. Frosting got on Madeline's nose. Her friend Sam laughed. Grandma wiped Sam's chin with a soft napkin. Grandpa gave everyone milk. Madeline sat on the big chair and took another bite.

"The candles made it hot," said Madeline. "I blew them out. Now it's cake time." Everyone clapped. Madeline blew a kiss at the empty candles.

Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard with Dad.

"Stay close," said Dad. Maria stayed close to Dad.

Then Maria saw the grill. The grill made a little smoke. She wanted to touch it.

"Hot," said Dad. "We do not touch the grill."

Maria stopped her hand. She found a stick. She held the stick near the grill. The stick got warm. Then the stick got hot. Maria dropped the stick on the grass.

"Hot," said Maria. "The fire makes it hot."

She wiped her hands on her hat. Then she went to the cold water bucket. Maria put one finger in the water. "Cold," she said. She put both hands in. The cold water felt good on her warm fingers.

Dad sat down on the bench. Maria sat right next to him. "I stay close," said Maria.

"You stay close," said Dad. "Good girl."

Maria watched the smoke go up, up, up. Her new hat kept the sun off her head. She waited with Dad until the corn was ready. It smelled so good.

"Cold hands, warm corn," said Maria, and she smiled.

Alice went to the store with her brother. They wanted apples for snack time. Alice was hungry already.

Mum said, "We need ten apples." Alice put apples in a basket. One, two, three. Then the basket tipped over. Apples rolled on the floor. "Oh no," said Alice.

Her brother knelt down with her. They tried to pick up every apple. Alice counted as they went. "One, two, three, four, five." Her brother found one more under the shelf. "Six!" Alice held up an apple. "Seven, eight, nine." They looked and looked. One apple was still missing.

Then Alice saw it. It had rolled to the big orange pumpkins. She picked it up. "Ten!" she said. "All the apples came back."

Mum smiled. "Why did they roll so far?" she asked.

Alice thought. "The floor is smooth," she said. "Smooth things roll fast."

She put the ten apples in the basket. She held the basket with both hands this time. Her brother carried the bread. Alice counted the apples one more time on the way home. "Ten apples for our snack," she said.

Lydia skipped all the way to the big stadium. She held Daddy's hand. "One, two, three, up we go," Daddy said as they climbed the steps.

The game began. Lydia sat in her seat. Then everyone stood up and waved. Tall people were all around her. Lydia could not see the game. Her tummy felt sad. She pulled Daddy's sleeve. "Too many feet," she said. Daddy looked down at her. Then he smiled and lifted her up on his shoulders.

Now Lydia was taller than everyone. "One, two, three, I can see!" she said. She clapped her hands. The crowd roared. Lydia waved her little flag. A man scored a goal. Everyone jumped. Lydia bounced on Daddy's shoulders. At last she saw the whole game, from way up high. "I see it because I am up," Lydia said. Daddy laughed. "Yes, you are," he said. "Wave your flag one more time."

Emilia went to the store with Mama. She saw a big red balloon. Emilia wanted the balloon for her friend Sam's present. But a boy was holding it. He was crying because his mama said it was time to go.

The boy put the balloon down. Emilia picked it up. Then she saw the boy still crying. He wanted it too. Emilia thought hard. She looked at the balloon. She looked at the boy.

"Here," Emilia said. "You take it first. Then it is my turn." The boy smiled and held the balloon. He gave it back to Emilia after one minute. Emilia counted the minute out loud, slow and deep, like a big drum. Then she hugged the balloon. At the store, the man at the door said, "One line, one turn, everyone waits." Emilia waited in the line. She got her turn. She paid with coins from Mama.

At home, Emilia gave Sam the balloon. "We took turns," she said. Sam squeezed it tight and laughed.

Chloe wanted to play the senses game. Mom said, "Name five senses, and win a star."

Chloe held a red apple. "I see it with my eyes," she said. Then she sniffed it. "I smell it with my nose." Mom clapped.

Chloe stopped. "What comes next?" Mom put the apple by Chloe's back. "No fair!" said Chloe. "My ears can't see it!" She turned around and grinned.

She bit the apple. "Crunchy! I taste it with my mouth." Then she touched her teddy bear. "Soft! I touch with my hands."

Mom held up the star. "Five senses, five body parts. You did it!" Chloe hugged the bear. "My hands feel squishy teddy!" she said, and took another big crunchy bite.

Andrew went to the little pool by the lake. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But Andrew felt shy. He sat at the edge and watched.

Dad held his hand. "Try one little kick," Dad said. Andrew held the rail. He put his face in the water. He blew out with his mouth. Bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! Andrew lifted his head. He laughed. "The bubbles pop because I blow," he said.

He tried again. He blew more air. More bubbles came. More bubbles popped. Then Andrew let his feet float up behind him. His legs did not sink. They sat on top of the water like a boat. "Dad, look! My feet come up when I blow!" Dad smiled and held him steady. After all that blowing, Andrew was tired. They lay on the towel in the sun. Andrew took a little nap. When he woke up, he said, "More bubbles now, please."

Chloe stood on her stool at the kitchen wall. She had toast and a butter knife. She wanted to do it all by herself.

She pushed the knife hard. The butter was cold and hard. The toast tore. A big hole! Chloe laughed. "Oops. Toast boat." Dad put a new slice in the toaster. He set the butter dish near the warm toaster. Soon the butter went soft and shiny. Chloe slid her knife across it. The soft butter spread like paint. "Soft butter goes on easy!" she said. "Cold butter makes holes."

Then came the milk. Chloe held the little jug with two hands. She poured too fast. Milk slipped down the side and made a puddle. She got a cloth and wiped it up. Then she tried again, very slow, like a sleepy turtle. Drip. Drip. Drip. Not one drop spilled.

"Look, Dad!" said Chloe. "Slow milk stays in the cup." Dad clapped. "Big girl milk," he said. "Stormy clouds outside, but our kitchen is dry." Chloe drank her milk and ate her buttery toast, every bite, even the crumbs.

Emilia ran into the clinic. She was first in line for her turn. She loved the doctor, but not shots.

"Nurse Amy, will the shot hurt?" she asked.

"A little," said Nurse Amy. "But try this. Let your arm go soft and loose."

Emilia squeezed her arm tight. It felt like a rock. Then she tried. She let her arm go soft. She wiggled her fingers and counted to three.

"One, two, three."

The needle went in. It was just a quick pinch!

"That was small!" Emilia said. "My arm was tight before. Tight made it hurt more. Soft made it hurt less!"

Nurse Amy put a band aid on. Emilia held up her arm.

"My arm feels a little weak," she said, "but it is still strong enough for a sticker!"

She picked a shiny star and held it high.

Henry ran to the park. He heard a bell ring. Ding, ding, ding! Henry used his ears to hear it. "The ice cream truck!" he said. But where was it?

Henry looked with his eyes. He could not see the truck. He turned his head all the way. There it was! "My eyes see it!" said Henry. The truck stopped by the sandbox. Henry dug in the sand. He made a big, round hole. "Look! An ocean!" he said.

The man held out ice cream. Henry sniffed with his nose. It smelled sweet. He licked it with his tongue. Yum! It tasted cold and yummy. A dog ran by. "Phew, that dog is smelly," said Henry. Henry patted the dog with his hand. The fur felt soft.

Henry sat on the bench. The dog sat too. "We can talk with our mouths," said Henry. He licked his ice cream again. "More tomorrow!"

Henry went to the library with Mom. Today was story time. Yesterday, the library had a cake party. Henry had licked the frosting off his piece. It was the last cake on the plate.

Henry looked at the big table. "Where is the cake?" he asked. Mom smiled softly. "The cake was yesterday," she said. "Today we have story time. The cake is all gone."

Henry frowned a little. He wanted cake now. "Can we get cake now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later we can bake one at home." Henry touched the empty table with his hand. It felt smooth and cool. "The cake is gone because yesterday is done," he said.

Then the librarian rang a little bell. Story time was starting now. Henry sat down on the soft rug. He picked a book about a red truck. "Can we read the truck book tomorrow too?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow we can come back." Henry hugged the book to his chest and turned the first page.

Hayden went to the library with Dad. He wanted a book about a big elephant. But where was it?

The books were all mixed up. He saw a book about apples. He saw a book about a teddy bear. He saw a book about a bus. No elephant anywhere.

Then Hayden saw little signs on the shelves. One sign had a cow on it. The cow shelf held cow books, pig books, and duck books. All the animals lived there!

He ran to the animal shelf. He hugged the books close to his chest. There was a blue book with a big gray elephant on the cover. It was heavy. His grip felt loose, so he held on tight.

"Look, Dad! Elephants are animals. Apples are foods. This is the animal shelf!"

Hayden sat down on a soft rug. He opened the elephant book. The pages made a swish sound. Then something fell out. It was a shiny bookmark shaped like a tiny peanut. The elephant in the picture seemed to wink at him.

"Elephants love peanuts," said Hayden. "This is for you, elephant." He put the bookmark right on the elephant's long nose.

Dad smiled. "Time to close the book soon. We can take it home."

"One more page," said Hayden. "The elephant is still hungry."

Lincoln put on his blue coat. He went to the corner store with Dad. "Can I pick the apples?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We need six."

Lincoln counted the red apples. One, two, three, four, five, six. Then he counted them the other way, starting from the other end. One, two, three, four, five, six. He frowned. It was six both times! How could that be? He counted them again, very slowly. Six again.

"The last number I say is six," said Lincoln. "So there are six." Dad smiled and put them in the bag. Then Lincoln saw two baskets of oranges. He counted one basket. Eight. He counted the small basket. Five. "This one has more," he said, pointing. He helped build a tall stack of them by the register. The stack did not fall. "Eight is more than five," said Lincoln. "Because when I count, the last number tells me."

Joshua ran into the big hall. There was a desk by the door. Grandma was sitting at the desk. She handed out spoons and cups. The sky outside was cloudy and gray.

"Time for soup," said Grandma. Joshua grabbed his spoon fast. Then everyone held hands in one big circle. "We say the blessing first," said Grandma. Joshua put his spoon down on the desk. He held Grandpa's hand and Mama's hand. Grandpa said the blessing. Joshua listened. Then everyone said, "Amen!" Joshua clapped. "Now we eat!" said Grandma. Joshua picked his spoon back up. The soup was warm and yummy.

A dog barked outside the window. "The dog wants soup too," said Grandpa. Joshua giggled. "Dogs can't hold hands," said Joshua. Grandpa laughed and laughed. "Blessing first, then soup," said Joshua, and he slurped his bowl.

Anna was at the playground. She saw the big slide. The slide looked like a dark dragon tail.

Anna wanted to go down it. But the ladder was tall. Her feet could not fit on the first step.

A boy named Sam stood by the ladder. Anna said, "Please help me climb." Sam held her hand. Up, up, up she went.

"Thank you, Sam," said Anna. At the top, Anna pretended to be a lion. "Roar! I am a lion on a mountain!"

She slid down fast. Whee! Then she bumped into Sam at the bottom. Sam fell on the grass.

"Sorry," said Anna. She helped Sam stand up. Sam smiled.

"Why did you say sorry?" Sam asked.

"Because I bumped you. Bumping hurts. Sorry makes it better," said Anna.

Sam nodded. "Want to be lions together?"

"Yes! Roar!" said Anna. Two lions ran around the playground.

Then Anna's shoe came untied. "Help, please," she called. Mama came and tied it tight.

"There," said Mama. "Now the shoe will fit just right."

"Thank you, Mama," said Anna. She roared one more time and ran to the swings.

William went to a big festival with his grandma. There was music and food and a long table. Outside, kids ran near a playground. One boy began to fall, and William helped him up.

At the table, everyone held hands. Grandma said they would say a blessing first. William did not wait. He grabbed a sharp piece of bread and put it in his mouth. Nobody else was eating yet. William looked around. He put the bread down on his plate.

Grandma smiled at him. She squeezed his hand. Then she said the blessing, and everyone said thank you together. After that, they all ate. William tried again at the next meal. He held hands. He waited. He said the blessing with grandma, word by word.

"You waited," said grandma. William picked up his bread and took a big bite.

Blake walked on the nature trail with Dad. She wanted to know a game for the long walk. Dad said, "Let's play the five senses game." He held up one finger. "First, eyes. What do you see?" Blake saw a green leaf. "I see a leaf with my eyes!" she said.

Then Blake heard water. She pointed to her ears. "I hear the water with my ears!" Dad smiled. They came to a pine tree. Blake touched the bark. "I feel the bark with my hands!" Next she sniffed the air. "I smell pine with my nose!" One sense was left. Dad poured a sip of water from his bottle into her cup. Blake drank it. "I taste the water with my mouth!"

Just then rain began to fall. Blake felt drops on her face. "The rain is wet because water falls from the sky," she said. Dad laughed. "You used your hands and your skin. That is neat!" Blake counted on her fingers: eyes, ears, hands, nose, mouth. "Five senses," she said. "I did it!" She jumped in a small puddle with both feet.

Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was falling outside. It made a thick white coat on the window.

"Today we count!" said Miss Ana. She clapped her hands. All the children stood in a circle.

Axel wanted to count the loud drum. Miss Ana said, "When we count, we say the numbers in a row. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Axel began. "One, two, three, five!" He hit the drum one time for each word. But there were ten crackers on the plate. The drum stopped at five. "Where did four go?" Axel asked.

Mia stood next to him. She pointed at her fingers. "Look. The words go in order. You skipped one." Axel looked at her fingers. He tapped each one as he said a word.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Ten taps. Ten crackers. All the children clapped. Miss Ana put a cracker in his hand.

Axel grinned. "The words have to stay in their line!" He ran back to the window to count the snowflakes, one by one.

Michael ran into Grandma's house. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights! Grandma had small clay lamps called diyas. Each one had a little cotton wick and a drop of oil.

"I want to light one!" said Michael. Grandma helped him. But when they set his diya on the porch, the wind blew. The flame went out. Michael set it out again. The wind blew it out again.

Then Michael saw Grandpa's lamp. It sat behind a big glass jar. The wind could not reach it. Michael found a jar too. He put his diya inside it. He lit the wick. The flame stood up tall. "The wind can't get it now!" he said. Grandma clapped. The pet dog barked at all the bright lights.

Soon Michael was sleepy. He fell asleep on Grandma's lap, with his little lamp still shining.

Bennett jumped into his big car seat. "Go, go, go!" he called. Daddy started the car. It went fast, then slow, then fast again.

Bennett looked out the window. A big truck went by. Vroom! A small bug sat on the glass. It was so tiny. Outside the sun was hot. Bennett touched the window. Hot, hot, hot! He touched his cold juice cup. Cold! "Hot window, cold juice," he said. Daddy laughed.

Daddy said, "We will get ice cream soon." Bennett clapped. Ice cream was yummy, yummy, yummy! They stopped at the ice cream shop. Bennett got a vanilla cone. He sat in the car and held it tight.

The sun was hot. The ice cream started to drip. Drip, drip, drip, right onto his cone. "My ice cream is melting!" said Bennett. He looked up at the hot sun. "The sun is hot. That makes it melt!" Daddy gave him a paper plate. Bennett put the cone on the plate and ate fast. "Big bites, Daddy, big bites! I will eat it all up!"

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Violet waited by the kitchen window. Then his car pulled up. "Grandpa!" she shouted. He hugged her tight.

On day two, Grandpa sat quietly at the table. He did not eat his toast. "I miss my sheep," he said. "At home, I paint them every morning." Violet knew what to do. She found paper and her paint pots. She put them right in front of him. Grandpa picked up a brush. He painted a funny sheep with a curly face. Then he laughed and laughed and ate all his toast.

"You were sad because you missed your sheep," said Violet. "Now you painted one, so you are happy." Grandpa nodded and gave her a big kiss. Violet painted a sheep too. They painted side by side, all week long, until the paper covered the whole kitchen table.

Andrew went to the park with his mom. The sun was bright. He ran to the slide. He put his hand on it. "Ow! It is hot," he said. The sun made the metal hot. He pulled his hand back fast.

"Let's wait," said Mom. They sat in the shade under a tree. Andrew heard leaves whisper over his head. He saw a snowy patch behind the fence. It felt cold when he poked it with his boot.

Then they walked past the little farm. A pink pig sat in the pen. Andrew wanted to pat it. "Stay back," said Mom. "The fence keeps us safe." Andrew waved at the pig instead. The pig wiggled its nose.

Later the sun went behind a cloud. Andrew touched the slide again. It was not hot now. He climbed up. He went down, fast and smooth. "The sun made it hot before," he said. Mom clapped. "You waited, and now you can slide."

Blake went to the library with her mama. There was a new rug by the story corner. It was blue like a lake. Blake sat down on the soft blue lake.

The teacher held up one duck puppet. "We will pass the duck," she said. Blake wanted the duck first. But a boy named Sam got it first. Sam made the duck quack. Then Sam passed the duck to Blake. Blake made the duck quack too. Then she passed it to the next kid. "Why do we pass it?" Blake asked her mama. "So everyone gets a turn," Mama said. One duck, many kids, so they took turns.

At the end, the teacher said, "We all win, because we all had a turn." Blake smiled and hugged the duck one more time. Then she put it in the basket. "Bye, duck," she said. "See you at the lake."

Iris wanted to wear her red shoes tomorrow. But she could not find them. She looked under her bed. She found one sticky candy wrapper there. "Yuck," she said. She kept looking.

"It is nighttime now," said Dad. "The shoes can wait until later. Tomorrow is not here yet." Iris sat on her bed. She did not want to wait. Waiting felt long.

Dad helped her look anyway. They looked slowly. They looked in the toy box. They looked by the door. Then Iris felt something tickle her toes inside her slipper. She wiggled her foot. Out fell a red shoe! The other red shoe was under the blanket.

"The shoes hid from me," Iris said. "I found them because I kept looking." Dad smiled and put the shoes by the door.

"Now I sleep," said Iris. "Then it will be tomorrow, and I will wear my red shoes." She pulled the blanket up to her chin and closed her eyes.

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with Dad. She wanted to find a book about bears. She looked and looked. There were so many books!

Dad pointed to a big letter on a sign. It was B. "That is B," he said. Brooklyn frowned. How would B help her?

Then she said the letter out loud. "B says buh," she said. Then she said her own name. "Brooklyn. Buh, buh, Brooklyn!" The B was at the start of her name!

She looked at the shelves again. She saw a word that began with B. She said the first sound. "Buh. Buh, bear!" The word said bear! She pulled the book out. A friendly bear smiled on the cover.

"Can you spell bear?" asked Dad. "B," said Brooklyn, proudly. "Then the other letters come after." She could not say them all yet, but she knew the first one.

"Maybe B can find more books," said Dad. Brooklyn walked along the shelf. She saw a word that began with B. "Buh, buh. Bunnies!" She found a bunny book too.

"Did B help you find them?" Dad asked. Brooklyn nodded. "Yes. B makes the buh sound. So my eyes find B first."

On the way home, they talked about dinner. "Bananas," said Brooklyn. "Bananas start with B too!" Dad laughed. Brooklyn hugged her bear book.

"Tomorrow," she said, "I want to find the letter C."

Sara dug little holes in the dirt. She dropped a seed in each hole. Then she covered the seeds with soft brown soil. "Grow, little seeds," she said. "Grow, grow." Her dog Max dug too. He hid a big bone in the corner of the garden. "Silly Max," said Sara. She patted his head.

Every day Sara watered her seeds with a small blue can. Green leaves popped up in the sun. But in the corner, by the tall wall, nothing grew. Sara waited and waited. She watered that spot too. Still nothing came up. Then she sat and watched all morning. The sun moved over the sky. The sun did not shine on the corner at all. "The seeds need sun," said Sara. "That is why they will not grow."

So Sara planted new seeds in the sunny spot. Soon the leaves grew tall there too. Tiny red tomatoes came out. "Look, Max!" said Sara. "The sun helped them grow." The sun began to sink behind the barn. Max dug up his bone and lay down in the warm grass. Sara held a pretty red tomato in her two hands. "Grow, little seeds," she whispered. "Grow, grow."

Victor wanted apple juice at snack time. Miss Ana held the big jug. Victor reached and grabbed. Miss Ana said, "Please ask with words." Victor said, "Please pour me juice." Miss Ana smiled. She pour, pour, poured the juice into his cup. "Thank you," said Victor. "You are welcome," said Miss Ana.

Victor took his cup with both hands. But his sock slipped on the floor. The cup tipped. Juice went splash, splash, splash. Victor felt his face go hot. "Sorry," he said to Miss Ana. "It slipped out of my hands." Miss Ana knelt down. "Accidents happen," she said. "Let's clean it up together." One towel, two towels, three towels. They wiped the floor till it was dry.

Then Miss Ana helped him pour a new cup, just a little bit. "Little cups do not tip," she said. Victor held it with both hands. He did not spill one drop. "Please works," said Victor. "I asked, and you helped me."

After snack, the class made red paper fire for their pretend fire truck. Victor glued on one flame, two flames, three flames. Then he got so sleepy. Nap mats came out, soft and quiet. Miss Ana tucked his blanket in. "Sweet dreams, Victor," she whispered. Victor closed his eyes and held his teddy tight.

Harrison had four little pots on the balcony. He filled each one with smooth, brown dirt. He pushed one carrot seed into each pot. Then he wrote a letter C on the pots with tape.

"Grandma, they are not growing," Harrison said. Two pots had tiny green leaves. Two pots had nothing at all.

Grandma came to look. She pointed at the pots. "Look where the sun is," she said. Harrison looked. The sun was bright on two pots. The wall made a big shadow on the other two.

"The sunny ones grew," Harrison said. "The dark ones did not."

Grandma smiled. "Sun helps seeds grow. Let's move them."

Harrison moved the pots into the sun. He gave each one a drink of water. Every morning he counted them. "One pot, two pots, three pots, four."

One day the dark pots had little leaves too. Harrison pointed at them and jumped up and down.

"Look, Grandma! The sun helped them!"

Joshua wanted to find his red ball. He looked under the bed. He looked behind the chair. The ball was not there.

Then he heard a loud sound outside. "Woof, woof!" The dog next door began to bark. Joshua jumped. His tummy felt tight. His hands felt cold. He was scared of the big sound.

Grandpa came outside with him. "Let's look at the dog," said Grandpa. They stood by the fence. The dog barked one more time. Then Grandpa clapped his hands softly. The dog sat down. It wagged its tail. "He barked because he wanted to say hello," said Grandpa. Joshua felt his tummy loosen. He was not scared now. He laughed, and the dog looked happy too.

Grandpa pointed at the grass. There was the red ball! Joshua felt so excited. He hugged Grandpa. "The dog barked, so we came out," said Joshua. "Then I found my ball." He threw the ball high in the air. "That was cool!" he said.

Claire was at Grandma's house. She wanted to play house with her teddy bear. But teddy was missing. She looked under the big chair. She looked behind the door. No teddy.

Grandma sat down beside her. "Let's make a bed for teddy," Grandma said. "Then teddy will want to come home." So Claire got a small box. She put in a soft sock. She laid a tissue on top, like a little blanket.

Then Claire heard a funny sound. Peep, peep! It came from the last basket on the shelf. Claire stood on her toes. There was teddy! A bird was singing a song outside the window, and teddy had been hiding near the sound. "The song brought the bird," Claire said. "The bird woke teddy up!" Claire put teddy in the new bed. She patted his head. "Night night, teddy," she said. Grandma smiled and turned off the little lamp.

Isaac jumped into the family car. He wanted his little blue dinosaur. But the dinosaur was not in his bag. Oh no! Where did it go?

"Last look!" said Mom. "We have to go now." Isaac sat in his seat. Then he remembered something. He had hugged the dinosaur when the car turned fast. The car had gone round the big corner. Everything slid to one side. Maybe the dinosaur slid too!

Isaac bent down low. He peeked under his seat. He saw a shoe. He saw a cracker. No dinosaur yet. He looked on the other side. He reached his hand way down. His fingers touched something bumpy. Something little. Something blue!

"I found him!" Isaac shouted. He pulled the dinosaur up high. "He slid under the seat when the car turned!" Mom laughed and clapped. The car began to go. Isaac hugged his dinosaur tight. "Soon we will be home," he said. "Then we can have a snack in the kitchen!" He spun the dinosaur around and around until he felt dizzy. The dinosaur got a big kiss right on his nose.

Natalie was in her playroom. She wanted to paint a green frog. But where was the green paint?

She looked in her paint box. She found red. She found blue. She found yellow. No green at all.

"Oh no," said Natalie. "My frog needs green."

She was hungry for her snack, but the frog came first. Natalie squeezed some blue paint. She squeezed some yellow paint too. She dipped her brush in both colors. She stirred them round and round on the paper.

The paint turned green! "Look at that!" said Natalie. Blue and yellow made green. She said it out loud: "Blue and yellow make green. That is why!"

She filled the whole page with green. Then she painted the frog's big eyes. She painted its little nose, right on its face.

"Mama, come see!" she called. "My frog is green!"

Mama came in and smiled. Natalie held up the painting.

"I made green all by myself," said Natalie. "Now can I have my snack?"

Margot wanted to draw a winter picture at school. She wanted a hill and a hat and big white snow. She picked up the tablet. She tapped the screen once. The screen stayed dark. She tapped it again. Still dark. She asked her teacher, "Why won't it wake up?"

Her teacher said, "Try the little round button. Hold it down."

Margot found the round button on the side. She pressed it with her finger. She held it and held it. Then the screen lit up. "The button makes it go," said Margot. "Tap does nothing. Hold makes it start."

She found the drawing app. It had a rainbow on it. She drew a white hill and a red hat and lots of snow. Then the timer rang. Play time was done. Margot pressed the button again. The screen asked, "Turn off?" She tapped yes. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, flat and neat.

"You put it away all by yourself," said her teacher. "That is a win."

Margot smiled at the shelf. "The tablet sleeps there now," she said.

Wesley was a small boy. He walked in the forest with his bear, Blue. Blue was hungry. Wesley had no spoon for pretend soup. He looked on the ground. He found a smooth brown stick. "This can be your spoon," he said. He stirred leaves in a little puddle. The stick made the soup. "Eat it all up," he said. Blue ate and ate. Then Wesley carried Blue to a mossy log. "This is our house now," he said. First they ate soup. Then they had a nap. A soft wind blew. The leaves went swish, swish. Wesley covered Blue with a big green leaf. "Good night, Blue," he said. "Sleep tight in our house." The forest went quiet and still.

Gabriella sat on a small chair in Miss Polly's music room. Miss Polly played a song on the piano. "Now we clap," she said. Gabriella clapped fast, fast, fast. The claps did not match the song. Her hands felt mixed up. She wanted to hide them under her legs.

Miss Polly stopped playing. She patted Gabriella's back. "Try again, little one," she said. "Listen first." Miss Polly played the slow beat. One, two, one, two. Gabriella listened. Then she clapped one, two, one, two. Her hands landed right on the beat. "My claps go with the song!" she said. "The claps are slow like the music."

"Now let's sing," said Miss Polly. They sang "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" together. Then Miss Polly went quiet. Gabriella sang it all by herself. She remembered every word. On the wall was a picture of a small sheep with a woolly coat. Miss Polly clapped for her. "One more song?" she asked. "Yes!" said Gabriella, and she began to sing.

Hazel went to the library with her dad. She wanted the book with the big red chicken on it. But she could not reach the shelf. It was too high.

A lady with a blue cardigan walked by. Hazel pulled her sleeve and said, "Book!" The lady did not move. Hazel tried again. "Book, please." The lady smiled. "Ah, you want the chicken book! Here you go." Her bag began to swing as she reached up high.

Hazel looked at the book. "Please got the book," she said. Her dad nodded. "Please helps people hear you."

On the way out, Hazel bumped into a boy. "Sorry," she said. He said, "That's okay." At the desk, the lady gave her a stamp on a fresh card. "Thank you," said Hazel. The lady gave her a big thumbs up. "Come back soon, Hazel!"

Logan stood at the big library desk. He wanted a book about trucks. The librarian gave him a card with his name on it. "Your very first card," she said. Logan held it with both hands.

He found a truck book on a low shelf. He sat on the floor and looked at the pictures. The wheels looked big and shiny. He smelled the pages. They smelled like paper and old rain.

"I want to keep it," Logan told his mom. "Forever and ever."

"You can take it home," Mom said. "But a stamp inside says when to bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Logan looked at the stamp. He put the book under his arm. His loose tooth wiggled when he smiled.

At home he read the book on his knee. Every night he turned the pages. Then the day came. The stamp day.

Logan carried the book back to the library. He set it on the desk. "I brought it back," he said. "Now another kid can read it."

The librarian smiled. "That was kind. And you can borrow it again."

Logan's tooth felt even looser. He picked a new book about cranes. "Thank you," he said to the librarian. He held his card tight all the way home.

Emily was at Grandma's house. She found a big book on the sofa. The book had little marks on every page. Grandma called the marks words. "The words tell the story," said Grandma. Grandma opened the front of the book. Then she turned the pages one by one. The story went from the front to the back.

"I want this book forever," said Emily. She hugged it tight. Grandma said, "The book is from the library. We can take it home. But we must bring it back by Saturday. Then other people can read it too." Emily held the book. She did not want to let it go.

They read the book together. It was about a green frog. The frog sat on a log by a pond. The frog was slimy and cool. In the garden, Emily bent down to see a real worm. She looked so long that her neck began to hurt. Grandma rubbed her neck softly. "The worm is slimy too," said Emily. "It is, little one," said Grandma.

On Saturday, they walked to the library. Emily gave the book to the lady at the desk. "You brought it back," the lady said. "Now someone else can read it." Emily looked at the book on the shelf. Then she picked a new one. She opened the front page first. "New words," said Emily. Grandma smiled and took her hand.

Dylan wanted a snack. He saw the big pot on the stove. Steam went up from the pot. "Hot," said Mama. "The pot can hurt you."

Dylan put his hand near the pot. The air felt warm. He pulled his hand back fast. He did not touch the pot. "The pot is hot because it is on the fire," Dylan said. Mama smiled and gave him a cold apple slice instead. It felt cool in his hand.

Then Dylan wanted to go outside. He ran to the door. But he stopped and looked back. Mama was still in the kitchen. "Stay close to me," said Mama. So Dylan held her hand. They went outside together.

Dylan saw a shiny tool on the grass. It had sharp teeth. He did not touch it. "Mama, this is not for kids," he said. Mama put it away high on a shelf. Then they sat on the steps. Dylan bit his apple. It went crunch. "Crunchy," he said with a big smile.

Stella loved the little kitchen at school. Today the baby doll would not stop crying. Stella held her close. "Why is Baby crying?" she asked. Then she saw it. Baby's arm had a big scratch.

Stella laid Baby on the table. She got a soft cloth. She patted the scratch, very gently. But Baby still cried.

Then Ben came over. "I can be the doctor," he said. He picked up a toy phone. "Ring, ring," he said. "Hello, Doctor? Baby has a scratch." He listened to the phone. Then he nodded. "The Doctor says she needs a bandage."

Stella found a sticker bandage. She stuck it on Baby's arm. She wrapped Baby in a small blanket. She gave her pretend milk from a tiny cup.

Baby stopped crying. Stella smiled big. "She is better now," she said. "We called the Doctor, and the Doctor helped."

Ben grinned. "You are a lucky mom," he said. "Your Baby has a bandage now."

Stella rocked Baby in her arms. "Shh, shh," she sang. "Time to sleep, little one." Baby's eyes closed, just like that.

Zoey found a big drum in the garage. It sat on a wooden stand. The wood was old and dusty.

She tapped the drum. It went boom. It sounded low and floppy. Zoey wanted a happy sound. She tapped it again. Still floppy.

Dad came in. He was not mean. He was kind. He gave her a small key. "The drum needs tight skin," he said. "Try turning this."

Zoey turned the key. She turned it a lot. The skin got tight. She tapped the drum. Ting! Now it sounded high and clean.

"Dad! Tight skin makes a good sound," she said. "Loose skin makes a floppy sound."

She tapped it fast. Ting, ting, ting. Dad tapped his knees. They played a song together.

Sienna stood at the gate. The playground was big. She held her mama's hand tight.

"Go on," said Mama. "Your teacher will call your name." Sienna walked to the sand table. She found a cup of water. She stirred it fast with a stick. Bubbles came up in the air. They popped one by one.

A boy came close. He looked at her shirt. There was a red tag on it. The tag had letters. "Sienna," he read out loud. "Hi, Sienna. I am Leo."

Sienna looked down at her tag. "You know my name," she said. "The tag tells you."

"Yes," said Leo. "That is what tags are for."

At the paint table, Leo mixed blue and yellow. The paint turned green. Sienna gasped. "It changed," she said. She made green too, with her own stick.

Then it was time for bubbles. The teacher blew thin, shiny bubbles. One landed on Sienna's shoe. It did not pop. It sat there like a little window.

"Look, Leo," said Sienna. "A bubble on my shoe."

Leo sat down next to her. "First days are fun," he said.

Sienna smiled at her red tag. "My name helped," she said. "It found me a friend."

Adam sat at the little red table. Ten apple slices sat on his plate. He wanted to count them all.

"One, two, five," said Adam. His friend Mia frowned. "That is not the song," she said. Adam sang the counting song in his head. "One, two, three, four, five." The numbers came out in a row.

He tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten apple slices! He touched each slice as he said a number. "Why did it work?" he asked. "I said them in the song order," he said.

Mia dropped her apple on the floor. Adam picked it up. Then he gave her one of his fresh slices. She took a big bite and smiled.

Outside, Adam found a leaf on the ground. He counted it. "One leaf." Then he found another. "One, two." Mia laughed. "You count everything," she said.

"Ten," said Adam. "Count with me."

Grandma's big TV was on. It was game night at Grandma's house. Georgia sat on the floor with her blanket.

Everyone watched the game. Aunts and uncles and cousins came too. Georgia wanted to see the ball. But the couch was big. The grown-ups were big too.

Then the team ran fast. The people on TV scored a point. Everyone jumped up. "Hooray!" they shouted. Everyone stood in front of Georgia. She could not see the TV at all. Georgia sat very still. She waited.

Soon the game went on. Everyone sat back down. Georgia could see the TV again. Then the team scored another point. Everyone jumped up again. "Hooray!" they shouted. Georgia could not see again.

Georgia thought and thought. When the people scored, everyone stood up. When they did not score, everyone sat down. So she got her little stool. She stood on the stool by the couch. Now she could see over everyone.

The team scored again. Everyone jumped up. But Georgia was up high on her stool. She could see the ball go in. She could see the striped shirts running on the green grass. "I see it! I see it!" she said.

Grandma looked at her and smiled. "Look at Georgia," said Grandma. "She waited and found a good spot." The game went on and on into the night. Georgia stood on her stool the whole time. When the last point came, she shouted with everyone. "Hooray!"

Rehmat lost her red ball in the backyard. "Ball, ball!" she called out loud. She heard a dog bark with her ears. The sound came from behind the big rock. Rehmat looked with her eyes. She saw the shiny ball on top of the rock, like a little red mountain. It was too high to reach. Rehmat closed her eyes and grabbed. She touched only leaves. "I cannot see," she said. "So my hands miss." She opened her eyes again. Now her hands found the ball. A smell came to her nose. It was sweet. Mom was cutting a mango at the table. Rehmat ran to her. Mom gave her a slice. Rehmat tasted it with her tongue. "Sweet!" she said. Then she shared one piece with the dog."Come here, boy!" she called. "This is for you."

Colton went to the store with Mom. He held his bunny. Then he let go to grab an apple. Bunny was gone. "Bunny is lost," Colton said. "Bunny is lost."

Mom knelt down. "Let's draw a picture of Bunny," she said. Mom drew a picture on her list. Bunny had long ears. Mom showed the picture to a worker. The worker smiled. "I will help you look," she said.

Then Colton had an idea. He went back to the apples. He looked where his feet had been. "Bunny fell here," he said. "Bunny fell because I let go." There was Bunny, on the floor by the apples!

Colton hugged Bunny tight. The worker clapped. Mom said, "You found Bunny because you went back to the same spot." On the way home, Colton drew a big bunny picture for his teacher. "Bunny is found," he said. "Found, found, found."

Leo went to the park with Mom. He wanted to find the red ball. He held Mom's hand on the way. "Stay close to me," said Mom. Leo stayed close to Mom.

The sun made the slide very hot. Leo put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He pulled his hand back fast. The slide was too hot to touch. So Leo sat in the shade instead. The shade felt cool and nice.

Then Leo saw something shiny near the fence. It was a rough old can with sharp edges. Leo wanted to kick it. But he stopped. Sharp things can hurt you. Leo did not touch it. He ran back to Mom. "I did not touch the sharp can," he said. Mom smiled and patted his head.

Leo found his red ball by the tree. He kicked the ball to Mom. Mom kicked it back. Leo laughed and held his tummy. "The slide was hot because the sun was on it," said Leo. Mom nodded. "Yes, little one. The sun makes things hot." Leo kicked the ball again, far and high.

Peyton sat at the big table in math club. There were two plates of cookies. The sweet smell made her tummy giggle. "We can each pick a plate," said her friend Ben.

Peyton wanted more cookies. But which plate had more? She counted the red plate. She started at the left end. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted again, from the right end. "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was the same!

Ben laughed. "You counted them twice, silly."

"I had to check," said Peyton. "The end number is still five. It does not care where I start."

The blue plate had four. Peyton picked the red plate. "Five is more than four. More cookies for me!"

Ben giggled and picked the last one.

Amira stood at the little table in the cooking classroom. Today she would make bread for her family. She mixed flour, water and yeast in a big bowl. Then she patted the dough flat like a pancake. "Now we wait," said Teacher Jo. "Why?" asked Amira. "You will see," said Teacher Jo, and she smiled. Amira waited. She watched. The dough got puffy. It grew big and fat. Amira put her hand on it. It felt soft, like a sheep's wool. "The yeast makes little bubbles," Amira said. "The bubbles push the bread up." She shaped the dough into a nice round loaf. Her friend Ben dropped his spoon. Amira picked it up for him. "Thank you," said Ben. The teacher put the loaf in the oven. Soon the whole room smelled warm and sweet. Amira carried the bread home in a basket. "I made this," she said. "It is big because the bubbles pushed it up." Her family ate it all up.

Brielle sat in the nursery. A little bed was by the sun. In the bed was her new baby brother. He was so cute.

Brielle was happy. She wanted to clap. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap! The baby woke up. He began to cry. "Waa, waa," he said.

Mom came in. She held her finger to her lips. "Shh," said Mom. "The baby was sleeping. He woke up because it was too loud."

Brielle nodded. She sat very still. She counted the baby's toes. "One, two, three," she whispered. "Four, five." The baby stopped crying. He closed his eyes. He went back to sleep.

"He sleeps because it is quiet," Brielle whispered. Mom smiled and kissed her head. Brielle looked at her brother. "I will clap tomorrow," she whispered.

Bennett ran into the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. He looked by the tall fence. He looked under the big tree.

Then he heard a sound. Sizzle, sizzle. It came from the grill. "Dad, what is that?" he asked. "The grill is hot," Dad said. "It can hurt your hand. Do not touch it."

Bennett stepped back. He put his hand near the grill from far away. He felt warm air. "The fire makes it hot," he said. "That is why it sizzles."

Just then he saw his red ball. It sat close to the grill. "Dad, my ball is there!" Dad picked it up with the long tongs. He held it out. "Here you are. Stay close to me and play here."

Bennett hugged the ball. "Thank you, Dad." He rolled it on the cool grass.

Sebastian went to the library with his mom. There was a craft table by the window. On the table were red paper, blue paper, and a big jar of glue. "I will make a fish," said Sebastian. He drew a fish with one fin, two fins, three fins. Then he wanted to put the paper fish on a big blue sheet. He dug in the craft bin for a spoon. He found one. He scooped a lot of glue. He spread it all over the blue paper. It was wet and shiny. He pressed his fish down.

The fish stuck. But the blue paper got bumpy. Little hills grew all around the fish. The paper had been smooth. Now it was not. Sebastian touched the hills with his finger. "Too much glue," he said. "The paper got all wet. That made the bumps."

A girl next to him was gluing too. She used one little dot of glue. Her paper stayed smooth. Sebastian got a new blue sheet. He made one dot. Then two dots. Then three dots. He pressed the fish down. The paper stayed flat and smooth. He held it up to the window. The sun made the red fish glow. "Mom, look!" he said. "One dot is enough. My fish is flat and happy." At home in the kitchen, his mom put the fish on the fridge with a magnet.

Jules sat at the dinner table. His tooth felt loose. He wiggled it with his tongue. Then he heard a sound. His sister Mia was crying. Her face looked sad. Jules knew sad faces. Sad faces have a turned-down mouth.

Why was Mia sad? He looked near her plate. Her potato had rolled off. It sat on the floor. "Did your potato go away?" he asked. Mia nodded. "Yes. I want it back."

Jules got down from his chair. He picked up the potato. He washed it at the sink. Then he put it back on her plate. Mia's mouth turned up. Now her face looked happy. Jules felt happy too. His heart went bump, bump, bump with excitement.

"You made me smile," said Mia. "I saw your sad face," said Jules. "So I helped." He wiggled his loose tooth again. It felt funny. He was a little scared it might fall out. But Mama sat near him. She held his hand. His scared feeling got small and small. Then Daddy said, "Ice cream for dessert!" Jules jumped. "Yay!" he said. His voice was loud and excited. Excited voices go up, up, up.

Grandpa came on the big train. Noah ran to meet him on the platform. Grandpa had a red bag and a big smile.

"I will stay for seven whole days," said Grandpa. "A week has seven days." Noah made a paper chain. It had seven paper rings. One ring for each day.

But Grandpa looked sad at supper. "I miss my tea at home," he said. Noah got the teapot. The teabag went into the bowl of hot water. It sat and sat. Then the water turned brown. "The tea makes the water brown," said Noah. "I see why now!" Grandpa laughed. "You got it, Noah." The first tea was too weak. The second cup was just right. "The first one was wrong because I took the bag out too fast," said Noah. The paper chain sank down in Grandpa's tea, but Noah dried it with a towel.

Each night, Noah took one ring off the chain. Six rings. Then five. Then one. On the last morning, one ring was left. "Last day!" said Noah. He held Grandpa's hand at the station. "Come back soon," said Noah. "I will make your tea just right."

Sadie stood in the new school hallway. She held her paper boat tight. The boat had a sail and a little flag. Her tummy felt funny.

A big door opened. Kids ran out to play. Sadie did not know where to go. She looked down the hall. So many doors! She held her boat closer.

A kind teacher stopped by her. "Where is your tag?" the teacher asked. Sadie looked. A tag was on her coat! It had her name on it. The teacher read the tag. "Sadie! Your class is this way."

The tag told the teacher her name. That is why the teacher knew her! Sadie smiled big.

In the class room, there was a water table. Sadie put her boat in. She stirred the water with her hand. The boat sailed round and round. The water made it move!

"My boat can sail here," Sadie said.

Levi wanted to paint a dragon egg. A big, green dragon egg. But the paint pots had no green.

Levi looked at the pots. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. "Red, yellow, blue." He said it again, like a magic spell. The teacher painted a thin line of blue on his paper. Then she painted a yellow line right on top of it.

Levi leaned close. The lines touched. They wiggled. They turned green! "It's a magic egg color!" he said. He dipped his brush in blue, then in yellow, and mixed them in his tray. Green, green, wonderful green. He painted a big round egg. He painted it all over, top to bottom.

When he finished, the egg was so green it seemed to glow. A dragon lived in there, Levi was sure of it. He held the paper up to his ear and listened. "I hear it tapping," he whispered. "It wants to say hello."

Everett ran to the swings. The sky was cloudy, but he did not mind. "One, two, three, up to the tree!" he shouted. The swing made him feel like a bird.

But the swings were full. A girl was on one. A boy was on the other. Everett wanted a swing so much. He stood and waited. Then he waited more.

The girl jumped off. "Your turn," she said. "You waited, so you go next." Everett got on the swing. His tummy felt like jelly. "Wee!" he cried. "Up to the tree!"

Then the boy said, "My turn again." Everett held the chains tight. He looked at the boy's face. The boy looked sad. Everett remembered waiting. Waiting was long. "Okay," said Everett. "You waited, so you go next." He hopped off. The boy smiled big.

Later they all played in the wood chips. "Let's cook a cake!" said Everett. They stirred leaves in a bucket. Each friend added one leaf. "One for me, one for you," said Everett. "One for me, one for you." The cake had a bit from everyone.

The bell rang. Time to go. Everett held the gate and counted friends going out. One, two, three. "All out!" he said. Then he ran to his mom, still holding one leafy cake piece. "Can we cook a real cake at home?" he asked.

Wyatt wanted to help Dad in the backyard. Dad was cooking soup on a little stove. "Stay close to me," Dad said. Wyatt stayed close to Dad.

The pot made a hiss. Steam went up, up, up. Wyatt put his hand near it. The air felt hot, not cold. He pulled his hand back fast. "Hot air," he said. "I will not touch the pot." Dad nodded.

Wyatt saw a shiny tool on the grass. It was sharp and wet from the sprinkler. He did not touch it. "Sharp tools can hurt," he said. Dad put it away high on a shelf.

Then Dad poured cold milk into a small cup. Wyatt took a little taste. "Yum," said Wyatt. "The milk is cold. The pot is hot. I stay close to you." Dad smiled and held his hand. "Good helper," said Dad. "Good helper."

Margot sat down at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. "I can count them," she said. "One, two, three, five, eight, ten!" Dad smiled. "Ten peas? Let's look again."

Margot poked the peas with her spoon. She counted slow this time. "One, two, three, four." The peas kept going. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the peas had a number. "Where did four go before?" she asked. "Maybe I jumped over it."

"You did jump," said Dad. "The numbers have an order. One comes before two." Margot tapped her spoon on the table. Tap, tap, tap. "One, two, three," she sang, like the song at school.

Then she held up her milk cup. It had a big owl on it. "Mr. Owl can count too," she said. "I pretend he is the counting teacher." She made a low owl voice. "Hoo, hoo. One, two, three." Margot laughed. "Owls are not scary at all," she said. "Not when they count."

She looked at Dad's plate. He had peas too. "Can I count yours?" she asked. Dad pushed his plate close. Margot pointed at each green pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad clapped. Margot ate a pea. Now she would count nine. She grinned and tapped the cup again. "Hoo," said Mr. Owl. "One, two, three."

Matthew put on his big red apron. "I wear my apron like a chef," he said. Dad smiled. "Let's buy food for dinner," said Dad. They walked to the farmers' market.

At the market, Matthew saw a shiny fish on the ice. "It looks like silver," he said. Dad said, "Yes. We can cook that fish for dinner." Matthew carried the bag. It was cold and heavy.

At home, Dad put a pan on the stove. "Hot pan, careful hands," said Dad. Matthew said it too. "Hot pan, careful hands." Then Dad put butter in the pan. Matthew watched. The butter was hard. Then the pan got hot. The hard butter turned to liquid and slid around. Matthew jumped a little. "The butter is all runny!" he said. "Why did it do that?" Dad said, "You tell me." Matthew thought. Then he said, "The pan is hot. Hot makes the butter melt." Dad said, "That's right. Heat melts butter."

Matthew helped put the shiny fish in the melted butter. It went sizzle, sizzle. He held Dad's hand and stayed back a step. Soon the fish smelled good. Mom came in and said, "Mmm, who is the chef?" Matthew held up his red apron. "I am!" he said. They all sat down. The fish was warm and soft. Matthew took a big bite and said, "Hot pan, careful hands, good fish!"

James was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma said, "Time for the park."

James grabbed his red coat. He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. "I can do it," he said.

Now for the zipper. James pulled it up. It stopped right away. He pulled again. It would not move. James made a sad face. "The zipper is broken," he said.

Grandma knelt down beside him. "Look at the bottom," she said softly. James looked. His coat edge was stuck in the zipper. That is why it would not go up. James pulled the cloth out. He held it away with one hand. He pulled the zipper with his other hand. Zip! It went all the way up.

"It was the cloth," said James. "The cloth was in the way."

Grandma smiled. "Yes, it was. You fixed it all by yourself." James felt very big. He ran to the door. "Let's go, Grandma! I want my sandwich at the park. All this zipping made me hungry and thirsty too."

Grandma laughed and picked up the little bag. James zipped his coat again, just to hear the sound. Zip! Zip!

Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. Snow! White snow was on the grass. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day!" Chloe laughed and jumped on her bed.

Chloe ran to the backyard. The snow was cold on her boots. It crunched under her feet. But the steps were slippery. Mom slipped a little. "Oh no," said Mom. "Be careful, Chloe."

Chloe had an idea. Dad kept a big bag of salt by the door. Dad put salt on the steps. "Watch now," he said. Chloe waited. Drip, drip, drip. Little holes opened in the ice. The salt was melting it! "The salt makes the ice go away," said Chloe. She put more salt on the path with her little cup. Drip, drip. Soon the steps were safe.

The mail truck came down the street. Chloe ran to the mailbox. A letter was inside! Mom read it to her. It was from Grandma. Chloe held the warm letter in her mittens. "Look, Grandma made a snowman on the paper," she said. "I will draw her one back."

Avery sat in her car seat. The seat belt clicked. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later." Avery looked out the window. A thin cloud slid by. "Where does the cloud go now?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "The cloud goes this way now. It went that way yesterday too." Avery pressed her ear to the window. She heard the road go rumbly rumbly. Yesterday the road had been quiet. Why? Then she saw why. Today the road was wet. The rain had come yesterday. Wet wheels made the big sound. "The rain made the road loud!" she said. "The rain came yesterday, and now the wheels go rumbly."

"What do we do at Grandma's house?" asked Avery. "We will bake cookies later," said Mama. "Today?" asked Avery. "Yes, today," said Mama. "And tomorrow we eat them again." Avery clapped her hands. The rain had come yesterday. The cookies would come later. Today was the car day, and the wheels went rumbly rumbly all the way.

Nova went to the park with her blue bag. "The ducks were here yesterday," said Nova. "Ducks are here today, too." She threw a small piece of bread. One duck ate it fast. That was funny.

"Now I want to ride the swing," said Nova. But a boy was on the swing. "You can ride later," said Mom. Nova waited. She sat on the bench. She looked at the ducks some more. Waiting was slow, but that was okay.

The boy jumped off the swing. "It is later now!" said Nova. She ran to the swing. Mom pushed her up high. "The sun is going down," said Mom. "We can come back tomorrow." Nova kissed Mom's cheek. "Tomorrow, ducks," said Nova, waving her bag.

Matteo had a library book. It was about a red truck. He held it in his lap. He opened the front cover first. "This is the start," said Mama. Matteo pointed at the little marks on the page. "What is that?" he asked. "Those are words," said Mama. "They say truck goes up the hill." Matteo looked at the words. Then he looked at the truck. The words told about the truck!

Matteo loved the red truck book. He wanted to keep it forever. But then Mama said, "Library day is tomorrow. We take the book back." Matteo held the book tight. "My book," he said. His tummy felt tight, like a little problem was sitting in it. "Other kids want to read it too," said Mama. "Someone else will borrow it, just like we did."

The next day, Matteo put the book in his bag. He popped the bag on his back. At the library, he set the book on the big desk. A lady smiled and said, "Thank you." Then Matteo found a shelf of new books. He picked one about a fresh yellow banana. He opened the front cover. The words were there, waiting for him. "We take this one home," he said. "And bring it back next time." Mama nodded. "Yes. Just like that." Matteo hugged the new book all the way home.

Rose sat in a big red seat. Dad sat on her left. Grandma sat on her right. The game was down on the green grass. It was so far away.

A spotted dog walked by with a man. Then something strange began. One row of people stood up. They threw their arms up high. Then they sat down. The next row stood up. Then the next one. It came closer and closer. Dad stood up. He put his arms up. Rose stayed in her seat. She missed it. The row behind her stood. Rose turned to look. Too late again.

Rose watched and watched. The far rows stood first. Then the near rows. She saw why. Each row waited for the row in front. Now it was coming back. It was almost at Dad. Rose planted her feet on the floor. She stood up tall. Up went her arms. Down she sat, just in time. Grandma laughed and clapped. "Again," said Rose. "Watch the front row." The wave came around once more. This time Rose stood up with everyone, right on time.

Max climbed the big yellow school bus. He held his backpack tight. He wanted to sit with his friend Sam.

Max looked at all the seats. Where was Sam? Max walked down the aisle. The bus floor bounced under his feet.

Then Max saw the bus window. Sam was on the other side of it! Sam had not gotten on the bus yet. Max waved through the glass. Sam waved back and climbed the steps.

Sam sat down next to Max. "You were outside the window," Max said. "That is why I could not find you!"

Sam laughed. He opened his lunch box. He shared a sweet red apple with Max.

The bus started to roll. Max looked out the window. The trees went by, then his school.

"That is where we learn," said Sam. "My big sister will teach us the song."

Max smiled and took another big bite.

Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted apples for a song. "We need apples to sing," she said.

Dad put one apple in the bag. Then two apples. Sienna tapped the bag. "One, two, seven, ten!" she said. Dad smiled. "Let's try again, slow and easy." He tapped the bag with her. "One, two, three." Sienna watched his finger. The words came in a row, like steps on stairs.

A man in a green hat walked by. He had a messy cart full of bread. He hummed a song. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Sienna listened. His words were the same as Dad's words, in the same order.

Sienna counted the apples again. "One, two, three, four, five." She got them all in the right row this time. She waited, then tried once more. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten apples!" said Dad. Sienna put the bag in the cart. The numbers went in a line, so she sang them in a line. She did a little dance by the apples. The man in the green hat waved. "Nice counting," he said.

At home, Sienna held up the bag. "Ten apples, Grandma! Want to sing with me?"

Logan ran to the window. "Mom! The sun is out! It is sunny!" He grabbed his sun hat. He wanted to play outside all day.

Then the wind came. It blew his hat right off his head! Logan chased the hat across the grass. The wind was too fast. Mom hung the hat on a hook. "Windy days need a warm jacket," she said, zipping him up.

Then drip, drop, drip. Rain fell on the roof. Logan heard it ping on the pots. He put on his rain boots. He splashed in a big puddle. Splash! Splash! His boots kept his feet dry.

Next, the sky turned white. Snow! Soft flakes landed on his mittens. Logan scooped up snow and patted a little snowman. He put a hat on it too.

Inside, they looked out the window. The sun came back. The little snowman began to melt. It got small, then smaller. "The sun makes it melt because it is warm," said Logan.

His dog barked and shook the snow off his back. Logan yawned a big, sleepy yawn. "One more look," he said. The snowman waved goodbye with one tiny stick arm.

Gabriel ran to the playground. The sun was hot on his face. He wanted to go on the big slide. But the big slide was too hot to touch!

He looked around. There was a small slide in the shade. Gabriel touched it. It felt cold. "The sun made the big slide hot," he said. "No sun, so this one is cold." He patted the small slide with his towel. "You are my friend now."

Down he went, slow and easy. Then a big kid zipped by, fast like a bird. Gabriel laughed. "You are fast. I am slow. But I go again and again!"

After the slide, Gabriel found the water fountain. He pressed the button. Water went splash into his hands. The water was cold and he splashed his hot neck. He sat on his towel in the shade. It was quiet there. The tall tree made everything quiet and cool.

Then the clouds came. The sun went away. Gabriel touched the big slide again. It was cold now! "The sun went away, so now it is cold," he said. Up he climbed, one step, two steps, three.

Gabriel went down the big slide. He flew fast, fast, fast. "Sun makes it hot," he shouted. "No sun makes it cold. And me? I make it fun!" He ran to the ladder for one more turn.

Juliette loved the water. Every Saturday, her swim team came to the pool. Her team was called the Little Fish.

Juliette wore her float belt. The belt had soft foam blocks. The belt made her stay on top of the water. Without it, she sank down low. With it, she floated up high. She kicked her legs and moved like a fish.

One Saturday, Juliette wanted to jump off the tall step. She stood at the edge. She jumped in. The water went up in a big splash. Then the splash went away. She was floating. Her belt had kept her up. "The belt helps me float," she said.

Coach Maya smiled. "Good kicking, Juliette."

After swimming, the team sat on the towels. Mom had brought apples for a snack. Soon they would go home for dinner.

At the last swim day, everyone on the team got a ribbon. It was shiny and blue. Juliette held it tight. "I got this because I swam all season," she said.

Mom clapped. Juliette waved her ribbon at Coach Maya.

"I will be a Little Fish again next year," said Juliette.

Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with her grandpa. The wind blew. Her furry coat was in her bag. "Put it on, Brooklyn," said Grandpa. "It is cold."

Brooklyn pushed her arms in. One arm, two arms. Then she pulled the zipper. The zipper did not go up. She pulled again. It still did not go up. Grandpa waited. He hummed a little song. Brooklyn looked down. The two sides of the zipper were apart at the bottom. She pushed them together. Click. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. "It goes up because the bottom is together," said Brooklyn. "The bottom has to be together."

Grandpa smiled. "That's right," he said. He pulled a carrot from his bag. "A snack while we wait." Brooklyn munched her carrot. She zipped her coat down and up again, just to see it work. The bus came around the corner. Brooklyn held her furry sleeve up high and waved and waved.

Audrey had a cough. It kept her awake at night. Mom said, "We will call the pharmacist." The phone rang. The pharmacist had kind voice.

Mom took Audrey to the pharmacy. The pharmacist gave her a bottle and a small cup. "Use the cup," said Mom. "The cup has lines on it. The lines show how much." Audrey looked at the lines. One line was for little kids. She was a little kid.

At home, Mom poured up to the line. Audrey drank it. It tasted like cherry. Then Mom stacked two pillows and one more. The pillows made a triangle. Audrey leaned back on the triangle. Her cough got quiet. She could breathe easy.

"The cup and the pillows helped," said Audrey. Mom tucked the blanket under her chin. "Yes," said Mom. "Now close your eyes." Audrey held her bear tight. The lamp made a soft yellow circle on the wall. "Good night, Mom," she said.

Mia was four years old today. She wore a crown of paper flowers. Her party was at the big park. Grandma set the cake on the picnic table. Baby Sam was sleepy. He rubbed his eyes. "He needs his nap," said Mom. She pushed him in the stroller under a tree.

The sky was cloudy. A cool wind blew. Dad lit the candles. But the little flames went out. He lit them again. They went out again. The wind was blowing them out! Mia held up her hands. She made a wall with her palms. Dad lit one candle. It stayed lit. Then he lit them all. The flames stood still behind her hands.

"Sing now!" Mia called. Everyone sang Happy Birthday. Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. Every candle went out at once. Grandma hugged her. "Make a wish," said Grandma. Dad went to lock the cake safe in the car. Sam woke up from his nap just in time for a big piece.

Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He saw a little sink in the corner. A nurse stood by it and smiled.

"Wash your hands first," the nurse said. "Use soap and count to twenty." Dylan put his hands under the water. He rubbed the soap all over. "One, two, three," he counted. "Four, five, six." The bubbles grew big and white.

"How long is twenty?" Dylan asked. The nurse held up her fingers. "Count my fingers ten times, then you are done," she said. Dylan counted and counted. "Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" The bubbles went down the drain.

"Now my hands are clean!" said Dylan. He looked at them shine. "Germs go down the drain because I washed them off," he said. "I will wash before I eat too. And after the potty!" The nurse clapped her hands. Dylan waved his clean hands like flags. "Look at me, whole world!" he shouted. "My hands are soap clean!"

It was a rainy day. Big drops hit the window. Asher held Mommy's hand at the store.

"Rain makes the window wet," Asher said.

The store did not sell toys. It sold paint and paper. A craft table stood by the door. Asher sat down to paint a frog. But there was no green paint. Only red, blue, and yellow cups.

Asher felt worried. "My frog needs green," he said.

Mommy smiled. "Try mixing two colors," she said.

Asher dipped his brush in yellow. He painted a stripe. Then he dipped in blue. He touched the yellow stripe. The paint turned green on the paper!

"Yellow and blue make green!" Asher said.

He painted one big green frog. Then he drew red lips and a blue hat on it. The rain went tap, tap, tap on the roof. Asher and Mommy walked home with the dry frog picture held up high.

Romy wanted her teddy bear. He sat on the high shelf. She was too small to reach him.

Romy looked around the playroom. The big chair was tall. The small chair was short. She pushed the big chair to the shelf. She climbed up. Still too short! Then she saw the big red block. She put the block on the chair. She climbed again. Her hand touched teddy's soft foot. She pulled him down.

"Got you!" she said.

Then the block began to slide. "Fast!" said Romy. The chair tipped over. The block fell. Bump! It hit the floor. Romy sat down and pouted. She was mad at the chair.

Her brother Ben ran in. "Was that you?" he asked.

"The block fell fast because it was big and heavy," Romy said. "Small things fall slow."

Ben picked up a tiny block. He let it drop. It fell slow and soft. Then he dropped the big block. It fell fast and hard. Bump again!

"See?" said Ben. "You taught me that!" said Romy.

Just then teddy's hat slipped off. Under it was a sign. It said "Kiss me here." Romy laughed. She kissed teddy on his soft head. Teddies don't get too hot or too cold, she thought. They are just right.

Naomi stood in the reading corner. She saw big books and little books. One book had a bear on the cover. The bear wore a red hat.

A librarian came over. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Naomi nodded. She got a new card with her name on it. The letters made her smile.

She took the bear book to the desk. "I want to keep this forever," Naomi said. The librarian smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "But other kids want to read it too. So you bring it back soon."

Naomi held the book tight. She tried to think. If she kept it, other kids could not read about the bear. That made her feel sad for them.

"Okay," she said. "I will bring it back." She drew a circle around the day on the paper. That was the day the book went back.

At home, Naomi read the bear book three times. Then she put it by the door. "I will see you again," she told the bear.
