Layla wanted to help Mom cook. She saw a big pot on the stove. "Can I stir?" she asked. Mom said, "Not yet. Wait for the soup." So Layla waited.

Mom gave her a small gift. It was an orange in a heavy bag. Layla touched it with her fingers. It felt bumpy. She smelled it with her nose. It smelled sweet. She heard the soup bubble. Her ears told her it was hot. "It talks!" said Layla, and she laughed.

Mom cut the orange. Layla tasted it with her tongue. "Sour and sweet!" she said. Then Mom let her stir. The spoon was too big, so her arm went slow. She tried again. The soup turned round and round. "My eyes saw it spin!" said Layla. "Because I stirred it." Mom kissed her head. "Good little cook," said Mom.

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's farm today. Yesterday, Grandma had called. "The brown egg is warm," Grandma said. "A chick will come out soon."

"Is it now?" Paisley asked. "Not now," said Mom. "We drive now. We get there later." Paisley looked out the window. A wild bird flew by. "That bird can fly now," she said. "I want to fly now too." Mom smiled. "Later, little one. First we drive."

The car went slow, then fast, then slow again. Paisley counted the cows. One, two, three. Then the car stopped. "We are here now!" said Mom.

Paisley ran to the coop. She looked at the brown egg. It was shaking. Tap, tap, tap. A small hole appeared. Then a wet little chick popped out. "It came out!" Paisley said. She thought hard. "The egg sat and sat. Then the chick came out. It took a long, long time." Grandma nodded. "Now you learn how chicks come," she said. Paisley touched the soft chick with one finger. "Hello, chick. You hatched today." Just then, the second egg began to tap too.

Audrey wanted the big red truck. Ben had it. Ben pushed the truck round and round the rug. It made a loud brmm sound. Audrey waited. She counted to ten. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Ben still did not stop.

Audrey grabbed the truck. The truck tipped over. Blocks went crash. A cup of water began to spill. Ben shouted, "My truck!" Audrey felt her face go hot. Dad came over on slow feet. He knelt down by the rug.

"Dad, I want a turn," said Audrey. "Then use your name and ask," said Dad. Audrey took a big breath. "Ben, can I have a turn, please?" Ben looked at the truck. Then he looked at Audrey. "Okay. When I get to the door," said Ben.

Ben pushed the truck to the toy door. Then he gave it to Audrey. Audrey pushed it to the door too. "Your turn," she said. Ben smiled. Dad said, "Look at that. Asking works." Ben gave Audrey the cup. Audrey drank her water. It was not spilled after all.

They took turns, one, two, one, two. The truck went back and forth all morning. Dad sat close by the blocks. The playroom was warm and sunny. "Best truck day ever," said Ben. "Best truck day ever," said Audrey.

Charlie was at soccer practice. There was one big yellow ball. Max wanted to kick it too.

Charlie grabbed the ball and ran. Max grabbed it back. Then the ball popped right out of both hands. It rolled under the bench. Nobody got to kick it.

Coach Zoe blew her whistle. "One ball, two friends," she said. "Take turns."

Charlie thought hard. He had an idea. "You go first," he said to Max. Max kicked the ball to the goal. Then Max sent it back with his foot. "Your turn, star player!" said Max.

Charlie ran and kicked the ball high. It went over the goal and landed in Coach Zoe's hat. Everyone laughed. "Oops," said Charlie.

The coach shook the ball out of her hat. "Good kick," she said. "See what happens? When you wait, the ball comes back to you."

Charlie nodded. "Grabbing made it roll away," he said. "Waiting sends it back!"

At the end, the team played a friendly little game. Max and Charlie shared the ball the whole time. "Best kick team ever," said Max.

Charlie smiled and kicked the ball one more time.

Iris sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big strawberry cake. But the cake box sat by the door, all closed up. "Not now," said Mama. "The cake is for tomorrow." Iris was mad. She tapped her spoon. Tap, tap, tap. The cat came in and gave the door a scratch. The door opened a little bit. Iris did not go to the cake. She looked at her plate. "Yesterday I had peas," she said. "Today I have rice. Today, tomorrow. Yesterday, today, tomorrow." She counted the days on her fingers. One, two, three. "Cake is tomorrow," she said. "That is after my sleep." Mama nodded. Iris ate her rice. She drank her milk. Then she rubbed her eyes. "Sleep comes first," she said. "Then it is tomorrow. Then cake." The cat jumped on her lap and purred. Iris patted its soft head, one pat, two pats, three pats. "Good night, cat," said Iris. "See you at cake time."

Milo wanted his red cup. It sat on a high shelf. He stretched up on his toes. His fingers touched nothing. The shelf was too high.

His dog Pip ran to him. Pip gave his hand a lick. Milo walked to the kitchen. Dad was washing a shiny pot. "Dad, can you help me, please?" said Milo. Dad smiled. "Yes, I can help." Dad got the red cup down. "Thank you," said Milo.

Then Milo ran too fast. The cup fell on the floor. Water went everywhere. "Sorry, Dad," said Milo. Dad got a towel. Together they wiped the floor. It took a long time. They wiped and wiped. At last the floor was dry and shiny. Milo looked at the cup. "The cup fell because I ran," he said. Dad nodded. Then Dad tucked Pip on his bed, and Milo sat down to drink his water, slow and careful.

James sat at the art table. He wanted to paint his favorite frog. The frog sat on a lily pad in a pond. But James looked in the paint box. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. There was no green.

James needed green for his frog. He waited. He looked at the jars again. Still no green. Then he had an idea. He put some blue on his brush. He put some yellow on top. He stirred them on the paper.

The paint began to turn. Blue and yellow made green! James stirred slowly. The green grew bigger and bigger. "My frog can be green," he said.

Then something funny happened. A drop of red fell on the green. The red spot turned brown. James laughed. "Red and green make brown," he said. He painted his brown spot as a log. His green frog sat right on top. Then he dipped his brush in the blue. "Now for my pond," he said.

Lily stood in the big kitchen. The cook, Ben, gave her warm toast. "Be my helper," he said. Lily wanted to butter the toast all by herself.

She pushed the butter with her knife. It slid around. Then Lily saw the toast was warm. The warm toast made the butter soft. The soft butter spread easy. "Look!" said Lily. "I made a butter map on my toast!" Ben smiled. The butter covered every bit.

Next came the milk. Lily held the cup. She poured from way up high. Milk splashed out. "Oh no," said Lily. So she held the cup close to the jug. She tipped it slow. The milk went in quiet. Not one drop fell. "I did it!" said Lily. Ben clapped. "Here is your milk, and here is mine," said Lily, handing him a cup.

Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She saw a little orange fish. "I want that one," she said. The man put the fish in a bag of water. Dad helped Ella carry it. The bag felt heavy but she was strong.

At home, they put the fish in a small tank. Ella wanted to feed him. She tipped the food jar. Lots of flakes fell in. "So many!" she said.

The next morning the water was cloudy. Ella could not see her fish. Dad said, "Try one little pinch." Ella picked up two flakes. She dropped them in. The fish ate them fast.

Day by day the water got clear again. "Too much food made the water cloudy," Ella said. "Little bit for the little fish." Every morning she gave one small pinch. The fish swam round and round, and his tail went swish.

Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her cup was empty. She wanted more milk.

"More," she said. Papa kept cutting his bread. "More," she said again. Papa still did not move.

Then Mama said, "Papa, please pass the bread." Papa passed the bread right away. Sienna watched with wide eyes.

She waited for her turn. "Papa, please may I have milk?" she asked. Papa got up and poured the milk. "Thank you," said Sienna. Papa smiled a big smile.

Sienna took a sip. She reached for the bread and bumped her spoon. Clang! Peas rolled under the table. One pea, two peas, three little peas.

"Sorry, Mama," said Sienna. "I bumped my spoon." Mama said, "You can ask for help." Sienna waited while Mama picked up one pea, two peas, three little peas.

After dinner, Papa said, "Want to go to the playground?" Sienna slid down the big slide, one time, two times, three times.

"Thank you, Papa," she said. "That was because I said please."

Camille sat down for dinner. Papa put one big corn bread on the table. Camille wanted the first big piece.

"I will cut it," said Papa. "Then we each take one piece." He cut the bread into four pieces. One piece was big. One piece was small. Camille grabbed the big piece fast.

Mama looked at her plate. "My piece is small," said Mama. Camille looked around the table. Papa had a small piece too. Baby Sam had crumbs.

"Wait," said Camille. "If I take the big one, you get the small ones." She put the big piece back on the plate. She pushed it to Mama. Then she took a middle piece for herself.

Just then a bug flew in the window. It landed near the bread. "Go away, bug!" said Camille. "That is our food." Papa carried the bug outside on a napkin.

"Dinner has a rule," said Camille. "We all get the same size, so it is fair." Then she smelled something. "Papa, your shoes are smelly!" Everyone laughed. Sam laughed too.

"Papa, wash your feet," said Camille. "Then come back for bread."

Jaxson ran into the kitchen. His tummy was rumbling. "I want a snack," he said. Mom had just come home from the shop. She was cooking soup on the stove.

Jaxson saw the big pot. Steam went up, up, up. He reached out his hand.

Mom said, "Stop! Stay by me."

Jaxson stopped. He held Mom's hand instead. He watched the steam rise. The pot was hot, like the sun.

Mom let him touch a cold apple from the fridge. "Cold," said Jaxson. "The apple is cold. The pot is hot. Hot things can hurt me."

Mom smiled. "That's right. Now let's find you a snack."

Jaxson took a big bite of the apple. "Yum," he said.

Bennett woke up in his bedroom. The sun was not there. Rain tapped on his round window. Tap, tap, tap.

Bennett wanted his swing. "Can I swing now?" he asked. "Not now," said Grandma. "The rain makes the swing wet. You can swing tomorrow." Bennett looked out. The swing hung by the tree. Rain dripped off the seat. Drip, drip, drip.

Bennett remembered yesterday. Yesterday the sun was out. Yesterday the swing was dry. Yesterday he went up so high. "Yesterday I swung and swung," he said. "But yesterday is all done." He missed his swing. He wanted it now.

So Bennett found his round red ball. He rolled it on the floor. He rolled it under the bed. "Later I will get my ball," he said. "Later, after my nap." He yawned a big yawn.

Grandma tucked him in. "Sleep now," she said. "Then tomorrow comes. Tomorrow the rain stops. Tomorrow the sun comes out." Bennett smiled. "Then the swing dries," he said. "Then I swing and swing." His eyes closed. The rain tapped soft. Tap, tap, tap.

Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. Her dog, Biscuit, sat under her chair. His tail went tap, tap, tap on the floor. Tonight there was a big bowl of grapes. Rosalie loved grapes. They were cold and sweet.

"Biscuit is hungry," Rosalie said. She picked up one green grape. She held it down low. Biscuit sniffed it. Then he turned his head away. Rosalie's dad shook his head fast. "Grapes can make dogs sick," he said. Rosalie looked at the grape. "Grapes are food for me," she said. "Not food for dogs." That was why Biscuit said no.

So Rosalie gave Biscuit his red ball instead. Balls are toys, and toys are good for dogs. Bisciet chased the ball under the table. Rosalie was thirsty from all the fun. She drank her water. "Does the ball speak?" she asked her dad. He laughed. "No, it just bounces." Biscuit rolled the ball right to her feet.

Jaxon went to his friend Mia's house. Mia had a drum. It went boom, boom, boom. "How does it stay so even?" Jaxon wondered. He clapped too fast. Clap-clap-clap-clap! The boom and the clap did not match. Mia tapped his hand, slow and slow. One clap, one boom. One clap, one boom.

"Now it fits!" Jaxon said. "The clap goes with the boom. That is why it sounds good." They sang a song about a young duck. Jaxon forgot the middle. He squished his eyes and thought. "Quack, quack, quack!" The words came back. Singing it again and again helped him remember.

Then Mia drew a rainbow on paper. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue!" they counted. They sang and clapped to the end. "Again!" said Jaxon, and his hands went boom, boom, boom.

Benjamin put on his red shirt. It was his team shirt for soccer. He ran out to the backyard. Coach Dad set a little ball on the grass. "Kick it to me," said Dad. Benjamin kicked it. The ball went way over Dad's head. It landed in the flower bed. A butterfly crawled onto the ball and sat there.

"Why did my ball fly so far?" Benjamin asked. He tried again. He kicked with his toe. The ball went crooked. Then Dad rolled a slow ball to him. Benjamin stopped it with his foot. He looked at the ball. He kicked it soft and low, with the side of his foot. The ball rolled right to Dad.

"My kick was soft, so the ball came to you," Benjamin said. Dad clapped his hands. "Kick it again," he said. Benjamin ran to the flower bed. The butterfly flew up. It went over the fence. Benjamin laughed and chased his ball. He kicked it low, low, low, all the way to Dad. "Goal," said Dad, and Benjamin gave him a big, juicy orange slice hug, sticky and sweet.

Wyatt sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to plant a paper flower in a paper pot. Miss Jo gave him paper shapes. "Make your flower," she said.

Wyatt picked up a circle for the flower. It rolled right off the table. He picked up a square. The square stayed still. It did not roll. Wyatt got upset. "My circle runs away!" he said. Miss Jo knelt by his chair. "Put some glue on it," she said.

Wyatt put glue on the circle. He stuck it down. The circle could not roll now. "The glue makes it stay," said Wyatt. He stuck on a rectangle pot and a green triangle leaf. Then he drew a little cat by his flower. "The cat likes my plant," said Wyatt. Miss Jo smiled and clapped her hands.

Hazel ran to the play corner at school. A little crib sat there with a doll inside. But baby doll had no blanket. Hazel wanted one very much.

She looked around the room. Ben had the play kitchen. Mia had the dress-up hats. Nobody had a blanket. Then Hazel saw the scarf basket. She took a soft blue scarf out. It was big. The baby was small. So she folded it. Once. Then again. Now it was just right. She laid it on the baby. "Warm now," she said. The baby stayed snug in the middle of the crib.

Mia came over in a big hat. "I am the doctor," said Mia. "Is the baby sick?" "No," said Hazel. "She was cold. The scarf fixed it." Ben brought a cup from the kitchen. "Warm milk," he said slowly, so the baby could rest. Hazel held the cup near the doll's lips.

The teacher walked by with quiet feet. She did not yell. She just smiled. Hazel rocked the crib, slow and gentle. "Sleep, baby," she said. "Sleep."
</br>

Grandpa came on the big red bus. He would stay for seven whole days. Ali counted on his fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

Grandpa liked to make pancakes in the morning. But Grandpa could not find his glasses. "Oh dear," he said. He looked in his bag. He looked under the table.

Ali wanted to help. He let Grandpa sit down. Then Ali looked in the kitchen. He saw something shiny in the pan cupboard. It was the glasses! Grandpa had put them there when he hid the chocolate.

"You sat on them?" asked Ali. "No, I hid sweets there," laughed Grandpa. "Then I lost my glasses too!" Ali laughed too. He put the glasses on Grandpa's nose.

"You found them because you are small," said Grandpa. "You can see down low." Ali felt very proud. He helped make the pancakes. He helped keep the kitchen tidy. Every morning after that, Ali looked in the cupboard first.

"Any more chocolate?" he asked. Grandpa winked. "Look in my shoe," he said.

Clara rides in the car to the field. Her team wears blue shirts. Today is her first real game.

Clara stands by the tee. The ball sits on the tee. She holds the bat with two hands. She swings. She misses. The team is quiet. She waits. She swings again. The ball goes pop and rolls in the grass.

Clara holds the bat tight. She runs with it. The bat is heavy. Her feet go slow. The coach calls, "Drop the bat, Clara!" Clara lets go of the bat. Her hands are free. Now her feet go fast. She runs to the base. She steps on it with one foot.

"You made it," says her friend Ben. Clara looks back. The bat lies in the dirt. She sees why her feet were slow. "The bat made me slow," she says. "My feet are fast with no bat."

The next batter hits the ball. Clara claps from the base. The sun feels warm on her head.

At home, Clara puts her bat by her bed. She pats it once. "Night, night, bat," she says.

Luka went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about trucks. Luka felt excited. His tummy jumped like a grasshopper.

He ran to the truck shelf. The truck book was gone! Luka felt angry. He stomped his foot. Then he felt sad. A big tear rolled down his cheek.

A girl named Mia saw him. "This book fell behind the shelf," she said. Luka peeked. There it was! A loud thump had made the book fall, because the shelf was wobbly. Luka picked it up. He was scared of the dark gap, but Mia held his hand. Luka smiled. "Happy again," he said. At home, he asked for water and a sweet apple. Mom read the truck book twice. "I love the library," Luka said.

Sienna ran into the community centre. It was stormy outside, so playtime was inside today. On the table sat two bowls of crackers.

"I want the one with more!" said Sienna.

She counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then the second. "One, two, three." Five is more than three!

Tom counted her bowl from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," he said.

"You got five too!" Sienna cried. "I counted from that side. You counted from this side. We still got five!"

She ate a cracker. "Five!" she said, holding up fingers. "I have five crackers, because five was my last number!"

Outside, the stormy sky rumbled. Inside, Sienna munched and grinned.

Parker stood at the edge of the backyard pool. His green swim ring sat in the water. It went up and down on the little waves. "I want to swim like a fish," said Parker. Dad put water wings on his arms. "Now kick," said Dad.

Parker jumped in with a splash. His arms floated up all by themselves. "My arms go up!" said Parker. He kicked his legs. He did not sink. He moved like a little boat. Dad clapped and cheered.

Then Dad took the water wings off. Parker held Dad's hand. His arms went down in the water. "No wings, no float," said Parker. "Wings make me float." Dad smiled. "We will practice more after lunch." Parker chased a leaf across the shallow end. "Look at me," he said. "I swim."

Emily wanted warm milk before bed. The milk in the fridge felt cold. "So cold," she said, and shivered.

Mom poured the milk into a pot. The pot sat on the hot stove. Emily watched. Big bubbles came up in the small pot. The milk went fast, fast, fast. Then Mom turned the knob. Now the bubbles went slow, slow, slow.

"Why did it get slow?" Emily asked. She looked at the knob. Mom had made the stove less hot. "Less hot makes it slow," Emily said. "Is that true?" Mom smiled and nodded.

Emily held her cup. The milk was warm now. She took a tiny sip. Then a big sip.

"Can milk swim in my tummy?" she asked.

Mom laughed, and poured a little more.

Milo went to the farmers' market with Grandpa. He saw big red tomatoes on a stand. "I want to grow one," said Milo. A farmer gave him a tiny seed. "Seeds need water every day," Grandpa said.

Milo planted the seed near the fence. He gave it water on Monday. On Tuesday he forgot. On Wednesday he forgot again. The pot looked dry. Nothing grew.

Milo was sad. "My seed is broken," he said. Grandpa knelt down by him. "The seed is dry. Dry seeds sleep. Let's water it together." Milo gave the seed a big drink of water. He watered it every day after that.

Soon a little green sprout popped up. A bird flew by with twigs for its nest. Milo clapped his hands. "Water made it grow!" he said. Grandpa smiled and gave him a hug.

Hunter ran to the playground after school. He looked in his cubby. His little blue dinosaur was not there. "Where did you go, Dino?" he asked. His heart felt heavy.

"I must find him," Hunter said. He thought hard. "Where did I play last?" He had played on the slide first. He looked under the slide. Only sand was there.

Then he had played in the grass. He had pretended the grass was a jungle. He walked to the jungle spot. He looked down. There was Dino, lying in the green grass!

"You were in the jungle the whole time," Hunter said. "I found you because I walked my steps again." He hugged Dino close.

His teacher smiled. "Time to go home, Hunter," she said.

"Okay," Hunter said. He held Dino tight. He was polite and said, "Thank you for waiting, Teacher." Then he waved goodbye to the slide, and to the grass. "Bye, jungle," he whispered to Dino. "Let's go home."

Connor was a little kid on a big trip. His family had a hotel room. Connor put his brown teddy on the bed. "We are home now, teddy," he said.

But then the lights went out. The room went dark. "Mom! Mom!" Connor began to yell. Mom came fast. "I am here," she said.

Dad held a little card. "Watch this," he said. He put the card in the slot by the door. Click. The lights came on. Dad took the card out. Click. The lights went off. Connor laughed. "The card makes the lights!" he said.

Connor tried it himself. Card in, lights on. Card out, lights off. "I can do it," he said. Then he saw teddy in the dark corner. Connor put the card in the slot. The lights came on. Ted was safe. Connor hugged him tight.

At night, Dad took the card to the desk. "Sleep now," said Mom. The room got dark and soft. Connor held teddy close. "The card is sleeping too," he whispered. Ted's brown ear touched Connor's nose.

Aiden sat on Grandpa's big couch. The room was loud and warm. One team, two teams, lots of fans. Grandma painted a little red star on his finger. "There," she said. "Now you are a fan too." Grandpa blew a long, sharp whistle with his mouth when the game started.

Then everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" They all stood up. They jumped. They waved their arms. Aiden could not see the TV. He saw backs and elbows and a big hat. "I can't see!" he said. His cousin Mia heard him. She pulled a small chair to the front. "Sit here," she said. Aiden climbed up. Now he was tall.

Just then his team scored. Aiden missed it. He missed the ball and the net and everything. His lip went down. Grandpa sat next to him. "Watch now," said Grandpa. "The TV will show it again." Aiden watched. One, two, three seconds went by. Then the ball came back on the screen. It flew and flew and went in! "Again!" said Aiden. "The TV shows it again!" Everyone laughed and jumped one more time. "Again, again!" said Aiden.

Hayden went to the pharmacy with his dad. His nose was runny and red. Dad got a small box of tissues. Then Hayden saw a little bottle of soap next to the tissues. It smelled like honey. He wanted it.

At home, Dad said it was time to eat. "First we wash," said Dad. Hayden let the water rain down on his hands. He rubbed the honey soap all over. His shadow sat small on the floor by the sink. Dad counted, "One, two, three." Hayden counted too. They counted all the way to twenty. The soap bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

Then Hayden ate his sandwich. His hands were clean. "No germs on my bread," he said. "Twenty seconds did it." Dad smiled and gave him one more bite.

Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Jo held up her hands. "We will clap and sing today," she said. The song was "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star."

Eva wanted to sing it all by herself. But her claps went too fast. Her claps ran ahead of the song. Then the words fell out of her mouth. She stopped and frowned.

Miss Jo clapped once. "Twinkle," she sang. She clapped again. "Twinkle," she sang. Eva watched. One clap came with one word. Not two claps. Just one.

Eva tried it. She clapped on "Twin" and skipped to "kle." The clap went in the middle of the word. That was the trick!

"Does one clap help?" Eva asked herself. "Yes. One clap for each big word."

The whole class clapped together now. Clap, word, clap, word. It was a huge sound, like soft rain on the roof.

Eva sang the rhyme from memory. She did not miss one word. She clapped on the beat all the way to "what you are."

Miss Jo smiled at Eva. "That was a big number of claps," she said.

"Twinkle, twinkle," Eva sang again.

Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He wanted to paint a green frog. Green was his favorite color. But Grandma had no green paint.

"Look in the basket," said Grandma. Weston found red, blue, and yellow. He saw a puzzle on the table too. A frog puzzle! The frog on the box was big and green.

Weston looked hard at his paints. No green anywhere. He dipped his brush in blue. He made a blue stripe. Then he dipped in yellow. He mixed them on the paper with his brush. Round and round went his wrist.

"Grandma! Look!" The blue and yellow made green! "Blue and yellow make green," said Weston. Grandma clapped her hands.

Weston painted his frog green. Then Grandma brought red juice with ice. The ice began to melt in the sun. Weston laughed and painted a red sun too. "My frog has a sunny day!"

Jackson went to the park with his dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his red cap. The cap was the color of a strawberry.

Then the trees began to move. "The wind came," said Dad. The wind blew a leaf right off a branch. The wind blew Jackson's cap off his head too. The cap flew over the grass. Jackson chased it. Dad caught it and put it back on. "The cap is light, so the wind took it," Jackson said.

Dad put Jackson's warm jacket on him. The jacket was heavy. The wind could not blow it away. Then gray clouds came. Rain fell. Dad opened the umbrella. "The rain can't get us," Jackson said. Dad smiled. "Here is our last stop," he said. They ran to the swings together.

Wren sat at the big table. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write her name. Her name had four letters, W, R, E, N.

She held the pencil in her whole fist. She wrote a W. It came out wobbly. She wrote an R. That was wobbly too. The letters fell over like sleepy babies.

"Why do my letters fall over?" Wren asked.

"Look at your hand," said Grandma. Grandma sat close by her side. "Try pinching the pencil with two fingers."

Wren looked at her hand. She was squeezing with all five fingers. She let go. Then she pinched the pencil with her thumb and one finger. The pencil sat on her tall middle finger, like a little rest.

She wrote a W. It stood up straight. She wrote an R. It stood up too. "The pencil wobbles when I squeeze it all," Wren said. "It stands still when I pinch it."

"Yes," said Grandma. "Pinch, pinch, pinch."

Wren wrote an E. Wren wrote an N. There it was. W, R, E, N. Her name, all by itself on the paper. Her face felt warm and happy.

"I did it alone!" said Wren. She held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma, look at my name!"

Jasmine skipped into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school. She held her lunch box with two hands. Then she saw a big problem. All the seats were full!

"Where will I sit?" she asked. Then she looked again. One table had an empty spot. A boy sat there with his own lunch box. "Is this seat free?" she asked him. "Yes," he said. "My name is Ben."

Jasmine sat down next to Ben. She opened her lunch box. Mom had packed a tasty apple and a cheese sandwich. The kitchen at school made warm noodles too. Ben had noodles on his tray.

Jasmine took a big bite of her apple. Crunch! "Your apple is loud," Ben said with a giggle. Jasmine giggled too. "Apples go crunch because they are hard," she said. Ben bit his soft noodle. No crunch at all.

"We are lunch friends now," said Ben. Jasmine smiled big. First days are good with a friend. She skipped her feet under the table, tap tap tap.

Arthur ran up to Nia's door. He could not wait to play. Nia opened the door with a big smile.

"Come see my doll," she said. "She is sick today."

They went to the playroom. A doll lay in a small bed. Nia put a blanket on her. "She needs a doctor," Nia said.

Arthur looked around. He wanted to help. He found a blue coat in the toy box. He put it on. "I am the doctor now," he said. Nia found a little cup. "Here is her medicine," she said.

The doll would not drink. She was just plastic. Arthur held the cup near her mouth anyway. He made a little slurp sound. Nia clapped her hands. "She drank it! She feels better!"

"Why did the doll get better?" Arthur asked. He thought hard. "Because we pretended the medicine worked," he said. Nia nodded fast.

"Now she needs a nap," Nia said. They made a nest of soft pillows. They tucked the doll in. Arthur whispered, "Sleep tight, little baby."

The doll's eyes stayed open. That was okay. In the game, her eyes were closed.

Then Nia said, "The baby is hungry when she wakes up." Arthur grinned. "I will make soup!" He stirred a pretend pot with a big spoon.

The doorbell rang. It was Arthur's dad. "One more minute," Arthur called. He fed the doll one last spoonful. "All done," he said. "She is a healthy baby now."

Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His eyes felt heavy. His spoon went down, down to his plate. He did not eat his rice.

"Papa, my eyes want to close," he said. Papa looked at him. "You did not nap today," said Papa. Muhammad thought about that. No nap. Now sleepy. "No nap makes me sleepy," he said.

Mama filled his cup with milk. He drank it all. Then he ate three small bites of rice. His tummy felt warm.

After dinner, Mama ran the bath. The water was warm and bubbly. Muhammad washed his toes and his arms. Then he put on his soft blue pajamas. He buttoned the top button all by himself.

Papa carried him past the desk by the window. The window was open a little. A cool breeze came in. Muhammad yawned a big yawn.

"Sleep now," Papa said. Muhammad closed his eyes. The breeze touched his cheek, soft and slow.

Maya was four today. Her party was at the big park. Grandma set the cake on the table. Mom put four candles on top. Maya wanted to blow them out.

Maya lit the candles with Dad's help. Then the wind blew. One candle went out. Then another went out. Maya frowned. "Why do they go out?" she asked. "The wind is blowing them," said Dad. Maya held her hands around the candles. The wind could not get in. The candles stayed lit.

"Quick, sing to me!" said Maya. Everyone sang the birthday song. When the song was done, Maya took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out at once. Everyone clapped.

Then Maya grabbed her juice cup to cheer. She waved it too fast. The juice began to spill. Grandma caught it with a napkin. "Easy," said Grandma, and she hugged her. At the next table, Ben sat very still and looked green from spinning on the merry-go-round. "Are you sick?" Maya asked. "A little," said Ben. So he sat by Grandma too, and they shared the cake.

Hazel went to the store with Dad. She held her bunny in her hand. Then she saw the apples. She let go of bunny to pick one up. When Dad said "Let's go," Hazel looked down. Bunny was gone.

Hazel walked back to the apples. No bunny there. She felt sad and slow in her feet. Then she thought about what she did. She had picked up an apple first. So bunny must have fallen near the apples. She looked under the apple shelf. She saw something soft and white. It was bunny! "You fell down because I let go," Hazel said. She gave bunny a big hug.

Dad put the apples in the cart. He gave Hazel a juice box, too. It had a picture of a blue lake on it. "Make bunny a seat," Dad said. So Hazel made a seat with her coat. Bunny sat in the cart all the way home. Hazel held the juice box and smiled at the little lake. "We found you," she whispered to bunny.

Athena went to the backyard with Dad. She wanted to find her red ball. "Stay close to me," said Dad. Athena stayed close to Dad.

She heard a loud train far away. Choo, choo! The train was far, far away. That was neat. Athena did not go near the train. Trains are big and fast. She just listened with Dad.

Then she saw the red ball. It sat by the grill. The grill was hot. Athena could feel the warm air on her face. She stopped her feet. "Hot," she said. She did not touch the grill. She put her hands behind her back, like Dad taught her. Hot things can hurt you.

Dad turned the grill off. They waited. Athena began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." She touched the air above the grill. Now the air was cool. The grill was cold now. Cold things are safe to touch.

Athena picked up her ball. "The grill got cold because you turned it off," she said. Dad smiled. "That's right. You waited, and you stayed close." Athena hugged her red ball. She rolled it on the grass, back and forth. "Safe and sound," said Dad. Athena rolled the ball again.

Ellie sat on the big doctor bed. Rain went tap, tap, tap on the window. The nurse came in with a tiny silver tray. "One, two, three," said the nurse. "On three, blow out like birthday candles." Ellie held Mama's hand. She squeezed it. Squeeze, one, two, three. Ellie took a big breath and blew. She blew and blew, like blowing out candles on a cake. "All done!" said the nurse. Ellie looked at her arm. There was a small round bandage on it. "It was just a tiny pinch," said Ellie. "It went away fast because I blew it out." "What a smart girl," said Mama.

Afterward they went to the ice cream shop. The rain had stopped. The sun was warm, warm like fire. Ellie got pink strawberry ice cream. One lick, two licks, three. "My favorite," she said, and she held up her bandage for the scoop of strawberry to see.

Ayla was at Grandma's house. It was a cloudy day. "We can play inside," said Grandma.

Grandma had a big box of letters. Each letter was a little wooden shape. Ayla tipped them out on the rug in the room. They made a clicky sound on the floor.

Ayla picked up a curvy letter. It looked like a snake. "S," said Grandma. "It says sss." Ayla slid the letter on the rug. "Sss," she said, like a snake hissing.

Then she held up a round letter. "Is this S too?" she asked. Grandma shook her head. "That is O. It says ohh." Ayla turned it around and around. The O looked the same every way she turned it! But when she turned the S, it looked different. It fell over and lay like a sleepy snake.

"Oh," said Ayla. "The S is wiggly. The O is round." She put S on the rug. She put O next to it. "Sss, ohh," she said.

"Shall we find your letter?" asked Grandma. "A for Ayla. It says ahh." Ayla dug in the pile. Click, click went the letters. Then she found one with two pointy legs. She held it up high.

"Ahh!" she called out. Grandma clapped. Ayla hugged the letter to her chest.

"Ah," she whispered to it, "you are mine."

Nathan walked up the big hill with his dad. It was Diwali night. Lots of little lamps glowed in the dark. They smelled like smoke and sweet flowers.

Nathan held his own clay lamp. He wanted to light it. He touched his wick to Dad's flame. It did not light. He tried again. Still dark. "Tell me why, Dad," Nathan said. Dad just smiled. "Try one more time. Wait a little first."

Nathan looked at his lamp. He remembered. He had washed his hands before dinner. Water had dripped on the wick. The wick was wet. So Nathan waited. He held the lamp in the warm air. He watched other lamps twinkle on the hill. He waited some more.

Then he touched his wick to Dad's flame again. This time it lit! A tiny orange light popped up. "The wick was wet," Nathan said. "Wet wicks do not light. Now it is dry!" Dad clapped. Nathan set his lamp on the grass. It glowed beside all the others.

Lea stood by the school gate. She held her small toy rabbit tight. "What if the teacher does not know my name?" she asked. Mama knelt down next to her. "Let's go and see," said Mama.

A teacher smiled at the gate. Lea hid behind Mama's legs. Then the teacher said, "Hello, Lea!" Lea looked up. How did the teacher know? She looked down at her shirt. A red tag was pinned there. It had her name on it. Letters make the tag say a name, she thought. The teacher read the tag, so the teacher knew her.

Lea let go of Mama's hand. She ran to the high slide. "Come play, rabbit," she said. She gave her animal a big hug at the top. "The teacher knows me," said Lea. "My tag said so."

Luna ran up to the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. Luna wanted a book about bunnies. She found one with a soft white bunny on the cover.

A kind man gave Luna her very first library card. "Mine!" said Luna. She held it tight. Then she asked, "Can I keep the bunny book forever?" The man shook his head. "You borrow it," he said. "You take it home. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too." Luna looked at the book. She moved it close to her chest. "Bring it back," she said. "So Sam can read it too. Sam likes bunnies." The man smiled. "Yes. That is how it works."

Luna gave the man her card. He stamped the book. Luna held the book like a gift. She would read it at home, in her cozy bed. When the bookmobile came back, her bag would be empty, and she would give the bunny book back. Then she would get a new one. "Bye, truck!" said Luna. She waved and waved.

Jasmine stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. Her dog, Biscuit, sat by her feet. He was big and furry. Dad held up a hoop. "Try again," he said.

Jasmine threw the beanbag. It went too low. It hit the grass. Biscuit ran to it and gave it a lick. "No, Biscuit," said Jasmine. She laughed and took it back. She looked at the hoop. It was up high. She looked at her hands. She held the beanbag way down by her knees. That was why it went too low.

So she lifted her hands up high. "One, two, three, throw!" she said. The beanbag flew up and went right in. Dad clapped. Biscuit barked.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. Jasmine held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. It rolled under the bush. She got it and tried again. This time she held out both hands. She pulled them in close to her tummy. The big ball landed right in her arms. "I caught it!" she said. Biscuit jumped up and licked her cheek. Jasmine patted his furry head. "One, two, three, throw!" she said, and threw the ball to Dad.

Emile sat in the vet's office with a small box. Inside the box was a gray kitten. The kitten was going home with him today. Emile wanted to hold her right away.

The vet smiled. "New cats need a quiet house," she said. "Loud noise makes them hide."

At home, Emile clapped his hands. "Come out, kitty!" he called. The kitten ran under the couch. Emile could not see her at all. It was getting late, almost bedtime.

Then Emile remembered. Loud noise makes them hide. So he sat down very still. He whispered, "Kitty, kitty." He tapped one finger on the floor, soft, soft.

A small gray nose peeked out. Then the whole kitten came out. She walked to Emile and rubbed his leg.

Emile gave her a gentle kiss on her head. "I love you, kitty," he whispered.

The kitten curled up in his lap and went to sleep.

Clara sat at the big art table. She was painting a butterfly. It had red wings and yellow dots. "So cute," she said. She fished in the crayon box for a black one. She wanted to add little legs.

Clara pressed her finger on the wing. The paint smeared. Now there was a red spot on her finger and a big smudge on the wing. "Oh no," said Clara. She looked at her finger. She looked at the wing. Why did it smear?

She touched the yellow dots next. Those were dry. Nothing came off. "The wet paint smears," said Clara. "The dry paint stays." So she waited. She counted to ten, twice. Then she touched the wing again. It felt dry and smooth. The paint stayed on the paper, right where she put it.

Clara picked up the black crayon. She drew the little legs. The butterfly was done. "Look at you," she whispered.

Grandpa came to stay at Maeva's house for a whole week. Maeva wanted to take him to the park. But first Grandpa said, "I need my nap." After lunch he slept in the big chair.

Maeva could not wait. She wanted to show him the slide. So she called to him from the door. "The park is far, Grandpa! Get up!" She did not mean to yell, but she did. Grandpa woke up fast. He sat up and rubbed his eyes. He looked tired still.

Mom gave Maeva a small job. "Make him a snack for the walk," she said. Maeva put bread and cheese in a little bag. She waited by the door, very quiet. She hummed a tiny song instead of calling.

Soon Grandpa came out in his blue coat. "My nap is done," he said, smiling. Maeva held his hand. They walked to the park together. Grandpa went down the slide, once, very slowly. Then something fell out of his pocket. It was a red balloon! "For you," said Grandpa. The balloon bobbed up in the sun. Maeva jumped for it and held the string tight.

Paisley wanted to help at snack time. Miss Dana held up the tray. "Can you count out crackers for your table?" she asked. Paisley nodded big.

She sang the counting song in her head. "One, two, three, four, five." She put five crackers in a bowl. Then she tried to go on. "Seven, nine, ten!" she sang out loud.

Ben started to giggle. "That is a joke song," he said. "You skipped some!"

Paisley looked at her bowl. It did not look full enough. She counted the children at the table. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. Eight friends, and only five crackers.

She closed her eyes. She sang the song slowly, like Miss Dana sang it. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She touched a cracker on each word. Now the bowl was full.

"Now everyone gets one," said Ben. He took his cracker and smiled.

Paisley could see her bowl. Eight crackers, eight friends. "The song has to go in order," she told Ben. "If you skip, the crackers skip too."

Then Miss Maya tapped her sharp pencil on the table. "Ten napkins next, Paisley."

"One, two, three, four," sang Paisley.

Julia put on her pajama shirt. It was soft and blue. But her teddy bear was gone.

Julia looked under the bed. It was dark there. Her tummy felt tight. "I am scared," she said. She grabbed her flashlight. The light made the dark go away. The tight tummy went away too.

Then she heard a bump. Julia got angry. She stomped her foot. "Who took my bear?" she said. She peeked in the toy box. There was teddy, stuck under a big book!

Julia pulled him out. "You hid from me!" she said. She felt so happy she did a little dance. Then Mama came in. "Time for bed," said Mama. Julia felt excited. She hugged teddy tight.

"Teddy was sad under the book," Julia said. "Now he is not sad." She gave him a sweet kiss on his nose. She pulled the blanket up. The flashlight clicked off. "Night night, teddy," she whispered.

Jack had a new pet. It was a shiny gold fish. The fish swam in a little bowl. Jack held his dad's hand all the way home.

"I will feed him now," said Jack. He got a big spoon. He put in a big spoon of food. The bowl got cloudy. The food made the water yucky. The fish hid behind a little green plant.

"That is too much food," said Dad. Dad helped pour out the old water. He added clean water. "Just a tiny pinch," said Dad. Jack took a tiny pinch. He dropped it in. The water stayed clear. The fish came out and ate it up.

"Too much food made the water bad," said Jack. "A tiny pinch is just right." The fish swam in circles. The birds began to sing outside the window. Dad put his arm around Jack. The fish blew a little bubble. "Good night, fish," said Jack.

Jacob went to the backyard with Grandpa. The sun was hot on the grass. Jacob wanted to play with the grill. It was black and big. "Not that," said Grandpa. "Hot things can hurt you." Grandpa put his hand far from the grill. He let Jacob feel the warm air. "See? Hot," said Grandpa. Jacob felt the hot air on his little hand. He pulled his hand back fast.

Then Jacob saw a brown stone in the grass. He touched the stone. It was not hot. It was cold and smooth. "This one is cold," Jacob said. Grandpa smiled. "Yes. Cold stones are safe to hold."

Jacob put the stone in his pocket. He wanted to show it to Mama. "Stay close to me," said Grandpa. Jacob stayed close. He held Grandpa's hand. They walked to the porch together. Jacob showed Mama the cold brown stone. "Cold stone," said Jacob. Mama said, "What a good finder you are." Jacob sat down by Grandpa and held his stone.

Charles sat at the dinner table. His hands still had blue paint on them from painting a dog. Mom said, "Wash first, then eat." That was a table rule.

The bread basket came around. Charles wanted two rolls. Dad said, "One for now. Then the basket goes around." Charles took one roll. He passed the basket to his sister. She was asleep in her chair, so he passed it on to Mom.

Then the mashed potatoes came. Charles reached for the big spoon. His cousin Leo reached too. Their hands bumped. "Who goes first?" Charles asked. Mom said, "You went first last night. Tonight Leo goes first." So Charles waited. Leo took some, then Charles took some. Then Leo passed him the butter without being asked.

Charles took a bite of his roll. It was warm and soft. "Sharing goes around, and around, and around," he said. Everyone began to laugh. Even the baby woke up and laughed too. Charles gave her a little wave, and she waved back with her tiny paint-free hand.

Brooks put on his swim cap. It had white sheep on it. His sheep cap was easy to see. His towel was snowy white and soft.

Today was the swim meet. It was the last one of the season. Brooks swam on the Turtles. He waited at the edge for his turn. Lily swam first. Then Ben. Then it was Brooks. He jumped in and kicked hard. He touched the wall. Maya went next. She tagged Maya's hand first. Then Maya could go. One swimmer, then the next.

Brooks looked for his goggles. Where did they go? He peeked under the towel. They did not hide there. He peeked in his bag. There they were. "I found them," said Brooks. Coach gave him a green ribbon. It was for the whole season. Brooks held it up high.

Aiden sat at the big table in the hall. Grandma held out her hand. "We say our blessing first," she said. Aiden picked up his cookie instead. He took a big bite. "Too late!" said Grandma. She laughed. "We need to say it before we eat." Aiden looked at his cookie. Half of it was gone already. "Oh no," he said. He put the cookie down. He put his hands together, just like Grandma. He closed his eyes tight. His boot tapped the floor under the table. "Thank you for the food," he said. "That is true," said Grandma. "Now we eat!" Aiden picked up his cookie again. Next time, he said the blessing first. Then he took the very first bite. "Before, not after!" said Aiden. Grandma clapped her hands.

Kayden wanted a warm cookie. He could not find one. "Where are the cookies?" he asked.

First he used his eyes. He saw the tall counter. He saw a big bowl. No cookies yet. Then he used his ears. He heard a beep, beep. The oven was hot! It was winter, so the warm oven felt nice on his face.

Next he used his nose. He sniffed, sniff, sniff. He smelled something sweet. His nose knew that smell! He remembered it from Grandma's house. He followed the sweet smell right to the oven.

Ding! The cookies were done. Mom gave him one. He touched it with his fingers. Warm! He took a little bite. His tongue tasted sugar and chocolate. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three cookies!"

"The oven beeped, so the cookies were done," Kayden said. "And my smelly socks did not help at all. Only my nose helped!"

Mom laughed. "That's right, sweet boy."

Kayden took another warm, sweet bite.

Blake wanted juice at daycare. The juice was hot from the sun. "Too hot," she said.

Miss Kim showed her a big pitcher. "The big pitcher is cold from the fridge." Blake touched it. Cold! She poured a little hot juice and a little cold juice. She sipped it. Warm. Just right.

Then Blake heard a boy talk about his slow snail. It moved so slow. Blake ran fast to see. "Wow, you are fast," said the boy. "My snail is small and slow. You are big and fast." Blake sat down alone next to the snail. She waited. The snail climbed up. Its bottom slid along the leaf. It went so slow, but it did not stop. "Look, it got to the top!" said Blake. "Slow can do it too."

Theodore went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about a spider. "Here is one," said Mama. The cover had a black spider on a web. Theodore held it tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. He opened the front cover first. He turned page one, then page two, then page three. The pages went front to back. The words on the page told the spider story. "The words talk to me," said Theodore.

Mama smiled softly. She showed him a little card. "The book has to come back on this day," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Theodore hugged the spider book. "One book about a spider. One book about how to bake bread. One book about a bear asleep in winter." He counted his three books. At home, he read the spider book two times. Then he put it by the door. "I will bring you back," he whispered to the spider, "so a friend can read you too."

Clara ran to school with a purple backpack. Inside was a horse magnet for show and tell. She was so excited. Show and tell was her favorite thing.

But at school, her friend Ben sat alone. His face looked sad. His bunny toy was lost. Then Max grabbed Ben's crayons, and Ben got angry. His face turned red.

Then thunder boomed outside. A big boom! Clara felt scared. She held her magnet tight.

Then she had an idea. "Ben, let's look for bunny," she said. They looked under the table. They looked in the box. The magnet pulled the table clip, cling! And there was bunny, stuck to a chair leg.

"I found him!" said Ben. A big smile filled his face.

"You were sad," said Clara. "Now you are happy."

Thunder boomed again. But now they laughed together. Even the scary boom felt small.

Sofia stood in the school hallway. Her red backpack was heavy on her back. The hallway had many little doors and many hooks on the wall. So many hooks! Which one was hers?

Sofa looked up at the hooks. Each hook had a little card on it. The cards had names on them. She could not read big words yet. But she knew her own name. It started with an S. She walked slowly and looked at each card.

Then she saw it. A card with Sofia on it. The card was red, just like her backpack. She hung her backpack on that hook. It fit! Why did that hook hold her backpack? Because the hook had her name on it. "The name tells me where to go," she said. She said it out loud, soft and slow.

A boy came to stand beside her. He looked sad and a bit mixed up. He could not find his name. Sofia pointed at the cards. "Look for the one with your name," she said. He found a card with a sheep drawn on it, and his name under the sheep. He hung up his bag too. Then he smiled at Sofia.

The teacher opened the big door. "Come in, friends," she said. Sofia took one more look at her red card. Then she walked in.

John sat in his car seat. He was hungry. "My snack, please," he said. Mom handed him a warm bottle of juice. The sun shone on it through the window. The juice got hot. John made a sad face. Mom put the bottle in the cool shade behind her seat. Soon the juice was cold again. John drank it all up.

A big truck sat next to them. It went very slow. A small car zoomed by. It went fast. John pointed at the truck. "Big is slow," he said. "Small is fast."

Then a big dog in the small car barked at them. It had a clean white bone in its mouth. John waved at the dog. The dog wagged its tail.

Maya ran into the garage. Dad kept his old drum kit there. Today it was hers to try!

She picked up a drumstick. She hit the drum very hard. BOOM! The drumstick bounced right out of her hand. It flew onto Dad's work bag.

"Oh no!" said Maya. She got the stick back.

Maya tried again. This time she held the stick with a loose hand. She tapped the drum. Boom, boom, boom. The stick stayed right in her grip!

"You did it!" said Dad. "Keep tapping, Maya!"

Maya tapped faster. Boom boom boom! She smiled big.

"When I squeeze too hard, the stick jumps away," Maya said. "When my hand is soft, the stick stays!"

She tapped and tapped. Boom boom boom, all the way to lunch time.

"Can we play again after my nap?" she asked.

Zayn put on his red shirt. His team was called the Red Foxes. They played inside the big room at the community center. The floor was cold under his feet, so he jumped up and down.

"Kick, kick, pass," said Coach Kim. Zayn ran to the ball. He kicked it too hard. The ball went far, far away. Then he saw why. A big kick makes the ball go far. A little kick makes it go close. He tried a little kick. One, two, three, tap. The ball rolled right to his friend Mia.

Mia caught it with her feet. She did not fall. She waved at Zayn. "Nice pass!" she said. Zayn jumped high. He was a Red Fox who could pass.

William was on the swim team. Every Saturday morning the pool was full of kids. The coach gave William a small red kickboard. "Hold it tight," said the coach. "Kick to the other side."

William held the board and kicked. But his kicks were tiny, like a little fish. He stayed in one spot. The water was cool on his toes. A big kid zoomed past him with big, slow kicks. William looked and looked.

Then William tried big, slow kicks too. Whoosh! The water pushed him along. He was moving! He went all the way to the wall. "My big kicks made me go fast," said William.

A small girl next to him was stuck like he had been. Her feet wiggled but she did not move. William paddled over to her. "Kick big and slow," he said. "Watch me." She watched. Then she kicked big and slow. Whoosh! She moved too.

"Fast legs, slow legs, fast legs!" she laughed. At the end, the coach gave them both a ribbon. William held his up high. "I got this because I kicked big," he said. The small girl splashed him with a happy kick.

Lily ran to the reading corner. She saw the librarian, Miss Jo, holding something small.

"This is for you," said Miss Jo. "Your very own library card."

Lily held it up high. The card had a red bird on it. "Now I can take a book home!" said Lily. "A real book, at my house!"

She picked a big book about a fire truck. The truck was red like a ball of fire. The cover felt rough on her hands. Miss Jo put the card on a string so it could hang around Lily's neck.

"I will keep this book forever and ever," said Lily. She hugged it tight.

Miss Jo smiled. "Let's try it first," she said. "Stamp, stamp." She put a date in the book.

At home, Lily read the book ten times. Then Sam came over. Sam wanted the fire truck book too.

"But it is mine," said Lily.

"It was mine first," said Sam. "I read it at the library. Now it is your turn. Then it is my turn again."

Lily looked at the date in the book. The book had to go back so Sam could read it. "The book comes back because other kids want it," said Lily.

She ran back to the library with Miss Jo. Then she got a new book about a yellow duck. Sam waved the fire truck book at her.

"Your turn again soon," said Sam.

"Next time I get two books," said Lily.

Ethan wants the red crayon at school. Mia has it. She is drawing a big dragon.

Ethan grabs the crayon. Mia begins to cry. The dragon loses one wing.

"Sorry, Mia," Ethan says. He gives the crayon back. Mia adds two more wings. Now the dragon can fly in the pretend clouds.

"Can I help you color, please?" Ethan asks. Mia nods. She hands him a blue crayon. It feels like a magic wand.

Ethan draws gentle rain. "The dragon needs rain to grow," he says. Mia laughs.

At clean-up time, Ethan drops the crayon box. All the colors roll under the table. "Can you help me, Teacher?" he asks. The teacher smiles and reaches down.

"I said help, so you helped me," Ethan says. "The crayons come out because we both reached!"

"You're welcome," says the teacher. "And thank you for asking so nicely."

Ethan holds up the blue crayon like a sword. "The magic wand works best with please," he whispers to the dragon.

The car was going fast. William sat in his big seat. He wanted to draw a dog. He looked in his bag for his red crayon.

But the red crayon was missing! William looked and looked. He found a dinosaur. That was a toy, not a crayon. He found an apple. That was food, not a crayon. He found a cracker, too. Yum. He took a big bite.

Then Mom turned the car. The bag tipped over. Everything slid to one side. "The car turned, so my things slid," said William. And there, under the apple, was the red crayon! It had been hiding all along.

William reached for it. He got it! He held it up high. "I found it!" he said. Mom smiled. William drew a big red dog on his paper. The dog had a long tail. "Next I will draw the apple," said William. He took another happy bite.

Michael sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to make a paper fish. Grandma gave him paper, glue, and shiny dots.

Michael put the shiny dots on the paper. He picked up the paper to show Grandma. The dots fell off. They rolled onto the floor. Michael felt sad. "My dots fell down," he said.

Grandma smiled softly. She put glue on the paper. The glue felt cold and slimy on Michael's fingers. Michael put a dot on the glue. He lifted the paper up high. The dot stayed on. It did not fall.

"The glue holds it!" said Michael. He put glue on the tail too. He put more dots on the fish. Then he held it up for Grandma to see. "Look, Grandma. My fish has shiny spots now."

Madelyn wanted a letter from Grandma. Yesterday, Mom put a letter in the mailbox. Madelyn saw Mom drop it in. The little door clanked shut. "It went away," said Madelyn. "The mail truck takes it," said Mom.

Today, Madelyn ran to the mailbox. She pulled hard. The door was stuck. She wiggled it. Then it opened. The mailbox was empty. "Where is Grandma's letter?" she asked. "It is still going," said Mom. "The truck is driving now. Grandma gets it later."

Madelyn frowned. "Later is a long time," she said. Mom smiled. "Not so long. Today the letter rides in the truck. Tomorrow it gets to Grandma." Madelyn looked at the road. The sun was warm on the mailbox. "Then Grandma reads it tomorrow," she said.

"Then she writes back," said Mom. Madelyn clapped her hands. "Her letter comes next!" she said. She patted the mailbox. "Goodbye, little box. I will see you tomorrow." Then she ran inside to draw a picture for Grandma.

Hailey wanted the red truck. Her brother Ben had the red truck. He pushed it on the floor. It went fast.

"Give it to me," Hailey said. Ben held it tight. His face looked sad. Hailey grabbed, and Ben cried. Then Mama came. She held up a little timer. "You can take turns," she said. "Ben goes first." The timer ticked. Hailey waited. Then it rang, ding! Ben gave her the truck. Now Hailey pushed it fast on the floor. When the timer rang again, she gave it back.

Hailey smiled. "The timer helps us share," she said. Ben smiled too. They sat close together. The truck rolled past them both. "It goes to me, then to you," said Hailey. Outside, a car went down the street. "Just like that car," said Ben. "One at a time."

Carter wants to find the top of the big slide. But his shoes are dirty. Ms. Amy says, "Wipe them first." Carter waits. He wipes and wipes. Now his shoes are clean.

He climbs up. A big boy runs fast past him. Carter goes slow. Slow feet do not slip. He hears the big boy say, "Ouch!" The big boy went too fast and fell down on his bottom.

Carter keeps going slow, step by step. He gets to the top. He sits down. He puts his hands up. He slides down fast. The wind feels cold on his face. At the bottom, his cheeks feel hot. He laughs and says, "Big slide, fast slide!"

Ms. Amy claps. "Slow up, fast down," she says. Carter nods. He runs to the back of the line. He wants to go again.

Blake went to the garden center with Dad. She picked out tiny carrot seeds. "I will plant a big number of seeds," she said. Dad laughed. "Ten is a big number for you."

Blake put the seeds in dirt. She made two pots. She watered one pot every day. She forgot the other pot. The watered pot grew little green tops. The dry pot grew nothing at all. "Hey!" said Blake. "This pot has no water. That is why!" She gave the dry pot a big drink.

Soon both pots had green tops. The tops grew tall. Blake pulled one carrot up. It was small and young. She washed it and took a bite. "Mmm," she said. "The next one is for you, Dad."

Matteo wanted his red socks. He could not find them. He looked under the bed. He looked in the toy box. No red socks.

Mom sat down next to him. "You wore them yesterday," she said. "Yesterday is the day before today." Matteo put his finger on his chin. Yesterday he played in the snow. His socks got wet. Mom washed them after that.

Matteo ran to the drying rack. There they were! His red socks hung up, still warm from the radiator. "I know why they are here," he said. "They got wet yesterday. You washed them yesterday. They dry now. Later they will be dry all done." Mom smiled and clapped her hands.

"Can I wear them tomorrow?" Matteo asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow comes after you sleep." Matteo got into bed. He pulled the blanket up to his chin. "Sleep now, socks," he whispered. "See you tomorrow." He closed his eyes. Mom turned off the light.

Harper went to the pharmacy with Dad. She saw a boy at the sink near the door. He was washing his hands. He sang a song while he washed.

"Dad, why does he sing?" Harper asked.

"Watch and see," said Dad.

Harper watched. The boy sang the whole song. Then he pointed at a sign. The sign said twenty seconds. "Soap needs time," the boy said. "A quick rinse does not work."

Harper wanted to try. Dad helped her reach the sink. She put soap on her hands. She sang her song, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She sang it all the way through. Then she rinsed the soap off.

"Dad, my hands are clean!" she said. "The song made me slow down. Slow soap wins!"

"Slow soap wins," said Dad, laughing. "Now let's go get your medicine."

At home, Harper washed before lunch. She washed after the toilet too. She sang every time. Her hands were clean. The soap had time to work.

Gabriel ran to Grandpa's house on his little bike. The sun was hot, so he parked the bike under the tree. "I want to paint," said Gabriel. Grandpa gave him a brush and some paint. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. But there was no green paint. Gabriel wanted to paint the green grass. Grandpa said, "Try things and see."

Gabriel dipped his brush in yellow. He painted a yellow sun. Then he dipped the same brush in blue. He made a dot on the paper. "Oh!" said Gabriel. The dot was green! Yellow and blue made green. He painted the grass with his new green. "Yellow and blue make green," he said. Grandpa smiled.

Then Gabriel chewed his apple while his painting dried. Grandpa hung it up on the wall. And there, at the bottom, Gabriel found one more surprise. A tiny green dot was on his thumb. "Grandpa, my hand is green too!" Grandpa laughed. "Let's wash it in the sink, and then we can paint some more."

Eliana went to the art gallery with her dad. A big monkey statue sat by the door. It looked thirsty, so Eliana pretended to give it her juice. "Here, monkey," she said.

Inside, Eliana saw paintings everywhere. One room was all red, blue, and yellow. "Those are the big colours," said a lady with paint on her hands. Eliana touched the wet yellow wall. Then she touched the blue wall next to it. Her fingers made green!

She stared at her hand. "Yellow and blue," she said slowly. "They cook up green!" She tried again on paper. Red plus yellow made orange, like a sunset. Red plus blue made purple, like a plum.

Eliana ran back to the monkey statue. She held up her purple fingers. "Look what I made!" she said. "Blue and red cook purple!" The monkey did not move, but Eliana was sure it winked.

At school, Miss Kim put out two plates of crackers. "Which plate has more?" she asked. Ethan wanted to answer, but he did not know.

He watched the crackers on the blue plate. He made a line with his finger and counted. "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was five. So there were five crackers.

Then he counted again. This time he started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." Five again! Ethan smiled. The last number was the same. It did not matter where he began.

Then he counted the red plate. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven crackers!

"Miss Kim!" said Ethan. "The red plate has more. It has seven. Seven is more than five."

Miss Kim clapped her hands. "Well done, Ethan."

Ethan picked up one naughty cracker that had rolled off the plate. He put it back in line, counted once more, and said, "Still seven!"

Hannah sat on the train with her teddy. The train went fast. Rain ran down the window in little lines. "Look, teddy, the rain is dancing," said Hannah.

Then Hannah wanted her yellow cup. "Where is my cup, Mama?" Mama looked in the big bag. She looked under the seat. No cup. "Your cup is at home," said Mama. "We can't get it till we go back." Hannah frowned. At home, the cup sat on the table. But the table was far, far away now. The train could not turn around for one little cup. "Silly train," said Hannah. Papa laughed. "Silly cup," he said. "It is home drinking all the juice by itself." Hannah giggled. She thought her cup might be lonely.

Mama held up a paper cup from the snack cart. "This cup can be yellow too," said Mama. She put a yellow sticker on it, a little sun with a smile. "New cup, new friend," said Hannah. She gave teddy a sip. Teddy got a dot of juice on his nose. Outside, the rain stopped. Hannah watched the sun come out. "The rain went home too," she said. "Just like my cup." Papa kissed her head. "Everything goes home," he said. The train went on. Hannah waved at the sun.

Tonight was candle night at Grandma's house. Eleanor put on her red dress. It was Diwali, the festival of lights.

Eleanor wanted to hold a candle too. Mama said, "First we light the big lamp. One lamp, two lamps, three little lamps." Eleanor counted with her. The flames jumped up, warm and bright. They smelled like sweet flowers. Then Mama gave Eleanor one small candle. It was messy with wax on her fingers. "Why does my candle go out?" Eleanor asked. Grandma smiled. "You tipped it. The wax ran out." Eleanor held it very still, straight up like a tree. The flame stayed on!

Grandma touched Eleanor's cheek. "Good holding, little one." Eleanor watched her flame dance. "My candle is still on," she said.

Sophie and Grandma went to the garden. Sophie had a little pig toy in her pocket. The pig had a round pink nose. Sophie patted his nose. Then she planted three seeds.

Every day Sophie came back. She wanted to see her seeds. She dug in the dirt to look. But the seeds did not grow. Sophie felt sad. "My seeds are broken," she said. Grandma held her hand. "Seeds need to sleep in the dark," said Grandma. "Let them stay under the dirt."

So Sophie stopped digging. She gave the seeds water instead. The sun came up each day. It was not late when she watered. Then one morning, Sophie saw a green sprout. "It grew because I let it sleep!" she said. Sophie turned her face up to the sun and smiled. The little pig watched too.

Elias stood on a small stool. He was at the big community kitchen. He wanted to bake bread for his mama and papa. He mixed flour and water and a little honey. He made a soft, round ball of dough.

He put the dough in a pan. He slid the pan into the oven. Then he waited. He waited a long time. He peeked in. The bread was still pale and flat. A tiny mouse ran along the wall. "Look, little mouse," Elias whispered. "My bread will not puff up."

Then he saw it. The oven was not hot. He had not turned the knob. No heat meant no baking. Elias turned the knob. A soft warmth filled the oven. He waited again. This time the bread grew round and gold. The kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

"Is it ready?" asked Mama. Elias tapped the bread. It sounded hollow inside. "It is ready!" he said. Papa tore off a piece and smiled. Elias cut a thick slice for himself. "Hot ovens make bread bake," he whispered to the mouse. "I turned it on, so now we eat."

Sara wanted to win a game at school. The game was called the five senses game. But she did not know all the answers yet.

Mama had an idea. "Let's play at home," she said. Mama put an orange on the table. Sara looked at it with her eyes. She smelled it with her nose. She touched the bumpy skin with her hands. Mama cut it open. Sara took a small bite with her mouth. Then Mama clapped, and Sara heard the sound with her ears.

"Now count them," said Mama. Sara held up her fingers, one at a time. "Eyes, nose, hands, mouth, ears." That was five. Then Mama shook a toy snake with a bell inside. Sara held it up high and listened. "I hear the bell with my ears," she said. Mama smiled. "You know all five now," she said. "Let's play one more time." Sara put the orange back on the table and began again.

Isla ran to the big slide. It was tall and shiny in the sun. "Too hot!" she said. Her hands let go fast. The sun made the slide hot, so it burned a little.

She went to the small slide instead. It sat in the shade of a tree. She touched it with one finger. This slide was cool. Down she went, slow at first. Then she went again, and she went fast. "Whee!" she shouted. A boy laughed. "You go fast when you stand up less," he teased. Isla sat down flat. She slid so fast her hair flew up.

After the slides, she was thirsty. Mom had a water bottle. The water was cold. Isla drank it all up. "The sun makes things hot," she said. "The shade makes things cold." Mom gave her a towel to sit on, and Isla lay in the shade. The towel was soft and cool, and soon she was not sleepy at all, wide awake and ready for the swings.

Samuel wanted his blue coat. It had a circle patch on the pocket. The coat rack was full of coats.

Samuel looked and looked. He saw a coat with squares. He saw one with triangles. Where was his circle?

Then he heard his teacher. "Time to go outside!" The room got loud. Samuel needed his coat fast.

He touched each coat. Squares had four sides. They felt pointy. His circle patch felt round and smooth. No points!

Then he felt something round. It rolled a little under his hand. It was the circle patch!

"Found it!" said Samuel. He put on the coat.

His teacher laughed. "How did you know?"

"The circle is round," said Samuel. "It rolled on my hand!"

The room was quiet now. Everyone was outside. Samuel ran out the door. "Wait for me!"

Olivia wanted to paint at the little table. But her brother Sam was already there. He had all the cups of paint. All six cups!

"I want blue," said Olivia.

"Blue is mine," said Sam.

Olivia frowned. She looked at the big sheet of paper. It was cloudy and grey, because Sam used grey on everything.

"How many cups do you have?" Olivia asked.

Sam counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

"That is not fair," said Olivia. "Six for you and zero for me."

Sam looked at her face. He pushed three cups across the table. "One, two, three," he said. "Now it is fair."

Olivia took the blue cup. She painted a big blue cat. Sam painted a red sun.

Then the brush fell on the floor. "I can fix that," said Sam. He picked it up and wiped it clean.

"Now you go first," said Olivia. "Then it is my turn."

They took turns, back and forth, back and forth. The picture got bigger and bigger.

Mama came to look. "What a lovely cat and sun," she said. "Who made this?"

"We both did," said Sam. "We shared the paint."

"And we took turns," said Olivia. She smiled and gave Sam the blue cup. "Now blue is yours."

Logan ran into the baby store. "Baby sister is coming soon!" he said. Mom held his hand. "We need a cozy blanket," she said. Logan saw a red one. He touched it. It was soft like his teddy bear. "This one!" he said.

Then Logan saw tiny shoes. They were so small. He put his shoe next to one. His shoe was much bigger. "Baby feet are little," said Logan. "So the shoes are little too!" Mom laughed. "That's right, Logan."

Logan picked a cozy blue hat. It fit on his hand like a mitten. He followed Mom to the strollers. Then a small surprise! Dad was hiding by the cribs. "I bought a crib already," said Dad. Logan clapped his hands. "Now baby sister can sleep!" he said. They all went home with the red blanket.

Mila sat at the little table. She had red paint and yellow paint. She wanted to paint a big apple.

First she painted the apple red. Then she wanted a yellow leaf on top. She put her brush in the yellow paint. She touched the red apple with it. Oh no. The yellow spot turned orange.

"Why did it turn orange?" Mila asked. She looked at her brush. The brush still had wet red paint on it. The wet paints mixed on the paper.

So she washed her brush in the water cup. She dried it on a paper towel. Now the brush was clean. She got fresh yellow paint. She sent the clean brush across the paper. The yellow stayed yellow!

She painted a little yellow leaf. It sat on top of her red apple. Her teacher smiled. "What a lovely apple," she said.

Mila held it up to the window. "Clean brush, yellow leaf," she said softly.

Ellie ran onto the green field. Her team wore white shirts. Daddy sat on the bench by the shed door. "Kick the ball, Ellie!" he called.

The ball rolled to Ellie. She stopped it with her hands. She picked it up and hugged it. The coach blew the whistle. "No hands, Ellie. Feet only. Hands mean the other team gets the ball." Ellie put the ball down. The other team took it, and they ran far away.

Ellie felt like crying. Daddy waved from the bench. "Try again," he said.

The ball came back. This time Ellie used her foot. She tapped it and tapped it. Then she kicked it hard. The ball went into the net! Ellie's team did win the game. Daddy lifted her up high. "You used your feet," he said. Ellie laughed and hugged her white shirt close.

Brooks ran to the big red slide. He wanted to play house, but he had no baby. Then he saw a stuffed bunny near the sand. "I can be your dad," Brooks said to the bunny.

He found a box for a bed. One, two, three leaves went on top. "Soft bed for you," he said. The bunny kept falling out. Brooks stopped and looked. The box was on the hill. The hill was slanted. That was why the bunny fell.

He thought hard. Then he moved the box to flat ground. "Flat ground, no falls," he said. The bunny stayed in the bed. It stayed and stayed.

A girl named Mia came over. "Can I be the doctor?" she asked. "Yes," said Brooks. "My baby needs a check." Mia tapped the bunny's tummy one, two, three times. "All better," she said. Brooks hugged the bunny tight. "Time for bed, little one."

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. There was a play room with a tall shelf of toys. On the table sat two plates of cookies.

"May I have cookies?" Clara asked. Miss Amy smiled. "You may have the plate with more," she said.

Clara looked at the plates. She could not tell which had more. So she counted the red plate. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Then she counted the blue plate. "One, two, three, four," she said. Four came last, so four was less than five.

Then Clara counted the red plate again. This time she started from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Five again! She counted once more from the middle. It was still five.

"It is five every time," Clara said. "I get the same answer."

She took the red plate. She ate one cookie, slowly and happily. Outside, a car went past the window, and the big bell began to ring. It was song time.

"Come on," said Miss Amy. Clara ran to the circle, holding her last warm cookie.

Lena sat in the big waiting room chair. Her feet did not touch the floor. She held a card with her name on it. She was going to the dentist for the very first time.

A lady called, "Lena, come in." Lena sat in a soft chair that tipped back. The dentist said, "I will count your teeth." Lena shut her mouth tight. The dentist could not see anything.

Then Lena saw a little mirror. She wanted to see it too. She opened her mouth very wide. "Ah," she said. Now the dentist could see every tooth. He counted one, two, three, all the way to twenty.

"Open wide, and I can see," said Lena. The dentist smiled and gave her a sticker. It was a shiny tooth.

Raphael went to the little pool by the lake. The water was cool on his toes. Dad helped him tie the strings of his swim shorts. "Now I will swim!" said Raphael.

Raphael put his face in the water. He came up fast. "Ow! My nose has water in it," he said. He tried again. Water went up his nose again. "Why does the water go in?" he asked. Dad said, "Try one thing. Blow out like this. Puff, puff."

Raphael put his face down. He blew out. Bubbles came out of his nose. He came up smiling. "The water stayed out!" he said. "My nose was too busy blowing bubbles!"

Dad laughed. "Good swimmer!" Raphael blew more bubbles. "Look, Dad! Bubble nose!" Then he splashed Dad with a big kick.

The lights went out. Matthew stood in the backyard with Dad. The porch light was off too.

"Is it dark everywhere?" Matthew asked.

They went inside. Dad found a flashlight. Dad clicked it. No light came out.

"Old batteries," said Dad. He put in two new batteries. He clicked again. Now a bright beam shone on the wall.

"New batteries make it work!" said Matthew. He clicked it on and off, on and off.

They sat on the step. Matthew shone the light on his toy bus. The bus looked yellow in the beam.

"How long do the lights stay off?" Matthew asked.

"Till the men fix the wires," said Dad.

Matthew held the flashlight on his bus. The little wheels gleamed. "Bus, we can see you," he said.

Aubrey woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter and a cup of milk. "I can do it myself," she said.

Dad put warm toast on her plate. Aubrey dug her knife into the cold butter. The butter made a big lump and tore the toast. She tried again on the warm part. The butter went soft there and slid on like paint. "Warm toast makes butter melt," she said. She spread it all the way to the corners.

Next came the milk. She lifted the carton up high and tipped it fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. The dog ran in and began to bark at the puddle. He stepped in it and left a stinky wet foot print on the floor.

Aubrey got a cloth and wiped the table. Dad wiped the dog's paw. Then she tried again. This time she held the carton close to the cup. She tipped it just a little bit. The milk slid in slow and quiet. Not one drop fell. "You have to pour slow," Aubrey told the dog. The dog wagged his tail and licked up her toast crumbs.

Zoey sat on the blue mat at daycare. Miss Rita held up a book. "This morning I went to the library," she said. "You can borrow books there and take them home."

Miss Rita opened the front cover. She turned page one, page two, page three. Zoey counted along. "One, two, three!"

The book was about a sweet little bear who patted every dog he met. Pat, pat, pat. Zoey laughed.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Zoey.

Miss Rita smiled. "But we must bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Zoey thought hard. Then she patted the book, soft and gentle, like the bear patted the dogs.
