"Bye bye, book," she said. "New kids are coming to read you."

She turned the pages one more time, front to back, all by herself. "One, two, three. The end!"

Eliana sat in the car seat. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "I wonder what a dentist does," she said.

Mama parked the car. They went in together. The dentist had a big chair. It went up and up, like a rocket. Eliana laughed.

The dentist looked in Eliana's mouth. "I see little bits of dirt on your teeth," she said. "We will wash them off." She used a tiny brush. It tickled. Then she put some paste on it. The paste tasted like bubblegum! "It tastes sweet," Eliana said. "Teeth paste can taste good?"

The dentist rinsed with water. The water washed the dirt away. Eliana looked in a little mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white. "The water made them clean," she said. "That is why they shine!"

In the car, Eliana was hungry. Mama had an apple in her bag. Eliana took a big bite. "My teeth feel so smooth," she said. She smiled all the way home.

Edouard sat on his bed with a new book. It was about a blue bird in a garden. He got it at the library with Mama. He had his very own card now, with his name on it.

"I want to keep this book forever," Edouard said.

Mama sat down next to him. "The book has a due day," she said. "We take it back so other kids can read it too."

Edouard held the book tight. "But I love the blue bird."

"You can draw the bird," said Mama. "Then your picture stays."

Edouard found his crayons. He drew the blue bird in the garden. Then he put the book in his bag.

"Tomorrow we take it back," he said. "Then a new book comes home with me."

"Good plan," said Mama. She tucked him in.

"Night night, blue bird," said Edouard.

Eliana stood by the gate. The playground looked very big. She wanted a friend, but everyone was new. A boy ran past her. A girl climbed the slide. Nobody knew Eliana's name yet.

Then Eliana saw something on her shirt. Her mom had pinned a tag there. It said ELIANA in red letters. A girl with a dog backpack came close. She looked at the tag. "Your name is Eliana!" she said. "My tag says Mia." Mia pointed at her own red letters.

"You read my tag!" said Eliana. "That is how you know my name!" Mia laughed. "The tags tell us," she said. "Clever tags." Then the sky turned stormy, so they ran inside together. "Sit by me," said Mia. Eliana sat down fast.

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. He held his little toy plane. Today he would meet the dentist. He did not know what a dentist would do.

"Will it hurt?" he asked.

"Let's find out together," said Mom. "Hold my hand in the big chair."

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a chair that went up and down. The dentist smiled. She held a tiny mirror. "Open wide," she said. "I will count your teeth." She counted out loud. "One, two, three." Brooks kept his lips shut at first. Then he opened them a tiny bit.

"Look, twenty teeth!" said the dentist. "Now they are clean and shiny."

Brooks jumped down from the chair. He waved his toy plane high.

"Teeth get counted because they get clean," he told Mom. "And it did not hurt one bit."

The dentist gave him a sticker shaped like a star.

Lillian wanted her teddy bear. He was a gift from the toy shop. But the hall was dark. She could not see. She felt scared. Her tummy felt tight.

Then Daddy turned on the light. The hall was bright now. Lillian looked around. There was no monster. There was only a coat on a hook. The scary dark was gone. Her scared feeling got small. She smiled a big, happy smile.

"Dark made me scared," said Lillian. "Light helps!"

She walked down the hall. She found her teddy under a chair. Daddy clapped for her. Lillian felt so excited. She hugged teddy tight.

Then she heard a loud crash. Oh no! The cat had knocked down a cup. Lillian ran to look. The cat looked sorry. Lillian giggled.

"Kitty made the crash," she said. "I heard it first!"

Parker wanted to steer the rocket. The rocket was a big cardboard box. Mia was holding the wheel.

Parker grabbed the wheel. "My turn!" he said. Mia pulled it back. The rocket wobbled. The rocket nearly tipped over. "The rocket is wobbly because we both hold the wheel," said Parker.

Mia found a sand timer. "You watch the sand," she said. "When the sand goes down, it is your turn." Parker watched the sand. It went drip, drip, down. Then the sand was all gone. Mia let go of the wheel.

Parker steered the rocket all alone. They flew past stars. Outside it was very dark and shiny. They landed at the moon park. The moon park had a bumpy slide.

"Your turn now," said Parker. He held out the wheel to Mia. Mia smiled. They took turns until the moon came up over the playroom window. "Next stop, the star park!" said Mia.

It was Sophia's birthday! She was three years old today. The bowling alley was loud and bright. The balls went rumble, rumble down the floor.

"Happy birthday, Sophia!" said Grandma.

Sophia picked a big blue ball. She pushed it hard. The ball went crooked. It rolled into the gutter. No pins fell down.

"You went too fast," said Dad. "The pins need you to wait. Then the machine sets them up again."

Dad showed her. He pointed his feet straight. He rolled slow. Crash! All the pins fell down!

Sophia tried again. She pointed her feet. She rolled slow. Crash! Eight pins fell!

"Too fast, they fall down wrong. Slow, they fall down right!" said Sophia. Everyone clapped.

Then came the cake. There were three real candles. Sophia made a wish and blew them all out.

"Do not forget the ice cream," said Grandma.

Sophia ate her ice cream with a little pink spoon. "Best birthday ever!" she said. Grandma gave her one more big hug.

Parker found the old paint cups at school. He wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green cup. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. No green at all.

Parker dipped his brush in blue. He made a blue stripe. He made a yellow stripe under it. Then he kept painting. The stripes touched. He rubbed his brush back and forth.

"Look!" said Parker. "The blue and yellow made green!"

His teacher came to see. "You made green all by yourself," she said. Parker painted big green grass. He painted a green frog too.

At play time, Parker went down the slide. He saw green grass at the bottom. "Same green as my paint!" he said.

His friend Mia slid down next. "Show me green paint later?" she asked.

"Yes," said Parker. "Blue and yellow. That is how."

Hailey wanted to make a house for her pet cat. She got paper and tape. First she taped a circle on top. The circle was round like a ball. It rolled off. "Oh no," said Hailey. "The circle rolls. It will not stay." She tried a square. The square was flat and had four sides that were the same. It stayed on, but the rain could not run off in her picture. Then she tried a triangle. The triangle had three sides and a pointy top. "This looks like a real roof," she said. Mom helped her pull the tape tight. The triangle roof stayed on. The cat jumped in. "The circle rolled because it was round," Hailey said. "The triangle stays because it is pointy." Mom smiled. "Nice work, Hailey." The cat curled up under the pointy roof. It was not scary at all. It was cozy.

Natale put on her red shirt. It was her team shirt for soccer. Dad walked with her to the backyard, where the coach was waiting.

Natalie wanted to pass the ball to her friend Sam. She kicked it with her toe. The ball jumped up high. It went over Sam's head. It hit the fence with a knock. Then it rolled under a bush.

"Why did the ball go up so high?" Natalie asked.

The coach rolled the ball back. Natalie looked at her foot. She tried again. This time she kicked the ball with the inside of her foot. The ball stayed low. It rolled right to Sam.

"Sam caught it!" said Natalie. "The inside of my foot keeps the ball down."

Sam kicked it back. Natalie trapped it with her foot. Then she passed it again, low and slow.

A little feather blew across the grass. The ball was quiet now, not bumpy. Natalie stepped on the crunchy leaves by the fence. They made a fun sound.

"Good pass, Natalie," said Dad from his chair. He clapped his hands.

Natalie smiled. She held the ball under her arm. "One more pass," she said. "Watch me, Dad."

Mila wanted tea for her toy cat. She looked in the playroom. She could not find her small teapot. "Where is it?" she asked. She found it under the cat's long tail.

Mila poured from the big teapot. The tea went all over the table. "Oh no," she said. She poured from the small teapot. The tea fit in the tiny cup. "The big one holds too much," she said. "The small one is just right."

The tea was pretend hot. She blew on it. Slow, slow, slow. Then she pretended to sip. "Is it hot or cold now?" she asked. "Cold," she said. "Slow blowing makes it cold."

The cat drank fast. Mila drank slow. "Just right," said Mila. She held the cup up to the cat's soft ear.

Elijah sat by the rink wall. Papa sat on one side. His friend Mia sat on the other. The big game was starting.

The glass in front of Elijah turned white and foggy. He could not see the players. He rubbed the glass with his mitten. A clear spot opened up. He could see the ice again. Then his warm breath touched the glass. The fog came back. Elijah rubbed it again, slow and slow. The spot opened up again. He kept the spot clear while he watched.

"The players are so fast," said Mia. Elijah watched and waited. The skates went zip, zip, zip. The air smelled cold and fresh. Then the puck slid toward the net. Nobody moved. Elijah held his breath.

The puck went in! "We got a goal!" Elijah shouted. Papa clapped his hands. Papa leaned down and gave Elijah a kiss on the head. Mia laughed and clapped too.

Elijah looked at the glass. His fog spot was still there. He pointed with one finger. "The glass gets foggy because I breathe on it," he said. He took a big breath and blew. Fog bloomed like a little white cloud. Then he rubbed it clean one more time and watched the players skate on.

Isaac sat at the dinner table. He had ten little peas on his plate. He wanted to eat them one by one.

"One, two, three," said Isaac. He pushed the peas with his spoon. Then he stopped. He did not know what came next. He made a small noise. "Stuck," he said.

Daddy was washing the big pot at the sink. He came over and sat down. "Want to sing it?" said Daddy. Daddy sang the counting song from play group. Isaac knew that song! He sang too. "Four, five, six, seven." The song went on. "Eight, nine, ten!" Now he knew them all.

Isaac looked at his plate. The song helped him remember. "The song says the numbers," he said. Daddy nodded.

Isaac ate the peas. He counted each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All gone! Daddy gave him a warm hug.

"Bedtime comes early tonight," said Daddy. "But first, one more song."

"Ten little peas went crunch, crunch, crunch," sang Isaac.

Margot sat on her big bed. She had a library book about a stinky skunk. She loved that skunk. She wanted to keep him forever.

"One skunk, two skunks, three stinky skunks," she counted on the pages. She read the words out loud. "Skunk. Bed. Hat." The words told her things! She turned the pages one by one, front to back.

Then Mama came in. "Library day is today," said Mama. "The book goes back so other kids can read it too."

"No! My skunk stays with me," said Margot. She held the book tight.

"But then no one else gets the skunk," said Mama. "And you can borrow a new book."

Margot thought. She took her crayon and drew her own skunk. Then she let the book sink down into the book bag.

"Bye, skunk," she said. "Hello, new book."

Noah put on his red shirt. It was his team shirt for soccer. He ran out to the backyard to practice.

Dad rolled the ball to him. Noah caught it with his hands. He held it tight and ran.

"No, no," said Dad with a smile. "In soccer, we use our feet. Not our hands. Try a little kick."

Noah put the ball down. He tapped it with his shoe. The ball went straight to Dad. Noah tapped it again. The ball rolled under the big tree, near the wooden horse on the swing set.

"Oops," said Noah. He ran to get the ball. "I guess I kicked it too hard," he said.

Dad nodded. "A soft kick goes a short way. A big kick goes far."

The sun was going down. They did not want to be late for dinner. Noah gave the ball one more soft kick. It rolled right to Dad's feet.

"Team practice done," said Dad.

Noah held up his hands. "See? No hands!"

Gabriel wanted his red ball. It rolled under the big chair. He could not reach it.

Gabriel felt angry. His face got hot. He stomped his foot. "Bad chair!" he said.

Mama came in. She was a kind woman. "Take a big breath," she said. "Then try again."

Gabriel took a big breath. His face did not feel so hot. He got down on his tummy. He reached far. Still no ball.

"I need a stick," Gabriel said. He found a wooden spoon. He pushed it under the chair. The ball rolled out. It rolled right to his hand.

"I did it!" Gabriel said. He jumped up and down. He felt so excited.

Then the doorbell rang. It made a loud noise. Gabriel felt scared. He held Mama's leg.

"It is just Grandpa," said Mama. Grandpa came in. He had a small dog. The dog licked Gabriel's face.

Gabriel laughed. He felt happy now. He threw the red ball. The dog ran after it.

Gabriel clapped. "Big breath first, then throw," he said. He took a big breath. He threw the ball again, far, far across the room.

Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted a cookie from the bakery. He held Mama's hand in the middle of the aisle. But the bakery was dark. The big oven was cold. No cookies today, said the baker. We bake them tomorrow. Theodore looked at the dark oven. He kicked his shoe on the floor, just a little kick. Yesterday we had cookies, said Mama. Today the oven is cold. Tomorrow we will come back. Theodore looked at the bread shelf. He picked a soft roll instead. He held it in both hands. Now he had something to eat. Later, at home, Mama put jam on it. Theodore took a big bite. Tomorrow we get cookies, he said. And tomorrow he did.

Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Kay's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Leon took a bite of his cheese snack. It was good.

Then the team got close to scoring. Everyone jumped up. "GO! GO! GO!" they all yelled. Grandpa yelled too. Aunt Millie yelled loudest of all. Leon covered his ears. Then the room got quiet. The TV man said, "We missed the play while you cheered!" Leon looked at the frozen picture on the screen. He thought and thought.

"Wait," said Leon. "When we yell, we can't hear the game." Mr. Kay laughed. "That's right, little buddy!" So Leon held up his hand like a traffic helper. "Yell now!" he said when there was a break. Everyone yelled like wild bears. "Shhh now," said Leon when the game came back. Aunt Millie tied a string on her wrist to remind her.

The team scored the last point. Leon jumped high. "NOW we can yell!" he shouted. And everyone did.

Daniel was at the little stove in his school cooking classroom. He was making muffins for his family. Mama would get the big one. Baby sister would get the tiny one.

Daniel mixed flour and milk in a big bowl. He cracked an egg. Some shell fell in. "Got you," he said, and fished it out with a spoon. Then he filled his muffin cups and set them in the oven to bake.

The timer rang. Daniel pulled the pan out with safe, big mitts on. But the muffins were flat like pancakes. Flat, flat, flat. He looked at the counter. A small jar sat there all alone. "The puffy stuff!" he said. He had left the baking soda in the jar. No puffy stuff, no puffy muffins. He laughed and laughed. Then he mixed a new bowl, tapped the baking soda in, and those muffins came out big as clouds. He put them in a basket and ran to find his teacher. "Look! Puff magic!"

Luca ran out to the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. It was not in the toy box. He looked behind the big green bush. No ball there.

Then he heard a happy sound. "Tweet, tweet!" A blue bird flew by. Luca followed it. The bird landed by the flower bed. And there was the red ball, sitting under a yellow flower!

Luca picked up his ball. It was dirty. "I will clean it," he said. He wiped it with a wet cloth. The ball turned bright and shiny again. Luca held it up high. "The bird took my ball to the flowers!" he said. "That is why I could not find it!" He laughed and kicked the ball across the green, green grass.

Wesley stood in the band room. A shiny trumpet sat on the stand. He wanted to play it for his mom today.

He took a big, big breath. He blew as hard as he could. Pfffffft. Nothing. Not one sound. Just air. He tried again. Harder! Pfffffft. Still nothing. A cymbal fell over with a clang.

Miss Paz came over. "Try little air," she said. "Tiny, tiny air."

Wesley took a small breath. He blew softly. Bzzzz! A sound came out! A big, funny sound. "Loud air makes no sound," said Wesley. "Little air makes the sound!"

Miss Paz laughed. He played again. Bzzzz! Bzzzz! His arms wanted to swing like a drummer's.

Then it was time to go. His mom was waiting. "Play for me!" she said. Wesley lifted the trumpet. He blew tiny air. Bzzzz!

His mom clapped and clapped. "Bravo!" she said. "After this, we can eat crunchy crackers at home."

Wesley grinned. Little air, big sound. He liked that trick.

John sat at the big art table. He wanted to make a house picture. He cut out a square for the house. He cut out a rectangle for the door. He cut out a triangle for the roof. Then he cut a circle for the sun. John put the circle on the table. The circle rolled off! It rolled under the chair. "My sun ran away," said John. His teacher helped him look. "Round things roll," John said. He picked up the circle with his finger. The teacher was melting crayons for a bright sun picture. "Careful," she said. "The warm wax can burn." John watched and waited. She poured red and yellow wax. It made a curly, swirly sun. John taped his square, rectangle and triangle flat on the paper. They did not roll at all. Then he pressed the curly sun on top. "Flat sides stay put," said John. "Only round things roll."

Myles ran into the backyard. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He wore his sun hat and his cool sunglasses. A turtle sat by the fence, in the warm sun.

Then the wind came. Whoosh! The wind blew Myles's hat right off his head. The hat flew over the grass. "Come back!" said Myles. He chased it and caught it. "Why did you fly?" he asked the hat.

Myles looked up. The wind pushed the tree leaves too. The leaves waved and waved. "The wind moves things," said Myles. "That is why my hat flew!" So he put the hat on and tied the strap under his chin. Snug!

Rain began to fall. Myles ran inside. He grabbed his rain boots and his yellow rain coat. He looked out the window. "Maybe tomorrow it will be snowy," he said. "Then I need my big warm mittens, so my hands will not freeze." The rain went drip, drip, drip on the glass. Myles watched and smiled.

Camille wanted to help Mama make soup. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Camille stood right by her side. One step, two steps, close to Mama.

The pot went on the stove. Steam rose up, up, up. Camille put her hand near the steam. The air felt hot. She pulled her hand back fast. "The steam is hot," said Camille. "My hand went away because it was hot." Mama nodded and smiled. Camille touched the cold jug of water instead. Cold felt nice and safe.

Then Camille saw the big knife on the counter. She did not touch it. "That is not for me," she said. She was a brave helper, and Mama let her fill the cups with cold water. One cup, two cups, three cups. "My dream is to cook like you," said Camille. Mama laughed softly and gave her a big warm hug.

Madison wanted to paint a green snake. She had red, blue and yellow paint. But there was no green paint at all. She looked and looked. No green anywhere.

She painted one snake red. She painted one snake blue. Then she painted a big yellow snake. She still wanted a green snake. So she dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow too. She stirred the paints on the paper. "Ooh!" said Madison. Blue and yellow made green! The green spread like magic grass.

"Green snake, green snake, come out to play," she sang. She made three green snakes. Then she shut her paint box tight. The snakes slid across the paper, all the way to the flower garden. "Because blue and yellow mix," said Madison, "green snakes can live in my yard."

Sophie sat in the car. She held a cookie in her hand. Today was a big day. Mom was bringing the baby home.

The baby had a small seat. The small seat faced the back of the car. Sophie looked and looked. She could not see the baby. "I want to see the baby," she said.

Dad counted the seats. "One, two, three," he said. "Try the middle seat." Sophie climbed over. She sat in the middle. Now she could see the baby's face. The baby was sleeping. "The baby sleeps because the car goes bumpy bumpy," said Sophie. "The bumps rock her, like my doll."

Mom smiled. Sophie took a deep breath. She whispered very softly. "Hi, baby. I am Sophie." The baby opened one eye. Then she made a small sound. Sophie broke her cookie in two. She kept one half. She saved one half for the baby, for later. "When you wake up," she whispered, "we will count things together. One cookie. Two cookies. Just you wait."

Benjamin wants to play house at daycare. He picks a doll to be his baby. The baby will not sleep. It keeps "crying" in his arms.

"You need a blanket," says Mia. She folds a small red cloth. Benjamin wraps the baby up. The baby gets warm and cozy. Now it stops crying and sleeps.

"It slept because it was warm," Benjamin says.

Next, the baby is hungry. Benjamin makes pretend soup from a cup and a leaf. The baby eats it all up. Then a big block tower falls down with a crash. It sounds like thunder. The baby looks scared. Benjamin hugs it close.

"Shh. That was just a mountain falling," he says. He rocks the baby. The baby falls asleep again. Benjamin smiles and tucks the blanket in tight.

The big family dinner was ready at Grandma's house. Aurora could smell the warm bread. She wanted to hurry to the table and eat.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "We hold hands first. Then we say our blessing together." Everyone stood around the table. Grandma took Aurora's hand. Papa took her other hand. Every person held on to someone.

Then Grandma squeezed Aurora's hand. Aurora squeezed Papa's hand. Papa squeezed Aunt Jo. The squeeze went all the way around, one hand at a time. Then the circle came back to Aurora. Everyone said the blessing together, loud and happy.

"The squeeze went all the way around," said Aurora. "It came back to me." Grandma smiled. "Yes. It goes around because we all hold hands." Aurora clapped. "We are lucky we have so many hands!"

After dinner, Grandma gave Aurora a pencil. Together they drew a big circle on paper. Grandma put a tiny hand in the circle for each person. Aurora counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five!" she said. Then she drew a line from hand to hand. "Look, Grandma. My squeeze will go here, and here, and here."

"Next Sunday, you can start the squeeze," said Grandma. Aurora jumped up and down. "I will squeeze your hand first!"

Violet put on her red dress. Her family walked to the big temple house. Today was Diwali, the festival of lights.

Inside, small clay lamps glowed everywhere. Violet's grandma gave her a lamp. "Hold it flat," Grandma said. Violet held it very still. Then a man walked past. The air moved. The little flame went out. The lamp was dark now. Violet looked at her grandma's lamp. It was still lit. It sat by the wall, where the air was still.

"I know why," Violet said. "The wind blew it out. The wind did not blow yours."

"Try again," said Grandma. They found a quiet spot by the wall. Grandma lit the wick with a match. Violet set her lamp down next to Grandma's. The flame stood up small and bright. Nobody walked past. Nobody blew. The light stayed on.

"It is not scary now," Violet said. "It stays when the wind stays away."

Grandma smiled and held her hand. The two little lamps glowed side by side all evening.

Violet was late for school. She had missed her breakfast. Her tummy made a little rumble.

At circle time, Miss Kim sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the children clapped. Violet clapped too. But her mouth would not say the words.

Miss Kim smiled. "Sing with us, Violet. Just say the words after me."

Violet tried. "One, two, three, four, six, eight, nine," she said. The boy next to her giggled softly.

Violet tried again. "One, two, three, four, six," she said. "It went wrong!"

Miss Kim clapped her hands. "Let's go slow. Say each word as I sing it."

"One," sang Miss Kim. "One," sang Violet. "Two." "Two." They went all the way to six. Then Miss Kim stopped.

"Now comes the next word," said Miss Kim. "Watch my mouth."

"Seven," said Miss Kim. "Seven!" said Violet. The word fit right after six, like a puzzle piece.

They sang the whole song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Violet said every word. Every word fit in its place.

"I did it!" said Violet. "Seven comes after six. That is why it went wrong."

Miss Kim gave her a cracker, and Violet ate it all up. Then Miss Kim sang the song one more time, just for her.

Clara sat at the little table. It was lunch time at school. Her soup was big and hot. Her friend Ben had a small cup. His soup was cold already.

"Mine is too hot," said Clara. She wanted to eat it now.

She looked out the window. A wild bird sat on the sill. It flapped one wing, then the other. The wind blew. The wing went up and down, up and down. Fast air moved over it.

Clara had an idea. Air can cool things. She picked up her spoon. She blew on the soup. One big blow. Two big blows. Three big blows. She blew slow. The steam still rose. She blew fast, like the wild wind. The steam went away.

Ben watched her. He tried it too. He blew on his cold soup. "Mine stays cold," he said.

"Yes," said Clara. "Cold stays cold. Blowing is for hot."

The teacher came with bread. Clara took one bite. "Just right now," she said. She smiled and blew a little kiss to the wild bird. The bird flapped both wings and flew away.

William was at summer camp. There was one big red truck. William wanted it first.

He grabbed the truck. His friend Max said, "No! My turn." Max started to cry. William felt sad too.

The teacher came over. She had two sand timers. One was big and one was small. She said, "When the sand runs down, it is a new turn."

William turned the big timer over. Sand fell down, bit by bit. He pushed the truck in the dirt. He made a long road for it. Max watched and waited.

Then the sand ran out. William gave Max the truck. Max turned the timer over. He pushed the truck now. William watched the sand fall.

At snack time, William sat with Max. They shared a bowl of crackers. William said, "The sand fell down, so it was your turn." Max smiled a friendly smile and said, "You waited for me."

Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. Rehmat wore her red coat. The coat was not zipped. Rehmat wanted to zip it all by herself.

She pulled the zipper. It did not move. She pulled it again. Still nothing! Rehmat looked down. The zipper slide was at the very bottom. It was not in the little slot yet. The zipper had to sit in the slot first.

Rehmat sat on the bank floor. She pushed the bottom of the coat into the slot. Click! It went in. Then she pulled the zipper up, up, up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to her chin.

"Cold air can not get in now," said Rehmat. Mama laughed. "Look at you! Zipped up like a big girl." Rehmat opened the coat. Then she zipped it again, just for fun. Zip, zip, zip.

A man at the bank gave Rehmat a shiny red apple. "For the girl with the good zipper," he said. Rehmat held it in her warm, zipped pocket.

Luka was at summer camp. He saw a paint table. Red, yellow, and blue pots sat there. He wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. He felt shy about asking. So he sat down and watched.

His teacher came. She poured a little yellow. Then she poured a little blue. Luka waited. He dipped his brush. He tried it himself. He mixed yellow and blue together. The paint turned green!

"Look!" said Luka. "Yellow and blue make green." The teacher smiled. Luka painted his frog. He added big eyes. He added little feet. Then he dipped red and yellow. He mixed them. Now he had orange too. He painted a small orange hat on his frog.

Joshua stood at the little table in the school cooking room. Today he would make pancakes for his family. He poured flour, one cup, two cups. He cracked an egg. He added milk. Then he stirred and stirred. The batter looked like thick mud.

"Careful," said Teacher May. "Don't stir too fast." But Joshua stirred fast, and the batter flew out. Splatter! A naughty drop landed on his nose. Joshua laughed and laughed.

He stirred slowly this time, round and round. The batter stayed in the bowl. Teacher May poured it into the hot pan. One pancake, two pancakes, three pancakes, four. They smelled sweet and buttery. Joshua packed them in a box. "Mama, Dada, and me!" he said. He carried the box all the way to the door, sniffing the warm smell.

Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red bumpy ball. Charlie wanted to kick it first.

Ben grabbed the bumpy ball at the same time. Charlie grabbed it too. She pulled hard. The ball hit her leg. It left a little scratch on her knee.

Dad knelt down next to her. "That scratch looks small," he said. "Let's find a way to play." Dad held up one hand. "We can count to ten. Then it is a new turn."

Charlie wiped her eyes. She held the ball. "One, two, three," she counted. Ben kicked the ball at ten. Then Charlie kicked it. The ball bounced over the cake table. Everyone laughed. Even Grandma jumped up to catch it.

"My turn went fast because I counted," said Charlie. She held the ball out to Ben. "You can go. I will wait."

Ben smiled big. The bumpy ball rolled and rolled across the grass.

Miles sat in the family car. He held his blanket tight. Today he would get his first big boy haircut. His tummy felt funny, but he marched up to the salon door anyway.

The hairdresser, Miss Jo, picked up a spray bottle. "Want to push it?" she asked. Miles pushed the button. Spritz, spritz! Water came out. His hair got wet. Wet hair stuck together in little dark points. Then Miss Jo cut with her scissors. Snip, snip. The wet pieces fell down like tiny rain drops. "Wet hair is easy to cut," Miles said. "It sticks in a line!"

Soon his hair was short and neat. Miles looked in the mirror. He saw a big boy with a big smile. At home he put his wet hands in his hair. "Mommy, wet makes it stay!" he said. Mommy laughed and hugged him tight.

Parker made a painting at school today. It was a red heart for his mom. It was her birthday gift.

"I want to take it now," said Parker.

Ms. Kim shook her head. "It is still wet. Wet paint makes spots on your bag."

Parker touched the paper. His finger came back red. He looked for his friend Leo. Leo was missing. Leo was home sick today. Yesterday Leo was here. Tomorrow he would come back.

Parker asked, "When will my painting be ready?"

Ms. Kim said, "Later. It needs time to dry."

So Parker waited. He played with blocks. He ate his snack. He looked at the painting again and again.

At last the paint was dry. The paper felt smooth. Parker held it up.

"Now I can bring it home," he said. "The paint dried because I waited."

Anna lost her soft bunny at school. She looked by the swings. She looked by the sand. No bunny. "Where are you, bunny?" she said.

Anna sat down on the little bench. She thought hard. "I had bunny when I sat here," she said. "Then I put my jacket down." She picked up her red jacket. She had to fold it to go down the short slide. Something soft was inside. It was bunny! Bunny was hiding in the jacket all along.

"Bunny was in my jacket," said Anna. "Bunny was in my jacket!" She hugged bunny tight. Her friend Tom ran over. "I looked by the park fence," he said. "No bunny there." Anna smiled. "Bunny was with me," she said. "Let's go on the slide together." Anna held bunny's paw and off they went.

Milo went to the park with his dad. He saw a hoop on the grass. He wanted to toss a beanbag into it.

Milo threw the beanbag hard. It went past the hoop. It landed far away in the sand.

He tried again. This time he tossed it up, high and soft. The beanbag dropped down. It fell right in. "It goes in when I toss it up," said Milo.

Then Dad rolled him a big ball. Milo used one hand. The ball bumped his fingers and fell. He got up fast and felt dizzy for a second. Dad waited, then rolled the ball again.

Milo held out both hands. He hugged the ball to his chest. He caught it!

"You did it," said Dad. He clapped and clapped.

The park felt like Milo's whole world that day. After, Dad filled Milo's water cup. Milo drank it all. "Again," said Milo, holding out both hands.

Eli sits on the small red rug at daycare. Miss Pam holds up a book. It has a picture of a red truck on the front. "This book is from the library," she says. "We can take it home, but not for always."

Eli wants the truck book for always. He holds it tight. "My truck book," he says.

Miss Pam sits down next to him. "The library lets us borrow it," she says. "Borrow means we take it home, then bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Eli opens the book. He turns the pages from the front. The truck goes up a hill. Then the truck goes fast down the hill. At the top of the last page, the truck sleeps. "It ends!" says Eli. "How does it start again?" He turns back to the first page. The words sit in little rows. Miss Pam reads them out loud. The words tell the truck what to do.

Eli looks at the words. "The marks talk," he says. "They say truck!"

Eli takes the book home. His mom reads it three times. On the last page, Eli pats the truck. "Good night, truck."

The next day, Eli brings the book back to daycare. He gives it to Miss Pam. "The book is for the other kids now," he says. "They read it too." Then he picks a new one, a book about a big yellow duck. He sits on the rug and turns to page one. "Read the marks, please," he says.

Lena put on her fox apron. It had a big orange fox on the front. Today she would make pancakes for the whole family.

She mixed flour, milk and one egg. Mom reminded her, "Do not forget the little spoon of baking powder." But Lena forgot it.

She poured the mix into the warm pan. The pancake stayed flat. It looked like a sad little plate.

"Why is it flat?" Lena asked.

Mom held up the small tin. "Because we left this out. It makes pancakes puff up."

Lena stirred the baking powder in. She poured a new pancake. It puffed up big and fat. "It got fluffy because of the powder!" Lena said.

The stack grew tall. Lena set the table fast. Then she took a big breath and did her loudest yell. "Pancakes are ready!"

Dad came running. Lena pointed at the tall warm stack and grinned.

Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. It was Diwali, the festival of lights. There were little clay lamps called diyas everywhere. Lillian wanted to light one all by herself.

Papa gave her a small diya. Lillian held the flame to the wick. It lit up. Then it went out. Lillian looked sad. She tried again. The wick lit up. Then it went out again.

The room was noisy with music and singing. Lillian looked at the big diyas on the table. Their flames stayed on and on. She looked at her diya. The oil was all gone. The big ones had lots of oil.

"The oil makes it stay on," Lillian said. Papa smiled. He poured more oil into her diya. Lillian lit the wick one more time. The little flame stood up tall. It stayed on. Lillian sat back and watched her light shine with all the others.

Henry jumped into the family car. "Are we at Grandma's yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "Grandma lives far, far away. First we need gas." Henry buckled his shoe taps together and waited.

Dad drove and drove. The car made a funny cough. Then it slowed down. Dad pulled over at a gas station. "Why did the car stop?" Henry asked. "Because the tank is empty," said Dad. "Cars need gas to go."

Henry watched Dad put the nozzle in the tank. It made a glug, glug sound. Then Dad closed the little door on the car. "Full tank!" said Dad. "Now we can go again."

The car zoomed back onto the road. Henry saw a stormy sky with big gray clouds. Rain tapped on the window. Soon the rain stopped, and a rainbow came out. "We did it!" said Henry. Then he yawned and fell asleep. When he woke up, Grandma was waving at her door.

Ibrahim wants to play outside. He looks out the big window. "Oh no," he says. "Rainy today." Little drops tap the glass. Tap, tap, tap.

Mama comes to the window too. "Rainy days need boots," she says. Ibrahim runs to the shoe rack. He puts on his red boots. He remembers his hat with ears. He gets that too. But wait. His robot toy is on the porch! It is sitting in the rain.

Ibrahim opens the door. He walks out in his boots. Puddle, splash, puddle, splash. He picks up the robot. It is wet, but it still beeps. "Good robot!" says Ibrahim. He hugs it dry with his towel.

Then the wind blows. Whoosh! His hat almost flies away. "Windy too!" says Ibrahim. He holds his hat with one hand. He holds the robot with the other hand. Mama lifts him up. "All safe and dry," she says. The robot beeps a happy little beep.

Evelyn lived in a little house with a red door. She wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by herself. Mama sang it, and Evelyn tried. The words fell out in a jumble.

Then Mama clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Slow and steady, like a clock. Evelyn clapped too. Her claps went fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Mama with a smile. "The song walks, it does not run."

Evelyn looked at her red block on the floor. She put it down. She listened first. Clap, clap, clap. Then she copied Mama. Clap, clap, clap. Now her hands went the same speed! The claps fit the song.

Evelyn clapped and sang at the very same time. "Twin-kle, twin-kle, lit-tle star." Each word sat on a clap. The whole rhyme came out, from start to end, with no jumble at all. Mama picked up the teddy bear and bounced him to the beat.

Evelyn gasped. "Mama! The claps are walking. The song walks too. That is why it works!" She hugged the teddy tight. "Teddy, now you sing." She tapped his soft paw, clap, clap, clap.

Kinsley ran to the slide at the park. Mom sat on a bench close by. The slide was long and slippery. Kinsley wanted to go down it, but the ladder looked high.

"Help, please," Kinsley said. Mom came right over and held her hand. Kinsley climbed up, one square step at a time. At the top, she sat down. Whoosh! She slid all the way to the bottom.

Then a boy bumped into her. "Sorry," he said. "It is okay," said Kinsley. She stood up and brushed off her knees. Mom clapped. "Thank you, Mom," Kinsley said.

"I slid fast because the slide is slippery," said Kinsley. Mom smiled. Then they walked home to cook lunch together. "Pasta, please!" said Kinsley.

Paisley came home with a goldfish. His name was Dot. He swam in his little bowl.

Paisley was worried. "Is Dot hungry?" she asked. Dad was there to help.

Paisley poured in lots of food. "This is yummy food," she said. But Dot did not eat it all. The food sank down. The water got cloudy and yucky. Dot hid behind his little castle.

Dad said, "Let's fix it." They scooped out the extra food. They put in fresh, clean water. Soon the water was clear again.

Paisley saw Dot come out of his castle. He wiggled his tail. He blew a tiny bubble.

"Now I know," said Paisley. "Too much food makes the water dirty." Dad smiled. "Just a little pinch each day."

That night the moon shone in the window. Paisley gave Dot one small pinch. Dot gobbled it all up.

"Good night, Dot," said Paisley. Dot blew one more bubble.

Georgia stood by the red barn. She wore her loose sun hat. The hat was too big for her head.

"I want to know my five senses," Georgia said to Grandma.

Grandma smiled. "Let's find them together."

Georgia sniffed the air. "I smell hay with my nose," she said.

Then the hen went cluck, cluck. Georgia covered her ears. "I hear the hen with my ears."

Grandma picked a ripe strawberry. Georgia put it in her mouth. "I taste sweet with my tongue."

A soft lamb walked near. Georgia touched its wool. "I feel soft with my hands."

"Now one more," said Grandma.

Georgia looked around. She saw a yellow duck. "I see the duck with my eyes!"

Grandma clapped. "Five senses. You found them all."

Georgia's loose hat slipped down over her eyes. "Now I see nothing!" she said.

Grandma lifted the hat up. The sun came back. Georgia saw the yellow duck again, splashing in the little pond.

"Hello, duck," said Georgia. "I see you."

Olivia stood by the coat hooks at school. It was cold outside. Her teacher said, "Coats on, everyone."

Olivia pushed her arms into her sleeves. The coat was on. Now came the zipper. She pulled the pull tab up. Nothing happened. The zipper did not move. She looked down. The two sides of her coat were apart.

She tried again, slowly. First she pushed the little metal tab into the slot at the bottom. Click. The two sides were stuck together now. Then she pulled the pull tab up. The zipper went up, up, up. "I did it!" said Olivia.

Her friend Sam was still pulling at his zipper. His coat was different. It had buttons. Olivia waited by the door. The clock on the wall ticked while Sam pushed each button through its hole. One, two, three.

At last Sam was done. "Ready," he said. They held hands and walked out into the cold.

Axel sat at the dinner table. He had ten green peas on his plate. Big news! He wanted to count them all by himself.

"One, two, three, four," he said. Then he stopped. What came after four? He could not remember. His tooth felt funny when he smiled, so he covered his mouth with his hand.

Dad held up his fingers. He tapped them one by one. "One, two, three, four," said Dad. He held up the next finger. He waited.

"Five!" shouted Axel. "Then six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He pointed at each pea as he said each word. Every pea got one word. No pea was missing.

Then Axel counted his spoonfuls of rice. One, two, three, all the way to the last bite. He did not forget a single word now.

"Can I count your peas too, Dad?" he asked.

"Ten carrots coming up," said Dad.

Luka sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted the gold sticker on the desk. But first, the doctor said, he had to try five things. Luka looked at the fish tank. Two small fish swim round and round. He saw them with his eyes. One.

Next came his ears. The doctor rang a little bell. Ding, ding. Then she said, "Close your eyes. Can you still hear it?" Luka shut his eyes tight. Ding. "Yes!" he said. "My ears work without my eyes!" Two.

He sniffed a sweet orange. His nose knew it. Three. He stuck out his tongue. The doctor put a tiny drop on it. Sour! He made a funny face. Four.

Then Luka touched the sticker. It felt smooth and shiny. Five. The doctor gave it to him. On the wall was a poster of a tree. Luka pointed at it. "What is the bottom part called?" he asked. The doctor smiled. "That is the root," she said. Luka stuck the gold star right on his shirt.

Jordan sat at the big table. The game was on the huge screen. Everyone wore blue hats. Dad's boot tapped the floor fast. Jordan colored his menu with a red crayon. He colored a big blue ball, just like on the screen.

But Jordan could not hear the game. He looked at the TV. The players ran. Their mouths moved. No sound came out at all. Jordan wanted to hear the roars. He wanted to hear the whistle. He put down his crayon. Then he saw small words at the bottom of the screen. The words told who scored! The score numbers changed too. Now Jordan knew what happened. The TV was quiet because the restaurant had it on mute. The words helped him watch.

"Look, the score says two to two!" Jordan shouted. Everyone cheered. Mom ordered frozen yogurt for the win. Jordan held up his menu. "I colored the ball for luck," he said. Dad gave him a high five. The whistle blew. Blue team scored! The score changed to three to two. "See, the numbers know!" said Jordan.

Iris wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Dad was folding towels in the hall. She pulled a stool to the sink. The tap was shiny and silver. She turned it with both hands.

The water came out fast. It was cold at first. Then it got hot. Very hot. Iris pulled her hands back quick. "Ow," she said. She turned the blue tap instead. The water turned cool again. "Hot water can hurt," she whispered. "I will use the cool side."

Dad heard her small voice. He came in fast. "Are you okay, Iris?" he asked. "The water got hot," said Iris. "So I moved my hands. Then I made it cool." Dad smiled a big smile. "You learn fast," he said.

He stayed close while she washed. She rubbed the soap on her hands. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. The water stayed cool and nice. Dad gave her a small towel. Iris dried her hands all by herself. "I did it," she said. Dad clapped his hands. Iris hung the towel on the shiny hook.

Liam sat in the school computer lab. A big tablet lay on the table. He wanted to draw a red truck on it.

Liam pushed the screen with his finger. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark and cool. He waited. Then he saw the round button on the bottom edge. He pressed it and counted slowly, one, two, three. The screen lit up bright. "I did it," Liam said.

He looked for the drawing app. It was a little square with a crayon on it. He tapped it with one finger. The app opened. Liam picked the red color and drew a big truck. He drew two round wheels. He made the line tight and small for the window. His teacher smiled.

Now it was time for snack. Liam had to put the tablet away. He pressed the round button on the bottom again. The screen went dark. He slid the tablet back onto the shelf, next to the other tablets.

Liam looked at his teacher. "When I press the bottom, the light goes out," he said. She nodded. Liam patted the tablet gently, like a sleepy cat, and ran off to find his crackers.

Madison stood at the big running track. Her beanbag was shaped like a pink pig. She wanted to toss it into a hoop on the ground.

Madison threw the pig. It fell short. She tried again. Still short. Then she held her arm straight and long, like a stick. She let go at the end. The pig flew far and landed in the hoop. "My arm was straight, so it went far!" she said.

Next, Dad rolled a big ball to her. Madison tried to catch it with one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. "Why did it fall?" she asked. "I only used one hand." So she held out both hands. Dad rolled the ball again. It went right into them. Madison hugged the big ball and laughed. The pig beanbag sat in the hoop, and Madison jumped up and down.

Arlo looked out the window. The grass was gone. White snow was everywhere. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day." Arlo clapped his hands. He wanted to play in the backyard.

He ran outside in his slippers. His toes felt cold right away. "Ow," said Arlo. He ran back in. "My feet are cold because I have no boots," he said. Mama smiled. "Yes. Snow is very cold. Boots keep you warm."

Mama helped him put on his boots. She helped him tie the laces. She pulled each tie tight. "Now my feet are warm," said Arlo. He stomped in the snow. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

Then Arlo saw his pet dog, Bingo. Bingo was shivering. "Why is Bingo cold?" Arlo asked. "Because dogs get cold too," said Mama. She put a little coat on Bingo. Bingo wagged his tail. Arlo patted his soft ears. Together they made a big snowball. It grew and grew. "Best snow day ever," said Arlo, and he threw his mittens up in the air.

Leon sat in a big chair. It was his first haircut at the salon. His mom stood right next to him and held his hand.

The hairdresser, Miss Jo, put a cape on Leon. The cape had rainbows on it. "Snip, snip," went the scissors. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. "Look, Mom," said Leon. "The snip makes my hair fall!" Mom smiled and said, "Yes, one snip, one little piece."

Miss Jo kept going. One snip, one piece. Two snips, two pieces. Three snips, three pieces. The hair fell down like soft rain. Leon watched every piece. His head felt lighter and lighter. Soon he got tired of sitting so still, so Miss Jo gave him a squeeze toy to hold.

At last the haircut was done. Miss Jo brushed off the cape. Leon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "New hair!" he said. Then Mom picked him up for a big hug. At home, Dad was going to cook pasta for dinner. Leon sat in his small chair, still in his socks, and told Dad all about it. "One snip, one piece," he said. "And now I have new hair!"

Owen was grumpy. He did not want to see Doctor Paz today. His tummy felt funny and the office smelled like soap.

First, Doctor Paz held up a picture. "Cover one eye," she said. Owen covered his eye with his hand. Now he could not see the duck with that eye. He took his hand away. The duck came back! "My eyes see it," Owen said. "My hand was in the way."

Then she looked in his ears. "Say aah," she said. Owen said, "Aah." Doctor Paz rang a little bell. Ding! Owen's ears heard it. Then she put a cotton ball over the bell. Now it was quiet. "The cotton stops the sound," said Owen. Doctor Paz laughed. "You are a smart patient."

Next came a taste test. Doctor Paz gave Owen a tiny cup. "Taste this." Owen tasted it. "Yuck! It is bitter!" Then he pinched his nose and tasted again. Now he could not taste it at all. He let go of his nose. Yuck came back! "My nose helps my tongue," Owen said. "That is silly!" Doctor Paz smiled. "Your nose and tongue are a team."

At the end, she gave him a warm sticker of a truck. Owen touched it with his fingers. It felt bumpy. He sniffed his bread snack in his bag. It smelled good. On the way home he said, "Dad, can we build a doctor office at home?" Dad said, "Yes. But I get the bell." Ding!

Anna sat at the big table. The soup was hot. Mama said, "Hold hands first." Anna held Papa's hand. She held Grandma's hand too.

Anna wanted to say the blessing. She was too young to know all the words. Her mouth opened. Nothing came out. Grandma smiled and pointed at the cow bowl. "Count with me," Grandma said. "One, thank you for the cow. Two, thank you for the corn. Three, thank you for us."

Anna counted with Grandma. "One. Two. Three." She did not need big words. She only needed to count good things.

The next night, Anna held hands first. She pointed at the bread. "One, thank you for the bread," she said. "Two, thank you for the soup." Then she stopped. She looked at Baby Ben. He was too small to eat soup.

"Three, thank you for Ben," Anna said. Ben banged his spoon. Everyone laughed. Papa gave Anna the first piece of bread. "You said it all by yourself," he said. Anna took a big, warm bite.

Edouard found a red book at school. On the cover he saw little black marks. "What are those?" he asked. His friend Mia said, "They are words. Words tell you things." Edouard opened the book. He held it tight. Page one, page two, page three. He turned the pages from front to back. On page three was a soft white rabbit. "A pet," said Edouard. "I want this book forever."

He asked his teacher, "Can I keep it?" She said, "No, Edouard. This book is from the library. You can take it home. Then you bring it back so other kids can read it too." Edouard felt sad. But he took the book home. He smelled the pages. They smelled like paper and sun. He read the rabbit book every night.

On Friday, his mom said, "Time to take the book back." Edouard held it tight one more time. Then he put it in his bag. At school, he gave it back. "Why do I give it back?" he asked. "So Sam can read it next." At circle time, Sam held the red book. He opened it to the rabbit. Edouard smiled and said, "Page one, page two, page three."

Claire ran to the toy shelf at daycare. The red truck was not there.

"Where is the red truck?" she asked.

Teacher Sam pointed. "Ben has it now. You can have it later, after snack time."

Claire looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. "Later is a long time," she said.

"Not too long," said Teacher Sam. "We play now. We eat later. Then the truck is free."

Claire went to the blocks. She played a game with Mia. They stacked the blocks up, up, up.

"Yesterday the truck was mine," said Claire. "Today it is Ben's. Tomorrow maybe it is mine again."

"That's right," said Teacher Sam.

Snack time came. Ben put the truck on the shelf. Claire ate her crackers slowly. Then she ran to the shelf.

The red truck was there. "Later came!" said Claire. "The truck is mine now."

She pushed it across the floor. "Now, now, now!" she said.

Zoey wanted to build a fish at daycare. She found paper shapes in a box. There were circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles.

She picked a big circle for the fish body. Then she tried to make a tail with a square. The square corners stuck out. "That looks funny," said her friend Ben.

Zoey looked at the picture of a fish on the wall. The tail had pointy ends and straight sides. "A triangle has pointy ends," she thought. She pulled a triangle from the box and put it on the circle. Now the tail looked just right. "The triangle fits because the tail is pointy," she said. Then she glued two small circles on top. Would they be good eyes? Yes! The eyes were round like the circles.

Next she wanted to make fins. Which shape had two long sides? She held up a rectangle. It was long on top and long on the side too. She put one rectangle on the fish's back. It looked like a perfect little fin. She added a square at the bottom for a fin too. The square had four sides, all the same.

Ben put the fish on the wall for everyone to see. "You were so brave to try new shapes," he said. Zoey tapped the triangle tail with her finger. It felt smooth and pointy. "Look," she said. "A circle, a triangle, a rectangle, and a square. My fish has them all!"

Elizabeth saw a big butterfly on the art table. It was blue and gold. She wanted to make one too.

She needed the glue. Ben had the glue. Elizabeth grabbed it fast. Ben's paper went crooked. It was not straight anymore. His butterfly wings fell off.

"One, two, three," said Elizabeth. She picked up the wings. She looked at Ben. "Sorry," she said.

Ben gave her the glue. "Thank you," said Elizabeth.

The glue was sticky and hard to squeeze. "Help, please," she said. Teacher Maya came and helped her hands. Squeeze, squeeze. One wing, two wings.

"Now it is straight," said Elizabeth. "Because I said sorry and please."

Ben smiled and stuck on one gold dot.

Alexander stood at the bus stop with his red coat. The bus would come soon. He wanted to zip his coat all by himself.

He pushed the zipper up. It went crooked and stopped. "Why won't it go?" he asked. He looked down. The two sides were not in the little slot together. One side was out.

He pulled the zipper all the way down. He put both sides into the slot. He heard a small click. Then he pushed the slider up, up, up. The zipper moved like a slow turtle. But it moved!

"My coat is zipped! I did it!" he said. Mama clapped. "You win, Alexander!" she said.

The bus came round the corner. Alexander was tired from trying, but he smiled. He got on the bus with his warm coat on. "I can zip it myself now," he said.

Grandpa came to stay at Olivier's house. "I will stay for one whole week," said Grandpa. Olivier wanted to know how long a week was. Was it as long as a day? Was it as long as a nap?

Olivier had an idea. He made a big paper sign. He drew seven suns on it. "Why seven suns?" asked Grandpa. "You will see," said Olivier. He hung the sign on the kitchen door.

Every morning, Grandpa would cook eggs. Then Olivier would look at the sign. One morning was gone, so he crossed out one sun. "Look, Grandpa! One sun is gone. That is one day." The next morning, he crossed out another sun. Then another, and another. The week got littler and littler.

Soon only one sun was left. Olivier felt worried. Would Grandpa leave forever? "When all the suns are gone, do you go away for always?" he asked. Grandpa smiled. "A week always ends. But a new week can start. And I can come back."

The last morning came. Grandpa cooked the eggs. Olivier crossed out the last sun. The sign had no suns at all. "The week is all done!" he said. Grandpa gave him a big hug at the park gate. Then Olivier ran home to draw seven new suns.

Eleanor ran to the park with her red ball. Then the ball rolled into the bushes. "Oh no," she said. She wanted it back.

Eleanor used her eyes to look. She saw green leaves and no ball. She used her ears to listen. She heard a small bump, bump. The ball was still rolling! Eleanor followed the sound with her ears.

A curly dog ran up too. The dog used its nose to sniff. Sniff, sniff, under the bench. The dog pushed the ball out with its nose. Eleanor reached out her hand and touched the ball. It was bumpy and warm.

"Thank you, dog," she said. She gave the dog a pat. Then she held the ball tight with both hands, so it would not roll away again.

Henri stood by a big table at the hall. Lots of people were there. Henri's grandma held his hand. "We say our blessing now," she said. Henri felt worried. He did not know the words yet.

"Watch first," said Grandma. "Then you can join in." Everyone at the table held hands. Their hands made a big ring. The ring went all around the long table, like a road over a hill.

Then everyone closed their eyes. They took a big breath. And they all said the words together. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for our friends." Their voices sounded thick and warm, like a big soft blanket.

Henri listened. The words were short. He said them in his head. Then the big breath came again. Everyone closed their eyes one more time. This time Henri said the words too. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for our friends." He said every word. Grandma squeezed his hand. Then bread came around, and Henri took a warm piece. "I said it," he told Grandma. She smiled and gave him some honey on top.

Sofia carried her towel down to the pool. The pool was right by the big beach. She could hear the waves.

"Today I will swim!" said Sofia. A boy named Sam was there too. He had a furry dog on a towel. The dog was waiting for him.

Sofia got in the water. It came up to her chin. She put her face in. The water went up her nose. It hurt! She coughed and coughed. "Why did that happen?" she asked.

Sam was blowing bubbles in the water. "Watch me," he said. He put his face in. Bubbles came out of his nose. No coughing!

So Sofia took a big breath. She put her face in the water. She blew bubbles out of her nose. The water stayed out! No coughing at all.

"Look, Dad!" she called. "My nose blows air! That keeps the water away!" She did it again. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles. Up she came, smiling wide.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Dad laughed. "Yes, little fish." The furry dog wagged its tail, and Sam clapped for her. Sofia splashed her feet. "Bubble time again!" she shouted, and down went her face.

Bennett stood in the pool changing room. His tummy was wet. His legs were wet too. His daddy held a big towel.

Bennett tried to put on his shirt. The shirt stuck. It would not go down. "Why will it not go on?" he asked.

Daddy patted him with the towel. The towel drank up the water. Bennett's tummy was dry now. Was that why the shirt stuck before? Bennett tried the shirt again. This time it slid right down. "Wet skin is sticky," said Bennett. "Dry skin is not sticky."

Daddy laughed and nodded. Bennett patted his own arms with the towel. He liked how soft it felt. Soon his legs were dry too. His pants went on fast, zip zip.

Bennett picked up his swim bag. He put his wet swimsuit inside. "The suit is wet because I swam in the pool," he said. He was not sad that swim time was over. Next week he would come back.

At the door, Bennett waved at the pool. "Bye bye, water," he called. "I will keep practicing my kicks."

Grandma was coming today! Anna jumped in the kitchen. "She will stay for one, two, three, four, five, six, seven sleeps," said Mama. Anna held up seven fingers. Seven sleeps was a lot!

Anna made a chart. It had seven paper cups on it. Each cup was for one sleep. "When you rip a cup off, that sleep is done," said Anna. That night, Anna ripped one cup. Six left!

Grandma ate pancakes with Anna. Grandma made messy flour hills. Anna made messy flour hills too. They laughed and laughed. Each night, Anna ripped one more cup. Six, five, four, three, two, one.

On the last night, one cup was left. Anna ripped it off slow. "Zero cups," she said. "Zero sleeps. That means you go home today." Grandma hugged her tight. "Bring the cups when you visit me, Anna."

Brielle woke up and looked out the window. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," she said. She put on her little yellow hat. The hat kept the sun off her nose.

Brielle wanted to play outside. She ran to the door, fast. But the sky got dark. Big drops fell. Drip, drip, drip. "Now it is rainy," said Brielle. She could not wear her sunny hat in the rain. Her hat would get all wet.

Mama gave her red rain boots and a blue raincoat. Brielle put them on. She stepped outside. The rain fell on her hood. Her feet stayed dry in the boots. The rain did not get in.

Then the wind came. It blew her hood off her head. "It is windy too," said Brielle. She held her hood with one hand. The wind could not take it now.

Later the rain turned soft and white. Snowflakes fell on her sleeve. "It is snowy," said Brielle. She met her friend Bella outside. They caught snowflakes on their mittens.

"The snow is cold," said Bella. Brielle looked at her warm mittens. "Rain needs boots," she said. "Snow needs mittens." Then she caught one more snowflake on her red boot.

Eliana was three today. The big room had balloons. Outside the window, soft snow fell on the slide. Nobody played on it now. Inside, everyone was warm.

Mama brought the cake. On top were three little candles. "Why three?" Eliana asked. Papa lit them with a match. The flames grew tall. Eliana counted one, two, three. "One candle for each year," said Gran, cutting a thick slice of cake.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew hard. All three flames went out. The smoke curled up in thin grey lines. "The candles went out because I blew on them," she said. Everyone clapped. Eliana ate her thick piece of cake. Baby Theo banged his spoon. Papa said, "Happy birthday, Eliana!" Outside, the snow kept falling, slow and quiet, on the empty slide.

Riley ran to the park. Her blue hair clip fell off somewhere. She wanted to find it.

First she used her eyes. She looked by the swings. She looked under the bench. No clip. "Maybe my ears can help," she said. She stood very still. She heard kids laughing. She heard a dog bark. No clip sound. A clip does not make noise.

Then she used her nose. She sniffed the big flower bed. It smelled sweet. She sniffed the dirt. It smelled dirty, like rain. Still no clip. "A nose can not smell a clip," she said.

Riley sat down in the sand. She put out her hands. She touched the sand, bit by bit. The sand was warm and bumpy. Her fingers went left. Her fingers went right. Then something hard and smooth touched her skin. It was the blue clip!

"Mom, I found it with my hands!" said Riley.

Mom smiled. "Your eyes looked and looked. But fingers can feel what eyes can not see."

Riley put the clip back in her hair. Then she licked her ice cream. Yum. "Mom, does my tongue help too?" she asked, and took one more lick.

Elliot ran to his toy box. He wanted to play house. He found his little duck toy, his teddy, and a small blanket.

"Baby duck is cold," said Elliot. He wrapped the duck in the blanket. But the duck kept slipping out. It slid onto the floor. Thump. Elliot picked it up. He wrapped it again. Thump. The blanket was too big and too smooth.

Then Elliot had a big idea. He gave the duck a name. "Your name is Ducky," he said. He rolled the blanket tight, the way Mom rolled his sleeping bag. Ducky stayed snug. "Ducky is warm now," said Elliot. He clapped his hands.

Next, Ducky was hungry. Elliot found a play apple. It was red and juicy. "Here, Ducky," he said. He held it to the duck's beak. He made a little munch, munch sound. "Ducky likes juicy apples," said Elliot. He patted Ducky's head, just like Dad patted his head.

Teddy wanted a turn too. "You be the doctor," Elliot told Teddy. Teddy checked Ducky with a spoon. It was a very good spoon. The phone rang in the kitchen. It was Mom calling them for a real snack. Elliot hugged Ducky tight and ran. "Come on, Ducky! Snack time!"

Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big red balloon by the door. But a girl was there too. Her name was Mia. She wanted the red balloon too.

Mia grabbed the string. Isaiah grabbed the string too. The balloon bounced between them. "One balloon, two hands," said the store man. "You can take turns. First Mia holds it. Then Isaiah holds it."

Isaiah let go first. Mia held the balloon. She counted to ten. Then she gave the string to Isaiah. Isaiah held the red balloon. It felt full and light in his hand. He counted to ten too. Then he gave it back.

"Taking turns works," said Isaiah. "One holds it. Then the other one holds it. Nobody cries."

The store man smiled. He reached under the counter. He pulled out one more red balloon! "A full basket of balloons was hiding here," he said. Now Mia had one, and Isaiah had one. "We both keep a balloon," said Isaiah. He waved to Mia all the way to the street.

Grayson packed his little blue bag. In went one bear, two socks, three crackers. "Trip time!" he yelled. The car was full. Dad put the map in the front. Mom put the food in the back.

At the campsite, Grayson jumped out. He saw a spotted deer by the trees. He saw a big fire pit. He saw his own little tent. "I sleep here!" he said. But then Grayson felt sad. His bear was not in his bag. The bear was home, far away.

"We can make a new bear," said Mom. She took out paper and a pencil. They drew a bear with round ears. Grayson held the paper bear tight at bedtime. The tent went flap, flap in the wind. Grayson said, "The wind makes the tent move." He yawned and closed his eyes.

In the morning, Dad held up something soft. "Look who came with us!" It was the real bear, tucked in Dad's coat pocket all along. Grayson hugged the bear, then the paper bear too. "Two bears! One, two!"

Charlotte rode her bike to the barbershop. Her dad walked beside her. This was her very first haircut.

The barber put a big cape on Charlotte. The cape was too big. It kept slipping off. "The clip is too weak," the barber said. "It cannot hold the cape." He got a strong clip instead. Now the cape stayed on.

The barber picked up his scissors. Then he stopped. Charlotte's hair was full of tangles. The tangles came from her bike helmet. "Why is my hair so tangled?" Charlotte asked. The helmet had rubbed on her hair on the ride.

The barber filled a spray bottle with water. He sprayed Charlotte's hair. Splash, splash. "Why does it need water?" she asked. He let her touch her wet hair. It felt soft now. The comb went right through it. Charlotte smiled. Wet hair was easy to comb.

The scissors went snip, snip, snip. Soon Charlotte had short, neat hair. "No more tangles," she said. "My hair is wet, so the comb can roll right through it."

Then she pedaled her bike all the way home.

Luke woke up early. Today was a big day. Grandma was coming for Eid.

Luke wanted to help make the sweet biscuits. But he could not reach the table. He got his little stool. Now he could reach!

Grandma showed him the dough. Luke could fold it over. He folded one piece. Then another. His hands were sticky. The dough was gone from the bowl. The bowl was empty.

"Grandma, no more dough!" said Luke.

Grandma smiled. "We made them all, Luke."

Soon the biscuits came out of the oven. They smelled so good. Luke counted them. One, two, three, all the way to ten.

The family sat together. Everyone ate the biscuits. Luke gave Grandma the biggest one.

Then Luke picked up crumbs. He put them in a small pile, like a little nest. "The crumbs fell because I ate fast," he said.

Grandma laughed. "Eat slower next time, little one."

Luke ate one more biscuit, slow slow slow. No crumbs fell. "Look, Grandma! I ate slow, so no crumbs!"

Grandma clapped her hands. "Yes, Luke. That is our clever boy."

Hailey went to the grocery store with Dad. They walked past the apples. They walked past the bread. Then they came to the big cold door. Frost was on the glass.

"It is freezing in there," said Dad. "Put on your coat, Hailey."

Hailey pushed her arms in. One arm went in fast. The other arm hid. She shook the coat. She wiggled. Pop! The arm came out. "I did it!" she said.

Now the zipper. Hailey pulled it up. It would not zip. She pulled again. Nothing. "Why will it not zip?" she asked. She looked down. The zipper pull was way up high, not at the bottom. She slid it down, down, down. Then she pushed the two sides into the little slot together. She pulled up. Zip! It worked!

"Is that true? Did you zip it all alone?" asked Dad.

"Yes! The pull has to start at the bottom," said Hailey.

Dad hugged her. A silly snowman sticker fell out of her sleeve. "Where did he come from?" Hailey laughed. "He came to shop too!"

They bought milk for a drink and seeds for the garden. Hailey wore her coat all the way home.

Jayden sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint a big orange ball, like the one he saw roll down the hill. But there was no orange paint. "No orange," said Jayden. His hands felt stuck.

Miss Rosa sat next to him. "Let's look at your paints," she said. "Red, yellow, blue. One, two, three." Jayden pointed. "Red, yellow, blue!" he said. The paint felt cool and wet on his fingers.

"Try red and yellow," said Miss Rosa. Jayden dipped his brush in red. Then he dipped it in yellow. He mixed them round and round. The bowl made a sloshy sound. "Look!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow make orange! They made orange because I mixed them!" He painted his ball. It was big and bright. "My ball!" he said. Miss Rosa smiled. "You made your own orange, Jayden."

Henri sat on the big train with Mama. He held his teddy bear tight. "Are we home yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "The train takes us far away. We sleep at Grandma's house tonight."

Henri had a little carton of milk. He put it on the tray. Then the train began to move. Chug, chug! The milk carton wobbled. It tipped over! Milk ran all over the tray. Henri looked at it. "The milk fell because the train moved," he said. Mama smiled. "Yes, the train made it jump."

Mama wiped the milk with a napkin. She gave Henri a new carton. "Hold it in your hands this time," she said. Henri held it tight. The train went faster. The milk did not fall. "My hands are strong," said Henri. "The straw was weak before. It bent and fell too."

The train went chug, chug, chug. Trees went by the window. Henri saw a cow in a field. He waved at the cow. "Bye, cow!" he said. Mama waved too. Henri put his head on Mama's arm. The train went soft and rumbly. He watched the wheels go round and round. "Mama, is Grandma far?" he asked. "A little far," said Mama. "But the train knows the way." Henri hugged his teddy. His eyes closed slowly. The train went chug, chug, all the way.

Hudson sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint a purple grape. He looked for purple paint. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. There was no purple paint at all.

Miss Ana put a brush in his hand. "You can mix two paints," she said. Hudson dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in blue too. He made a dot on the paper. The dot was purple! "Red and blue make purple," he said.

Hudson tried again. He made another dot. It was purple too. He hummed a little song while he painted. Then he painted a big purple grape.

He wanted to make a green leaf next. He dipped his brush in yellow. He dipped it in blue. He made a dot. It was green! The paper got wet, so he had to wait. He waited and watched the paint dry.

Then he added one more dot with his fingernail scratch on the paper. "Look, my grape!" he said.

Alice sat in her car seat. The car went hum, hum, hum. "Are we at Grandma's now?" Alice said. "Not now," said Dad. "We get there later. Later comes after now." Alice watched the trees go by. One tree, then another tree, then another.

Alice had a bag on her lap. It was heavy. It had bread inside for Grandma. "Yesterday we made this bread," Alice said. "Yes," said Dad. "Yesterday is the day that is done. Today we drive. Tomorrow we play with Grandma." Alice put a berry in her mouth. It was sweet.

The sky got dark. Alice's eyes got heavy too. "Sleep now," said Dad. "Grandma later." Alice slept in her seat, soft and warm. The car went hum, hum, hum all night.

Alice woke up. The car was still. There was a door, and there was Grandma! "You slept a long time," said Grandma. "Now it is tomorrow!" Alice hugged her heavy bag. "The bread made yesterday is for today," Alice said. Grandma took the bread and smiled. "Come in," she said. "We will eat it now."

Everly could not sleep. She wanted tomorrow to come now. Tomorrow was Grandma's birthday party.

She got out of bed. She went to find Daddy. "Is it tomorrow yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. "First we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Everly drank some water from her cup. There was lemon in the water. She took a little taste. It was sour! She made a funny face. Daddy laughed softly.

"But I want tomorrow now," said Everly.

"Sleep comes first," said Daddy. "Yesterday we made the cake. Today we set the table. Tomorrow we will eat it."

Everly looked out the window. The moon was up now. The sun would come later. She got it. The moon goes, then the sun comes, then it is tomorrow.

She climbed back into bed. She hugged her bear. She closed her eyes. She waited and waited.

The room got light. The sun was up! Everly jumped out of bed. "The sun came!" she said. "Sleep went away. Now it is tomorrow!"

Ellie sat at the dinner table. She tapped her spoon on her plate. Her peas rolled round and round.

"I want Grandma," said Ellie. "Is she coming now?"

"Not now," said Mom. "Grandma comes tomorrow."

Ellie frowned. Her tummy felt upset. Tomorrow was too far away.

"What is tomorrow?" asked Ellie.

Mom did not say. She started to fill her own plate. "Eat your peas first," she said.

Ellie looked at her spoon. She piled three peas on it. The spoon looked like a little green boat. She sailed the boat to her mouth. One, two, three. The peas were gone.

"Pea boat, pea boat," said Ellie. She made another boat. Then another.

The sky outside got dark. The lamp made a warm yellow circle on the table.

"Now it is night," said Mom. "Sleep comes at night. After sleep, it is tomorrow."

Ellie ate her last pea. She thought hard.

"So I sleep," she said, "and then it is tomorrow? Then Grandma comes?"

Mom smiled and nodded. Ellie slid down from her chair. She ran to find her pajamas.

"Come on, bed," she called. "Hurry up and be done."

She lay down and closed her eyes tight. In the morning, Grandma knocked at the door.

Dylan ran to the park with his red ball. The weather was warm and sunny. The grass smelled fresh and green.

He saw a girl on the swing. She was pushing her feet hard. Her mouth turned up. She was laughing loud. "She is happy," Dylan said. Then a boy dropped his ice cream. His mouth turned down. His eyes got wet. He was sad.

Dylan bounced his red ball. It went high. It went over the bushes. He could not see it. His tummy felt tight. He wanted to cry.

A big dog ran by. The dog barked. The sad boy jumped back. His eyes got wide. He was scared. The dog sniffed the bushes. Out came the red ball! The dog pushed it with his nose.

Dylan clapped his hands. His heart went fast, like a drum. He felt excited. He picked up his ball. "Good dog," he said. "You found it because you sniffed the bushes." The dog wagged his tail.

Anthony went to the library with Mama. He was hungry, so he held her hand tight.

"Story time is today," said Mama. "Yesterday we missed it. Today we are here!" Anthony put the book from yesterday on the desk. He heard the librarian say, "This book was due yesterday. Thank you for bringing it back." Anthony smiled. Yesterday was the day before today. Now he knew.

"Can we get a cake book now?" Anthony asked. "We can look now," said Mama. "We will read it later, at home." They found one, two, three cake books. Cake today, cake tomorrow, cake every day!

At home, Anthony turned the pages. "Look, Mama. We mix the cake now. We eat it later." He tapped the picture. "Later comes after now!"

Sofia sat in the car with her teddy bear. "The dentist will count my teeth," she said to Mama. "One, two, three, teeth," she counted, tapping her teddy's smile. Mama smiled too.

At the dentist's office, Sofia sat on a wooden bench. It felt smooth and cool. A tall chair waited for her. Sofia could not reach the big chair by herself. The dentist helped her up. "Open wide," he said. Sofia opened her mouth. He counted out loud. "One, two, three," all the way to twenty. Sofia's teddy sat on her tummy. The dentist peeked in the teddy's ear too, and they both laughed.

"There, all clean," the dentist said. He gave Sofia a small sticker. In the car, Mama buckled her in. Sofia held up the sticker. "My teeth got counted," she said. "Twenty of them, Mama. Twenty."

Michael was four years old. He went to school with his red backpack. Today his class would play outside. But first, everyone had to put on their shoes.

Michael felt shy. He sat alone by the wall. He pushed his feet into his shoes all by himself. The teacher smiled at him. Then Michael stood up to walk. Ouch! His feet felt funny. His toes bumped into each other. He fell down on the soft mat.

His friend Lily came over. "Try swapping your shoes," she said. Michael pulled the shoes off. He put the left shoe on his left foot. He put the right shoe on his right foot. He stood up again. He walked to the door. No ouch! No falling!

"The shoes hurt because they were on the wrong feet," Michael said. Lily clapped for him. Outside, they ran to the sandbox. Michael smelled the fresh bread from the kitchen. Lunch was coming soon. After lunch came a nap on his little mat.

Later, Michael drew a picture on the classroom computer. He drew two shoes. One said L and one said R. He showed it to his teacher. "I can put on my shoes all by myself now," he said. Then he wiggled his happy toes inside his right-way shoes.

Baby Mia was crying. She was in her basket in the nursery.

Lincoln did not want her to cry. He did not want to be alone with the crying. He ran to find Mom. "Come quick," he said. Mom was feeding Mia soon.

"Maybe she is hungry," said Mom. "Babies cry when they need milk."

Linlin watched. Mom gave Mia milk. The crying stopped. Mia made small sounds. Her eyes closed.

Lincoln saw the answer. "She cried because she was hungry," he said. "Now she is full."

Mom smiled. "Yes. Now she can sleep."

Later Mia cried again. Lincoln was big now. He ran to fetch Mom. He did not say a word. He just pulled her hand. Mom picked up Mia.

"You told me," said Mom. "Good helper."

Lincoln patted Mia's soft blanket. It smelled like milk and soap. Mia yawned and went to sleep.

Victor wanted to build a big tower in the playroom. He put a circle block at the bottom. The circle had round sides. It rolled away! The whole tower fell down. "Oh no," said Victor.
