Mama sat next to him on the rug. She gave his knee a little kiss. "Try again," she said. Victor picked up a square block. The square had flat sides. It did not roll. It sat still. He stacked more squares on top. Then he found a triangle for the roof. "Flat sides stay," said Victor. "Round sides make it fly off the rug!" He clapped his hands. Mama laughed. "Can I add one?" she asked. She put a rectangle by the tower. It made a door. Victor knocked on it. "Come in!" he said.Victor wanted to build a big tower in the playroom. He put a circle block at the bottom. The circle had round sides. It rolled away! The whole tower fell down. "Oh no," said Victor. Mama sat next to him on the rug. She gave his knee a little kiss. "Try again," she said. Victor picked up a square block. The square had flat sides. It did not roll. It sat still. He stacked more squares on top. Then he found a triangle for the roof. "Flat sides stay put," said Victor. "Round sides roll away!" He clapped his hands. Mama laughed. "Can I add one too?" she asked. She put a rectangle at the base. It made a door. Victor knocked on it. "Come in!" he said.

Aiden sat on the small red rug. His teacher had a big basket of books. Aiden picked one. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He went from the front to the back. On the last page was a picture of a brown dog. The teacher pointed at the words. "Those marks say good night, dog," she said. Aiden looked at the marks. The marks could talk!

The teacher said the books came from the library. "You can take one home," she said. Aiden wanted the dog book. He wanted to keep it forever. He hid it in his cubby. A boy named Sam looked in the basket. Sam wanted the dog book too. Sam got upset. "It's not here," he said. Aiden saw Sam's sad face.

Then Aiden had an idea. He lift ed the dog book out of his cubby. He gave it to the teacher. She put a paper card in it. "The card says bring it back," she said. Aiden took the book home. He read it front to back. On Friday, he brought it back. Sam smiled and hugged the book. "My turn," said Sam. Aiden clapped his hands.

Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was coming today! She wanted to give the baby a gift. She looked in her toy box. She found a red truck. She found a flat blue hat. Nothing felt just right.

Then Natalie saw her crayons. She could make a picture! She glued a photo of herself onto big paper. She added shiny stars. She made a road on the paper with a gray crayon. The road went right to the baby's crib. "This road shows the baby how to find me," she said.

The door opened. Mom carried in a tiny bundle. "Meet your baby brother," said Mom. Natalie tiptoed close. The baby's eyes opened. He looked at the paper. Then his mouth made a tiny O. Natalie giggled. "He likes the stars!"

Then something surprising happened. The baby grabbed Natalie's finger. He held on tight. Natalie laughed. "He is holding my hand because I am his sister," she said. She put the picture on the wall by his crib. The baby watched the stars shine. Natalie waved and said, "Goodnight, baby brother. I will see you tomorrow."

Austin sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to hear his own heart. "Can I hear it?" he asked. The doctor smiled. She put small cups in Austin's ears. The cups had a long tube. "Now listen," she said. Austin heard a thump, thump, thump. "That is my heart!" he said. He heard it with his ears.

The doctor let him look at his skin with a tiny light. Austin saw his arm up close with his eyes. He touched a squishy ball on the table. His fingers felt it. He smelled a sticker that smelled like grapes. His nose knew it. The doctor gave him a candy. Austin tasted sweet on his tongue.

Austin gave his mother a grape sticker. "Your ears heard my heart," he said. "The cups made it loud." His mother laughed. Then Austin yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy," he said. The doctor said, "Big hearts need big naps." Austin closed his eyes right there in the chair.

Hunter was hungry for soup. Mom made a big pot of it. Hunter had a small bowl. Mom had a big bowl.

The sky outside was stormy. Rain tapped on the window. A little bird sat under the roof to stay dry.

Hunter blew on his soup. He blew fast. Then he blew slow. "Still hot!" he said. Mom sipped hers. "Mine is cold already," she said. Hunter looked. Her bowl was big and deep. His bowl was small and flat.

He waited a little more. The small bowl let the heat go out fast. Then he took a sip. "Cold enough!" he said. "My little bowl wins!"

Mom laughed. "My big bowl loses," she said. "But I get more soup."

Hunter slurped his soup. The rain went tap, tap, tap.

Madelyn wanted to build a house for her toy sheep. She looked at her blocks. Some blocks were squares. Some were triangles. Some were rectangles. Some were balls, round like circles.

She put a ball on the floor first. Then she put a square block on top. The block slid off. The round ball rolled away. "Oh no," said Madelyn. "The sheep has no wall."

She put the square block down instead. It sat flat and still. She stacked another square on it. Then another. The wall stood tall. The round ball had rolled because it was round. The flat square did not roll. It stayed.

Madelyn made four walls. On top she put a triangle, like a little roof. Under the roof, the sheep fit just right. "Your house is not weak," Madelyn told the sheep. "It is strong."

The sheep sat in its square house. Madelyn smiled and patted the triangle roof.

Raphael was at school. He made a real clay star. It had five points. His teacher Mia smiled at it.

Then Ben grabbed the star. It fell and broke. Raphael made angry fists. His face went hot. "You broke my star," he said. Mia knelt down beside him.

"Why is my face hot?" Raphael asked. "Because you are angry," said Mia. "Big breaths can help." Raphael took a big breath. Then another. His fists let go. His face felt cool again.

Ben said sorry. He helped fix the star. The glue made the points fit back on. The star was whole again.

Raphael jumped up and down. "I feel excited!" he said. Mia laughed. "Me too," she said. She put the real clay star on the shelf, up high, where it would be safe.

Everett sat at the dinner table. He wanted the sweet corn. It was summer corn, his favorite.

"Close your eyes," said Dad. Everett closed his eyes. He could not see the corn. He peeked with one eye. There it was, yellow and bumpy.

Then Everett held his nose. He took a bite. He froze. "I can't taste it!" The corn tasted like nothing at all.

Dad laughed. "Let go of your nose, silly boy." Everett let go. Now the corn tasted sweet again.

"Your nose helps you taste," said Everett. He sniffed the corn with his nose. He listened to it crunch with his ears. He felt the rough little kernels with his fingers.

"I need my whole face for corn," said Everett. Dad laughed and gave him one more piece.

Lennon spotted the red crayons on the shelf. They were up too high. She wanted the red one for her apple picture.

She pulled a chair and stood on it. The chair wobbled. It tipped over. Blocks fell everywhere and her elbow hit Omar's tower. "Sorry, Omar," she said. Omar nodded and started to build again.

Lennon looked up at the shelf. How could she reach now? Miss Ada had a phone on her desk. Maybe that could help? "Miss Ada, can you help me, please?" Lennon asked. Miss Ada smiled and got the red crayon down. "Thank you," said Lennon. She drew a big red apple. "The magic word made it come down," she said. Then she put the chair back where it belonged. "I did it all by myself," she said, "with a little help."

Cooper sat in the middle of the car. His cup fell on the floor. It rolled far, far away.

"Can you help me, please?" Cooper asked. "Yes, I can help," said Dad. Dad reached back. He got the cup.

Dad bumped Cooper's knee. "Sorry," said Dad. "It's okay," said Cooper.

Cooper drank his water. "Thank you," he said. Dad smiled. "You said please, and I heard you," said Dad. "That is why I could help."

The car was quiet now. Cooper looked out the window. "One red car," he said. "One blue truck. One big bus." Dad laughed at the window game.

"Where is the sun?" Cooper asked. Then he answered himself. "The sun went to sleep. Night is coming." Cooper held his cup tight. Dad patted his knee softly. Cooper watched the cars go by, all the way home.

Gabriella went to the old community kitchen with her dad. Today she would bake banana bread for the whole family. She pulled her stool up to the big counter.

First she needed butter. The butter was cold from the fridge. Gabriella poked it with her finger. It was hard as a rock. She tried to stir it into the bowl. Little hard lumps hid in the mix. "Why won't it mix?" she asked. Her dad said, "Let's wait a bit."

They set the butter on the warm counter. They peeled the bananas, soft and sweet. They looked at the river out the window. They waited some more. Then Gabriella poked the butter again. Now her finger went right in. She stirred it, and it went smooth as a river.

The old kitchen smelled warm and sweet. The bread came out golden brown. Gabriella clapped her hands. "The butter got soft because it waited in the warm!" she said. "Now we can eat!"

Rowan wanted to make a sandwich. The bread was square. He put it on the plate. Round cheese would not stay on the square bread. It slid and slid. Then the cheese fell off. It made the milk spill. "Oh no," said Rowan.

His mom helped him wipe the milk. "Try again," she said. Rowan looked at the bread. It had four flat sides. The cheese was round like a ball. Round things roll. That was why it slid off. So Rowan turned the round cheese into a square. He cut it with a safe knife. Now the cheese had four sides too.

The square cheese sat on the square bread. It did not roll. It did not slide. Rowan cut the sandwich into two triangles. A triangle has three sides. He counted them. "One, two, three!" He ate his sandwich and sang a happy song. Then he found a triangle cookie in his lunch box. "A surprise triangle!" said Rowan.

Cooper wanted his red ball to roll all the way to the toy house. He pushed it slow. The ball stopped. "Hmm," said Cooper. "Why did it stop?"

He tried again. He pushed the ball fast. The ball rolled and rolled. It went all the way to the toy house. "Fast makes it go far!" said Cooper. He clapped his hands. Then he rolled a big ball and a small ball. The big ball was too big for the door. The small ball went right in. "Small fits," said Cooper.

He sat down to rest. His toes were warm in his socks. He touched the window. It felt cold like ice. He pulled his toe back. "Brrr," he said. Then he smelled cookies. A sharp, sweet smell came from the kitchen. Cooper ran to find them. "Fast feet!" he said.

Isla wanted to find her soap. It was a new soap. Mama went to buy it today. Isla could not see it on the shelf.

"Use your nose," said Mama. "The soap smells like flowers." Isla sniffed with her nose. She smelled something sweet. She followed the smell. There it was, under the towel.

Isla touched the soap with her hands. It felt smooth. Mama turned on the water. Isla heard the splash with her ears. The soap popped in her mouth a tiny bit. "Yuck," said Isla. She made a face. "Soap is not for tasting," said Mama. Isla washed her hands and made them tidy. Then Mama kissed her soft cheek. Isla smiled. "My nose found the soap," she said.

Jasmine wanted to make a party for her teddy bear. She got out her paints. She had red, blue, and yellow paint.

She painted a red hat. She painted a blue hat. She painted a yellow hat. Then she wanted a green hat. But there was no green paint.

Jasmine looked and looked. "No green," she said. She made a dot of blue. She made a dot of yellow. The two dots touched. The paint turned green!

"Blue and yellow make green," said Jasmine. She dipped her brush again. More blue. More yellow. More green. She painted a big green hat, and it was her best one.

The paint had to dry. Jasmine waited. She waited slowly. She gave teddy a cracker because he looked hungry. She marched around the table one time. Then two times. She sat down and waited some more.

At last the hats were dry. Red, blue, yellow, and green. Jasmine put them on the table. She put the green one on teddy's head.

"Now we can have our party," she said.

Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. The window was snowy and white. The cook gave him warm toast, soft butter, and a small pitcher of milk.

Colton spread the butter. The hard butter tore the toast. He looked at the warm toast. "Why does the butter tear it?" he asked. He held the toast near the stove. The toast got warmer. The butter went soft. Now it spread smooth like paint. "The warm toast makes soft butter," he said.

Next came the milk. Colton held the pitcher up high. The milk splashed out. It splashed like a turtle diving into a pond. He tried again. This time he kept the pitcher low, close to the cup. He poured slowly with two hands. Not one drop fell. He did it. "All the milk is in my cup," he said. He took a big drink.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. It was dark! Kai held Dad's hand. "Oh no!" said Kai.

Dad found a flashlight. Dad stepped across the kitchen floor. Click! The light came on. "A candle party!" said Dad. He lit one pretty candle. Mom put apples and crackers on a blanket. Kai laughed and clapped.

Kai wanted cold milk. He pulled the fridge door open. Dad ran over. "Shut it quick!" said Dad. "The cold will run out." Kai pushed the door shut. He waited. Then he opened it fast, grabbed the milk, and shut it again. "I did it!" said Kai. He drank his milk by the candle. Outside, the porch light popped back on. "The lights are home!" said Kai. Dad blew out the candle. "Goodnight, candle," said Kai.

Julia wants to play outside. She looks out the big window. The sun is not out today. Rain drops tap, tap, tap on the glass. Julia holds her yellow hat in her hands.

"Rainy day," says Julia. "I need my boots."

She counts what she needs. "One hat. Two boots. Three raincoat." The raincoat is red with white dots. It has a little triangle on the pocket. Julia puts it all on. It takes a long time. She pulls and wiggles each boot.

Mama opens the door. Puddles sit on the path like little ponds. Julia steps in one. Splash! Her socks stay dry inside the boots. "Dry feet," says Julia. She steps in another. Splash, splash!

Then the wind comes. It blows her yellow hat up, up, off her head. The hat lands in the bush. Julia waits. The wind slows down. She walks over slowly, slowly, and picks it up. She holds the hat on tight with both hands.

Julia looks up at the sky. Something soft and white falls on her nose. "Snowy!" says Julia. One snowflake, two snowflakes, three. Mama brings out warm mittens. Julia wears them and catches snow on her tongue. "Tasty," she says. "Cold and tasty." Then she waves at the snowy sky.

Felix found a book about crabs at daycare. Miss Ana said the book came from the library. Felix held it tight. He wanted to keep it forever.

Felix opened the book. He saw little black marks under the pictures. "What are those?" he asked. Miss Ana said, "Those are words. They tell the story." Felix turned the page. The crab was there. He turned more pages, one by one, all the way to the back. Then the story was done.

At snack time, Felix ate a salty cracker. He put the book next to his cubby. "This book is mine now," he said. Miss Ana shook her head. "The book needs to go back," she said. "It goes back on Friday. Then other kids can read it too."

Felix felt a surprise in his tummy. He did not want to give it up. He looked at the crab book. He looked at his friend Sam. Sam was looking at it too.

"Sam can look at it first," said Felix. He held the book open. "We start at the front," he said. Sam nodded. They turned the pages together, slow and slow, until the very end.

Connor sat down for dinner. He put his toy monkey on the chair too. "Monkey is hungry," said Connor. Dad gave Connor a bowl of peas. Connor held a pea up to the monkey's mouth. The pea rolled down and fell on the floor. Pip! Connor tried again. The pea fell again. Monkey did not chew. Monkey did not swallow.

Then Connor put the pea in his own mouth. Munch, munch, gone! Dad laughed. "Monkey is a toy," said Dad. "Toys do not eat. Foods are for eating." Connor looked at his plate. Peas were food. Banana slices were food. Monkey was not food. So Connor ate the banana all by himself.

"You wear a bib, and monkey gets nothing," said Dad. Connor picked up his fork. "Careful, that end is sharp," said Dad. Connor smiled and fed himself one big pea. "Peas fall down because monkey has no mouth that works," he said. Dad clapped. "My big boy eats the food, and the monkey just watches."

Henry ran to the park with his dad. Yesterday it had rained. Today the sun was warm. "Where are the puddles?" Henry asked. All the wet spots were gone. The rain came yesterday, not today. That was why the ground was dry.

Henry wanted to splash, but there was no water. He felt a little angry. His sweater was too warm now, so Dad put it in the bag. They went down the slide. They dug in the sand. "Later we will get ice cream," said Dad. Henry had to wait until later. Waiting was hard, but he kept playing.

A truck drove by with a big water tank. It sprinkled the flowers near the fence. Water made a little pool on the path! Henry stomped his boots. Splash, splash. "New water today!" he laughed. Dad took a photo. "Tomorrow we can look at the picture and remember," he said. Henry clapped his wet hands.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her macaroni was warm and bumpy in her spoon. She wanted to show her father her picture. But his face looked down, and his mouth was a flat line.

Zoey looked at the cat clock. She looked at her father again. His eyebrows hung low. She had seen that face before. Her brother made it when his ice cream fell. "You are sad," Zoey said. Her father nodded. "My cup broke today," he said.

Zoey slid her picture across the table. It had a big yellow sun. "The sun makes me happy," she said. Her father looked at it. Then the corners of his mouth went up. Up, up, up, like a slide at the park. "Now you are happy!" said Zoey. She felt so excited she jumped in her seat. The dog came to chase the macaroni that fell. Everyone laughed, even Zoey's father, with his big smile.

Evelyn sat at the little table. She had paper and glue. She wanted to make a lion. She glued on a round yellow head. She glued on a tail.

Now the lion needed a mane. Evelyn picked up a red crayon. She pressed hard on the paper. Nothing showed. She pressed again. Still nothing. Her paper stayed white.

Evelyn tried the glue on the crayon. That did not work either. Then she saw the paint pots. She dipped a brush in orange paint. She touched the paper. Orange lines showed up! Wet paint sticks to paper, she thought. The crayon was dry, so it made no lines.

She painted a big orange mane. Round and round her brush went. The mane got bigger and bigger. "Look at my lion!" she said. Her teacher smiled. "What a big orange mane," she said. Evelyn held up her lion so everyone could see it.

Stella loves book day at daycare. The noisy bus takes them to the library. Stella finds a book about a red fox. She points at the marks under the fox. "What are those?" she asks. The marks are words, and the words tell the story. Stella turns the pages. She starts at the front. The fox is small at first. At the back, the fox is big. "The book goes front to back," she says.

Stella wants to keep the fox book forever. She hides it in her cubby. But Miss Kim looks for it. The book belongs to the library. You can borrow books and take them home. But you must bring them back by a certain day. Other people want to read them too.

Stella marches to the desk. She gives the book to the librarian. The librarian stamps a card with a big stamp. Stella borrows the book the right way. At home, she reads the fox story to her cat, front to back, with her pencil tucked behind her ear.

Layla sat on the rug. She wanted to build a tall tower. She put one block on another. "I have an idea," she said. "I will make it very tall!"

Then the big dog barked outside. Boom! The sound was loud. Layla felt scared. Her tummy felt tight. She dropped her blocks and ran to Mama.

Mama held her hand. They stood still. They waited. The dog went quiet. Layla's tummy felt different now. The scared feeling got small.

"Because the dog is quiet, I am not scared," said Layla.

She went back to the rug. She was excited to build again. She stacked the blocks slowly. One, two, three. The tower stood tall.

Layla smiled a big, happy smile. "Look, Mama! My tower!"

But then her little brother crawled over. He pushed the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. Layla felt angry. Her face got hot.

She took a big breath. She waited. The angry feeling got small too.

Layla built the tower again. This time it was different. It was even taller.

The lights went out. The house went dark. Jules looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. The snow looked white in the dark.

"Where is the light?" Jules asked. Dad said, "We need the flashlight." They looked in the big drawer. The flashlight was there. Jules clicked it on. But it made only a tiny beam. "Why is it so small?" Jules asked. Dad said, "The batteries are old." They put in new batteries. Jules clicked again. Now the light was big and real. It shone all the way to the fence.

Jules counted with the light. "One stone. Two stones. Three stones." Then he saw the bird bath. The light stopped on the ice. "Fish live in water," said Jules. "Do fish live in ice?" Dad laughed. "No, little fish swim far, far away." Jules shone the light up at the falling snow. Each snowflake glowed. "One, two, three, too many!" he said.

Dad made sandwiches by flashlight. Jules ate his on a blanket. He clicked the flashlight on and off. On, off, on. "The lights will come back," said Dad. Then the kitchen light blinked. It came back on. Jules waved his flashlight at the bulb. "Hi, big light," he said. "You found your batteries too."

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there. "I lost bunny," she said.

Grandma gave Aubrey a cup of milk. "Think," said Grandma. "Where did you play last?" Aubrey sipped her milk. Then she remembered. She had played in the garden. She had played with the watering can.

Aubrey ran to the garden. She looked by the flowers. No bunny. She looked under the bench. No bunny. Then she saw the watering can. It was lying on its side. Aubrey looked inside. There was bunny, all wet! "The water went in," said Aubrey. "The can fell over. That made bunny wet."

Grandma hung bunny on the line in the sun. "The sun will dry him," she said. Aubrey waited and waited. At last bunny was warm and dry. Aubrey hugged him tight. "Bunny, you can share my cookie," she said. Grandma smiled and cut the cookie in two.

Victoria was at the beach with her dad. Behind the sand was the little local pool. Victoria wanted to swim in it. But she could not swim yet.

First she sat on the pool step. The water came up to her tummy. Her dad held her hands. "Kick your legs," he said. Victoria kicked and kicked. But she stayed in one place. She tried again. Kick, kick, kick. Still no moving.

Then her dad said, "Try big slow kicks, not fast little ones." Victoria made one big slow kick. Then another. Her body moved forward through the water. She was swimming a little bit! "My big kicks make me go," she said.

After that, they took a break. They sat on the sand. The wind blew on Victoria's wet arms. She found a slimy green bit of seaweed and dropped it fast. Then they went back to the pool. Kick, kick, kick. Big and slow. Victoria moved all the way to the wall.

"I did it, Dad!" she said. "The water went splash, splash, splash."

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had paper, glue, and seeds. He wanted to make a flower picture for his mom.

First he put glue on the paper. Then he set the seeds on top. But the seeds slid down the paper. One seed fell off the table. Mohamed picked it up and put it back. It slid again.

Mohamed looked at his hands. The glue was wet and sticky on his fingers. "Wet glue makes things slip," he said. He held each seed in place. He counted to ten, slow and quiet. Then he let go. The seed stayed.

He made petals with the seeds, one by one. He made a stem with a green string. Mom came in with a clean cloth. She wiped his sticky hands. "A flower for me?" she asked. Mohamed nodded. He picked up the picture to show her. But the picture was heavy on one side. The seeds there were still wet. They slid to the corner of the page. Mohamed laughed. "Wet glue makes things slip," he said again. He laid the picture flat on the table. He put his hands on top, like a bird sitting on a nest. He counted to ten again.

The seeds stayed put. Mom hung the flower picture on the wall. "It can dry there," she said. Mohamed smiled and waved to his flower. "Stay there, little seeds," he said.

Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. She picked out little seeds. "Carrots," said Ruby. "And beans!" Dad got a big bag of soil. A noisy crow sat on the roof. "Caw, caw," it called.

At home, Ruby planted her seeds in two pots. She put one pot in the sun. She put the other pot in the sun too. Every day, Ruby watered one pot. "Grow, grow, little seeds," she said. The other pot got no water at all.

Soon a tiny green leaf came up. Then two leaves. Then three. Ruby clapped her hands. But the dry pot had nothing. Not one leaf. The soil was hard and cracked. Ruby touched it. "Oh," she said. "This pot is so dry." She thought and thought. "The dry pot has no water. That is why nothing grows." She gave it a big drink.

Day by day, Ruby watered both pots. "Grow, grow, little seeds," she said. The first new leaf peeked out at last. Ruby smiled and called to Dad, "Come see! Water helped it live!"

Carter wanted his toy pig. It was on the big counter. The pot on the stove was making steam. "Is it hot up there?" he wondered.

Carter reached up with his hand. Grandma held his arm. "Stay close to me," she said. "The pot is hot. The pot can hurt you."

Carter touched the cold fridge instead. "Ooh, this one is cold," he said. "The pot is hot. The fridge is cold. They are different!" The steam moved up, up, up. Carter watched it go.

Then Grandma got the pig down for him. She put it in the sink. The sink was warm and soapy. Carter washed his pig with bubbles. "Pig was dirty," he said. "Now pig is clean. The soap made him clean!"

Grandma smiled. "Yes it did," she said. "Now let's dry him with the soft towel."

Felix stood in the band room. He held a small trumpet. He wanted to make a big sound. He blew air into it. Nothing came out but air.

The teacher sat next to him. "Try again," she said. "Take your time."

Felix blew again. Still no sound. He felt upset. A bird sat on the window and looked in.

The teacher smiled. "Watch me," she said. She made her lips buzz like a bee. Then the trumpet sang out loud.

Felix buzzed his lips. He put them on the trumpet. He blew. The trumpet sang!

"It buzzed because my lips buzzed!" said Felix. He did it again. And again. He did not stop.

The bird on the window flew up. It climb higher and higher. Then it sang too.

Felix played one more song, nice and slow.

Milo went to the library with his mom. The library was busy. Lots of kids were reading. Milo found a book about a dog. The dog chased a ball up to a tree. The dog chased a cat, too. Milo loved this book.

He sat down on a small red chair. He opened the book. The words were on every page. "Dog," Milo read. He knew that word. The words told about the dog. He turned page one, then page two. He read all the way to the end. The front came first, and the back came last.

"I want to keep this book," Milo said. "Forever and ever."

Mom shook her head. "We can take it home," she said. "Then we bring it back."

Milo held the book tight. He did not want to let go.

The next week, Milo came back to the library. A girl sat in the red chair. She had his dog book. She turned the pages, one by one.

"That is my book," Milo said.

"It was yours," said the girl. "Now it is mine."

Mom smiled. "And after her, it can be yours again."

Milo watched the girl read. He waited. She read slow. She read to the very last page. Then she closed the book and gave it back.

Milo took it. He opened the front page. "Dog," he read again. He was happy to start at the beginning. "My turn," he said.

Logan stood at the hotel pool. He held Dad's hand tight. "The water is big," Logan said. "I will hold you," said Dad. Logan stepped down the steps. The water was warm on his toes.

Logan saw a girl floating on her back. Her arms were out wide. Her tummy was up like a boat. She looked so calm. Logan wanted to try. Dad held his back in the water. "Take a big breath," said Dad. "Put your tummy up." Logan took a big breath. His tummy went up. His legs came up too. He was floating! "Air in my tummy makes me float!" Logan said. He saw the blue color of the sky above him.

Dad kept one hand under him, just in case. Logan splashed a little with his hands. The water made tickly sounds by his ears. A cute little duck toy floated past him. "Look, it floats too," said Logan. Dad laughed. "You and the duck," said Dad. Logan kicked his feet gently and stayed floating. Then Dad lifted him up for a warm towel hug.

Cooper went to the big game with Mom and Dad. The ice was white and shiny. A big robot mascot walked around and waved. Cooper wore his red shirt to match his team. His team was the red team, and red was his best color.

Cooper wanted to see the puck. But the seats were full of tall people. "I can't see!" he said. Then everyone cheered. The red team scored a goal! But Cooper missed it. Everyone had stood up. When people cheer, they stand up. That is why he could not see.

So Cooper got ready. He watched the red team skate fast. He heard the crowd begin to roar. Quick, quick, up he climbed onto Dad's shoulders! The red team scored again. This time Cooper saw the puck go in. He saw the robot do a happy dance. "We saw it!" Cooper shouted. "We saw it!" The smelly old skates in his bag did not matter now. He waved his red flag high, high, high.

Grayson went to the playground with Mom. He wanted to go on the big slide. Mom said, "Keep close to me." Grayson held her hand. The sun was warm on his face.

Near the slide there was a metal bench. Grayson put his hand on it. He pulled his hand back fast. The bench was hot! The sun made it hot. "The sun made it hot," Grayson said. Mom touched it too. "Yes, the sun is real and strong today," she said. "Hot things can hurt. Let's find the shady slide."

They found the little slide under a tree. It felt cool and smooth. Grayson slid down, one, two, three times. He laughed and laughed.

Then Grayson saw something shiny in the grass. It was a broken bottle. "Don't touch," said Mom softly. "Sharp glass can hurt." Grayson kept his hands behind his back. Mom picked it up with a bag. Then it was time for pizza under the shady tree. Grayson ate a real big slice. "Hot bench, cool slide, safe hands," he said. Mom smiled and kissed his head.

Jaxon ran to the gate. Grandpa was here! Grandpa had a big bag. "I will stay for a week," said Grandpa. Jaxon did not know how long a week was. Was it as long as a nap? "Grandpa, what is a week?" he asked. "It is seven days," said Grandpa. "Seven!" said Jaxon.

Grandpa gave Jaxon a rubber snake. It was long and green. "Are you afraid of it?" asked Grandpa. "No!" said Jaxon. "It is a toy." Jaxon made the snake hop in the grass. Grandpa laughed and they went out to play.

Each morning Jaxon put one stone in a jar. One stone. Two stones. Three. The jar got more full each day. On the seventh morning, the jar was full. "The jar is full," said Jaxon. "Seven days went by!" Grandpa picked up his big bag. "I will come back soon," he said. Jaxon waved and waved until the car went down the road.

Sienna sat in a big chair at Grandma's house. Grandma had a little salon in the back room. It had a mirror and a sink. Today Sienna would get her very first haircut. "Do not cut it all off!" said Sienna. Grandma laughed. "I only take little bits. Snip, snip, little snip." First Grandma sprayed water on Sienna's head. "Why is my hair wet?" asked Sienna. "Wet hair lies down flat," said Grandma. "Flat hair is easy to cut." Sienna touched her wet hair. It was not puffy anymore. It lay down like a sleepy cat. "My hair went flat because of the water," said Sienna. "That is right, smart girl," said Grandma. Then came the scissors. Snip, snip, little snip. Sienna watched the mirror. A tiny piece of hair fell down. It landed on her bib like a small brown mountain. "Look, Grandma! A hair mountain!" said Sienna. Grandma kept cutting. Snip, snip, little snip. Then Grandma held up the mirror so Sienna could see the back. Sienna held her teddy bear tight and looked. Her hair was short and neat and still there. "You did not cut it all off," said Sienna. "I told you," said Grandma. "Only little bits." Sienna patted her head. "Hair mountain, flat hair, little bits," she said. "Now we look pretty together," said Grandma, spinning the chair round and round. "Again!" said Sienna. "Spin me again!"

Jacob ran into the kitchen. "Pasta!" he yelled. "Pasta, pasta, pasta!"

He grabbed his fork. He was ready to eat. But Mama put her hand on the bowl. "Wait," she said. "We say the blessing first."

Jacob looked out the window. White snow was falling on the trees. He looked at his plate. "But I want pasta now," he said.

"Watch me," said Mama. She folded her arms. Grandma folded her arms. Big sister Lily folded her arms. Jacob folded his arms too. They went like this: one arm, then the other arm.

"Dear God," said Mama. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for snow to play in. Amen."

"Amen!" said Jacob. It was a big word. He said it loud.

Then Mama picked up the bowl. Steam went up, up, up. It smelled warm and cheesy. Jacob skipped to his chair, one, two, three skips.

There was broccoli on his plate too. "That is ugly broccoli," said Jacob.

"Eat one tree," said Grandma. "Just one."

Jacob ate it. Then he ate all his pasta. "We bless first," he said. "Then we eat!"

Grandma smiled. "That's right, big boy."

Lillian lost her bunny. Bunny was soft and gray. Lillian wanted to find him.

"Where are you, Bunny?" she said. First she looked under the bed. No bunny there. One. Then she looked in the toy box. No bunny there. Two. Then she looked by the big chair. No bunny there. Three.

Lillian sat down on the rug. She thought hard. "Where did I play with Bunny last?" she said. "I played with Bunny in my bed. Then I got up to get my shirt."

Lillian went back to her bed. She pulled the blanket back. Bunny was hiding under the pillow! He had been there the whole time. "The blanket was on top of you," Lillian said. "That is why I could not see you."

Lillian hugged Bunny close. "Now you can sleep with me," she said. She tucked Bunny under her warm blanket. His little ears felt cold, so she covered them too.

"Good night, Bunny," Lillian said. "One hug, and one more."

"Sleep tight, little bunny."

Penelope went out to the backyard. She wanted to paint a picture of her red apple. She put the apple on the grass. She got her paints and a clean brush.

She looked for red paint. The red pot was empty. "Oh no," she said. She found blue paint and yellow paint. She put some blue on her brush. She painted the apple. It looked all blue. That was not right.

She dipped her brush in the yellow pot too. She painted on top of the blue. The apple turned green! Penelope blinked. She touched the green paint with her finger. "Blue and yellow make green," she said. "The blue did it. Then the yellow did it too."

She painted big green leaves all around her apple. Then she painted the sky blue above it. A soft wind moved the paper. Penelope picked up her broom. She gave the patio a little sweep to clean the paint drips. Then she held up her picture to the sun. "Look, apple," she said. "Now you have green leaves."

Livia ran to the door. "Is it shot day?" she asked. Mom said yes. Livia loved the doctor's sticker prize at the end. But she did not love the shot.

At the office, the nurse typed on her computer. "You are next," she said. Livia held her teddy tight. She squeezed her arm into a hard ball. "Ow!" The nurse said, "Try a soft arm. A tight arm makes it hurt more." Livia let her arm go soft like a noodle. Quick quick, the shot was done! "It was small," said Livia. "My arm was soft, so it was small."

Mom clapped. The nurse gave her a bandage and a shiny star sticker. Livia held it up high. "Next time I will make my arm soft too!" she said. Then she ran to the toy corner, fast as a rabbit.

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. The grass was still wet. His team had red shirts. Cooper liked his red shirt a lot.

"Time to play," said Coach May. She looked at Cooper's legs. "Where are your shin guards?" Cooper looked down. He had socks, but no guards under them. "No guards, no playing," said Coach May. "A kick can hurt your legs."

Cooper sat on the bench. He watched his friend Sam kick the ball. Sam ran fast. Sam drank water at the break. Cooper wanted to run too.

Then Mom came running. She had Cooper's shin guards in her bag. "You left them in the car," she said. Cooper slid them on under his socks. "Guards on, playing on," he said. Coach May smiled.

Cober ran onto the field. He kicked the ball. It went into the net! "I can play because my guards are on," Cooper said. He kicked the ball again, pretty and far, all the way to Sam.

Today Hudson turned three. His family had a party at the bowling alley. Grandma held his hand. Hudson wore red bowling shoes. On his score card, he draws a big round ball with his crayon. It was his turn. He wanted to knock down all the pins.

Hudson rolled his ball, but it rolled very slowly. It stopped in the middle of the lane. Not one pin fell down. "Problem," said Hudson. He looked at his ball. It stopped because it was too slow. Daddy said, "Want to try again?" Hudson picked up a new ball. This time he pushed it hard with both hands.

The ball rolled fast, fast, fast. Crash! Six pins fell down. Everyone clapped. "It went fast because I pushed hard," said Hudson. Grandma gave him a hug. Then the cake came, with three candles. Hudson blew them all out. "Happy birthday to you," everyone sang. Hudson sat close to Grandma. He felt safe and happy. He ate his cake and smiled.

Jaxon sat in the family car. "We are going to the salon," said Mom. "You will get your first haircut."

At the salon, a lady named Bea put a cape on Jaxon. The cape was like a big bib. Bea picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. One snip, two snips.

Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They did not stick to Jaxon. The cape caught them, like it catches everything.

Jaxon watched in the mirror. A light made his hair shine. He saw a bit of hair fall. He touched his head. It did not hurt at all. "The hair is not on me anymore," he said. "The cape caught it because it is wide." Bea smiled. "That is right. The cape keeps you clean."

Mom had an egg sandwich in her bag for later. Jaxon got to share it after the haircut. He took a bite and smiled. "I like my haircut," said Jaxon. "Snip, snip," said Bea. "One happy boy, all done."

Jaxon looked in the mirror one more time. "Nice hair," he said.

Rosalie ran into the art room. She wanted to paint a big sun. But the paint pots were just red, yellow, and blue.

"Where is orange?" she asked. The sun needed orange! She looked and looked. No orange pot anywhere.

Rosalie dipped her brush in the yellow. She made a yellow dot on her paper. Then she dipped in the red. She put red on top of the yellow dot. She stirred it with her brush.

"Orange!" she shouted. "Red and yellow make orange!" That was true. She had made a brand new colour all by herself.

She painted her sun. It was big and orange and bright. Then she wanted purple grapes. She tried red and blue together. Purple! She clapped her hands.

Her teacher smiled. Rosalie pointed at her paper. "Look what I made!" she said.

Later, her father came to pick her up. Rosalie held up the painting. "Can we write my name on it?" she asked. Her father found a crayon. He wrote R-O-S-A-L-I-E at the top.

"Sun day!" Rosalie said, and she hugged the painting tight.

Lena was at daycare. Teacher Mia had a big bag. Out came library books. "We can borrow these," said Teacher Mia. "We take them home. Then we bring them back, so other kids can read them too."

Lena picked a book about a cat. She held the book. She turned the pages. The cat kicked a ball on page two. The cat ate with a spoon on page four. Lena pointed at the marks on the page. "Cat," she said. The words meant cat.

Lena hugged the book. "I want to keep it forever," she said. "The library needs it back," said Teacher Mia. Lena looked at the book. She looked at her friend Sam. Sam wanted the cat book too. Lena gave Sam the book. "You read it now," she said. "Then it goes back to the library." Sam opened the front cover. "Read it front to back," said Lena. Sam turned page one.

Naomi had a library book. It was about a beautiful dragon. She hugged it at bedtime. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

Mama shook her head. "We take it back on Friday. Then other kids can read it too."

Naomi hid the book under her pillow. The dragon could live with her! She counted the pages. One, two, three, four. The words on each page said what the dragon did. She read them front to back. The last page said, "The dragon flies away."

Naomi heard a tiny sound. Tap, tap. The book was wiggling! "The dragon wants to go fly," she said. "That is why she is tapping."

In the morning, Naomi did not forget. She carried the book through the kitchen. She put it right in her bag. "Fly, dragon," she whispered. "I will get a new dragon book soon."

Florence stood in the backyard. She held a small beanbag in her hand. A big hoop lay on the grass. She wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Florence threw the beanbag. The wind began to blow. The beanbag sailed up and then tipped sideways. It fell in the grass, far from the hoop. Florence got the beanbag and tried again. The wind blew once more. The beanbag tipped away again.

Florence watched the leaves on the tree. When the leaves hung still, she threw. The beanbag flew straight and dropped right into the hoop. "The wind pushed it," said Florence. "Now the wind is asleep."

Then Dad rolled a big ball to her. Florence held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. She put both hands out, close together. Dad rolled the ball again. Florence caught it with her two hands. "I got it!" she said. Just then a butterfly landed right on the hoop. Florence held her ball and smiled. "Come play too," she said.

Jules wanted a snack. He saw a big watermelon on the table. "Can I have some?" he asked. Mama said, "Yes, but it is late. Let us hurry."

Jules used his eyes to look at the watermelon. It was green on the outside. "What is inside?" he asked. "Knock on it and listen," said Mama. Jules knocked on the top with his knuckles. Knock, knock! He heard a deep sound. "It sounds full!" he said.

Mama cut the watermelon. Jules used his nose to smell it. It smelled sweet. His mouth got watery. He took a big bite. His tongue tasted the juicy fruit. "So sweet!" he said. The juice ran down his chin. He touched the rind with his fingers. It was smooth and hard.

"Why did we knock on it?" Jules asked. Mama said, "A ripe one sounds deep. A bad one sounds dull." Jules knocked again. Deep sound. Ripe! He ate one more piece and licked his fingers.

Evan stood at the gate of the school playground. His backpack felt light on his back. Mom gave him a hug and waved goodbye.

Evan wanted to play on the slide. But he did not know any kids. He stood still. His zipper got stuck on his jacket. He pulled and pulled. Then a girl came over. She looked at the tag on his backpack. It said his name in big letters. "Hi, Evan," she said. "I am Mia." Evan smiled big.

The teacher blew a whistle. It was time for a break and a snack. Evan sat with Mia under a tree. He shared his crackers. The sun made warm light on the grass. Evan looked at Mia's tag. It said her name too. He pointed at it. "Mia," he said. "The tag tells me your name!" Mia laughed and clapped. "Come on," she said. "Let's go to the slide!"

Milo was at Grandma's house. Grandma was painting at her table. "This flower is blue," she said. "But my blue paint is all gone."

Milo wanted to help. He hurried to the paint shelf. He found a jar with blue on the lid. But it was empty. He found a jar with yellow paint. That one was full.

Milo climbed on his chair. He squeezed the yellow paint into a cup. He added a drop of blue from Grandma's little tube. The colors swirled in the cup. Milo stirred with a smooth wooden stick.

The paint turned green! Milo looked and looked. "Yellow and blue make green," he said. "That is why Grandma has no green flower."

Grandma laughed and clapped. "Paint me a green leaf, Milo." Milo made a big green leaf. Then he made three more. Grandma hung them on the wall.

After all that work, Milo was sleepy. Grandma made him a soft bed for his nap. "You helped me today," she said. She tucked the blanket up to his chin. Milo yawned. "Yellow and blue make green," he said. Grandma kissed his head. "Good night, my helper."

Elizabeth wanted to wear her bear pajamas tonight. But where were they? She looked under her bed. She saw one sock. She looked in her toy box. She saw two blocks. She looked in the bathtub. She saw her yellow duck.

Then Elizabeth touched the bathtub. It was wet. "Hmm," she said. "The pajamas are not here. The bathtub is wet. Mommy washed clothes today!" Elizabeth ran to the laundry basket. She looked inside. She saw three shirts, two towels and her bear pajamas!

But the pajamas were damp. Mommy hung them near the warm heater. Elizabeth waited. She zipped up her doll's coat while she waited. At last the pajamas were dry and warm. She put them on. She rubbed her eye, big and sleepy. Mommy tucked her in, snug and safe. "Wet clothes dry by the heater," said Elizabeth. "Goodnight, bear."

Iris was at school. She painted a big red apple at the art table. Then the teacher rang a little bell. "Snack time," said the teacher. Iris wanted the crunchy crackers. She ran to the door of the snack room.

The teacher held up her hand. "Look at your hands, Iris," she said. Iris looked. There was red paint on her hands. "Are they dirty?" asked Iris. "Yes, they are," said the teacher. "So we wash them first."

Iris went to the sink. She turned on the water. She rubbed the soap. Bubbles grew and grew. Pop, pop, pop. Iris laughed. She had not seen so many bubbles. The paint went down the drain. Now her hands were clean.

Iris washed and washed until they sparkled. She walked to the snack room and got her crackers. She took a big bite. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "The paint is gone," said Iris. "Because I washed my hands, my crackers stay clean." She held one up to the teacher. "A clean cracker for you," said Iris.

Leo put seeds in a pot on the balcony. He patted the dirt down flat. Then he waited. He waited all day. Nothing came up.

"Hello, little seed," said Leo. "Wake up!"

His friend Mia lived next door. She leaned over the railing. "Seeds need water," she said. "Did you give it a drink?"

Leo ran to the kitchen. He filled a small orange cup. He poured the water on the dirt. "There," he said. "Now you can work, little seed."

Every morning Leo gave the pot water from the orange cup. One day a green nose poked out of the dirt. Then two little leaves stood up.

"The water helped you," said Leo. "No water, no seed. Water, and up you pop!"

Mia laughed from her balcony. "You are a good farmer, Leo."

Leo held up his cup. "More water, please!"

Alexis was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Her name was Rosie.

Rosie slept in a little basket. Then Rosie woke up. She cried and cried. "She is mean," said Alexis. "She is loud!" Grandma smiled. "Babies cannot talk," she said. "Crying is how she talks."

Grandma held Rosie near Alexis. Rosie kept crying. Grandma said, "Try one thing at a time." Alexis gave Rosie a soft blanket. Rosie still cried. Alexis patted Rosie's head. Rosie still cried. Then Alexis put his finger near Rosie's hand. Rosie grabbed it and stopped.

"She stopped because I gave her my finger," said Alexis. "She wanted to hold on." Grandma laughed. "Yes, it worked. She wanted to hold something warm."

Dad came in with milk in a small bottle. "Rosie is hungry too," he said. "You can help." Alexis sat very still. Dad let Alexis hold the bottle. Rosie drank and drank.

"You are a good big brother," said Dad. "You are like her teacher." Alexis grinned. "Rosie, I will show you everything. But not my toy cars. Those are mine." Rosie made a small burp. Alexis laughed so loud that the cat ran under the chair.

Aaron sat on Grandma's big red blanket. "Let's play a game," said Grandma. "Tell me your five senses."

Aaron frowned. "I don't know them all." He wanted to get it right.

Grandma rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Aaron covered his ears. "That is loud!" he said. "My ears hear it!" Grandma smiled. "Ears are one," she said.

Next she held up a yellow lemon. Aaron sniffed it. "Pee-yew! My nose smells it!" "Noses are two," said Grandma. Aaron licked his lips. "My tongue tastes. Three!"

Grandma gave him a soft kitten. Aaron petted its warm fur. "My hands feel it. Four!" Then he looked out the window. He saw a blue bird. "My eyes see it. Five!" he shouted.

"You said them all," said Grandma. "Ears, nose, tongue, hands, eyes." Aaron clapped his hands. He said the list again, all by himself. He got none of them wrong this time.

"Say it once more," said Grandma. Aaron took a big breath. "Ears, nose, tongue, hands, eyes!" The kitten purred in his lap, and Aaron giggled.

Jasper stood at the little table in his classroom. Ten number cards lay in a box. His teacher had said, "Put them in a row, one to ten."

Jasper laid the cards out. One, two, three, four, five, six. He put the next card down. Eight, then nine, then ten. He looked at his row. It felt wrong.

"I know," said Jasper. "Eight comes after seven. A card is missing." He looked under the table. He looked by the doll home in the corner. There it was, the seven card, tucked in a tiny bed.

Jasper picked it up and slid it in its place. Now the row went one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. He counted it out loud. It sounded just like the song.

"Seven was hiding," said Jasper. "That is why my row was broken."

His teacher smiled. "Now it is all better."

Jasper sang the counting song all the way to the shelf.

Zoe sat in a big chair at the clinic. Her mom held her hand. A friendly nurse named Sam came in with a small tray. Zoe saw the tiny needle and made her arm stiff like a rock.

"Will it hurt a lot?" Zoe asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Sam. "Try to let your arm go soft. A tight arm hurts more. A soft arm hurts less."

Zoe looked at her stiff arm. She made a fist. Then she tried to let it go soft, like a sleepy cat. Her arm felt wobbly and loose.

Sam touched the soft skin. "That is just right," he said. "Look out the window while I count."

Outside the window, Zoe saw a garden with red flowers. A bee flew from one flower to another. Zoe kept looking at the bee. She kept her arm soft.

"One, two, three," said Sam. "All done!"

"That was it?" asked Zoe. "That was just a little pinch!"

The tight arm would have hurt more. The soft arm hurt less. Zoe had found that out all by herself.

Sam put a happy bandage on her arm. "You were brave," he said.

"Can I open the sticker box?" Zoe asked. She picked a star sticker and stuck it on her shirt. "I want to show the garden bee," she said, waving from the window.

Jaxson woke up hungry. "I want toast," he said. Mom put bread in the toaster. Jaxson watched. He waited. He waited some more. "Is it time?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mom. Then the toaster went pop! The bread jumped up, hot and brown. "The bread popped because it got hot!" said Jaxson. He laughed. "Pop, pop, pop!"

Jaxson ate his toast. It was warm and yummy. He got some crumbs on the floor. Mom handed him a little brush. "Let's make the floor tidy," she said. Jaxson brushed the crumbs away. "Tidy floor!" he said. "Tidy boy," said Mom, and she kissed his head.

After breakfast came a bath. Jaxson splashed and played with his duck. Then Dad helped him get dressed. "Where are your socks?" Dad asked. Jaxson looked. One sock was under the table. One sock was in the toy box. "You silly socks!" said Jaxson. "Come here!" He put them on his feet, one by one. "Warm toes," he said. Dad called out, "Story time, Jaxson!" Jaxson ran to the couch. He held his duck. "Read the duck story," he said. Dad opened the book. "Once there was a little duck," he read. Jaxson snuggled close, and his warm toes wiggled.

Olivier ran to Grandpa's house. He wanted his little red car. But the car was gone. "Where did you go?" Olivier called. "Oh car, you are so naughty!"

Grandpa was in the garden. "Where did you play with it last?" he asked. Olivier thought hard. He looked at the park across the fence. "I pushed the car near the park," he said. So Olivier looked by the fence. He looked in the grass. No car there.

Then Olivier thought again. The car was small. Small things can hide in big places. "My toy went where I went," he said. So he walked his own steps. Through the gate. Past the big chair. Then to his blanket for nap time. He lifted a corner. There was the red car, tucked under the blanket! "The car was cold, so it hid!" Olivier called. Grandpa laughed. Olivier rolled the car down his knee. Vroom, all the way to Grandpa's slipper.

Max put on his big blue apron. It went down to his toes. Today he would make pancakes for his family. One, two, three, mix! That was his job.

Outside, the rain went tap, tap, tap on the window. Inside, Max looked into his bowl. The batter was lumpy. Big lumps. Little lumps. Lumpy, lumpy, lumpy. His tummy said, "I want smooth pancakes!"

So Max stirred. One, two, three, mix! The lumps got smaller. He stirred more. One, two, three, mix! The lumps went away. "The lumps went away because I mixed!" said Max.

The teacher poured the batter into the hot pan. Sizzle, sizzle! Then bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop. Max flipped the pancake high. It did a little jump.

At last the family came to eat. Max said, "I mixed it smooth!" Daddy took a big bite. Mama took a big bite. Baby took a tiny bite. Max counted the empty plates. One, two, three! Then he patted his full tummy and said, "More pancakes, please!"

Joshua went to the park with his blue bunny. He put bunny down on the grass. Then he ran to play ball with his dad. The ball bounced high. Joshua laughed and kicked it back. It was not too hard for him. He was getting good at it.

Then Joshua looked for bunny. Bunny was gone! Joshua wanted to cry, but he took a big breath. He thought and thought. "I played ball here first," he said. "Bunny was in the soft grass near the swings." He walked back to the swings. He looked down low, near his feet. There was bunny, hiding in the tall green grass! Joshua hugged bunny tight.

A little girl came by. "Do you want to share my ball?" she asked. Joshua smiled. "Yes, please," he said. He put bunny safe in his bag. Then he kicked the ball far, far up into the sky.

Arthur rode the city bus with his red bus. "Where did you go?" he asked. Snow fell on the windows. Arthur peeked under his seat. Only dirt and an old ticket lived there.

He thought and thought. "I had my red bus when we got on," he said. "The bus stopped. I slid forward." So his red bus slid too! Arthur looked under the seat behind him. There it was, by a gum wrapper. "You slid back when the bus stopped!" he said. He picked it up and held it tight.

Arthur tried a little test. He put the red bus on his knee. The bus stopped again. The red bus slid, just a little. "It moves because the big bus stops!" said Arthur. "That is so neat." The snow kept falling, and Arthur held his red bus all the way home.

Alexander woke up and sniffed the air. Something smelled sweet! He used his nose to smell it. Was it cookies? He ran to the kitchen on his little feet.

Mom was baking cookies. "These are for the school sale," she said. "We will sell them at the big table." Alexander wanted a cookie now. But the cookies were too hot to touch. He touched one with his finger and pulled it back fast. "Ow! Hot!" His fingers told him it was hot.

Then he heard a sound outside. His ears heard a funny sound. "Hoo! Hoo!" He looked out with his eyes. It was an owl in the tree! The owl was awake at night. That was funny, because Alexander slept at night.

Mom gave him a warm cookie. He put it in his mouth. His tongue tasted sugar and butter. It was so good! Alexander said, "My nose found the cookies first. My nose knew before my eyes!" Mom laughed and handed him a glass of milk.

Ibrahim woke up in his small bed. The sun was up too. He wanted to play outside with his red fire truck. "First we get dressed," said Mama. One sock, two socks. One shoe, two shoes. Ibrahim pulled his shirt too fast. Rip! The sleeve tore a little. "Oops," he said. "Slow hands next time," said Mama. She helped him put on a good blue shirt. Then she made warm toast. Ibrahim ate it all up. But then he stepped in a puddle by the sink. His socks got wet. He tried to put his shoes on. The wet socks felt cold and squishy. "Wet socks, cold toes," said Ibrahim. Mama dried his feet with a soft towel. One dry foot, two dry feet. New socks went on. Shoes went on. Ibrahim hugged Mama and ran outside with his fire truck. "The wheels go fast," he called.

Edouard was alone in the playroom. He wanted to count his blocks. "One, two, three," he sang. Then he stopped. What came next?

He tried, "One, two, three, seven!" That felt wrong. He frowned at the blocks.

Then he remembered the counting song. He loved that song! He sang it out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The words came out in a line, one after another.

"Now I know!" said Edouard. He touched each block as he sang. "One, two, three!" Three blocks! The numbers only worked when they came in order. That was why his trick had gone wrong.

He turned to the toy cars next. A car had dirt on its wheel. He wiped it clean. Then he counted the cars, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five!"

"Ten cars!" he sang at the end. He ran to show his mother. "Mama, listen! One, two, three, four, five!"

Eliana wanted the big red pencil. Her brother Sam had it. "My turn first," said Sam. "Then you." Eliana stamped her foot. It was hard to wait. The pencil was so red and shiny.

Mama sat down next to them. "You can use the timer," she said. She turned the dial. It went tick, tick, tick. Eliana watched the little hand go around. She smelled the orange peel Mama was peeling. Then the bell rang, ding! Sam gave her the pencil. "Your turn," he said. Eliana drew a big cat with whiskers.

The bell rang again. Eliana did not want to stop. But then she thought, "Sam waited for me. Now I wait too." She gave Sam the pencil. He smiled. "Your cat is funny," he said. Then he added a hat on the cat. Eliana laughed. "I wish I had a hat too," she said. Mama set the timer again. Tick, tick, tick.

Nathan stood by the little pool near the lake. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But every time he put his face in, water went up his nose. Then he coughed and sat on the step.

"You can blow out," said his friend Mia. She put her face in the water. Bubbles came out of her nose. Nathan watched. Mia lifted her head. "See? Bubbles," she said. Nathan took a big breath. He put his face down. He blew bubbles out of his nose. No water went in. He did not cough. He lifted his head and laughed. "The water stays out when I blow!" he said.

Across the lake, a brown cow drank at the edge. A duck paddled by. Nathan's mom waved from her towel. "I did it!" Nathan called. He felt very happy. He put his face in again. More bubbles, no cough. He kicked his legs behind him, splashing small waves. "Tomorrow I will swim all the way to the rope," he said. The sun was warm on his wet head, and he blew one more big bubble.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Ten cookies sat on a big plate. Mom said, "Count them. Then you get the one from the bigger pile!"

Oliver counted from the left. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then he counted from the right. "One, two, three..." The last number was ten again! "Mom! Ten from this side too! Ten both ways!"

"You got it," said Mom. "Ten cookies, no matter where you start."

A small bee buzzed at the window. Oliver laughed at the busy bee. He picked the soft cookie with the most chips. He counted them. "Nine chips!"

Oliver took a big bite. It was soft and sweet. He did not cry when a crumb fell. He just grabbed a napkin.

"Tomorrow I count my toy cars," he said.

Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Dad put down a big orange bowl of soup. "We say our blessing first," said Dad. Emmett wanted to say it all by himself.

"Fold your hands," said Dad. "Close your eyes. Then repeat after me." Emmett folded his hands. He closed his eyes. It was dark! He could not see Dad at all. But he could hear Dad's voice, nice and slow.

"Thank you for our food," said Dad. "Thank you for our food," said Emmett. "Thank you for our family," said Dad. "Thank you for our family," said Emmett.

Dad clapped. "You said the whole blessing!" Emmett opened his eyes. He looked at Dad, then at Mom, then at his orange soup. "When my eyes are closed, my ears work better!" said Emmett. Dad laughed. "I like that," he said. Mom smiled and picked up her spoon.

Zachary wanted to draw a cat for Mom. The cat would be orange. He saw the tablet in the basket by the big chair.

He tapped the screen once. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark and quiet. Zachary tapped it again. Still nothing. He sat down on the rug and thought.

"How does it wake up?" he asked. Then he remembered. Daddy held the little round button. Zachary found the button. He pushed it and held it. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen grew bright. It was on!

Zachary was so happy he almost forgot to sit still. He looked at the little pictures. One had a paintbrush on it. He tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. He picked orange. He drew a big cat with a long tail. He drew it fast because he was excited. Then he drank some juice from his cup. He drew tiny whiskers too.

Mom came in. "Is the tablet all done now?" she asked. "Yes," said Zachary. He pressed the round button and held it. The screen went dark again. "The button makes it sleep," he said. He put the tablet back in the basket, all by himself. He carried his orange cat to Mom.

Mila was going on a trip. Her family would sleep in a tent. There were no plugs at the campsite. Mila did not know that yet.

She put her little lamp in the car. She put her teddy bear in too. At the campsite, the sky got dark. Mila pressed the button on her lamp. The lamp stayed dark. She pressed it again. Still dark.

"There are no plugs here," said Mama. "The lamp needs a plug. A flashlight needs batteries."

Dad gave Mila a flashlight. It had batteries inside. Mila pressed the button. The light came on! It made a bright circle on the tent wall. The lamp was dark because it had no plug. The flashlight was bright because it had batteries.

Mila put the lamp back in the car. She held the flashlight all night.

"I will bring you next time," she told the lamp.

Teddy sat by her feet. Mila felt proud. She fell asleep in the soft glow.

Joshua stood near the big piano in the music room. He wanted to play a real song. He hit the keys very hard. The sound was loud and bumpy. It sounded like a car horn. Joshua did not like it. "I can't do it," he said. Miss Rosa was near him. She smiled. "Watch my hands," she said. She touched the keys soft and slow. The song came out pretty.

Joshua tried again. He hit the keys soft and slow too. Now the song sounded nice. "Soft hands make a nice song," said Joshua. He played it again. Soft and slow, soft and slow. Miss Rosa clapped. Joshua laughed and played some more. Then he stopped and put his small hand on top of hers. "You play with me," he said.

Charles got on the big bus with Grandma. He held his sleepy bunny by its long string. The bunny was soft and warm.

The bus went bump, bump. Charles sat down. "Where is bunny?" he said. His hands were empty. The string was gone too. Charles wanted to cry.

Grandma said, "Let us look where you sat." They walked back. Charles got on his knees. He peeked under the seat. The bunny had fallen down. It was hiding by a shoe. "Lost things stay where they drop," said Charles. He pulled the string, and out came the bunny.

A girl nearby smiled at him. She had thrown her ball under her seat too. It rolled out to his feet. He picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," she said. Charles hugged his bunny tight. The bus went bump, bump, all the way home.

Nova sat at the craft table at camp. She was making a picture for her old teddy bear, the toy she loved best. She wanted to cover it with glitter.

She squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. One dot, two dots, ten dots, a hundred dots! The paper got very wet. Then the paper tore. A big hole sat right in the middle of her bear.

"Oh no," said Nova. "My bear has a tummy hole."

Her friend Sam peeked over. "Too much glue makes the paper soggy," he said. "Then it rips."

Nova tried again on new paper. This time she made little dots. Dot, dot, dot. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then she shook the glitter on top. The glitter snowed down over her bear like sparkly snowflakes.

The paper stayed whole. The bear shined.

Nova held it up to Sam. "Look! Little dots, no hole," she said.

Sam clapped his hands. "The best bear at camp," he said.

Nova gave the picture a hug, and a bit of glitter snowed onto her nose.

Sofia went to the bank with her dad. It was cold outside. Dad said, "Put on your coat, please."

Sofa pushed her arms in. The coat was on. Now came the zipper. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. But the zipper did not move. The two sides would not join. "Hmm," said Sofia. "Why won't you zip?"

She looked down at the bottom of her coat. The two sides were apart there. What if the bottom had to come together first? Sofia pinched the bottom of the zipper with her fingers. She held it tight. Then she pulled the little tag. The zipper went zzzzzip, all the way up! "It works when the bottom is together," said Sofia. "That is why!"

At the bank, warm air seemed to float around her. Sofia held her coat closed so it would not fall open. Outside after, the cold wind blew. But her coat was not weak against it. The zipper stayed shut.

"Look, Dad," said Sofia. "I did it all by myself." Dad smiled and gave her a big hug.

Luca was at the farm. He had small seeds in his hand. "One for the dirt, two for the dirt, three for the dirt," he said. He patted the dirt on top.

Luca waited. He looked and looked. Nothing grew. He asked his grandpa, "Why won't my seeds grow?" Grandpa just said, "Seeds need water, every day."

So Luca got the little blue watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Drip, drip, drip. The water went down into the ground. He did it each morning. One can, two cans, splash.

A naughty rabbit came near. It sniffed at the dirt. Luca clapped his hands. "Go away, rabbit. That is my garden." The rabbit hopped off to eat grass.

One morning, Luca saw green tips. Tiny leaves pushed up. "The water helped the seeds," he said. "They grew because I watered them."

Grandpa took a picture of Luca by the little plants. Luca smiled big. Later they went to the pond. Grandpa tried to fish. Luca waved at his garden. "Grow, grow, grow," he said softly. The little leaves were still there, waving back in the wind.

Amira ran to math club. She was ready to play. On the table sat two buckets of blocks. One bucket was red. One bucket was blue.

"Which bucket has more?" asked Mr. Tom.

Amira hoped the red bucket had more. It looked big. But she wanted to know for sure. She pulled out the red blocks. She counted them. "One, two, three, four, five." Five! The last number she said was five.

Then she tried again. This time she started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." Five again!

"It is the same," said Amira. "I started there, and then there. Both times, five."

She counted the blue blocks too. "One, two, three, four." Only four.

"The red bucket has more!" said Amira. She smiled big. "Five is more than four."

"Good counting," said Mr. Tom. Amira stacked the five red blocks into a tall tower.

Rowan runs to the swings at the playground. He wants the red swing most of all. But a big girl is on it. Rowan waits. One swing, two swings, three swings go back and forth.

The girl jumps off. Rowan runs fast. Then a small boy bumps him. The boy falls down on the soft wood chips. Rowan feels scared that the boy will cry. "Sorry," Rowan says. He helps the boy up. The boy smiles. "Thank you," the boy says.

Now the red swing is free. Rowan climbs on. But he cannot make the swing go. He kicks his legs hard. The swing still stops. A lady walks over. "Can you push me, please?" Rowan asks her. The lady pushes gently. The swing goes up, up, up.

"Thank you," Rowan calls. He laughs in the wind. He tells the lady, "You pushed, so I went high. One push, one big swing!" The lady laughs too. "Again, please," says Rowan. The swing goes up once more.

Kinsley woke up and looked out the window. It was snowing outside. Big soft flakes snowed down on the grass. "Mommy, can we paint today?" she asked. "Yes," said Mommy. "But first I make tea."

Mommy put the kettle on the stove. The stove got hot. Kinsley reached up her hand. Mommy held her fingers back. "Hot things can hurt," Mommy said. Kinsley pulled her hand down fast. She touched the cold window instead. The glass felt cool on her fingers.

Kinsley picked one spot to sit. It was close to Mommy. She could see Mommy and the kettle too. She opened her jar of paint. The red paint was her best one. She made a picture of the snow. White dots went all over the page. She looked at the stove again. The kettle began to sing. Steam came out, and Mommy moved it away.

"I stayed close to you," said Kinsley. Mommy kissed her head. "That is true," said Mommy. "Now let me see that snow picture."

Wesley wanted his rubber duck. The duck was not in the tub. He looked with his eyes. He saw soap and a towel. No duck.

Then he heard a little squeak with his ears. The sound came from under the sink. Wesley bent down. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled toothpaste. The duck was by the toothpaste cup.

He reached with his hands and touched the duck. It was smooth and warm. "Found you," he said.

Mom filled the tub. Wesley put his toes in and touched the warm water. He brushed his teeth and chewed the little toothbrush softly. Then he sat up straight in the water and held the duck high.

"Squeak, squeak," said the duck. "Splash time," said Wesley.

Paisley had a library book about a funny red fox. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight.

Mama sat on the bed. "Show me your book," she said. Paisley opened the front cover. The words there said PAISLEY. "That word is my name!" she said. Mama smiled. She turned the pages one by one, from the front to the back. The words told about the fox. "The words talk to you," said Paisley. "Words say things."

Then Mama showed her a paper card. It had words on it too. "The card says take the book back," said Mama. "Other kids at school want to read the fox book too." Paisley pouted. But then she thought about her friends. They could read the fox after her.

"Tomorrow we take it back," said Paisley. "Then we get a new book."

Mama tucked her in. Paisley patted the fox book one more time.

Zayn put on his red shoes all by himself. "We need shoes for the library," he said. "Silly, the library is not outside," said Mama. Zayn giggled. "My toes like shoes."

At the desk, a kind man gave Zayn a little card. It had his name on it. Zayn picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. He held it tight. "Mine forever!" he said.

At home, Zayn hid the book under his bed. But the next week, the man called. The book had to go back so other kids could read it too. Zayn frowned, then smiled. "I will bring it back. Then I get a new one!" He zipped up his shoes. "Library day!"

Miles stood in the pool changing room. He put on his little swimsuit. His towel had a big owl on it. The owl looked at him with round eyes.

"Time for swim class," said Dad.

Miles had a problem. Last week, water went up his nose. It hurt. He did not like that. "Dad, will water go in my nose again?" he asked.

"Let's see," said Dad. They walked out to the pool. The water was blue and shiny. Coach Amy held Miles's hands. "Now put your face in the water," she said. "Blow out like a dragon."

Miles put his face in. He blew bubbles. Bloop, bloop, bloop. He lifted his head. No water in his nose! He blew air out, so water could not get in. "Dad! I blew bubbles and my nose is dry!"

"Good try, Miles," said Dad. "One more time?"

Miles put his face in again. Bloop, bloop, bloop. He came up laughing. Then he bumped into a girl with his elbow. "Sorry," said Miles. The girl smiled.

At the end, Miles sat on the step. His owl towel was warm and soft. "I can do it," he said. "I blow out, and the water stays out. Watch me next time!"

David got on the school bus. It was his first day of school. He held his mama's hand, then let go. "Which seat is mine?" he asked. "Any seat that is empty," said the bus driver.

David found a seat next to a tall girl. She had a big pink bow. The tall girl smiled at him. The bus went beep, beep, and started to roll.

David looked out the window. He saw his house get small. He saw trees go by fast. Then he saw a dog. The dog ran after the bus. David laughed. "Why is the dog running?" he asked. "Because the bus is fast," said the tall girl. "The wheels go round and round. That makes the bus move. The dog wants to chase it."

David looked down at the wheels. They were big. They went round and round, just like she said. "Wow!" said David. "Wheels make the bus go!"

The tall girl had a phone in her bag. Her mama gave it to her. "My mama said the phone can call home," she said. "If I need help, I press the green button. She will teach me how after school."

The bus stopped at the school. The doors opened wide. David jumped down the steps. He saw a big red door. He saw kids running to the line. "This is school!" said David. He ran to the door as fast as the dog.

"Wait for me!" he called to the tall girl. She ran too, and her pink bow flapped like wings.

Everett did not want to open his mouth. He sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The man in the white coat smiled. "First we look," he said. He held up a little picture. Everett used his eyes to see it. It was a red truck. Then Everett closed his eyes. He could not see the truck at all. "My eyes see," said Everett.

Next the man shook a small bell. Ding, ding. Everett used his ears to hear it. He covered his ears with his hands. The bell went quiet. When he let go, he heard it again. "My ears hear," said Everett. His mom clapped. "Good trying," she said.

The man held a little orange for Everett to smell. His nose sniffed. It smelled sweet. Then came a tiny taste of juice on a stick. Everett's tongue tasted it. "Orange!" he said. At last the man tapped Everett's knee. His leg jumped up all by itself. His skin felt the tap. Everett wanted a sticker for being brave. But first the man said, "Say ah." Everett climbed down from the chair, took a big breath, and opened his mouth wide. The wet popsicle stick went in, then out. "All done," said the man. He held out a shiny sticker. Everett stuck it on his hand. "My hand can hold it," he said.

Madelyn wanted her red cup. It was up on the big counter. She reached up high. The cup did not move. She reached again. Still no cup.

Mom was in the kitchen. Madelyn said, "Cup." Mom looked at her. Then Mom waited. Madelyn thought hard. She tried new words. "Cup, please." Mom smiled big. "Yes! You asked so nicely." Mom got the red cup down. Madelyn held it with two hands.

Next, Madelyn wanted juice. She said, "Juice, please." Mom poured it in. Madelyn took a drink. "Thank you, Mom," she said. Mom clapped her hands.

Outside, the dog began to bark. A butterfly was on the fence. The dog jumped and barked at it. Then the butterfly flew away. The dog lay down. Soon the dog was asleep. Madelyn said, "The dog barked, so the butterfly flew." Dad heard her. "Good thinking, Madelyn!" Then Madelyn waved at the fence and said, "Bye, butterfly. Please come back tomorrow."

Mia ran into the baby store. "The baby is coming soon!" she said. It was windy outside. The door went bang behind her. Snow fell past the big window. Mia had an idea. She would pick a cup for the baby.

Mia found a shiny red cup. It had a duck on it. "The baby will love this!" she said. Mom shook her head. "Watch this," said Mom. She gave the cup to a doll baby. The cup was too big. It did not fit in the doll's tiny mouth. Milk went all over.

Mia looked and looked. Then she found little bottles. They were small like her hands. Mom put a bottle to the doll's lips. It fit just right. "Babies drink from bottles," said Mia. "Not big cups!" She put the red cup back. She hugged the little bottle all the way to the car.

"Baby sister can drink now," said Mia. She patted Mom's big, warm tummy. "See you soon!"

Victoria had a cold. She had to stay in bed all day.

She wanted to play outside. But the sky was cloudy. Mom said, "Rest today. Then you can play."

Victoria drank water. One cup. Two cups. Three cups. She ate warm soup. She slept a long nap.

Her brother Ben came in. He brought her teddy bear. "I hope you feel better," he said.

Victoria drank more water. One cup. Two cups. Three cups. She slept again.

The next morning, her nose was dry. Her cough was small. "Mom! My nose stopped running!"

Mom smiled. "You drank lots of water. Water helped your body get strong."

Victoria looked out the window. The sky was blue now. She saw the big tree in the yard.

"Can I go out now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Wrap up warm."

Victoria ran to the tree. She touched its rough bark. "I was sick, tree. Now I am better!"

Edouard sat in the music room at school. Miss Rosa played a song on her drum. Boom, boom, boom, slow and steady. "Now we clap!" she said.

Edouard clapped very fast. Clap-clap-clap-clap! But his claps did not match the drum. He got all mixed up. He stopped. "Why am I wrong?" he asked. "The drum goes slow," he said. "I clapped too fast. That is why." So he waited. He listened to the boom, boom, boom. Then he clapped slow, like the drum. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. It fit!

Next Miss Rosa sang a rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Edouard only knew half of it. His brother sang this one at home, but the song felt so long. Edouard tried. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," he sang. Then he forgot the rest. He tried again. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are." He did it! He laughed out loud.

Miss Rosa laughed too. "You did it, Edouard!" she said. Edouard clapped a slow clap for himself. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. "I can do the whole song," he said, "all by myself!"
