Alexander went to the baby store with Mom. Mom said a baby was coming soon. Alexander wanted to pick a cup for the baby. He saw a red cup and a blue cup. Which one would the baby like?

He picked a cup with two handles. "Why two handles?" he asked. Mom let him hold a bottle filled with water. It was slippery and almost fell. Alexander held it with two hands and it stayed. "Two hands hold better," he said. The cup had two handles because babies hold with two hands!

He spun around in a happy circle. "The baby can drink all by himself!" Mom laughed and put the cup in the cart. At home, Alexander set the cup by the small baby bed. "I will show you how it works," he whispered to the empty bed.

Ava sat at the art table. She had a big pile of paper shapes. She wanted to make a house. "I will take the square for the walls," said Ava. She put a small square on top. Then she put a red triangle on the very top. "A roof!" she said.

Now Ava wanted wheels. She found two circles. She put a circle on the edge of the table. It rolled away! It rolled under the chair. "My circle is lost," said Ava. Her tummy felt tight. Miss Rosa came close and sat down beside her. "It is right here," said Miss Rosa. She picked up the circle and gave it back.

Ava tried again. She put the circle down flat. It stayed. She turned it up on its side. It rolled again! Ava watched. Then she said, "It rolls because it is round." She put both circles down flat, nice and safe. They did not roll. They did not get lost.

Ava painted her house with a rectangle door. She got blue paint on her skin, so Miss Rosa helped her wash it off. Ava held up her picture. The wheels were two big circles, sitting still. "Look at my house!" said Ava.

Madison ran onto the basketball court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak on the floor. Today was her first game with her team.

Madison wanted to score a basket. She threw the ball up high. It hit the rim and fell down. She tried again. It bounced off the side. Madison sat down on the dry, warm floor.

"Why does the ball not go in?" she asked her coach.

"Think about where your feet are," said Coach Kim, kindly.

Madison looked down. She stood very close to Coach Kim. Then she saw her spot on the floor. It had a small star sticker on it. She had not been standing on her star! She moved back and put both feet on the sticker. She threw the ball again. It went swish, right into the net.

"My feet were too close," said Madison. "The star is my spot."

Coach Kim smiled and clapped. "Good noticing, Madison."

The weather outside was sunny through the big window. Madison bounced the ball and giggled. "Can I try from my star again?" she asked.

"Yes," said Coach Kim. "You sure can."

Josephine's class had a bird nest up on a shelf. Miss Penny put five little eggs inside it. "Let's count the eggs," said Miss Penny. Everyone sang, "One, two, three, four, five."

Then it was snack time. Josephine wanted to pour juice into cups. Miss Penny put out ten cups in a long line. "Can you pour a little juice in each one?" she asked. Josephine felt worried. Ten was a lot. "What if I miss a cup?" she asked. Miss Penny smiled. "Just count as you pour."

Josephine poured. "One, two, three, five," she said. A boy named Max looked grumpy. "You missed a cup!" he said. It was still empty. Josephine looked at it. "I skipped four," she said. "That is why it is empty."

Miss Penny nodded. "The number words go in order. Four comes before five." Josephine filled the empty cup last. Then she counted all ten cups with her finger, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Every cup was full.

Max was not grumpy anymore. He took a big sip of juice. "Ten cups, ten sips," he said. Miss Penny gave Josephine a hug. "You counted them all," she said. Josephine sat down with her own cup. Outside the window, a bird flew by. Josephine whispered, "One bird, going home to her nest."

Milan went to the store with Dad. He wanted a book about trucks. He found a blue book on a low shelf. The cover had little marks on it. "Those marks are words," said Dad. "They say truck." Milan traced the marks with his finger. The words told him what the book was.

He opened the book at the front. He turned the pages one by one. The story went from the front to the back. The last page had a big picture of a red truck.

Then the book made a slip of paper fall out. Milan picked it up. It had more words on it. He asked Dad to fetch the shop lady. She read the slip. "This book is from the library," she said. "Someone left it here." Milan held the blue book tight. He wanted to keep it forever. The lady smiled. "You can take it to the library and borrow it," she said. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back, so other kids can read it too." Milan gave the book one more hug. Then he put it in his little bag. "I will bring it back," he said. "But not today."

Ava held her pink backpack tight. It was her first day of school. Mom held her hand. "Where do I put my bag?" Ava asked. "Let's look for your name," said Mom.

There were little boxes on the wall. Ava saw the letter A. Then she saw her whole name, AVA. "That box has my name on it!" she said. She put her pink backpack inside. "My name shows me my spot," said Ava. Mom smiled and nodded.

At snack time, Ava opened her backpack. There was bread from home, and a small surprise too. A sticker was inside, shaped like a star. Ava showed it to her teacher. "You can wear it," said the teacher. Ava stuck it on her shirt. She sat with Mom and ate her bread. "I like my box," said Ava. "It waits for me all day."

Beatrice sat on Grandma's soft couch. She wanted to draw on the tablet. But the screen was dark.

She pushed the little button once. Nothing happened. She pushed it again. Nothing. Then Grandma held her hand over the button. They counted together. "One, two, three." The screen lit up! "It came on because we held it down," said Beatrice.

She found the drawing app. It had a little ball of colors on it. She tapped it and drew a big red ball. "Look, Grandma! A ball!"

When she was done, she tapped the button again. The screen went dark. She helped Grandma sweep the crumbs off the couch. "Tablet sleeps now," said Beatrice.

Lucy ran into the playroom. Her big teddy sat on the wide mat. Her small mouse sat in the toy car.

"Teddy wants soup!" said Lucy. She got her little pot. She poured and poured. Oh no! The soup did spill. It went all over the mat.

Lucy looked at the puddle. "Why did it spill?" she asked. She looked at the pot. The pot was small. Teddy was big. A big teddy needs a big pot!

Lucy found the big pot. She poured the soup in. "Drink, Teddy!" she said. Teddy got lots of soup. Not one drop did spill.

Then Lucy pushed the car. She pushed it fast. Then she pushed it slow. Her friend Mouse went for a ride. "Fast!" laughed Lucy. "Slow!" she said next. The car rolled to Teddy's feet.

Adam ran to the red truck at the playground. It was his favorite toy. But Leo was already holding it. Leo pushed the truck on the ground. Vroom, vroom.

Adam grabbed the truck. Leo pulled it back. The truck fell. Both boys made a sad face. The playground felt noisy around them. Miss Maya came over.

"Adam, you can ask for a turn," she said. Adam took a big breath. "Leo, can I have a turn, please?" Leo looked at the truck. He did not let go yet.

"First I go down the slide," Leo said. "Then you can have it." Adam waited on the bench. He counted the slides. One, two, three. Leo ran back with the truck. "Here you go," Leo said. Adam held it tight. "Thank you, Leo," he said. Then Adam drove the truck to Leo. "Your turn now," Adam said. Leo smiled a big smile. "You waited for me," Leo said. "That was kind." Adam clapped his hands. The two boys sat in the sand. They pushed the truck back and forth. Vroom, vroom, all morning long.

Evan sat on the grass with his paints. He had red, blue and yellow. His friend Mia came over with her toy truck. "Can you paint my truck?" she asked. "It can be green like the grass."

Evan looked for green paint. There was no green cup. Evan felt worried. Then he looked at his brush. Yellow paint was on it. He dipped it in the blue cup. He stirred it round and round.

The paint turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," said Evan. He painted the truck green, top to bottom. Mia smiled big. "Thank you," she said. "That was so polite," said Evan's mom from the door. The truck rolled over the green, green grass.

Colton had a library book about bears. He held it at bedtime. The cover felt smooth. He did not want to give it back. He wanted to keep it forever.

"Read it again," Colton said. Dad opened the book. He turned the pages from the front. He went page by page, all the way to the back. The words told Dad what to say. Dad pointed at the words. "These little marks talk," Dad said. Colton looked closely. The marks sat in neat lines. When Dad read them, out came a story about a big brown bear.

The next morning, Colton put the book in his bag. "Where is bear going?" he asked. "Back to the library," said Mom. "Someone else wants to read him too." Colton held the bag tight. His tummy felt funny. He walked slow. He looked at the book one more time.

At the library, Colton set the book on the desk. Then he looked at the shelf. There were lots of books there. He could take a new one home. He picked a book about a red fire truck. The pages felt smooth too. Colton hugged it. "This one talks too," he said. "Read it in the truck?" Dad laughed. "At bedtime," he said. Colton held the book all the way home. "Turn the pages slow," he said. "I want to see every fire truck."

Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. Tonight was the lantern festival. Everyone would float little boats on the water.

"Can I bring my boat?" Sarah asked. It was a paper boat, soft at the edges. Mama smiled and said yes.

Sarah put a candle in her boat. Then she put in a stone, a flower, and a button. The boat went into the water. It went down, down, down. It sank!

"Why did my boat sink?" Sarah wondered. She looked at Papa's boat. It had only one candle in it. It floated so well.

Sarah counted on her fingers. One candle, one stone, one flower, one button. "Too many things!" she said. "My boat sank because it was too heavy."

She made a new boat. She put in one candle only. Into the water it went. It floated and floated, all the way to the middle of the pool.

The little flame bobbed up and down. Sarah clapped her hands. "Look, Mama! One candle, and it floats!"

Then the flame went pop and turned green for a second. Sarah gasped. "The candle can change colors too?"

Mama laughed and held her hand. "Make a wish, Sarah."

Sarah squeezed her eyes shut. "I wish my boat could float forever."

Kinsley sat on the playroom floor. She had red, blue and yellow paint. She wanted to paint a tree. But she had no green paint. A tree needs green leaves. She looked and looked in the box. No green anywhere.

She made a sound with her mouth. "Hmmm." Then she had an idea. She put some blue paint on her paper. She put some yellow paint on top. She mixed them with her brush. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said. She painted a big tree with high branches. The leaves were all green.

Then she tried more. Red and yellow made orange. Blue and red made purple. Her paper had many colors now. Her big brother came in. "Wow," he said. "How did you get green?" Kinsley held up her brush. "I mixed blue and yellow," she said. "I made it myself."

Her hands were messy. Mom helped her wash them at the sink. The water turned colors as it ran. Then Kinsley ran back to her tree. She painted one more green leaf on the high branch.

Norah came home with a small fish. It was red and shiny. She set the bowl on the table. Her teddy bear sat close by. "The fish will watch us," said Mom.

Norah tapped the bowl. Tap, tap. The fish hid in the little castle. It would not come out. Norah tapped again. The fish hid more. "The fish is hiding because I tap," said Norah. So she stopped tapping. She sat very still. She poured tiny food bits into the water. The bits smelled like the sea.

Then out came the fish. It swam in a circle. It ate the food. It blew a small bubble. Pop! Norah laughed. "Smart fish," she said. Mom hugged her. The teddy bear watched too. The fish swam and swam, happy in its new home.

Weston ran to the playground. He felt excited. His tummy jumped like a bunny.

He saw the tall slide. He wanted to go on it. He climbed up, up, up. Then he looked down. The slide was very tall. His tummy felt cold. His eyes got big. "Mama," he said, "I feel scared."

Mama stood close by. "You can hold my hand," she said. "Scared can get small when Mama is near."

Weston held her hand. He looked down again. The slide did not seem so tall now. His cold tummy turned warm. "Mama is near," he thought. "So scared got small."

He slid down fast. Whee! He laughed. He felt happy. A little girl slid down too. She fell on her bottom. She began to cry. She felt sad.

Weston picked up her hat. It had flown off. "Here," he said. She stopped crying. "Thank you," she said. She smiled a big smile.

Weston felt happy again too. Then a boy grabbed the swing and pushed hard. The little girl frowned. "That makes me mad," she said.

"Tell him with words," said Mama. "Say, I was using that."

The girl said it. The boy said, "Oh, sorry." He got off the swing.

Weston sat on the swing. Mama pushed him. He went high, high, high. A puppy ran up with the boy's ball in its mouth. That was a surprise!

"Big feelings get small," Weston told Mama. "When you say them out." Mama kissed his head. "Yes," she said. "And swings make them small too." Weston laughed all the way down.

Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to paint her cat. Her cat at home was brown, with round eyes.

She picked up the brown paint. The teacher held up a beet. "This is a root," she said. "It gives us pink paint." Juliette sniffed it. It smelled like dirt.

First Juliette painted a square body. She painted a rectangle tail. Then she painted triangle ears, sharp at the top. Last she cut two little wheels from paper for a cat cart. She cut the wheels square, with four sides.

She pushed the cart. The square wheels would not roll. The corners bumped and stopped.

Juliette waited. She looked at the wheels. Then she cut two new wheels, round like her cat's eyes. Round had no corners. She pushed the cart again. It rolled all the way across the table.

"The corners stopped it," said Juliette. "Round wheels go."

She took a bite of her cracker. It was square, but it tasted just fine.

Zoey sat in the big waiting room. She was going to get her first haircut. She held Mama's hand tight. There was a fish tank near her chair. Zoey did not want the fish to see her cry.

"I don't want them to cut my hair," Zoey said. "It will not grow back."

Mama said, "Let's ask the lady with the scissors."

The hair lady smiled. "I will show you something," she said. She held up a piece of Zoey's hair. Snip. She cut one little piece. Then she put it in Zoey's hand.

"Feel it," the hair lady said. "Your hair is still on your head. Only this bit came off."

Zoey touched her head. Her hair was all still there. "The hair stays on me!" she said. "Only the little piece gets cut."

"Good thinking," the hair lady said. "Now we can cut the rest. You will get a fun new look."

Zoey climbed up into the tall chair. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell like soft snow. It tickled her nose and she laughed.

At dinner that night, Zoey still had her new short hair. Her baby brother made a sour face at his peas. Zoey made a sour face too. Then she smiled.

"My hair got cut," she told him. "And it is still on my head."

She patted her head one more time, just to check.

Oliver went to the cultural center with his mom and his grandpa. It was New Year day. There were red lanterns and drums. The room smelled like warm rice.

Everyone wanted to eat the dumplings. But the dumplings were all gone. Oliver saw a long line at a big table. His tummy made a little growl. "The dumplings are gone because so many people came," he said.

Grandpa held his hand. "We can make more," Grandpa said. They went to the kitchen. Oliver helped fold the dumplings. He pressed the edges with his fingers. The dough was soft and cold. A lady gave him a secret job. He hid one coin in one dumpling, wrapped up pretty in a red paper. "The coin brings luck," she whispered.

The new dumplings went into the hot pot. Soon the line had food again. Oliver ate three. He bit something hard. It was the lucky coin! Grandpa laughed and clapped. Oliver held up the shiny coin. "I found the secret one!" he said.

Violet put on her red boots at daycare. It had snowed last night. "Yesterday there was no snow," said her friend Ben. "Today the snow is here." Violet looked out the window. The yard was all white and cold.

Teacher Mia held up a big pot. "We will pour warm water on the ice today," she said. "Now we pour. Later we can play." Violet held her little cup. She poured the water on the icy step. The ice went drip, drip, drip.

But Ben poured his water on the snow. The snow stayed white. It did not melt. "Why did my water not work?" Ben asked. Violet looked at her step. Then she looked at his snow. Her water went on hard ice. His water went on soft snow. "The snow is too big," Violet said. "The step is small."

Teacher Mia smiled. "We can try again tomorrow," she said. "Tomorrow the sun will come out. The sun is warm too." Violet clapped her hands.

"Now it is warm water," said Violet. "Later the sun will help." The class lined up at the door. Violet poured one more cup on the step. It went drip, drip, drip again. "Goodbye, ice," said Violet. "See you tomorrow."

Aubrey stood on her helper stool. "Can I do it myself?" she asked. Mom slid the toast to her. The first piece was warm and soft. Aubrey pushed the butter hard. The toast tore and a hole appeared. She looked at the hole. "The toast was too soft," she said. Mom gave her a new piece that was cool and firm. Aubrey pushed the butter again. This time the butter glided. It spread all over. No hole!

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one hand. The jug was big and heavy. Milk sloshed over the side. A puddle grew on the table. "Why did it spill?" she wondered. She looked at the jug, then at the cup. She put the cup on the table and held the jug with two hands. She poured slow, slow, slow. The milk went up, up, up the side. It stopped just at the top. Not one drop spilled.

Aubrey took a big bite of toast and a sip of milk. "The cup needed to sit still," she said. Mom clapped. "You did it all by yourself." Aubrey smiled. "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

Felix stood at the big table in the community kitchen. Today he would make his own snack. First, he tried to spread the butter. The butter was cold from the fridge. It tore his toast into little pieces. One piece, two pieces, three pieces.

Then Felix saw the bowl of soft butter sitting by the warm stove. He took a bit on his knife. The soft butter slid across new toast like a smooth road at the beach. "Soft butter does not tear the toast," Felix said.

Next came the milk. Felix held the cup low on the table. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. The cook smiled. "I did it," said Felix. He drank his milk and ate his warm, buttery toast. His itchy sweater sleeve brushed his chin as he grinned.

Evan wanted to paint a green egg at daycare. He looked for green paint. There was no green pot on the table. Only red, blue and yellow were there.

Evan tried red. His egg turned red. "Not green," he said. Miss Kim came over. "Try mixing two colors," she said. Evan dipped his brush in blue. Then he dipped it in yellow. He stirred on the egg. The paint turned green! "It worked!" said Evan. "Blue and yellow make green!"

Tommy hurried over to look. "That is neat!" he said. "Can I try?" Evan gave him the brush. Tommy mixed red and yellow. His egg turned orange. "Wow," said Tommy. "Red and yellow make orange!" Evan smiled and painted a big green stripe. "Mixing is fun," he said.

Ruby came to Grandma's house. Papa Joe had drive his old blue car to pick her up. Now it was lunch time.

Everyone sat at the big table. Ruby grabbed her spoon. But the spoons did not move. "Why?" she asked. Grandma held out her hands. "We hold hands first," said Grandma. "Then we say thank you."

Papa Joe held one hand. Grandma held the other. Ruby's sock feet did not touch the floor. "Thank you for our food," said Grandma. "Thank you for our food," said Papa Joe. Ruby squeezed her eyes shut. Her voice was small. "Thank you, food!"

Then all the spoons moved at once. "Hey!" said Ruby. "We say it, then we eat!" Grandma laughed. "Yes, smart girl."

After lunch, Ruby had a nap on the fuzzy yellow blanket. She woke up and asked, "Is it dinner yet? I want to say the thank you part."

Mason stood by the curb. The big yellow bus came up the road. It stopped right in front of him. The doors were shut. Mason waited.

The driver pushed a handle. The doors swung open. "The door opens because the driver turns it," Mason said. He held the shiny rail and climbed one step at a time. His hand was small on the big rail.

He found a seat by a window. He looked out at the glass. His mom waved on the sidewalk. Mason waved back. The doors closed with a soft sound, and the bus began to roll. The houses went by the window, one, two, three.

A girl sat down next to him. She had a red backpack, just like Mason. "First day," she said. "First day," said Mason. He felt happy inside.

The bus stopped at the school. The doors opened again, because the driver turned them. Mason held the rail and stepped down. He held his new backpack with both hands. "Bye, bus," he called. The driver smiled and gave a little wave.

Amelia wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked at the paint pots. There was red, yellow, and blue. "No orange," she said. "Where is orange?"

Her friend Tom giggled. "The paint fairy ate it," he said. Amelia laughed. "Silly Tom." She picked up her brush. She put red on her paper. Then she put yellow next to it. She poked the two spots together. The paint squished under her brush. It turned orange!

"Look, look!" said Amelia. She held up her paper. "Red and yellow make orange." She painted a big orange pumpkin. Tom painted a blue nose on his face. It was very silly. Amelia grinned. Orange was her new favorite color. She said, "Red and yellow, sit in the pot!" And they made orange for her work.

Ryan sat at a little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name. He held his pencil in his whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. The Y looked like a squiggle.

The librarian, Miss Kim, sat down next to him. She did not say much. She just pinched her own pencil with two fingers. Ryan watched. He thought about the crab at the beach. The crab pinches with two claws.

Ryan pinched the pencil with two fingers too. Now his hand felt steady. He wrote a big R. It came out clear. He wrote the Y. Then A. Then N.

"Look," Ryan said. "The letters come out right because I pinch!"

Miss Kim smiled. "Yes, they do." Ryan frowned at the paper. "My juice made my mouth sour. Writing did not."

He wrote his name one more time. The last N was the best one.

Grayson looked out the window. Big white flakes fell down. No school today! He ran to tell Mom. "Mom, wake up! Snow!"

Mom smiled. "The snow came in the night. The roads are all white, so no cars can drive. That is why school is closed." Grayson clapped his hands. "A snow day!"

He wanted to build a snowman. But first he needed his boots. He could not find one boot anywhere. "Mom, help! My boot is lost!"

Mom got down on the floor. She looked under the bed. There it was, under Grayson's toy plane. "Your boot was hiding," said Mom.

Grayson pulled on his boots. The snow was deep and bumpy. He made a big round snowman with Dad. Then he gave Mom a carrot for the nose. "Snow closed school," said Grayson, "so we can play all day."

Felix stood by the wooden fence. It was his first day of school. He wanted a friend to play with. But all the kids were new too. Nobody knew his name. He tried to say hello. The kids ran to the slide. Nobody knew his name.

Then Felix looked down. His teacher had pinned a picture card on his shirt. It was a tag with his name on it. A girl pointed at it. "Felix!" she read. "Do you want to play tag?" Felix smiled big. "Yes!" he said.

Felix ran and ran. When he got tired, he looked at his tag. He remembered why the girl knew his name. "The tag told her," he said. The girl laughed. "I have a tag too! It says Mia." They held hands by the fence.

Isabella went to Ms. Rosa's music room. She saw a shiny drum and a little toy cat. The cat had a long tail.

"I want to sing the whole song," said Isabella.

"First we find the beat," said Ms. Rosa. She tapped the drum. One, two. One, two.

Isabella clapped too. But she clapped fast, fast, fast! She got to the end of "Twinkle, twinkle" before the drum did. "Oops," she said. "I ran away from my song!"

Ms. Rosa laughed. "Clap when the drum claps. One, two. One, two."

Isabella looked at the drum. She waited. Drum, clap. Drum, clap. Then she sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The song stayed with the drum the whole way.

"I did it!" said Isabella. "The drum holds my song."

"Then the cat wants a turn," said Ms. Rosa. The cat tapped the beat with its tail. One, two. One, two.

Isabella clapped and sang. The cat's tail went up, up, up.

"Next time, can the cat sing too?" asked Isabella.

Zachary stood in the school computer lab. He wanted to draw a big blue pond on the tablet. But the screen was dark. "It is broken," he said.

Miss Ana smiled. "Just press the round button," she said. "Hold it down and count." Zachary pressed the little round button. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen lit up like morning. "The button makes it turn on!" he said.

He tapped the green drawing app. It opened with a pop sound. He drew a blue pond with three fish. Then it was time for lunch. Miss Ana said, "Push the button to make it sleep." Zachary held the button again. The screen went dark. He set the tablet on the shelf, careful and slow.

"Look, Miss Ana," he said. "I pressed it, and it went to sleep."

Elizabeth's grandma came to stay. She would sleep in the guest room for seven whole days. Elizabeth counted them on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said.

The guest bed had big soft blankets. Grandma tucked them in tight, like a nest. But at night, Grandma could not sleep. Elizabeth heard her turn and turn. In the morning, Grandma had dark circles under her eyes.

Elizabeth thought and thought. The room faced the street. Cars went by with bright lights. "The light wakes Grandma up," Elizabeth said. So she found a thick quilt and hung it over the window. That night, the room stayed dark and still.

Grandma slept and slept. In the morning she smiled. "What a good sleep," she said. "I love this cozy room." Elizabeth loved it too. She counted the days left. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Stay in your nest, Grandma."

Jasmine went to the park with her dad. They wanted a picnic in the sun. The sky was sunny and bright. "Yay, sun!" said Jasmine. She wore her shiny red hat. It was shiny because the sun made it glow.

Then the wind began to blow. The wind blew her hat right off. It blew the leaves. It blew the trees. "Why did the sun go away?" Jasmine asked. She looked up. "The wind moved a big gray cloud," she said. "The cloud took the sun away." Then rain began to fall. Drip, drop, drip.

"Rain needs rain boots," said Dad. He helped Jasmine put on her yellow coat. She pulled the hood up over her neck. "The hood keeps the rain off my neck," she said. They sat under the roof by the swings. They ate crackers and watched the rain. "Rainy days are good too," said Jasmine. She put out her hand and caught a drop.

Mohamed sat in his big bed. He had a library book about a turtle. "Turtle," he said, pointing at the picture. He turned the page. More turtle! He turned another page. The pages went from the front to the back.

On the last page there were little black marks. "What are those?" Mohamed asked. His dad read them out loud. They said the turtle could grow big in the pond. The marks were words! Words told about the turtle. Mohamed looked and looked. Did the book have more words? He turned the book around. The room went dizzy for a second. The book was all upside down.

"I want to keep this book forever," Mohamed said. He hugged it tight. Dad shook his head. "It has to go back to the library tomorrow. It is library day." Mohamed felt sad. "Why does it go back?" he asked. Dad said other kids want to read it too. Mohamed thought and thought. Other kids. Reading his turtle book?

"Can we get it again?" Mohamed asked. "Yes," said Dad. Mohamed put the book by his shoes so he would not forget it. In the morning, the book waited by the door. Mohamed patted the cover. "Bye, turtle book," he said. "A new kid will read you now."

Samuel went out to the backyard in the morning. The sun was shining. It was sunny. But Samuel wanted to build in his sandpit, and he could not see. The sun was too bright in his eyes.

"What can help me?" he asked. He ran inside and got his hat. He put the big hat on his head. Now the sun was out of his eyes. Samuel could build his sand castle. "The hat helps because it stops the sun," he said.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind blew his hat away! "Oh no," said Samuel. The wind blew and blew. He held his hat with one hand and patted the sand with the other. The wind stopped, and the yard was quiet again. Samuel smiled and put the last scoop on his castle.

Naomi sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to build a tower of blocks. But she was thirsty first. She drank water from her little cup.

Then she saw a ball. She gave it a push. The ball rolled away. "Why did it roll?" she asked.

Naomi picked up a square block. She pushed it on the rug. The block did not roll. It just slid and stopped.

She picked up the ball again. It was round all over, like a circle. She pushed it. Round things roll.

So she stacked square blocks and triangle blocks and rectangle blocks for her tower. They stayed put. At the top she put nothing round.

"Square blocks can't roll away," said Naomi. "So I win. My tower is safe."

Her tummy growled. "Snack time," said Mama from the door. Naomi ran to the table. She picked up her fork. She looked at it. "My fork has squares on the handle," she said. "Good. It won't roll off my plate."

Wyatt stood at the bus stop with Mama. The sun was out. "Sunny today," said Wyatt. He wore his big sun hat. The wind came. It went whoosh. His hat flew off his head. "Come back, hat!" said Wyatt.

Mama laughed. She picked up the hat. "The wind pushed it," she said. Wyatt put the hat back on. He held it with both hands. "I hold it," said Wyatt. "The wind can't get it!" The wind went whoosh again. The hat stayed on. "Ha!" said Wyatt.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell. Drip, drop. Wyatt was warm. He had his raincoat on. He zipped it up to his chin. "Rainy, rainy," said Wyatt. The bus came. He climbed the steps. "Bye bye, wind!" he said. The wind went whoosh.

Grandma poured two bowls of strawberries. One bowl was red and big. One bowl was small. "Which bowl has more?" Grandma asked.

Sarah looked and looked. She could not tell. So she counted. She touched each berry. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." The big bowl had seven.

The cat came by. Its paws were dirty, so Grandma said, "Cat, go outside." The cat sat by the door and waited.

Sarah counted the small bowl. She started with the berry on top. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted again. This time she started with the berry at the bottom. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five!

"Grandma! I counted that way, and I counted this way," Sarah said. "Both times, the last number was five."

Grandma smiled. "So which bowl has more?"

"The big bowl has seven. Seven is more than five."

Sarah ate her seven berries, one by one. "One, two, three," she said, and she kept counting to the very last one.

Brielle got to school early. It was writing time. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

She grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The B came out big and fat. The letters ran into each other. "Oh no," said Brielle. "My name looks like a blob."

Her friend Milo laughed, but not a mean laugh. It was a silly joke about the blob. Then he showed her his hand. He held his pencil near the tip. He used just two fingers and his thumb, like a little pinch.

Brielle tried the pinch. She held the pencil near the tip too. She wrote B, then R, then I. She stopped to count the letters left. E, L, L, E. She wrote them one at a time.

"Look!" said Brielle. "When I pinch the pencil, my letters come out small and neat." She held up her paper. Her name was all there.

"Nice writing," said Milo.

"I will write it again," said Brielle. She pinched the pencil and began the B.

Charlotte went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a cat. Cats were her favorite.

The picture books sat in big bins. Each bin had a label. One bin said animals. One bin said toys. One bin said foods.

Charlotte looked in the animals bin. She found a book about a dog. She found a book about a fish. But no cat book.

Then she looked in the toys bin. There was a book about a cow. A cow was not a toy! A cow was an animal, like a cat. So the cow book was in the wrong bin. That is why she could not find it. Maybe someone had mixed the bins up.

A cart rolled by with a squeaky wheel. The librarian stopped and smiled. "That book looks silly sitting there," she said.

"I can fix it," said Charlotte. She put the cow book in the animals bin. Then she looked again. Under the dog book was a cat book!

"Found it!" she did not yell, but she wanted to.

She sat down with her dad. The cat in the book chased a ball of yarn.

"Is yarn a toy?" Charlotte wondered. She turned the page to see.

Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair was in two little puffs. Today she had to get a shot in her arm. She did not want a shot. She held her arm stiff and tight, like a wooden stick.

The nurse came in with a small tray. "Can you hold still for me?" she asked. Mila squeezed her arm even tighter. It felt hard as a rock. The nurse shook her head. "A tight arm makes the shot hurt more," she said. "A soft, floppy arm helps it hurt less."

Mila looked at her arm. She let her shoulder go soft. She let her arm droop down, loose and floppy like a noodle. "Okay," she said. "My arm is soft now."

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Mila blinked. "That was small," she said. Then she got a bright bandage with stars on it.

On the way out, Mila did not hurry. She held her sticker up to the light. "Soft arm, small pinch," she told her mama. "See my stars?"

Lennon went to the store with Dad today. Yesterday they had no bananas left. So today they would get more.

"Look," said Dad. "This banana is green."

"Can we eat it now?" asked Lennon.

"Not now. Green means later," said Dad. "It turns yellow later. Then we can eat it tomorrow."

Lennon held the green banana. It felt hard. She put it in the cart, next to a small toy mouse. She made the mouse whisper, "Wait, banana, wait."

Then Lennon's legs felt weak from walking. Dad saw her rubbing her eyes. He picked her up. "You need help now," he said. "Rest now, walk later."

At home, Lennon put the banana on the window sill. "Tomorrow you will be yellow," she whispered.

The next morning, the banana was yellow. "It changed because I waited!" said Lennon.

Dad peeled it. Lennon took a big bite. "Today it is ready," she said. "Today is the best day."

Ayla sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted the green sticker on the wall. But first she had to wait.

The room had balloons. They floated up by the roof. One floated down to Ayla. She touched it with her hands. It felt smooth and cool.

The doctor came in. "Look here," he said. He held up a card with grass on it. Ayla used her eyes to see it. Then she covered her eyes with her hands. Now she could not see the grass! She moved her hands away. She could see it again. "My eyes make me see," said Ayla.

The doctor tickled her toes. Her skin felt the tickle. He shook a little bell. Ayla heard it with her ears. She held her nose closed. She tried to smell the sweet orange the doctor held out. She could not smell it. She let go of her nose. Mmm, now she could! She took a tiny taste with her tongue. Sour and sweet.

Then Ayla got mad because the visit was over. The doctor gave her the green sticker. She put it on her shirt. "Thank you," she said. The balloons floated up, and Ayla waved bye-bye to them.

Mateo ran into Grandma's house. "Where is the baby?" he asked. Grandma pointed to a soft blue blanket. A tiny baby was inside. "That is your new brother," said Grandma.

Mateo wanted the baby to laugh. He poked the baby's tummy. The baby did not laugh. The baby made a small frown. Mateo tried again. Still no laugh. He felt sad.

Grandpa held up the baby's little hand. Mateo put one finger near it. He tickled the tiny palm. The baby grabbed Mateo's finger and held on tight. The baby made a small smile. "Grandpa, look!" said Mateo. "I tickle his hand, and he holds me!"

Grandma laughed. "Babies love to grab fingers," she said. Mateo wiggled his finger. The baby held on and on. Then Mateo gave the baby a cold spoon from a glass of water on the table. The baby grabbed that too.

"He can hold everything," said Mateo. "Not me," said Grandpa, holding up his big hand. "Too big!" Mateo laughed. The baby squeezed his finger again, like a tiny hello.

Leah had a new swimsuit. It had a scratchy tag. Mom said, "I will cut the tag off." Snip, snip went the scissors. Now the suit felt smooth.

Leah sat on the wood bench in the changing room. The room was quiet after her swim class. She shivered. Her legs were wet. Why was she so cold? She looked down. Water sat on her skin like little beads. "Maybe the water makes me cold," she said. She picked up her big towel. She patted her arms. She patted her legs. She patted her hair too.

The water went into the towel. Her skin was dry now. The shivering stopped. "Mom, look! The water went away, and I am warm!" Mom smiled. Then Leah pulled on her socks. One sock had a hole. Her toe popped out and said, "Hello!"

Hudson stood in the big school gym. He had a red beanbag in his hand. On the floor was a hoop. He wanted to get the beanbag in it.

He threw the beanbag very low. It slid along the floor and missed. The beanbag made a soft sound on the wood.

Hudson tried again. He held his arm up high. He let go up high, not down low. The beanbag flew up and dropped into the hoop. "I did it!" said Hudson.

Then Coach Maya rolled him a big blue ball. It hit his tummy and fell. His hands were too far apart. "Why did it fall?" Hudson asked. "My hands were messy, all over." He put his two hands close together. He made a big bowl with them. Coach Maya rolled the ball again. Hudson caught it and held it tight.

"I can show you," Hudson said to his friend Ben. He held his arm up high. The beanbag went in the hoop. Ben clapped his hands.

Asher ran to the big slide. His tummy felt bouncy and jumpy. "I am so excited!" he said. He wanted to slide down all by himself.

He climbed up the ladder. It was very tall. Then he looked down. His legs felt wobbly. "I'm scared," he whispered. He sat at the top and did not move.

A girl named Mia climbed up too. "Want to go together?" she asked. Asher nodded. Mia went first. Asher held the sides and went slow. Whee! He slid down and landed in the soft sand. "I did it!" he laughed. His mouth made a big smile. He felt happy.

But then a big boy ran by and bumped him. Asher fell down in the sand. His face got hot and scrunched up. "That made me angry!" he said. Mia helped him stand. Then Asher spun in a circle, round and round, until he felt dizzy and fell laughing into the sand.

The big boy came back. He looked down and his eyes were watery. "I fell too," he said. "I feel sad." Asher patted his arm. "Come spin with us," he said. "Spinning makes me laugh." So they all spun in one big circle, round and round, until they toppled over together in the sand.

Adam had a library book about trucks. He loved it so much. He wanted to keep it forever.

At bedtime, Dad said, "Time for your book." Adam opened the front cover. The pages went one way, to the back. Dad pointed at the little marks on the page. "Those are words," he said. "They tell the story." Adam traced a word with his finger. "The words say truck!" he said.

Then Dad said, "We must take the book back on Friday." Adam held the book tight. "Why?" he asked. "Other kids want to read it too," said Dad.

Outside, a soft storm was starting. Rain tapped the window. Adam smelled his dog's stinky paws on the blanket. He giggled.

"I will not forget Friday," Adam said. He put the book by the door. Then he snuggled down. The rain went tap, tap, tap.

"Good night, truck book," Adam whispered.

Ethan ran up to the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. The librarian smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" Ethan nodded big. She wrote his name on a small blue card. Ethan held it with both hands.

Then he found a book about a squishy red tomato. He hugged it tight. "This book is mine now," he said. The librarian shook her head. "You can take it home. But you must bring it back so other kids can read it too." Ethan looked sad. Then he looked at the tomato book. "Okay," he said. "But just for a little while."

At lunch, Ethan showed the tomato book to Mama. He put the book on the table. It sat by his cheese. After lunch he read it three times. That night, the book went under his blanket. Tomorrow he would read it again. Soon he would bring it back. Then he would get a new one. Ethan patted the cover and whispered, "Good night, tomato."

Maya ran to the park with her bear, Brown. She loved the park so much. Today she would play house under the big tree.

A boy nearby threw a paper plane. It zoomed up and glided down. "Again!" Maya shouted. Then she set up her house. A flat stone would be the table. A leaf would be the bed for Brown.

Maya laid Brown on the leaf. But the leaf was bumpy. Brown rolled off. Thump! Brown fell in the grass. Maya tried again. Brown rolled off again.

She looked at the leaf. It was not flat. The bumpy parts pushed Brown right off. "The bed is too bumpy," Maya said. So she found a smooth, flat leaf. She patted the dirt under it. She laid Brown down. Brown stayed put. Maya clapped.

Then she found a small stick. It became a spoon. She stirred dirt and water. "Soup for Brown!" she said. The soup was warm from the sun.

The paper plane came gliding back. It landed right by the leaf bed. Maya laughed. "Brown, you have a new friend!"

Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. He looked and looked. Red, blue, yellow. Red, blue, yellow. No green.

Then Leo came over. Leo was grumpy because he had no red paint. Hayden had lots of red paint. He pushed his red cup over to Leo. Leo smiled and said, "Thank you."

Hayden was still stuck. He dipped his brush in blue. He painted a blue frog. Then he dipped the brush in yellow too. The blue and yellow mixed on the paper. The frog turned green!

"Blue and yellow make green," said Hayden.

Miss Ana helped him hang the frog by the window. The sun made the wet paint shine. Then Miss Ana let him pet the class pet, a soft brown bunny. "Nice green frog," said Leo.

Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen with her grandma. A big chef hat was too big, so grandma let her wear a small one instead. On the counter sat warm toast, soft butter, and a cup.

"Can I do the butter?" Paisley asked. Grandma cut a tiny piece of butter and put it on the knife. Paisley pressed hard. The butter ripped a hole in the toast. A little piece fell to the floor. "Oh no," said Paisley.

"Try again," said grandma. She set out a new slice of warm toast. Paisley slid the knife slow and soft this time. The butter went on like paint. "Gentle hands work," said Paisley.

Next came the milk. The jug was heavy. Paisley lifted it high and the milk splashed out of the cup. A white puddle grew on the counter. She felt a little lost. Grandma held her hand around the jug. "Tip it slowly," said grandma. Paisley tipped it just a little. The milk slid down the side of the cup and filled it up. "Slow tipping makes no splash," said Paisley.

Grandma wiped the puddle with a cloth. Through the window, Paisley saw a tree in the sun. They sat on two stools and ate the toast and drank the milk together.

"Mmm," said grandma. "Best toast in town."

Clara ran to the water table at school. "Look, a big boat!" she said. She put it in the water. It went slow. Then Sam came with a small boat. His boat went fast! "Why is yours fast?" Clara asked.

Sam pushed his boat again. "My boat is small," he said. "Small boats go fast." Clara tried her big boat. It went slow, slow, slow. She wanted a fast boat too.

Then Clara had an idea. She took the small boat and put the big boat on top. "Now they go together!" she said. Sam pushed hard. The big boat went fast with the small boat on its back. "Look, look!" said Clara.

Teacher Mia brought warm cocoa for snack. Clara touched her cup. "Hot," she said, and blew on it. Then she took a big drink. "Now it's cold enough!" After snack, Clara sat down to draw an ocean with two fast boats on it. "This one is big," she said, pointing. "This one is small." Sam yawned, all sleepy. Clara drew a bed for him in the picture, right next to the ocean.

Violet put on her new swimsuit. It was blue with white dots. Dad drove her to the pool by the lake. The lake water was far away. The pool water was close and blue.

Violet stood on the step. "I want to swim," she said. "But water goes in my nose." Dad held her hand. "Watch me," he said. He put his mouth in the water. He blew out. Bubbles came up. Bloop, bloop, bloop.

Violet tried it. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out. Bubbles came from her lips. No water went in her nose. She blew bubbles again and again. Then she kicked her feet. Dad held her tummy. The bubbles came up, and she did not cough. "Blowing keeps the water out," Violet said.

They sat by the pool in the warm light. Violet took a big bite of her apple. Dad wrapped her in a soft towel. "Swim again tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Violet. "Bubbles first."

Amelia wanted to make a ice cube last all day at school. She put one big ice cube and one tiny ice cube in her cup. The tiny one was as small as a mouse. "Which one will melt first?" she asked her friend Tom.

At play time, they ran to look. The tiny cube was gone. The big cube was still there. Amelia clapped her hands. "The small one melted fast," she said. "The big one melts slow."

The sun was hot on the shelf. So Amelia moved the cup to a cold spot near the window shade. Tom watched with wide eyes. "Will the big one melt now?" he asked.

Amelia waited and watched. The big ice cube sat still. It did not melt. "It melts slow because it is big," she said. "And it is cold here, not hot." The water in the cup did not grow one bit.

At tidy up time, Amelia put her cup in the sink. The big ice cube was still there, small now, but not gone. "You can come to my house," she told the ice cube. Tom laughed. "You talk to ice!" he said. Amelia giggled and waved the cup goodbye.

Weston saw a big table at the festival. There was warm bread on it. He wanted some right now. He grabbed a piece, but Grandma held his hand.

"Not yet," she said. "First we say our family greeting. We hold hands. We say it together. Then we eat."

Weston pouted. His tummy made a growly sound. But he took Grandma's hand anyway. He took Papa's hand too. Everyone made a big circle, like a cloud around the table.

Grandma started the greeting. Weston listened. Then he said the words too, loud and silly. "Good bread, good friends, good day!"

Then everyone laughed and picked up bread. Weston took a big bite. "It is salty!" he said, with his mouth full.

Grandma smiled. "You said it with us. Now the bread tastes even better."

Weston looked around. "Everyone eats after we all say it. That is why we hold hands!"

"Yes," said Papa. "One big word, one big bite."

Weston licked his fingers. "Can we do it again? I want more bread."

"First, the greeting," said Grandma, and she held out her hand.

The lights went out. The room went dark. Sienna held Mama's hand tight. "It's too dark," she said.

Mama got her phone. She tapped the back of it. A little light came on. Sienna looked and looked. Then she said, "The light comes on because you tap it." Mama smiled. "Yes. Let's keep it on."

They walked to the kitchen. Sienna's hands were wet from washing them. She wiped them on her towel. Then she tapped the phone too. The light got brighter. It made a circle on the wall.

They made a tent with a big plastic sheet. They sat inside it. The little light shone on the plastic. It looked like a star. Sienna yawned. The rain tapped the window outside. The phone light stayed on, small and warm. "Night night, light," Sienna whispered.

Lincoln was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Her name was Ivy.

Grandma had baked bread. Lincoln could smell it. "Yum," he said. The bread was warm and squishy. He pressed it with his finger. It popped back up.

Then the car came. Daddy carried Ivy inside. She was tiny. She had a little red face. Then Ivy began to cry. "Waa, waa."

"Why is she crying?" Lincoln asked. Grandma held Ivy close. "Let's see. Is her sock too tight? No. Does she need a burp?" Grandma patted her back softly. Burp! Ivy kept crying.

"Is she hungry?" Lincoln asked. Grandma said, "Let's try." Mommy gave Ivy milk. Ivy drank and drank. The crying stopped. Ivy went to sleep.

"She cried because she was hungry," Lincoln said. He counted her tiny toes. One, two, three, four, five. One, two, three, four, five. Ivy slept and slept.

Lincoln gave her a soft pat on her head. "I will help feed you," he whispered.

Nicholas sat on his bed. He had a library book about bears. He loved the bears so much. He wanted to keep the book forever.

He looked at the front cover. There were little marks on it. "Mama, what are these?" he asked. Mama said, "Those are words. They say Bear Book." Nicholas tapped the words. Words could talk! He turned the pages one by one, front to back. The bears went for a swim. Then they went to sleep. "What comes next?" he wondered.

Then Nicholas put the book under his pillow. "Now it is mine," he said. But the next day, Mama came in. "That book is from the library," she said. "We borrowed it. We must take it back so other kids can read it too." Nicholas made a sad face. His tummy felt tight, like a hurt.

Nicholas tried to hide the book in the bath toy box. That was wrong. Books do not like baths! Mama found it just in time. It was dry and safe.

So Nicholas made a plan. He asked, "Can we bring it back and borrow it again?" Mama smiled. "Yes, we can borrow it another day." Nicholas hugged the book one more time. He said, "Bye bye, bears. See you soon." Then he put it in the bag all by himself.

Eloise stood by her bed. The room was dark. She heard a noise. Thump, thump. Eloise began to freeze. Her legs would not move. "Something is under my bed," she whispered. Her tummy felt funny. She was scared.

"Mama!" she called. Mama came in fast. She knelt down by the table and looked under the bed. She pulled out a shoe. Then she pulled out a book. The big book had fallen down. That was the thump. "The book made the noise," Mama said. "The dark makes big noises feel scary." Eloise looked at the book. Her scared feeling got small. A happy feeling grew big.

Mama turned on the little lamp. The room was warm and bright. Eloise was not sad anymore. She hugged her bear tight. "Book go night-night," she said. Mama laughed and kissed her head.

Harrison went to the library with Dad. He wanted a book about dogs. "Where do dog books live?" he asked. "Let's look slowly," said Dad. "We will find one."

They walked past a big shelf. The books there were about food. Apples, bread, and milk. "Not dogs," said Harrison. They walked past another shelf. Those books were about toys. Balls, blocks, and drums. "Not dogs," said Harrison. They tried one more shelf. Those books were about animals. Cats, ducks, cows, and, yes, dogs!

"The dog books live with the animals," said Harrison. "Dogs are animals, so they are here." He pulled out a black book with a big yellow dog on it. He sat down on the soft rug. He turned the pages, one by one. Dad sat close and waited.

Then Harrison made a dog sound. "Woof, woof," he said, very quiet. He tried the page again. The woofs worked. A girl on the rug looked up and smiled. Harrison held the book out to her and said, "Look. A dog. Woof, woof."

Anna held her daddy's hand. The big yellow bus stopped in front of her. The door opened with a whoosh.

Anna climbed the steps. She looked for a seat. "I want the window seat," she said. A boy named Sam sat by the window. "Can I sit with you?" she asked. "Yes," said Sam. "I like to look out too."

Anna looked out the window. She saw a plane up in the sky. "The plane is so fast!" she said. "It goes fast because it has big wings," said Sam. "Wings go whoosh." Anna laughed. "Whoosh!" she said. "My arms are little wings." She flapped her arms like a bird. Sam laughed too.

The bus went bump, bump, down the road. It stopped again. A new girl got on. Anna waved. "Sit here!" she said. "We can look for planes."

At school, the teacher said, "We will paint today." Anna painted a big yellow bus. She painted a plane above it. "That is my bus," she said. "And that is my plane. I am so smart!" The teacher smiled. Anna smiled too. Then she painted one more thing. It was Sam, waving out the window.

Myles sat on his bed with his library book. It was a book about a big red truck. He wanted to keep it forever. "My book," he said. "Mine forever."

Myles turned the pages. He started at the front. He went to the back. "Books go front to back," he said. He saw little marks on the page. His big sister Rosa read them out loud. "Those marks are words," she said. "The words say what happens."

Then Rosa pointed at a paper slip in the book. It had a day on it. "The book goes back on that day," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Myles held the book tight. He did not want to give it back.

The next day Rosa helped him wrap the book in a fresh paper bag. It was clean and new. Myles carried it to the library. He set it on the desk. "Book goes back," he said. The librarian smiled. "You can borrow a new one," she said. Myles picked a book about a dog that likes to chew bones. He hugged it. "Front to back," he said, and turned the first page.

Luca stood at the bus stop with Mama. He was ready to go see Grandma. The sun came out. It was sunny and warm. Luca pulled off his hat. "Too hot," he said.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind grabbed Luca's hat. The hat flew up in the air. Luca reached and reached. "My hat!" he called. Mama held his hand tight. A kind man caught the hat. "Here you go," he said. Luca put the hat back on. He held it with both hands. "The wind took it because it was light," Luca said.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was rainy. Mama opened her big umbrella. Luca stood under it. The rain tapped on top. Tap, tap, tap. Luca stayed dry. He did not get wet at all. "The umbrella stops the rain," Luca said. Mama smiled and nodded.

Luca chewed his little cracker while they waited. He watched a puddle grow by his boots. "In spring we get lots of rain," Mama said. "Rain helps the flowers grow."

The bus came at last. Luca held Mama's hand. They climbed the steps together. Luca waved to the man with the hat. "Bye bye, rainy day!" he said.

Sofia stood by the tent with her small red bag. "What goes in the bag?" she asked. Mom knelt down beside her. "We pack a bag for a trip," Mom said. "Why?" asked Sofia. "Because we cannot use our things at home when we are far away."

Sofia put in her bunny and her socks. She wiggled her hand into her mitten. The mitten felt loose. "It is too big now," she said. "Your hand grew this year," said Mom. Sofia looked and looked. Her fingers went all the way to the end last summer. Now the mitten slipped off when she waved.

At the campsite, Sofia found a big flat stone. She sat on it and pretended the stone was a boat. "Row, row," she said. A wind came through the trees. The leaves shivered. The tent wall puffed out like a balloon. "Why does the tent move?" Sofia asked. Dad smiled. "The wind pushes it," he said. Sofia held up her hand. The wind pushed her fingers back. "The wind pushed me too!" she said. She pushed the tent wall with her palm, and it puffed out the other way. "Now I pushed the tent," she said, and she did it again.

Iris went to the pharmacy with her dad. The pharmacy sold soap, and Iris saw a pink bottle. "Can we buy it?" she asked. Dad said yes.

But there was a rule at preschool. You must wash your hands with soap for twenty seconds. Iris did not know how long twenty seconds was. At snack time, she washed fast, like a bunny hop. Then she ate her crackers.

The next day, her tummy felt bad. She had to stay home. "My hands were not clean," she said. "I washed too fast."

Her teacher sang a hand song. It took twenty seconds to sing. Iris sang it while she washed, all the way to the end. Now she sang it before eating and after the toilet too. The sun came in the window. Iris held up her hands. They were smart, clean hands, and they smelled like flowers.

Henry sat in his car seat. The sun was hot on his arm. "I am hot," he said. "Can I have cold air?"

Mom drove up a big hill. The car went slow. Henry rolled down his window a little. The air was warm.

Then they went down the hill. The road went flat. Mom made the car go fast. Wind came in the window. The wind was cool on Henry's arm. It felt like cold air.

"The fast car makes wind," said Henry. "The wind makes me cool." He put his hand out a little bit. The wind pushed on his hand. When the car went slow, the wind stopped. When the car went fast, the wind came back. Henry made his hand go in and out, in and out.

A big truck went by. It was bigger than their car. A little blue car went by too. It was smaller. Henry waved at the little car.

At the ice cream shop, Mom had to pay. She gave coins to the man. The man gave Henry a cold ice cream. It was cold like the wind from the window. Henry licked it and smiled.

"I like fast cars," said Henry. "They make wind for me."

Daniel went to the park with Grandma. He wanted to find the ducks. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Daniel held her hand.

They passed a big grill by the picnic tables. It was smoking. Daniel reached out one finger. The air above the grill felt hot on his skin. He pulled his finger back fast. "Hot," said Daniel. Grandma nodded. "The grill is hot, so we do not touch it." Daniel put his hands in his pockets. That was a good plan.

Then they heard a splash. The ducks were in the pond! Daniel ran, but he stopped and looked back. He waited for Grandma. They walked to the water together. Daniel took off one shoe and put in one toe. The water was cold. "Brrr!" he said. The sun was going down. It was getting late. "The ducks go home when it gets late," said Grandma. Daniel waved. "Bye, ducks. See you next time."

Jake had a cold. He was resting in his big bed. His nose was red and dry. He wanted water, but the cup was empty.

Mom filled the cup up. She put it on the little table. Jake drank and drank. Soon his nose felt better. His throat did not hurt. "Why did water help?" Jake asked. Mom said, "Water helps a sick body."

Jake wanted to see if it was true. He drank more water before his nap. He woke up and his nose was soft again. "The water fixes my nose!" he said. He hugged his teddy bear, who was feeling shy in the corner. Jake smiled. He put his shoe by the door so he could play outside tomorrow. Then he drank one more sip. "Good night, cup," he whispered.

Grayson found a big box behind the couch. He climbed inside it. The box smelled like cardboard and old crayons. "This is my house," he said. He knocked on the wall. Knock, knock. His toy bear sat all alone in the corner. The bear was cold, Grayson thought. Bears need blankets. He wrapped the bear in a soft towel. Then he gave the bear a pretend drink from an empty cup. "Drink your milk," said Grayson. The bear tipped over. "Oh no!" said Grayson. "Are you sick?" He thought hard. "Yes. You need a boot." He put his rain boot next to the bear like a bed. He tapped the boot three times. "That is my magic spell," he whispered. The bear sat up tall. Grayson clapped. "The spell worked because I tapped three times," he said. "More milk, bear?"

Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pink pencil and white paper. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He squeezed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed down hard. The pencil tip went through the paper. "Oh no!" said Gabriel. "The paper did rip!"

A woman came to the table. It was Grandma. She held up her own hand. "Look at my fingers," she said. Gabriel looked. Grandma pinched the pencil with two fingers, like a little crab. Gabriel tried it too. He pinched the pencil with his thumb and one finger. He made the letter G. He made an A. He made a B! The paper did not rip. The letters were wiggly, but they were there.

"Grandma, look!" said Gabriel. "When I pinch soft, the paper stays good." He wrote his whole name, all the way to the last L. "G-A-B-R-I-E-L!" he shouted. "Now I can write it again!" And he pulled a new piece of paper close.

Bennett stood in the music room. His teacher sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Bennett clapped fast, fast, fast. Then he forgot the words. The song fell all apart.

His friend Mia showed him the big yellow drum. "Try this," she said. The drum went boom, boom, boom. It was slow and even, like a clock. Bennett clapped boom, boom, boom too. He did not clap fast this time. His claps fit right into the song. "My claps go with the drum," said Bennett. "The drum keeps them steady."

Now the teacher hid the paper with the words on it. Bennett closed his eyes. He thought of stars. He sang every word. Then he drank his milk and smiled. "Again!" he said.

Oliver sat at the dinner table. He wanted his brown bread before dinner. "Can I have bread?" he asked. Mom said, "First we count the beans."

Oliver looked at his plate. He did not know where to start. So he sang his counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out in a long line, like a train.

He pointed at a bean and said, "One." He pointed again. "Two." The words went in the same order as the song. "Three, four, five." He counted five beans.

"Where did the words go after five?" he asked. He sang the song again, slow. Then he knew. "The song gives them to me in order," he said.

Mom smiled. "Now fetch the bread basket, please."

Oliver carried it back, one hand on each side. "One basket," he said, "and it is for me."

Evan wanted a picnic in the backyard. He got his basket and his red trike. He would ride the trike to the big tree.

First he went to his little desk. Mom kept the picnic things there. He put in one apple. He put in one banana. He put in one cracker. Apples, bananas and crackers are foods. Foods go in a picnic basket.

Then he saw his blue ball. The ball went in too. Then his toy duck went in. Then his drum went in. The basket got very full. It was too heavy to ride with.

Buster the dog ran up. He sniffed the basket. He barked and barked. Evan thought about it. Buster did not bark at the ball. He did not bark at the duck. He barked at the apple. "Buster smells the food," said Evan. Dogs like to smell foods.

So Evan took out the toys. He rolled the ball under the tree. He set the duck on the grass. He kept the foods in the basket. Now the basket was light. Evan rode his trike to the tree.

He sat and ate his favorite apple. Buster sat with him. "One apple, one banana, one cracker," said Evan. Buster wagged his tail and got a tiny bite.

Isabelle went to the farm with her grandma. Grandma had a gift in her bag. It was a shiny little bell. Grandma hid it behind the hay.

"Find the bell," said Grandma. Isabelle looked at the cows. She looked at the hens. No bell yet. So Isabelle used her eyes to look. "My eyes find things," she said. Then she saw something shiny by the red boot. "The bell! My eyes found it."

Grandma rang the bell. Ding, ding! "My ears heard it," said Isabelle. She covered her ears. The sound went away. She took her hands off. Ding! The sound came back. "My ears hear sounds," she said.

Then Grandma held out fresh bread. Farmer Joe had begun to bake it that morning. Isabelle smelled it with her nose. "My nose smells bread," she said. She touched the soft bread with her fingers. "My fingers feel soft." She took a little bite. "My tongue tastes it. Yum!"

A small goat walked up. It nibbled Isabelle's hair. Isabelle laughed. "Goat, that is my hair!" The goat blinked at her. Grandma laughed too. Ding, ding, went the shiny bell.

Josephine sat down for soup time at daycare. Her bowl was big. Max had a small cup. The soup was hot. Steam went up, up, up. Josephine wanted to eat now. "Too hot," said Teacher Ann. "We wait." So Josephine waited. She gave her teddy bear a kiss. Then she touched the side of her bowl. Still hot. Max touched his small cup. "Mine is warm now," he said. He ate his soup. It went fast. Josephine touched her big bowl again. Still hot. She waited some more. She watched the steam get small. At last the bowl felt warm. "The big bowl got cold slow," said Josephine. "The small cup got cold fast." She took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "Worth the wait."

Alexis sat at the big table. He had a heavy red truck in his pocket. Mom had helped him wash his hands before dinner. His ears could hear the spoons clink.

At school, Mia had grabbed the truck. Alexis had grabbed it back. Then Mia cried. Then Alexis cried too. The teacher gave the truck a spot on the shelf. She said they could each have a turn. Alexis waited. He counted to ten. Mia pushed the truck down the ramp. Then Alexis had his turn. He pushed it too. The truck rolled far. Mia clapped.

"Dinner is ready," said Dad. Alexis put the truck on the table. "Mia, your turn," he said. He slid the truck to his baby sister. She laughed and held it with both hands. Alexis counted to ten. One, two, three. His sister gave the truck back. "My turn," said Alexis. He made the truck drive over the bread.

Jacob stood in the bathroom. His new toothbrush was lost. "I want my blue toothbrush," he said. Daddy was there, brushing his own teeth.

Jacob looked with his eyes. He saw the sink. He saw the big mirror. No toothbrush. He listened with his ears. He heard water drip, drip, drip. No toothbrush. He touched the furry bath mat with his hands. It was soft. No toothbrush there. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled Daddy's minty toothpaste. "Mmm," said Jacob.

Then Jacob closed his eyes to guess. He reached for his cup. He missed it. The cup fell over. Clang! "Oh," said Jacob. "I missed it because my eyes were shut." He opened his eyes and picked it up. There, behind the cup, was the blue toothbrush! Jacob smiled. He put a little paste on it. He brushed his teeth. His tongue tasted the mint. "Minty," he said. Daddy said, "All clean, little man." Jacob spat, rinsed, and held Daddy's hand all the way to bed.

Ivy went to the library with Dad. She wanted to draw a cat on the new tablet. Dad said, "First you press the little round button." Ivy pressed it. The screen stayed dark. "Oh no," said Ivy. "The cat is asleep!" Dad laughed.

Then Dad showed her the button on top. Ivy slid it to the side. The screen woke up. "The button has to say green," said Ivy. She tapped the green dot. A picture of a paint brush came up. She tapped it. Now she could draw! She drew a cat with big ears and a hat.

At the end, Dad said, "Time to put it away." Ivy pressed the top button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in its basket. "In summer I will draw the cat again," she said. Dad said, "It will remember your cat." Ivy whispered, "Good night, cat."

Jaxon put on his red hat. The big game was on TV today! Aunt May came with chips. Grandpa came with a whistle. Even the boy next door came to watch.

Then the TV went dark. "Oh no," said Jaxon. "The game is lost!" Everyone looked for the problem. Grandpa looked behind the couch. Jaxon looked under the rug. He found his toy turtle there, but no game.

Jaxon marched into the kitchen. There was Dad, holding the TV plug. "The fan needed the plug," said Dad. "So the TV went off." One plug, one dark TV. Jaxon got it. "Put it back, Dad!" he yelled. Dad plugged in the TV. The game came back, big and bright.

The crowd on TV got loud. The buzzer went beep, beep, beep. "That means someone scored!" said Jaxon. Grandpa blew his little whistle. Aunt May jumped up. Chips went everywhere. Jaxon hugged his turtle and cheered too. "We win," he said. "All of us!"

Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread and fresh milk. A farmer gave Ezra a cup of juice too.

At home, Dad cut the warm bread into toast. "Can I teach you to butter it?" Dad asked. Ezra took the knife. He pushed hard. The toast tore. "Why did it rip?" Ezra asked. Dad gave him a new piece. The toast was warm and soft. Ezra touched it. The butter went soft too. It sat flat on the bread. He slid the knife gently. The butter spread all over. "Warm toast makes butter soft," Ezra said. He said it again. "Warm toast makes butter soft!"

Then Ezra poured the milk. He held the cup up high. Milk splashed out. He put the cup on the table, low and still. He poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. "Low cup, slow pour," said Ezra. He poured Dad's milk next. Not one drop.

Dad took a big bite of toast. "Mmm," said Dad. "More, please."

Leah went to the library with her mom. She wanted a book about dogs. Leah loved dogs. She loved their soft fur and wet noses.

She looked on a shelf. She found books about bears, cats and ducks. "So many animals," said Leah. The animal books all sat together on one shelf. That was why she could not find dogs at first. Dogs were animals too! Dogs were with the cats!

Next to that shelf was a shelf of toys. Cars, balls and blocks had their own books too. Then Leah found a shelf of food books. Apples, bread and eggs sat together in a big picture book.

Then Leah saw a book with a face on it. The face had a big nose and ugly green bumps. "What is that?" she asked. It was a book about frogs! Leah patted the frog picture. "Hello, frog," she said. "You are an animal too. You sit with the dogs."

Mom smiled. "Which book do you want, Leah?" Leah held the dog book in one hand. She held the frog book in the other hand. "Both," said Leah. "Animals are my favorite."

Sienna sat at the big camp table. She was making a sun out of paper. The sun needed yellow paper, glue, and a paper bag for the scraps.

First she cut a big circle. Then she squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. So much glue came out! The paper got very wet and shiny.

She spread the glue with her hand. Now her hand was dirty and sticky. "Sticky, sticky, sticky," she sang. Her friend Leo laughed. "Your hand is a glue hand!" he said.

Then Sienna tried to pick up her sun. The wet paper tore. "Oh no!" she said. "My sun ripped!"

She looked at the torn sun. Then she looked at the glue bottle. She thought and thought. "Too much glue makes paper wet," she said. "Wet paper rips!"

Next she made a new sun. This time she made one small dot of glue. Just one dot. The paper stayed dry. The sun did not rip. It was a good sun.

Leo held up his art. His paper had ripped too. There was a hole right in the middle. But Leo grinned and peeked through the hole with one eye. "Look!" he said. "My ripped paper is a mask!"

Sienna peeked through her old torn sun too. "Two masks!" she said. Then she hung her new sun on the wall, right up high.

Jasper wanted to feed the fish in his little tank. He put his hand in the toy box. He pulled out a toy banana. He held it over the water.

"Fish do not eat toy bananas," said Grandma. "Toys are not food."

Jasper looked at the banana. It was hard and shiny. It could not be lunch. He had a problem now. What do fish eat?

He went to the kitchen with Grandma. He saw real food there. Apples, bread, and a small can of fish flakes. "I guess the fish eat this," Jasper said.

He was gentle with the little flakes. He dropped three into the tank. The fish swam fast. It gobbled them up.

"Toys are for playing," said Jasper. "Food is for eating." The fish wiggled its tail at him.

Lea sat at the big art table. She was making a picture of a cat. One cat, two ears, three whiskers on each side. She squeezed the glue bottle to stick on paper eyes. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out like a white river.

Lea pressed the paper eyes down. They slid off. She pressed again. They slid again. The paper got wet and floppy. Lea felt worried. "My cat is falling apart," she said. Miss Amy came over. She sat close by Lea. "Let's look together," she said.

Lea looked at the glue bottle. It was almost full when she started. Now it was nearly empty. "I used too much glue," Lea said. "Wet glue makes paper slip and slide." Miss Amy smiled. "Yes. A little dot will hold," she said.

Miss Amy helped Lea cut a new cat. Lea made one small dot for each eye. One dot, two dots, three dots for the whiskers. She waited a bit. The glue got sticky, not wet. The eyes stayed on. The cat was done, just as the bell rang for snack. Miss Amy said, "You can cook your lunch story later, and this little cat can come too." Lea hugged the cat to her chest. "He is my baby cat," she said. "He will ride in my bag."

Ellie sat at the big table. Everyone was there. Grandma was there. Grandpa was there too.

The food smelled good. Ellie wanted to eat now. But Mom held her hand and said, "We wait. We say our blessing first."

Ellie folded her hands like Mom. But she did not know the words. She looked down at her plate. Everyone was quiet and waiting.

Grandpa smiled at her. He said the words slowly. "Thank you for our food." Ellie listened. Grandpa said the words again. "Thank you for our food."

Ellie tried too. "Thank you for... food," she said. Her words were a little different. But that was okay. Grandpa clapped. "Good try, Ellie!"

Then everyone said it together. "Thank you for our food." Ellie said it with them. She said every word. "The food comes after the words," Ellie said. "First we say it. Then we eat."

Mom kissed her head. "That's right, Ellie." The bowls went around the table. Grandpa put warm rice in Ellie's bowl.

After dinner, Ellie helped Mom bathe the baby. She sang the blessing to him. "Thank you for our food." The baby kicked his feet in the water.

"Say it again," said Grandpa from the door.

Ellie said it again.

Sofia climbed into the car. She held her favorite toy bunny. "Today I see the dentist!" she said. "Hurry, Daddy, hurry!"

Daddy drove fast but safe. Sofia looked out the window. She saw the dentist building. It had a big tooth on the sign!

The dentist had a little mirror on a stick. "Open wide," she said. Sofia opened her mouth very wide. The mirror bounced light inside. Now the dentist could see all the way back. "I can count your teeth!" she said. "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

"Twenty!" said Sofia. "I have twenty teeth because I opened wide!"

Then the dentist gave her a sticker. But that was not all. In the box was a tiny tooth toy for bunny! Sofia laughed and held it up. "Bunny opened wide too," she said.

Rehmat sat on the playroom floor. She wanted her teddy. She could not find him. "Do not worry," said Mama. "Let us look."

Rehmat put two cars on the ramp. The big car went down fast. The small car went down slow. "Big car is fast!" she said. Then she saw it. The big car had stopped by a big box. The big box was too heavy to lift. Rehmat felt grumpy. Her teddy was inside, she was sure.

Mama helped her tip the box over. Out came teddy, warm from sitting near the sunny window. Rehmat touched him. "Teddy is hot," she said. Mama brought a cool cloth. Soon teddy felt cold and nice. On teddy's paw was a letter, the letter R, just like her name. Rehmat pointed at it and laughed. "R is for Rehmat!" She hugged teddy tight and sat close to Mama.

Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make pancakes for his family. Grandma said, "Let's cook them together."

Parker mixed the flour and milk. Then he poured batter into the hot pan. The pancake came out pale and soft. Grandma said, "It is not done yet. Watch the bubbles." Parker waited. Little bubbles popped up all over the top. "Now flip it," said Grandma. Parker flipped it with the spatula. The other side turned golden brown. "The bubbles mean it is ready to flip," said Parker. Grandma smiled.

Then Parker saw a bird at the window. It was building a nest in the big blue pot by the door. "The bird needs some string," said Parker. He put soft string on the step. The bird took it for her nest.

Dad came in from the porch. He had let his bike ride down the hill and back. "Something smells good," said Dad. Parker set the table with blue plates. Everyone ate the pancakes. Dad took a big bite and said, "These are the best ones yet."

Weston wanted to play house in the backyard. He set his teddy bear on a square blanket. "You be my baby," he said. Weston stirred dirt and water in a pot. That was pretend soup for lunch.

Then teddy fell off the blanket. He landed in the wet grass. Weston ran to him. "Are you okay?" he asked. He hugged teddy close. "Sorry I put you near the edge," he said. Weston found out why teddy fell. The blanket was on a hill. The hill made teddy slide down.

So Weston moved the blanket to the flat square of patio. He set teddy in the middle. "Now you will stay," he said. Mom sat on the step and watched. Weston fed teddy his pretend soup, one spoonful at a time. "Time for bed, baby," Weston whispered.

Audrey sat on the little red mat. She wanted to find a book about bears. But she could not read the words yet. Her arm reached up to a shelf, and she pulled down a big book. It was stuck between two others, so she tugged it free.

On the cover was a letter she knew. It was B. "B says buh," she said softly. She looked at the word under it. The first letter was B. "Buh, buh, bear!" she said. She had found the bear book.

Then she did it again. A book with D on the front. "D says duh," she said. "Duh, duh, dog!" That one was about dogs. Audrey hugged the book. "The first letter tells me," she whispered. She carried both books to the cozy corner to read.

Sadie ran to the playground with her grandma. The sun was hot on the slide. Sadie put her hand near it. The slide felt hot, too. "Ouch," said Sadie. She pulled her hand back fast.

Grandma sat on a short bench under a tree. Sadie wanted to slide. She waited. She touched the slide again. Still hot. She waited some more. A cloud came and covered the sun. Sadie touched the slide one more time. Now it felt cool. "The sun made it hot," said Sadie. "The cloud made it cool." She climbed up and slid down. Whee!
