Then Sadie saw something shiny in the sand. It was a piece of glass. She almost picked it up. But glass can cut fingers. Sadie did not touch it. She ran to grandma and held her hand. They walked back together, slow and easy.

A little dog ran by. It turned around and licked Sadie's nose. Sadie laughed and laughed. "Again," she said. "Do it again."

Aubrey sat in the school computer lab. In front of her was a black tablet. It did not look at her. It was dark and still.

"I want to draw a cat," said Aubrey.

The teacher said, "Try the little round button."

Aubrey found the button on the side. She pushed it. She waited. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen woke up. It was bright. The tablet was on because she pushed the button! "I did it," said Aubrey.

Next she looked for the drawing app. She saw a little orange square. She tapped it with one finger. The page opened. It was white and empty. Aubrey picked a green color. Then she picked yellow. The green and yellow mixed into something new on the screen. It looked like grass in the sun. She drew a big cat on the grass.

A boy next to her had a dark screen. He looked sad. Aubrey showed him her button. He pushed it and counted, "One, two, three." His screen woke up too.

Then it was time to go. The teacher said, "Put the tablets away."

Aubrey pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She slid the tablet into the soft blue basket, just like that. "Bye bye, cat," she said.

Alexander wanted to draw with his new pencil. Mom was cooking soup in the kitchen. The pot went "pssss" on the hot stove. Alexander stood next to Mom. He held her apron with one hand.

"Can I see the soup?" he asked. "You can look from here," said Mom. "The pot is hot. Hot things can hurt you." Alexander looked at the steam. The steam went up like a little cloud. He put his hand near, but not close. He felt warm air. He pulled his hand back. "It is hot because the stove makes it hot," said Alexander. Mom smiled. "Yes, that is right."

Then Alexander sat at the table. He drew the pot and the steam with his pencil. He drew Mom too. Mom put a cold cup of water beside him. He touched the cup. It felt cold. "Cold is safe for my hands," he said. Mom clapped. "You learned something new today!" The sun came in the window. It was a sunny day, and the soup smelled good. "Lunch is ready," said Mom.

Josephine ran straight to the story corner at the library. Today was song day! But the singing lady was not there yet. Josephine wanted to sing "One, two, buckle my shoe." She could not remember what came next.

She looked on the shelf. She pulled out one red book. Then two books. Then three, four, five. Soon her pile was very big. The singing lady came in and laughed. "What a big pile!" she said. "Let's count it together."

They pointed and sang. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The numbers came out in the same order every time! Josephine said, "The words go in a line, like the books!"

She stacked the books in a straight, tall tower. Then she found a book about doctors and medicine to take home. "Ten books is too many," said the singing lady. Josephine giggled and put eight back. "Two to keep," she said. "One, two!"

Julia went to the band room at school. She saw a big drum, a small drum, and a shiny flute. Julia wanted to play the big drum. Its name was Boomer. The teacher let her try.

Julia hit Boomer very, very hard. The sound was so loud. She jumped back and put her hands over her ears. The loud boom made her friend Sam cry. Sam was upset. Julia was upset too. She did not want to hurt his ears.

Julia looked at her drumstick. She tried again. She tapped Boomer soft and slow. Boooom. A gentle sound came out. Then she tapped a little harder. The boom got a little bigger. Julia smiled. "Soft tap, small boom," she said. "Hard hit, big boom!"

Sam came close. Julia handed him a drumstick. "Tap soft," she said. Sam tapped soft. The drum said boooom, nice and low. Sam laughed and laughed. Julia gave him a hug.

Then they tapped together, soft, soft, soft. Boomer sang like thunder far away.

Evan ran to Grandma's fridge. Magnets lived there, all different letters. Evan wanted to find the letter E. It was his letter, the first letter of his name.

He searched and searched. So many letters! He found M and A. He found a B that looked a bit shy, hiding behind a pot. Then he saw it. E! He jumped up and down. "Grandma, I found E!" He held it high like a trophy.

"E says eh," said Evan, and he said it loud. "Eh, eh, eh, like Evan!" Grandma laughed and clapped. A feather from her hat floated down. Evan tried to catch it. It made him laugh too. Then he climbed onto a chair and put the E right at the top of the fridge. "E for Evan stays up high," he said. "The E found me because it has three little lines, and I know it now!"

The big blue bookmobile came to Matthew's street. Matthew held his mama's hand. He had a new card in his fist. It was his very first library card.

"I want a book about trucks," said Matthew. The librarian found a red truck book. Matthew hugged it tight. "This book is mine now," he said. "I keep it forever."

"You can take it home," said the librarian. "But you must bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Matthew held the truck book close. He did not want to let it go. At bedtime he read it three times. In the morning, he read it again.

The next week, the bookmobile came back. Beep, beep! Matthew ran to the door. He gave the truck book to the librarian.

A girl was there. She took the truck book. She sat down to read it. "She likes my truck book," said Matthew. He gave a big smile.

Mama helped him pick a new book. It was about a duck. A loose duck feather fell out of the pages. "A feather!" said Matthew.

The bookmobile drove away. Matthew waved. "Come back soon!" he called. He began to sing a little duck song. His mama sang too, all the way home.

Henry ran into his classroom. His backpack was heavy. It had crayons and a toy car inside.

Henry looked at the wall. Many little boxes sat there. Each box had a name on it. Henry put his backpack in a box. Then a girl came. "That is my box," she said. "It says Mia."

Henry looked. Yes. The name said Mia. "Where is my box?" he asked. Mia pointed. "Find your name."

Henry walked slow. He touched each name with his finger. Sam. Nina. Ben. Then he saw it. Henry. His name was on a blue box.

"My name is on my box," Henry said. "That is how I know it is mine." He put his heavy backpack inside. The box was just right.

Later the teacher said, "Time for pretend play." Henry grabbed a kit. It had a bandage in it. "I will be the doctor," he said. "My teddy has a sick paw."

Mia held out the teddy. "Can you fix him?" she asked.

"Yes," said Henry. "I will touch his paw. Then he gets a bandage." He stuck it on. The teddy looked very brave.

Myles sat at the little table in art class. Sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Myles wanted to make a paper boat. He wanted it to roll to his friend Sam.

Myles cut a square for the boat. Then he cut two more squares for wheels. He taped them on. He pushed the boat. The boat did not roll. It stopped. It tipped over on its side.

Myles looked across the room. Mia had a toy car. Her car rolled far. Myles looked at the wheels. Her wheels were round like a ball. "Your wheels are circles," Myles said. Mia smiled. "Circles roll," she said.

Myles cut two circles. He taped them on his boat. He pushed the boat again. The boat rolled across the table. It rolled right to Sam. Sam laughed and clapped.

"My boat rolls now," said Myles. "The squares made it stop. The circles make it go." He hopped down from his chair. He rolled the boat back home. The round wheels went round and round.

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist had a fuzzy puppet with big white teeth. Grace held it and laughed.

Then the dentist said, "You get a cookie after your checkup." Grace wanted that cookie very much. But the dentist said, "First, wash your hands."

Grace looked at her hands. They looked clean. "Do germs hide on them?" she asked.

"Let's find out," said the dentist. He took her to the sink. Grace put soap on her hands. The dentist said, "Now we count to twenty." Grace rubbed and counted. One, two, three. The bubbles grew soft and white. At twenty, she rinsed. The bubbles and germs went down the drain.

"I get it," said Grace. "The soap needs time to catch the germs." She dried her hands and ate her cookie. It tasted sweet.

After the cookie, Grace drank her cup of ice water. "Do I wash again after the toilet too?" she asked.

"Yes," said the dentist. "Twenty seconds, every time." Grace smiled at the fuzzy puppet. "Ready, germs? Nowhere to hide!"

Ibrahim went to Zayd's house. Zayd had a tablet. Ibrahim wanted to draw on it. But the screen was dark and still. He tapped it. Nothing happened. He tapped again. Still nothing.

"Press the round button," said Zayd. "Hold it down." Ibrahim pressed the little round button. He held his finger there. One, two, three. The screen lit up, bright and warm like sunshine. "It woke up!" said Ibrahim. "My finger made it wake up."

Zayd showed him a green square with a crayon on it. "Tap this," he said. "It is the drawing app." Ibrahim tapped it. Now he could draw. He drew a big red circle. He drew a silly cat with three eyes. "Your cat looks surprised," laughed Zayd. Ibrahim drew a blue square shape next. Then a yellow one. "I learn fast," he said proudly.

When he finished, the tablet began to blink. "Oh no, it is tired," said Ibrahim. "Batteries get low," said Zayd. "We must put it away." Ibrahim pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. He set the tablet on the shelf, soft and safe. "Sorry, tablet," he whispered. "Sleep well, tired friend."

Jayden wanted to give his mom a present. He found a small ice cube in his cup. "This can be my present," he said. He put it in his hand.

The ice felt very cold. Jayden shivered a little. Then he saw steam rising from the pot on the stove. The pot was hot. He did not touch the pot. Mama had told him, hot things can hurt you.

Jayden wanted to show Mama his ice present. He walked to the door. Then he remembered, stay close to Mama. So he stayed in the kitchen. He sat down on his little stool.

The ice began to melt in his warm hand. Drip, drip, drip. Soon there was only water. "Oh no," said Jayden. "My ice is gone."

Mama looked at his wet hand. "The ice melted because your hand is warm," she said. "Would you like a new present to give me?" Jayden nodded. They picked a red crayon together. Jayden drew a big red heart. He gave the paper to Mama. "A present for you," he said. Mama smiled and put it on the door.

Joshua went to Mia's house. Mia had a big toy kitchen. Joshua wanted to make soup too.

Mia said, "First we need a pot." She put the pot on the little stove. Joshua put in a red ball. That was the tomato.

Joshua stirred and stirred. He used a big wooden spoon. Round and round went the spoon.

"Where is the door to the oven?" Joshua asked. Mia pointed. Joshua peeked in. Oh! The oven was cold. Was that okay? Mia said the pretend oven could not get hot. That is why it was safe.

Then Baby Bear got sick. Joshua held Baby Bear. "Baby needs a nap," he said. He patted Baby Bear's back, soft and slow. Baby Bear's eyes closed.

"Why did Baby Bear go to sleep?" Joshua wondered. He patted again. Slow patting made Baby Bear sleepy. Fast patting woke Baby Bear up! Joshua laughed.

He patted slow, slow, slow. Baby Bear slept and slept. Baby looked so tired after the long day.

Joshua gave Baby Bear a blanket. He made pretend soup for Mia too. Round and round, the spoon went swish.

Then Daddy Bear came home. Mia made a big voice, "I'm home!" Joshua ran to the door. He opened it wide.

Daddy Bear said, "Something smells good!"

Charlotte was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the rug. Charlotte wanted to draw a big hill on it. But the screen was dark and blank.

Mia said, "Press the little button on top." Charlotte pressed it. The screen lit up. "The button makes it turn on," said Charlotte.

She pressed the round blue spot. The drawing app opened. Charlotte drew a green hill and a yellow sun. She took her time. She drew a small cat on the hill too.

Then the drawing was done. "Now we put it away," said Mia. Charlotte pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She heard the soft click.

"Can I do it one more time?" asked Charlotte. "Yes," said Mia. "The button works every time." Charlotte pressed it, and the sun came back.

Sarah ran into the library. She wanted a puppy book! "Where are the puppy books?" she asked Mom.

Mom pointed to a big shelf. Sarah saw a picture of a cat on a sign. She bent down to look. Cat books, bunny books, bird books! All the animals sat on one shelf.

But one book was in the wrong spot. It was a book about cake. Cake is food, not an animal! Sarah held it. The cover felt rough. She carried it to the food shelf. Apples, bread, milk, all together.

"The cake book goes here," said Sarah. "Animals go with animals. Food goes with food."

A librarian smiled. "Thank you, Sarah!"

Sarah ran back to the animal shelf. She found the puppy book! She hugged it tight.

"Puppy books live with the animals," she said. "That is why I found him!"

Max sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to write his name. His brother had a new pencil for him.

Max grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He tried to write an M. The pencil wobbled. The M looked like a squiggle. Max frowned at it.

He watched his brother write. His brother held the pencil near the tip. He used just two fingers and his thumb. Max looked at his own hand. He held his pencil way up high, far from the point. He slid his fingers down, close to the tip. He pinched it with two fingers and his thumb.

Max wrote an M. It did not wobble. "It holds still now," Max said. "My fingers are close to the point." He wrote an A, then an X. He wrote M-A-X three more times.

The ink had to dry, so Max waited. Then he held the paper up. "Look, brother! It says Max!"

Nicholas wanted to play house at Grandma's house. He looked for a baby doll. He found a box under Grandma's bed. He counted the dolls inside. "One, two, three," he said. But all the dolls looked grumpy. Their faces were flat and sad.

"Why are the dolls sad?" he asked. Grandma said, "Maybe they need a mama." Nicholas tried holding a doll like a baby. He wrapped it in a small towel. He rocked it in his arms. Then the doll's head fell back. It looked right at him with a smile. The towel made the head stay up!

Nicholas picked up the second doll. He wrapped it too. He rocked it and sang a little song. Grandma clapped her hands. "The towel makes the head stay up," said Nicholas. "Now all my babies can smile." He gave the third doll a big hug.

Willow ran to the play corner at school. She wanted to play house. Her friend Milo was there too. "You be the dad," said Willow. "I will be the mom."

Willow picked up the baby doll. The doll's eyes were open. "The baby is awake," said Willow. "She needs a nap."

She wrapped the doll in a small blanket. She rocked it in her arms. She sang a soft song. But the doll's eyes would not close. Willow looked at the doll. The eyes stayed open because the doll was lying flat on her knee!

Willow sat the doll up. Then she tipped her back slowly. Click! The eyes shut. "The baby is asleep," said Willow.

Milo tiptoed over. "Shh," he said. "Let's make soup now." Willow smiled and put the doll in the little bed.

Gianna was at Milo's birthday party. A big dig truck sat on the toy table. It had a long arm and a scoop. Gianna wanted it. She grabbed for it. But Ben had it first. He held on tight. The truck stopped moving.

"You both pulled," said Milo's mom. "The truck has to wait for calm hands." Gianna let go. She sat on her hands. "Can we take turns?" she asked. "Yes," said Ben. "You can dig the sand first."

Gianna dug a hole with the scoop. She piled the sand thin and tall. Then she gave the truck to Ben. He made a big hill. Then it was her turn again. "Why does the truck work now?" she asked. "Because we take turns!" she said. Turn, turn, turn. They played until the cake came out.

Olivia went to the garden center with Dad. She held a little tray of seeds. The sun was warm on her nose. There were tomatoes, carrots, and beans. Olivia wanted to grow beans best.

She filled a pot with soft brown soil. Her hands smelled like dirt and rain. She pushed three bean seeds into the pot. Then she set the pot in the shade under a table. Dad said, "Put it in the sun, too." So Olivia put the pot in a sunny spot.

A loud truck came by the gate. It dropped off many bags of soil. The truck honked and rolled away. Olivia did not jump this time. Dad was holding her hand.

Every day Olivia gave the pot a little water. On day five, a green sprout popped up. It bent toward the sunny window. "Look, Dad! It is leaning to the light!" Olivia turned the pot around. The next day the sprout bent back to the sun. "The sun pulls it," she said.

But then the hot weather came. One leaf turned brown and dry. "Dad, the leaf burns in the hot sun!" Dad nodded. "So we move it to the shade at noon." They moved the pot together. The leaf rested in the cool shade. Olivia patted the soil gently. "Grow, little bean," she said. "I will keep you safe." The sprout stood tall and green in the evening light.

Ivy came to the cemetery with Mama and Nana. They brought a picnic basket. They sat on a dry, soft blanket near Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone felt warm in the sun.

Nana opened the basket. She took out bread, cheese, and little cakes. "We eat first," said Ivy, reaching for a cake. Mama held her hand gently. "Wait," said Mama. "At Grandpa Ben's stone, we say our family blessing first. We say thank you before we eat."

Nana held out her hands. Ivy put her small hands in theirs. One hand was warm. One hand was soft. "Now we all say it together," said Nana. Nana said the words. Mama said the words. Ivy did not know the words yet. She listened. "Thank you for the sun. Thank you for the food. Thank you for family."

Then Nana said, "Now we eat." Ivy picked up a cake. It was sweet and good. "I want to choose a cake for Grandpa Ben," said Ivy. Nana helped her set one little cake on the flat stone. Ivy put her hand on the warm rock. "We hold hands, then we talk, then we eat," said Ivy. Nana gave her a big smile. "Yes," said Nana. "That is how our blessing goes." Ivy licked the crumbs from her fingers. "Again next time," she said.

Maverick went to Grandma's house. He heard a little sound. "Waah, waah." It came from the toy box. Grandma held his hand. "It is just your baby doll," she said. "The doll is not really sad. But you can pretend."

Maverick picked up the doll. He held it like Grandma showed him. He gave the doll a bottle. It was empty, but he tipped it anyway. He made a little sip sound. The crying stopped. Maverick looked up big-eyed. "The doll stopped crying because I fed her," he said.

Then he gave the doll a toy pig to hug. The doll patted the pig. "Say thank you," said Maverick. He made the doll's voice soft and polite. "Thank you."

Grandma smiled. She sat in the old swing on the porch. Maverick sat close with his baby. The swing went back and forth. The doll went to sleep. So did the little pig.

Emma stood at the little table by the tent. Daddy was there too. He had a sharp knife, and he cut the bananas. Emma kept her hands far away from the sharp part.

Now it was Emma's turn to cook. She poured pancake mix into the pan. The pan sat on the camp stove. It was getting hot. Emma waited. A frog hopped by her shoe. She watched the pan, not the frog.

Then Emma saw little holes in the pancake. Bubbles! Big bubbles came up. Daddy said, "Now flip it, Emma." She turned the pancake over with the spatula. It was not runny anymore. It puffed up big and round. "The bubbles made it ready," said Emma. Daddy smiled. They put the pancake on a plate. Emma took a tiny taste. "Yum!" she said. "More for Mommy too!" The frog hopped away into the grass.

Anna lost her toy robot. She felt sad. "Where did it go?" she asked.

Anna used her eyes to look. She saw the bed. She saw the chair. No robot there. Then Anna used her ears. She heard a little beep, beep. "Is that my robot?" she said. "Yes, it is!" The robot beeped because she had pushed its button before she put it down.

Anna followed the sound. The beeps came from the basket of socks. She used her hands to touch the soft socks. Something hard was under them. She pulled it out. It was her robot!

Anna hugged it. "My nose did not find you," she said. "My ears did!" Then Mommy called, "Snack time!" Anna smelled apples. She used her tongue to taste a sweet bite. She touched the robot's button. Beep, beep!

Jake wanted to play house. He had a teddy bear, a blanket, and a small cup. But his teddy bear looked sad on the floor.

Jake picked up the teddy bear. He wrapped it in the gray blanket. He held it like a baby. "Time for milk," he said. He tipped the little cup to its mouth. Then he patted its back, soft and slow.

The teddy bear still sat crooked. It kept sliding down. Jake tried again and again. Then he saw why. The blanket was too big. It pushed the bear out of his arms.

Jake folded the blanket in half. Now it was small. He wrapped the bear snug and tight. The bear stayed put in his arms.

"See, Robot?" Jake said to his toy robot on the shelf. "Big blanket made you slip. Small blanket helps you stay." He rocked the bear side to side. The room felt quiet and warm.

Robot watched with his shiny gray eyes. Jake sang a tiny song. "Sleep now, baby bear," he whispered. The bear's head rested on Jake's shoulder.

Austin ran to the big slide at the playground. The sun was hot on his hands. He touched the slide. "Ow! Hot!" said Austin. He could not go down alone.

Dad came with a water bottle. He poured cold water on the slide. Splash! The water ran down, down, down. Austin touched the slide again. Now it felt cold. The hot sun made the slide hot. The cold water made it cool. "Big slide, big splash," said Austin.

Austin climbed up slowly. Then he went down fast. Whee! A little dog ran by the fence. It was small, like a toy horse. "Fast dog, slow me," said Austin. He slid down one more time. Dad held out his arms. Austin landed right in them.

Nova went to her friend Milo's house. It was still early. The sun was just coming up. Nova had brought her baby doll. The doll was small and soft.

"Let's play house," said Milo. Nova held her doll. "The baby is crying," she said. "She needs milk." But Nova had no bottle. Milo looked around the room. He found a yellow block. "This can be the bottle," he said. Nova tipped the block to the doll's mouth. She made little drinking sounds. "There, there," she said softly. The doll went quiet. Nova smiled. "The baby stopped crying because we fed her," she said.

Then Milo put chairs in a row. "This is our bus," he said. "You can drive, Nova. I will hold the baby." Nova sat at the front. She turned a plate for the wheel. The cat crawled under the chairs. It rode on the bus too. "Next stop, the park!" said Nova. Milo laughed and bounced the doll on his lap. "One ticket for the baby, please," he said. "And one fish ticket for the cat."

Liam ran to the toy box at daycare. "Truck!" he shouted. He felt so excited. His tummy jumped like a bunny.

Then Ben grabbed the truck. "My truck!" said Ben. Liam's face got hot. His hands made fists. He was angry. He wanted to push Ben. He stomped his foot. It was very loud.

Miss Rosa came over. "Liam, you look angry," she said. "Big breaths help." She took a big breath in. Liam copied her. He breathed in. He breathed out. His fists opened. His tummy felt slow and calm now. "The big breath made the angry go small," said Liam. "Yes," said Miss Rosa. "You did it all by yourself." She helped him pat Ben's back gently. "Truck please?" asked Liam. Ben smiled. The room was noisy and warm. Liam and Ben rolled the truck on the rug together.

Emile runs into art class. Today he wants to paint a house. A big house with windows!

He dips his round brush in paint. He moves it on the paper. Round and round. The window comes out as a circle. But a circle is round like a ball. House windows are not round like balls.

Emile looks around the table. Nobody is playing with the sponge stamps. He is alone at his spot. He picks up a sponge. It has four flat sides. He taps it in green paint. He presses it on the paper. A square! A window with four flat sides!

He finds a triangle sponge too. Tap, press. A roof! He finds a long rectangle sponge. Tap, press. A door!

"Look, a house!" says Emile. His teacher smiles. She takes out her phone. Click! She took a picture.

Emile points at the circle window. "Round brush makes circles," he says. "Flat sponge makes squares!" He taps the sponge again. One more window goes on the house.

Eva went to the playground with Grandma. The gate was open. Eva ran in fast. "Wait for me," said Grandma. Eva stopped and held Grandma's hand.

Eva wanted to play on the big slide. But the sun was on it. She put her hand near it. The slide was hot. Eva pulled her hand back. "One, two, three," she said. She waited and counted some more. Grandma waited too. Then a cloud came. The slide got cool. Eva touched it. Now it was not hot. She slid down. "The sun made it hot," said Eva. "The cloud made it cool."

Next to the slide, Eva saw a shiny can on the ground. She did not touch it. She asked Grandma to pick it up. Grandma put it in the bin. "Good girl," said Grandma. Eva counted the swings. "One, two, three, four swings." She found a free one and climbed on. "Stay close, Grandma," said Eva. "I will," said Grandma. "I like to watch you fly."

Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a green leaf for the class tree. But there was no green paint. There was only red, yellow, and blue.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Zoe. She tapped each pot. "Where is green hiding?"

Her brush was polite and waited quietly. Zoe dipped it in yellow. She put yellow on the paper. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She put blue right on top of the yellow.

Something magic happened. The two colours swirled. They held hands. They turned into green!

"Green!" said Zoe. "Yellow and blue make green!"

She painted a big leaf. Then she painted more. She put leaves all over the paper. The class tree filled up with green.

Tom came to look. "How did you do that?" he asked.

Zoe held up her brush like a magic wand. "Yellow plus blue," she whispered. "That is the secret spell."

Sebastian stood in the backyard. Dad put a hoop on the grass. Dad gave him a small beanbag. Sebastian wanted to make it land inside the hoop.

He threw the beanbag hard. It sailed way over the hoop. It landed in the flowers. Sebastian ran and got it.

He tried again, softer this time. The beanbag went up high. It came down. It dropped right into the circle. Sebastian clapped his hands. "It went up, then it came down in!" he said.

Then Dad rolled him a big ball. Sebastian held his arms out stiff. The ball hit his arms and bounced away. His hands were like hard wood.

Dad rolled the ball again. This time Sebastian let his arms go soft, like a pillow. The ball touched his hands and sat there. He had caught it. "My arms are soft, so the ball stays!" said Sebastian.

Two busy little hands held the big ball all the way to Dad.

Ivy ran to the sandbox on a hot summer day. She had ten little stones in her red cup. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then Ivy jumped. The cup tipped over. The stones went spill, spill, spill into the sand.

"Oh no," said Ivy. "My stones are hiding." A boy named Sam came over. He dug with her, slow and careful.

Ivy picked up stones one by one. "One, two, three," she said. She kept going. "Seven, eight, nine." She looked all around. One stone was still lost. It was under the slide. Sam pointed to it.

"Ten!" said Ivy. "All ten are back. Counting tells me if they are all here."

"Count me too," said Sam, and he laughed.

Olivier dug a little hole. He dropped a seed in. Then he patted the dirt on top. His pink boots squished in the mud.

Papa gave Olivier a watering can. Olivier poured water on his seed. "Will it grow now?" he asked. "Let's wait and see," said Papa.

The next day, Olivier ran to the garden. He saw two spots of dirt. One spot was dark and wet. One spot was dry. Where had he poured the water? The wet spot had a tiny green sprout. The dry spot had nothing at all. "Oh!" said Olivier. "The water helped this one. That dry seed got no drink." He poured water on the dry spot too. He patted the dirt gently, like patting a puppy.

On the way home, Papa gave him a cookie. Olivier munched and wondered, "Will my sprout be big tomorrow?" He looked back one more time. The little green sprout stood up tall, like it was waving goodbye.

Eliana was at Grandma's house. She wanted to read her library book forever. The book had a purple cover and a picture of a bear. On the first page, words sat in a row. "Grandma, what do the words say?" she asked. Grandma turned the pages from front to back. She read every word out loud. The words told about a bear who could crawl under a fence. Words were like magic. They talked without a mouth!

Eliana held the book tight. "This book is mine now," she said. But Grandma pointed at a little paper slip inside. The slip had words on it too. Grandma read the words. The book had to go back to the library. Other kids wanted to read it too.

The next day they drove to the library. Eliana gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then the lady smiled and gave it right back. "You can borrow it again," she said. Eliana hugged the purple book. "It comes back to me!" she said. On the way home, she drew a map to the library, with a big bear on it.

Isaac sat in the waiting room. He held his favorite teddy bear. His father sat right next to him. Today Isaac would get a shot. He did not want a shot. "It might pinch," Isaac said. "I will hold your hand," said his father.

A nurse came in. "Squeeze your bear tight," she said. Isaac squeezed the bear. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." It was done! The shot was very fast. Isaac looked at his arm. There was a small round bandage on it. "The bear helped me," Isaac said. "I squeezed him and it went fast!"

Isaac got a sticker with a star on it. He put it on his shirt. His father picked him up. Isaac waved to the nurse. "The shot is done!" he said. Then he hugged his teddy bear tight.

Elena woke up and saw white outside. "Snow! Why is there snow?" She ran to the window. "Because it snowed all night!" School was closed. Mama said, "Let's go play." Elena put on her boots and her big red coat. Outside, the street was quiet and white. She made a snowball. She held it and held it. Then she opened her mitten. "Where did my snowball go?" It was just water! She made another one. Again, it melted in her warm hand. "My hands are warm. Warm hands make snow melt!" She laughed and made one more. She let it sit on the cold sidewalk instead. It stayed a snowball! Down the street, Papa tapped the icicles on the porch. Tap, tap, like a little hammer. An icicle fell down. "Catch it, Elena!" She ran, and the icicle dripped, dripped, dripped in her warm hand. "It's turning to water too!" she shouted. Elena stomped her boots and shouted to the sky, "Warm makes snow melt! Warm makes snow melt!" Mama said hot cocoa was ready. Elena stomped inside, still laughing. The snow stayed out on the cold street. It waited for her.

Matteo woke up when the sky was still dark. "School today," said Mama. Matteo put on his socks. One sock went on his foot. Then the other sock. It took a long time. Mama waited.

Matteo wanted his red truck to come too. "It will not fit in your hand when you paint," said Mama. So Matteo put the truck in his backpack. The zipper went zzzz. The truck was hidden inside. "The backpack holds it," said Matteo. "It is too big for my pocket."

At school, Matteo hung his backpack on a low hook. It was just his size. He painted a big sun. Then he unzipped his backpack. The red truck was still there. "The hook kept my spot," said Matteo. "Truck, we did it."

Jasper had a special red car. He played with it every day. Now the car was gone. "Oh no," said Jasper. He looked and looked.

Miss Maya came to help. "Let's go back where you played," she said. "One, the slide. Two, the sandbox. Three, the big tree." Jasper ran to the slide. No car. He dug in the sandbox. No car. A leaf fell from the big tree. Then he saw something under the leaf. It was his special car!

"The leaf hid it," said Jasper. "The car was there the whole time." Miss Maya smiled. "The car got lost because you left it under the tree," she said. Jasper held the car tight.

Miss Maya had an idea. "Let's fix a pocket for it." She pinned a little pouch on Jasper's shirt. Jasper put the car inside. "Safe now," he said. "One slide, two sandbox, three tree, and my car is home."

William wanted the red truck. His sister Mia had the red truck. She pushed it fast across the floor.

"Can I have a turn?" William asked. Mia said, "Wait for my turn to end." William sat down on the rug. He watched the truck go. He waited and waited.

Soon Mia said, "My turn is done. Now it is your turn." William held the truck. He pushed it fast. It went all the way to the toy box.

"Your turn lasted long," said Mia. "I counted to ten." William counted too. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. "Turn done!" he said. He gave the truck back to Mia.

Mama called, "Dinner time!" William helped Mia shut the toy box. Then they ran to the table together.

"Your turn, then my turn," said William. "That is fair." Mia smiled and hugged him.

Florence found a pink flower in the backyard. She wanted to tell Grandma all about it. But she forgot the words for it.

"Can you guess the words?" asked Grandma. "Let's count your helpers."

Grandma touched Florence's eyes. "One. Eyes see the flower." Florence looked at the pink petals. "Eyes see!" she said.

Grandma touched her ears. "Two. Ears hear." A bee went buzz. Florence laughed. "Ears hear the bee!"

"Three," said Grandma, touching Florence's nose. "Nose smells." Florence sniffed the flower. It smelled sweet. "Nose smells sweet!"

"Four," said Grandma, and she touched Florence's ears again. Florence shook her head. "No! Ears is two!" Grandma giggled. "You got me! Four is your tongue. Tongue tastes."

"Five," said Florence. She touched her own hands. "Hands touch the flower." She petted one soft petal. "Hands touch soft!"

Then Grandma closed Florence's eyes with her fingers. "No peeking. Guess what this is." Florence sniffed. Sweet. "The flower! My nose knows!"

Noah ran onto the green grass. It was soccer practice. Coach Maya held one big blue ball. The ball was blue like the ocean.

Tommy got the ball first. Tommy kicked it to the cone. Noah wanted a turn right away. He ran fast and grabbed the ball with both hands. Tommy fell down and started to cry. Coach Maya blew her whistle. Nobody could play now.

"Noah, look," said Coach Maya. She pointed at Tommy. "When you grab, Tommy falls. Then we all stop." Noah looked at Tommy's sad face. Noah felt mad at first. But then he saw why Tommy cried. "I grabbed too hard," Noah said. "That is why you fell."

Coach Maya had a plan. She held up a paper. "We will write the names down," she said. "Tommy first. Then Noah." She wrote both names with her pen. Noah sat on the grass and waited. He counted to ten. Then Tommy kicked the ball and said, "Your turn, Noah!" Noah kicked it all the way to the far cone.

After practice, Coach Maya gave Noah a big hug. "You waited," she said. "That was hard and you did it." Noah smiled and held her hand. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked.

Rehmat looked out the kitchen window. Snow was falling on the grass. No school today. "Snow day!" said Mama.

Rehmat was hungry. She wanted warm milk. Mama put snow in a small pot. "We will melt it," said Mama. Rehmat counted the snowballs going in. One snowball. Two snowballs. Three snowballs. Mama put the pot on the hot stove. Rehmat waited. She watched and waited.

The snow began to melt. One snowball got small. Two snowballs got small. Then all the snow turned into water. But it was only a little water. "The snow was mostly air," said Mama. Rehmat looked at the tiny bit of water. "Snow is big, but water is small," she said. They melted more snow, one, two, three, four. At last there was enough. Mama warmed the milk. Rehmat drank it slowly. "Snow made my milk," she said, and smiled.

Charles sat at the dinner table. His toe tapped under his chair. "Pancakes now?" he asked.

Mom shook her head. "Pancakes are tomorrow," she said. "Yesterday we had no eggs. Today I went to the store. I got a tiny carton of eggs."

Charles picked up his fork. He looked at his plate. There was rice and chicken on it. "But I want pancakes today," he said.

"We eat dinner now," said Mom. "Later we can have a pear. Pancakes come after sleeping. Tomorrow means after this night."

Charles took one bite of chicken. Then he took another bite. He thought hard. "So yesterday there were no eggs," he said. "Then today you got eggs. So tomorrow we can make pancakes!"

"That is just right," said Mom. She smiled at him. Dad came and sat in his big chair. He gave Charles a tiny piece of pear.

"Now we eat together," said Dad. Charles picked up the pear with his fingers. He put it in his mouth. It was sweet.

"After I sleep, it will be tomorrow," said Charles. "Then pancakes!" He wiggled his happy toe under the table. Mom kissed the top of his head.

Raphael ran to the toy corner at daycare. His friend Mia was rocking a baby doll. The baby had no blanket. Mia said the baby was cold. Raphael wanted to help the baby.

He looked around. What could be a blanket? He saw a thick sock on the floor. It was big and warm. He put the sock over the baby. "Now the baby is warm," said Raphael. Mia rocked the baby some more. The baby went to sleep.

Then Raphael picked up a small block. He held it like a bottle. He tipped it to the baby's mouth. "Baby is hungry," he said. "The block is the milk." Mia clapped her hands. "A block can be a bottle!" she said.

Raphael wondered what else could turn into something new. He looked at his shoe. Could a shoe be a car? He pushed it across the rug. Vroom, vroom! The shoe was a car now. "Thank you, shoe," said Raphael. "You are my fast car."

David woke up and looked out the window. The sky had dropped snow all night long. The grass was gone. The road was white. There was no school today. "Snow day," said Mom. David put on his boots.

Dad helped him fish his red sled out of the shed. "Be careful on the big hill," said Dad. David climbed up. He sat down. He pushed off. But the sled went slow, slow, slow. He looked at the ground. The snow was thin here. He could see little bits of grass. David climbed up again. He dragged the sled to the deep, thick snow. He sat down. He pushed off. The sled went fast, fast, fast.

"I know why," said David. "Thick snow makes me go fast. Thin snow makes me go slow." Dad laughed and waved. David climbed the hill one more time. "Here I go," he said.

Elizabeth ran to the swings at the park. There was only one swing left. A boy was already on it.

Elizabeth wanted that swing very much. Her tummy felt tight. She stood still and watched. The boy swung up high, then down low. Then he stopped and got off. He held the swing out to her.

"You waited, so it is your turn," he said.

Elizabeth sat on the swing. "You waited, so it is your turn," she said to herself. That was why she got the swing. She had waited, not pushed.

After swinging, Elizabeth found her mom on a bench. Mom had a small cake with her. It was a round cake with pink icing. "We will share it," said Mom. Mom cut the cake into two equal pieces. One for Elizabeth, one for Mom. The pieces were the same size. That is what fair means, Elizabeth thought.

A little girl came by. She looked at the cake. Elizabeth looked at her one piece. Then she looked at the girl. Elizabeth broke her piece in two.

"This half is for you," Elizabeth said.

The girl smiled big. She sat down next to Mom on the bench.

"Thank you," said the girl. "I have cookies. You can have one."

Elizabeth took the cookie. It was round like the cake. She bit it, and it was sweet.

"Sharing makes more, not less," said Mom.

Elizabeth ate her cake. The sun was warm. Mom held her hand. The swing went back and forth, all by itself.

Emily sat in her car seat. Her tummy made a big growl. "I want a snack," she said.

Daddy played a game. "Guess what is in the bag," he said. He knocked on the bag, tap tap. Emily giggled. "A cow?" she asked. "No, a cow is an animal. It says moo." Daddy opened the bag. "It is a banana. A banana is food. You can eat it!"

Emily took a bite. Yum. Then she saw something on the window. "A spider!" she said. "Is it food?" Daddy laughed. "No, silly. A spider is an animal too. It lives outside." The spider sat very still. "Are we safe?" Emily asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "The window keeps us safe. The spider cannot get in."

Daddy knocked on the window, tap tap. The spider jumped. Then it crawled away. "Bye bye, spider," said Emily. She waved her banana at it.

Grandpa came to stay at Bennett's house. "How long?" Bennett asked. "One whole week," said Grandpa. "That is seven sleeps." Mom helped Bennett make a paper chain. It had seven red links. Each night, they would tear one off.

In the morning, they went to the market. "Let's try the bread stand," said Grandpa. They got there early. The bread was still warm and fresh. Later they passed a tank with a turtle. The turtle hid in its shell. Bennett clapped, and it hid more. "Too loud," Bennett said. He whispered, and the turtle peeked out. "It comes out because I am quiet," Bennett said. Grandpa nodded.

Each night they tore one link off. One link fell, then two, then three. On the last night, one link was left. Bennett held Grandpa's hand. "Only one more sleep," he said. Grandpa smiled. "Then I will come back soon." Bennett tore the last red link, and they waved it together like a tiny flag.

Today was Ayla's first day of school. She ran into the big cafeteria with her lunchbox. It was winter, so Mom had packed warm soup.

Ayla did not know where to sit. She counted the long tables. One table. Two tables. Three tables. Then she saw a little card on table four. The card said AYLA. "That is my name!" she said. She sat down fast.

Her friend Ben sat across from her. He had warm soup too. Ayla opened her lunchbox. "Smelly broccoli!" she said with a giggle. Ben laughed. Then came the surprise. He opened his box and he had smelly broccoli too!

Ayla clapped her hands. "We are the same!" she said. She took a big bite and said, "I know where my seat is. It has my name!" Ben held up his broccoli. "Broccoli friends!" he said.

Sarah sat at the big table. She wanted to make a paper garden. She had green paper and red paper and little yellow flowers.

Mama gave her the glue. "Just a little bit," said Mama. Sarah squeezed the bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out in a big puddle. It was white and wet and cold on her fingers. She pressed a flower down. The flower slid away. She pressed it again. It slid again.

"Oh no," said Sarah. The paper got soft and yucky. A hole grew where the glue sat. Too much glue made the paper wet. The wet paper tore.

Mama sat down next to her. "We can fix it," said Mama. She gave Sarah a new green paper. "Try one little dot." Sarah made one small dot of glue. She pressed a flower on it. She counted to five. The flower stayed. It did not slide at all.

Sarah made dot after dot. The red tulip stayed. The yellow daisies stayed. Her garden filled up with flowers. "Little dots hold," said Sarah. Mama smiled and hung the garden on the fridge.

Billie ran to the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Billie wore her sun hat. "Why do I need this hat?" she asked. Her mother smiled and pointed up. "The sun is hot," she said. Billie felt her hat keep the sun off her head. "My hat stops the sun!" she said.

Then the wind came. It was a windy day now. The wind grabbed Billie's hat. Off it flew! The hat rolled down the street. "Come back!" Billie shouted. She ran and ran. The wind pushed the hat again. But then the hat hit a bush and stopped. Billie picked it up. "The wind blew my hat because it is light," she said. She held it tight with both hands.

Big clouds came next. Drip, drop. Rain fell. It was a rainy day. Billie had no raincoat. Her mother opened a big umbrella. They stood under it together. Billie put out one hand. Rain tapped her fingers. "The rain can't reach me here!" she said. The rain got the road all wet and shiny.

The bus came at last. Billie climbed up the big steps. She looked out the window. Way up on the hills, she saw white. "What is that?" she asked. Her mother said, "That is snow." Snowy places need thick, warm coats. Billie hugged her own warm coat. "One day I will play in the snow!" she said. The bus went beep, and off they drove.

Maeve sat on the big bus with her grandma. She held her bunny. The bus went bump. The bunny fell down. Maeve could not see it anywhere.

"Oh no," said Maeve. "Bunny is lost."

Grandma held her hand. "Let's look where bunny fell," she said. "Things fall down, and then they stay close." Maeve looked under the seat. She saw something soft. It was bunny! The bus went bump again, and bunny slid a little more. "The bus moves bunny," said Maeve. "Because the floor is not straight." She caught bunny and hugged him tight.

"Good looking," said Grandma. "Bunny is safe now." Maeve smiled. She held bunny all the way home.

Ryan wore his blue sweater to daycare. Outside the window, gray clouds sat low in the sky. Little flakes of snow began to fall.

"Time to clean up," said Miss Kim. Ryan looked for his ten red blocks. He could only see a few. He wanted all ten for his tall tower.

Ryan began to count. "One, two, three." Only three blocks sat on the rug. He looked under the table. "Four, five, six." Three more blocks were hiding there. He looked in the toy box. "Seven, eight, nine." Now he had nine.

One block was still lost. Ryan sang his counting song, the one from circle time. "Eight, nine, ten." He walked slowly around the rug as he sang. There, by the doll house, was block ten.

"The song helps me look," Ryan said. He stacked all ten blocks up, up, up. Outside, the snow fell soft and white.

Lily wants to paint a letter for Mom. It is school time, and the paint table is open.

She takes a big paper. It is as big as her arms. Sam takes a small paper. It is as small as his hand. They paint together. Lily makes red hearts. The paint feels slimy on her fingers. She says, "Big and small, slimy paint, here we go."

Lily wants to put her letter in her bag. But the paint is wet. It will smush. Teacher says, "Let's put them in the sun." The sun is hot. The shade under the tree is cold. Lily puts her letter in the hot sun. Sam puts his in the shade.

A snail walks by. It goes slow. A boy runs fast to the swings. Lily waits. She counts, "One, two, three." Her big letter is still wet. Sam's small letter is dry. She looks and looks. Then she sees it. "Small dries first," she says. "Big needs more sun."

She counts to ten. At ten, her letter is dry. The hearts shine red. Lily holds it up high. "My letter for Mom," she says. "Big and dry and all done."

Gabriel wanted to roll his red ball to the kitchen. He gave it a big push. The ball was a circle, so it rolled fast. It rolled under the table. "Come back!" said Gabriel. He reached out his arm. His arm was too short. He could not catch the ball.

Gabriel looked around for help. He found a square block. He pushed the square block with one finger. It did not roll. "Silly block," said Gabriel. "You are too flat on the bottom." Then he found his triangle hat and his rectangle book. He pushed them too. They just slid. "No, no," he laughed.

Only circles can roll. Gabriel grabbed his long rectangle ruler. He poked it under the table. The ball popped out. "I catch you!" said Gabriel. Then Mama clapped from the doorway. "My shape boy!"

Madison went to the library with her dad. The floor by the door was wet and slippery, so she walked slowly. She saw a big rug with ten ducks on it.

A lady sat down to sing. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. "Once I caught a fish alive." Madison clapped. She wanted to sing too. But when the song ended, her mouth felt mixed up. What came after five? She had said the words her own way at home. She said, "One, two, five, nine, six." The lady smiled, but the song did not sound right.

Madison thought hard. Why did the song sound wrong? She asked her dad, "Did I say them wrong?" He said, "Try again. Listen first." The lady sang again. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out in the same order every time. That was why the song worked!

Madison followed the words with her finger, duck by duck. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." It sounded right now. "The numbers go in a line," she said. "Just like ducks at the park." She sang it all by herself, and the lady gave her a gold star sticker.

Charlotte wants to paint with her big brother Leo. He is at the table with the red pot. "My turn first," says Leo. "Then you." Charlotte waits. She taps her toes. She counts one cup, two cups, three cups on the table. Leo paints a red bee. "Your turn now," he says. He gives her the red pot. Charlotte paints a red flower. Then Leo wants red again. "But it is my turn," says Charlotte. "You had it first. Now it is mine." Mom nods from the sink. "Charlotte is right," says Mom. "We take turns. That is fair." Leo thinks, then smiles. "Okay. You paint one more bee. Then I go." Charlotte paints a slow, sleepy bee. "This bee is asleep," she laughs. Leo claps. "Good job, Charlotte. Your turn is fun too."

Sarah wanted to wash her hands all by herself. She stood on her old step stool at the sink. Dad stood near the door.

Sarah turned the tap. Hot water came out. Steam went up, up, up. Sarah pulled her hands back fast.

"The water is hot," Sarah said. "Hot water can hurt me." She turned the tap the other way. Now the water felt cool and nice.

Dad smiled. "Good thinking, Sarah," he said.

Sarah washed her hands with soap. Bubbles grew big and white. She splashed a little. Then she saw Dad's razor on the sink.

"What is that?" Sarah asked.

"That is a razor," Dad said. "It is sharp. It can cut you. Little hands do not touch it."

Sarah nodded. She kept her hands in the bubbles. She did not touch the razor.

Then Sarah saw the water rising in the sink. She turned the tap off. The water stopped. "I did it," she said. "I turned it off all by myself."

She jumped down from her stool. She held Dad's hand. They walked out of the bathroom together.

"Wash hands, no touching sharp things," Sarah said.

Dad laughed. "You are a big helper now," he said.

Emilia took a warm bath. The water smelled like soap. Then Mama lifted her out. Emilia was dripping wet.

Soon Emilia shivered. Her arms felt cold. "Why am I cold?" she asked. Mama gave her a soft towel. Emilia rubbed her arms and her legs. The drops went into the towel. Warm came back! "Wet makes me cold," said Emilia. "Dry makes me warm."

Then Emilia put on her pajamas. One arm, then the other. She pulled them up all by herself. "I did it!" she said.

Papa set his phone on the table. It buzzed. Grandma was calling. Emilia waved hello at the screen. Then the phone went quiet. Baby Tom was asleep, so they all whispered. Emilia ate her bread. Then she yawned a big yawn. Mama picked her up and carried her to bed.

Elijah sat in the big salon chair. The chair was too tall for him. Papa gave him a little boost. A man named Sam put a dark cape on Elijah. The cape was dark like night. Elijah wanted to look like Papa. Papa had short hair.

Sam turned on the buzzer. It made a funny sound. Bzzz, bzzz. Elijah giggled. Sam cut the hair on top. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the dark cape. "Look, Papa! My hair fell!" said Elijah. Sam smiled. "The buzzer makes it fall," said Elijah. "The buzzer does the work!"

Sam held up a mirror. Elijah saw a boy with short hair. The boy looked just like a little Papa. Elijah patted his head. "All gone!" he said. Sam laughed and gave him a sticker shaped like a star.

Zoey wanted a special snack. She got her little bowl and ten crackers. She put them on the table, one by one.

Daddy said, "Let's count them first." Zoey touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, six." Daddy smiled. "Wait. What comes after four?" Zoey looked at her hand. She held up five fingers. "Five comes after four!" She counted again, slow and patient. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten crackers, all in a line.

Zoey ate one cracker. She counted the rest. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Nine now! Daddy said, "You ate one, so now there are nine." Zoey laughed. "One went in my tummy!" She drew a picture of her ten crackers. At the top she wrote wiggly marks. "Ten crackers," she said. "One, two, three, all the way to ten."

Grace stood in the school hallway. Her backpack was on. Her shoes were new. This was her very first day.

"Where does my backpack go?" she asked. The hallway had many hooks. A boy named Tom put his backpack on a hook. Then a girl put hers on a hook too. Grace did not know which hook was hers. She began to freeze like a small statue.

Then she saw it. A little card on one hook. It had her name on it. Grace. "That is my hook," she said. "My name is on it!" She hung her backpack there. It did not fall down. It stayed because the hook held it.

Tom looked at her. "Last one to the classroom is a silly goose!" he said.

"Not me!" said Grace. She ran past Tom. Outside the window, the street was sunny. Grace laughed all the way to her classroom.

Milan wanted to find the ice cream cart at the park. He could not see it anywhere. He looked with his eyes. He saw swings and a big slide. No ice cream cart.

Then he stopped and stood very still. He heard a little bell with his ears. Ding, ding! Was that the ice cream man? Milan sniffed with his nose. The air smelled sweet, like vanilla. His mouth watered, and he could almost taste it on his tongue. He ran toward the sound. The bell rang louder and louder. There it was! The cart was hiding behind a big tree. "How did you find me?" the ice cream man asked. "My ears heard your bell," said Milan. "The bell rings, so I can hear it. That is how I know where you are."

Milan got a vanilla cone. It felt cold on his fingers. "You are a lucky boy," said the ice cream man. "A lucky elephant likes vanilla too," he laughed, and pointed at a toy elephant on his cart. Milan licked his cone and smiled. His eyes, ears, nose, tongue and fingers had all helped him today. "One more thing," said the man. He rang the bell right by Milan's ear. Ding! "Now your tongue can taste the sweet, and your ears can hear the ring," he said. Milan took one more big lick.

Maria went to the music studio. The room was hot. The teacher, Miss Anna, opened the window. A little breeze came in.

Maria sat at the big piano. "I want to play the lion song," she said. "The lion roars."

Maria pressed one key. The sound was very quiet. The lion sounded like a tiny mouse. She pressed the key again, soft and slow. Still tiny. "Oh no," said Maria.

Miss Anna smiled. "Try again," she said. Maria pressed the key hard and fast. Boom! The sound was big and loud. "The lion is roaring!" said Maria. "I pressed hard, so it is loud. I pressed soft, so it was small."

She pressed soft, soft, then hard. "Little mouse, little mouse, big lion!" Maria laughed. Miss Anna clapped.

"Now let's build the whole song," said Miss Anna. Maria played soft for the mouse. She played hard for the lion. The song grew and grew. At the end, Maria pressed the key as hard as she could. "Roar!" she said.

Abigail looked out the window. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on the swings. The park was white all over. "No park today," said Mama. "The snow closed it."

Abigail wanted to play outside anyway. She put on her boots. She put on her red coat. She clapped her mittens together. Then she held a snowball in her hands. The snowball got small. Then it was gone! Water ran down her mittens. "It turned to water," said Abigail. Her warm hands made the snow melt.

Abigail picked up another snowball. This time she did not hold it long. She set it on the step and patted it flat. Then she went inside and found her toy frog. She put the green frog on the windowsill. Soon the sun came out. The snow on the step got shiny, then wet, then it was gone too. "The sun melts it," said Abigail. Mama laughed and gave her cocoa. Abigail took a sip and watched the white park drip, drip, drip.

Ivy did not want a shot. She sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. "Can we go home now?" she asked. Mom said, "First, one little check. Then we go." A nurse came in with a small light. "Can you hold still?" she asked. "I will look at your eyes." Ivy held still. The light was bright. Her eyes saw it blink.

The nurse put headphones on Ivy's ears. "Tell me when you hear a beep." Ivy waited. She waited some more. Beep! "I hear it!" said Ivy. "My ears heard it first," she said. "The beep made my ears feel funny, so I talked." The nurse smiled. "That is just right."

Then the nurse held out an orange sticker. "Smell it," she said. Ivy's nose sniffed. "Orange!" she said. The nurse gave her a tiny taste of sweet syrup on a spoon. Ivy's tongue tasted it. "Sweet!" Last, the nurse touched Ivy's arm with a cotton ball. "Feel this," she said. Ivy's fingers felt it, soft like a kitten. "You used your whole body team," said the nurse. "Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands." Then it was shot time. Ivy squeezed Mom's hand. It was over fast. "All done," said the nurse. Ivy picked a pink bandage. "My eyes pick pink," she said.

Kayden ran to the big sports field. Mom and Dad and Grandma came too. "Look, the game is starting!" said Dad. The players kicked the ball fast. Everyone jumped up and waved.

"I want to play one day," said Kayden. "That is my dream!" He clapped his hands. He stomped his feet. "Go, go, go!" he shouted.

Then big gray clouds came. The wind blew and blew. Kayden shivered. "Brrr!" he said. "The wind makes cold weather," he told Grandma. Grandma smiled. She pulled a soft blanket from her bag. She wrapped it around Kayden. "Warm now!" he said.

The sun came back. The crowd cheered loud. The team kicked one more goal. "We won! We won!" everyone shouted. Kayden threw his arms up high.

A player ran over and waved at the crowd. Kayden waved back. "I saw you, little fan!" the player called. Kayden hugged his blanket tight and jumped up and down.

Isaac ran to the backyard with his toy stove. Today he would make a pretend feast for Mom and Dad. He put a red bowl on the stove. He stirred in dirt, water, and three yellow leaves. He gave his meal a name. "I will call it Backyard Soup!" he said.

Mom sat down at the little table. Dad came too. Isaac served the soup in red cups. But the soup was too runny. It ran right off the spoon. "Why is it so watery?" Isaac asked. He looked at his bowl. "Oh! I put in lots and lots of water," he said. "Just a little splash next time."

He stirred in more dirt, bit by bit. The soup got thick. It did not run off the spoon. It went pop, pop, pop with big air bubbles as he stirred. Isaac filled three bowls. Mom took a tiny pretend sip. Dad clapped his hands. "Backyard Soup for everyone!" said Isaac.

Luke ran into the storytime room. Today he would get his very own library card! It was round and blue, like a little moon. He got to wear it on a string around his neck.

Luke picked a book about seeds. A seed goes in the dirt. Then a plant grows up! He hugged the book tight.

"I want to keep it forever," said Luke.

The librarian shook her head with a smile. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Luke read the seed book at bedtime. He read it at breakfast too. Then he ran back to the library.

"Here is my book!" he said. "I brought it back so someone else can read it."

Then he picked out three more.

Violet was on the swim team. Today was the big relay race at the pool. The water smelled like sunshine and chlorine. Her goggles felt tight on her little nose.

"Wait for Tom to touch the wall," said Coach May. "Then you jump in." Violet wondered why she had to wait. She stood on the edge and watched the water splash.

Tom swam fast. His arms went round and round. He came closer and closer. Violet jumped too soon! She hit the water before his hand touched the wall. Beep! The whistle blew. "Too early," said Coach May, kind and calm. "You dived before Tom touched. That is why we have to start again."

They tried again. Tom swam. His hand came near. Violet waited, waited, waited. Tap! His hand hit the wall. Then Violet jumped in. The water was cool on her skin. Her legs kicked and kicked. She touched the wall at the end, and her whole team cheered.

"A surprise!" said Tom. "We did it!" Violet laughed. "We take turns in the wall game," she said. And everyone jumped in for one big happy splash.

Everly ran into the big room. It was full of books. She picked a book about a red fire truck. "I want this one," she said. A lady at the desk gave Everly a little card. It was her very first library card. Everly held it tight.

"Can the book be mine forever?" Everly asked. "No," said the lady. "It is just for now." Everly made a sad face. "Then what?" she asked. "You take it home. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too." The fan above the door began to blow on Everly's hair. Her hair went up like a bird. "My hair is flying!" she laughed.

Everly put the book in her bag. She waved to the fire truck book. "Bye bye," she said. "I will bring you back. But first you come home with me." She skipped out the door.

Mackenzie was four today. She wore a big hat with a number four on it. Her family and friends came to the bowling alley with her.

First Mackenzie had to trade her shoes. "These shoes are too big," she said. "Big shoes help you not to slip," said Grandma. Mackenzie took the heavy ball. She threw it in the air. The ball went thump on the floor. It did not go near the pins. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

Daddy knelt down beside her. "Try again," he said. "Let me help." He showed her how to swing her arms. This time Mackenzie let the ball touch the floor. The ball began to turn and turn. It rolled straight down the long floor. Crash! All ten pins fell down. "Hooray!" everyone shouted.

"I did it! I did it!" said Mackenzie. Her friend Ben clapped and clapped. Then it was Ben's turn. He rolled his ball too, and seven pins fell.

After the game, they ate pizza and cake. Mackenzie licked her lips. "My pizza is salty," she said with a giggle. Mommy gave her a cup of water. Then Daddy brought out a surprise. It was a pink cake with four candles. Mackenzie blew and blew. All the candles went out. "Make a wish," said Grandma. Mackenzie closed her eyes tight. Then she took one more big bite of cake.

Zayn ran to first base. His shoes slid in the dirt. Thud! He fell on his bottom. "Ow," he said. Coach Peppy blew her whistle. "Zayn, why did you slip?" Zayn looked at his shoes. "My shoes are smooth," he said. "The dirt is loose." Coach Peppy held up her own shoes. They had little bumps on the bottom. "These are cleats," she said. "The bumps dig into the dirt."

Zayn wanted to try them. At the next game, he wore his new cleats. The big clock above the field showed it was time to play. He hit the ball and ran. His feet did not slide one bit. The cleats went deep into the dirt and held on. "Safe!" said Coach Peppy. Zayn grinned at first base. "My shoes have little teeth now," he said. "Grrr!" His friend Ben laughed. "Silly shoes," said Ben. Zayn stomped his feet. "Roar!" he said, and they both giggled all the way to the dugout.

Emily sat in her bed. She had a book from the library. It was about a curly sheep. Emily wanted to keep it forever.

Dad came in. "Time to read," he said.

Emily opened the book. She pointed at the marks. "Dad, what are those?" Dad read them out loud. The marks said, "Sheep sleeps on a hill." Emily gasped. "The marks talk!"

"Yes," said Dad. "Now turn the pages this way." He showed her. The story went front to back.

They read slowly. They read all the sheep pages. Dad said, "We must take it back on Friday. Other kids will read it too."

Emily held the book to her chest. She did not want to. She thought and thought.

Then she found paper and a pen. "Dad, draw the sheep words for me." Dad wrote, "Sheep sleeps on a hill." Emily put the paper under her pillow.

"Now I will always remember the sheep," she said.

Dad opened the window a little. Cool air came in. He kissed her head.

On Friday, Emily put the book in her bag. At the library, the sheep book went into the bin. Emily waved. "Bye, sheep. Someone else will read you now."

A boy picked it up right away. He opened it front to back. Emily smiled at him.

"He reads the marks too," she said.

Beatrice woke up and saw white. Snow was on the window. Snow was on the grass. "No school today," said Dad. "It snowed too much, so school is closed." Beatrice gasped. A snow day at home!

They went to the big sledding hill. Beatrice went down, down, down. Whee! Then she wanted to feed the birds. She looked under the snow for a worm. She dug and dug. No worm! The ground was cold and hard, so the worms were hiding deep down. Beatrice laughed. "Silly worms! They are sleepy today."

A little bird hopped near her sled. It looked at her mitten. Beatrice shared her bread crumbs instead. The bird pecked them up fast. Then it sat right on the sled, like a tiny rider. "Your turn," said Beatrice. "Hold on tight!"

Rowan was in the backyard with his dad. He saw a little brown bird by the fence. "Dad, the bird is hungry," said Rowan. "I will feed it."

Rowan ran to his toy box. He got his play apple and his play bread. He put them on the grass. The bird hopped close. Then the bird did not eat them. The bird flew away.

"Maybe toys are not food," said Rowan. His dad smiled. "Let's get real seeds," said Dad. They got seeds from the kitchen. They put the seeds on the grass. The bird came back. It pecked the seeds. Peck, peck, peck.

"The bird eats real food, not toys," said Rowan. "Toys are for playing." Then Rowan took his toy blocks. He made a big stack of blocks. The bird ate seeds. Rowan played with toys. Dad sat nearby in the warm sun.

Rowan looked at the bird. "Eat more, little bird," he said.

Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She had a stuffy nose. The doctor gave her a cookie to share. Everly took a little bite. "It tastes like nothing," she said.

She looked at the cookie with her eyes. It was brown and round. She sniffed it with her nose. But her nose was all plugged up. She could not smell it at all.

Everly pinched her nose shut. She took another bite. Still no taste! Then she let go of her nose. She heard the doctor say, "Take a big breath." Everly sniffed and sniffed. Slowly, her nose opened up a tiny bit.

She took one more bite. "Yum! Now it tastes sweet!" Everly was not angry anymore. She clapped her hands. "My nose helps my mouth taste," she said. The doctor read her chart and smiled. "That's right, Everly."

Everly touched the cookie with her fingers. It was bumpy and a little warm. She listened to the paper crinkle under her. "Can I have one more cookie, please?"

Livia could not find her bunny. She looked in the toy box. No bunny. She looked under the table. No bunny. "Where did you go?" she asked.

Miss Rosa came to help. "Where did you play last?" she asked. Livia thought hard. "I played in the sand," she said. "Then I washed my hands." Miss Rosa smiled. "Then we look on the way back."

They walked down the hall. Livia spoke in a small voice. "Bunny, where are you?" Then she saw something spotted. It was her bunny's spotted ear, sticking out of a basket of towels! Livia picked it up and hugged it tight. "You were hiding near the towels because I dried my hands there," she said. Miss Rosa laughed. "You found it all by yourself." Livia held her bunny close and smiled all the way to snack time.

Anna stood in the band room. She held a big silver trumpet. "Now I will play it," she said. She blew and blew. But no sound came out. Just air. Just wind.

Her friend Tom laughed, but not mean. "You sound like a sleepy dragon," he said. Anna was not afraid. She tried again. Big air, small air, fast air. Still no sound.

Then the teacher picked up her own trumpet. Anna watched her lips. They went bzzz, like a bee. Anna tried the bee lips. Bzzz. Into the trumpet. Toot! A big sound came out.

"I know why now," Anna said. "My lips have to buzz first!" Tom clapped. Anna tooted again and again. "A bee lives in my trumpet," she said. "A hungry bee. It wants my cookie."

Jaxon ran to the park. He saw the big red slide. He wanted to go first.

A girl was already at the ladder. "My turn," said Jaxon. "No," said the girl. "It is my turn now."

Jaxon stopped and looked. One girl was on the ladder. One boy was waiting behind her. They stood in a line. Why do they stand there? Jaxon wondered.

Jaxon walked to the back of the line. He waited. The girl went down. Whee! The boy went down. Whee! Then it was Jaxon's turn. He climbed up. He went down fast. It was fun!

"Again," said Jaxon. He went to the back of the line again. Waiting meant everyone got a turn. He saw that all by himself.

Next Jaxon found the water table. Splash! He put his hands in. A boy came over. "Can I splash too?" the boy asked. Jaxon moved over. They both splashed together. Two kids, one water table, room for both.

A turtle sat by the little pond. It looked strong and slow. "Hello, turtle," said Jaxon. The turtle slid into the water. Splash! Jaxon laughed.

The park helper rang a bell. All the kids came to the circle. Time for a story. Jaxon sat down too. Everyone sat. Everyone listened. Jaxon whispered, "I can follow the bell."

Then the story began, and Jaxon clapped his hands. "The end!" he said, "Again, again!"

Mya stood at the school gate. The gate was huge. It was taller than Dad. Mya pushed it, but it did not move. "Why won't it open?" she asked. Dad said, "Let's look for a clue." Then Mya heard it. Ding, ding, ding! The bell rang inside. The gate clicked and swung open. "The bell opens the school!" said Mya.

Mya hugged her backpack. It had a horse on it. The horse had a red saddle. "One horse, two feet, three kisses for the horse," said Dad. He kissed the backpack three times. Mya laughed. "Silly Dad. Horses do not go to school." Then she looked at the gate. More kids came in. They did not push the gate. They all stood and waited. Ding, ding, ding! The bell rang again, and the gate clicked again. "See? No pushing," said Mya. "Just wait for the bell."

A boy named Sam ran to the gate. He pushed and pushed. The gate stayed shut. "It will not open!" said Sam. Mya held up her hand. "One, two, three," she counted. Ding, ding, ding! The gate swung wide open. Sam fell right through and landed on his bottom. "The bell did it," said Mya. "The bell says go!" Sam got up and dusted off his pants. "You are the bell boss," he said. Mya marched through the huge gate. "Come on, horse," she said. "School is open."

Ryan ran into Miss Kim's music room. Today he would play the big piano. His tummy jumped with happy butterflies.

Miss Kim put Ryan's small hands on the keys. Ryan wanted to play fast, fast, fast. His fingers slipped and hit wrong notes. Bump, boom, blonk. He tried again. Wrong notes again.

"Why do I keep getting the wrong sounds?" Ryan asked. Miss Kim smiled. "Try it slow. Let's see."

Ryan played the notes very slowly. One, two, three, four. Each finger landed on its own key. Every note rang out clear. Then he played a little faster. Still clear!

"Slow hands help me pass the tricky part!" Ryan said. He played the song from the top. Slow first, then fast. Not one wrong note.

Miss Kim clapped. Ryan stood up tall. He felt so proud. "Can we do it one more time?" he asked.

"One more time," said Miss Kim. Ryan put his hands on the keys.

Zayn was a small boy on a big trip. The family had a hotel room. Zayn ran to the door. He pulled and pulled. The door did not open.

"My hands don't work!" said Zayn.

Daddy laughed. "Try the little card," he said. He gave Zayn the key card.

Zayn stood near the door. He put the card in the slot. The card had to slide in, then slide out. Beep! A little light turned green.

"The light said yes!" said Zayn.

He pushed the door. It opened! Mommy clapped. "The card made it open," said Zayn. "No card, no door. Yes card, yes door!"

Zayn tried again. Slide, beep, green light. "It opens because of the card!" he said.

The door swung wide. "Big room!" said Zayn. He ran in and jumped on the bouncy bed.

Arnaud was ready to sleep. He had his pajamas on. He had his teeth brushed. But he could not find his favorite cow. The cow was soft and white. Arnaud looked under the bed. He looked in the toy box. No cow. His mouth turned down. His eyes felt wet. "I feel sad," he said.

Then he saw a big shape by the curtain. It was tall and dark. Arnaud's tummy got tight. He pulled the blanket up high. "I feel scared," he whispered. He called, "Papa!"

Papa came in and turned on the little lamp. The dark shape was just Arnaud's coat on the chair. Arnaud sat up. "The dark made it look big," he said. "The light makes it look small." Papa smiled. "Yes. Light helps us see."

Then Papa lifted the coat. Something fell down with a soft plop. It was the white cow! Arnaud clapped his hands. He jumped up and down on the bed. "I feel excited!" he said. He hugged the cow tight.

Papa tucked him in again. Arnaud held the cow close. His eyes got heavy. He gave a big yawn. Papa turned off the lamp, but left the little one on. The room felt warm and soft. Arnaud patted the cow's head. "Night night, cow," he said. Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Evelyn went to the park today. Yesterday the ice cream truck did not come. Evelyn wanted ice cream so much.

"Is the truck here now?" she asked Mama.

"Not now," said Mama. "The truck comes later, after lunch."

Evelyn looked down the road. It was empty. She heard only a bird. She waited. The road was still empty.

Evelyn picked a dandelion while she waited. She made it a present for Mama. "This is for you," she said.

"Thank you," said Mama. "Now we wait a little more."

Evelyn heard a song far away. It came closer and closer. Then the big white truck turned the corner. Evelyn's eyes went wide.

"The truck comes later, and now it is later!" Evelyn said. She clapped her hands.

Mama bought a little pink ice cream. Evelyn sat on the bench and licked it slowly.

"Tomorrow can we come again?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow."

Evelyn smiled and took one more lick.

Jules ran to the garden with a big bag of seeds. "Today we plant!" he said. Grandpa gave him a small shovel. The sky was blue and warm. It did not snow today. That was good, because seeds like warm dirt.

Jules dug a little hole. He dropped a seed in. Then he patted the dirt down. He made ten holes in a row. He wanted big red tomatoes for lunch!

Jules waited. He looked at the dirt. Nothing happened. He waited more. Still nothing. "Where are my tomatoes?" he asked. The dirt was dry and cracked. A green frog hopped by. Even the frog looked thirsty!

Jules got his little watering can. He poured water on the dirt. He watered every single day. Then one morning, a tiny green leaf popped up! "The water helped!" Jules shouted. "Seeds need water to grow!" He jumped up and down. Day by day, more leaves came. Soon a small red tomato hung on the vine. Jules picked it and held it high. "Grandpa, look! My seed made lunch!"

Beatrice went to the mall with Mama. They walked past the toy shop. Then they came to a salon. A lady with scissors said, "First haircut?" Beatrice nodded. She did not feel bad. She felt big.

The lady put a big cape on Beatrice. Then she sprayed water on Beatrice's hair. Pss, pss. The wet hair stuck together in little lines. Beatrice looked in the mirror. "My hair sticks now," she said. Snip, snip went the scissors. The wet pieces fell and stuck to the cape. They did not go in her eyes or her mouth. Beatrice sat very still and waited.

At the end, the lady brushed her off. Mama unlocked the car with her key. Beatrice touched her short hair. "It got short because you cut the wet lines," she said. Mama smiled and buckled her in.

Elijah went to the store with Mom. He did not skip ahead today. He walked slow, holding her hand. Then he saw a small red shelf by the bread. It said LITTLE LIBRARY on top. Elijah knew those were words. Words say things you can read.

He found a book about a big yellow truck. The cover had a cute dog in the truck. Elijah opened the front. He turned the pages one by one, front to back. "It has words in it too," he said. "The words tell the truck story."

Mom read the little card in the back. It had a day on it. That day was the bring back day. Elijah held the truck book to his chest. He wanted to keep it forever. It was his dream book.

Then a girl came to the shelf. She looked and looked. She wanted the truck book too. Her face went sad. Elijah looked at her. He looked at his book. He looked at the card with the day on it.

"You can have a turn," he said. "I will bring it back on the card day. Then the book comes back here for you." The girl smiled big. Elijah smiled too. He carried the book to the front, nice and flat, so the pages would not bend. "See you soon, truck," he said.

Leah stood at the classroom door. She held a card with a letter on it. The letter was B. It looked hard to her.

"Is that a D?" said her friend Tom.

"No, it is a B," said Leah. "B says buh. B for banana!" She pretended to munch a big banana. "Buh, buh, buh."

Tom laughed. Then his sock began to slip down his foot. He pulled it up. "You munched the letter," he said. "Silly Leah."

The teacher called the next card. Leah looked at it. It was M. She knew this one. "M says mmm," she said. "Like when you eat something yummy!" She rubbed her tummy. "Mmm, mmm, mmm."

"You always make eating sounds," said Tom.

"That is my trick," said Leah. "The letter makes a sound. I make the sound too. Then I remember it!"

She held up the M card. It looked like two little mountains. "Mmm," she said, and marched around the table like a small mountain climber.

Tom marched too. "Mmm," he said. "This is fun."

At the door, the teacher smiled. "One more card, Leah."

Leah looked down. It was S. She wiggled like a snake. "Ssssss," she said.

Tom giggled so much his sock slipped again.

Abigail was at Grandma's house. She wanted to paint a green hill. Grandpa had red, blue and yellow paint. But there was no green paint at all. Where could green be hiding?

Abigail looked at the paints. She dipped her brush in blue. She made a blue hill. It was not right. She dipped her brush in yellow. She made a yellow sun. Still no green. Then some blue dripped onto the yellow sun. The spot turned green!

"Look, Grandma! Blue and yellow made green!" said Abigail. She mixed more blue and yellow together. She painted a big green hill with a friendly little rabbit on top. She painted red flowers too.
