At nap time, Abigail had to sleep. But first she put her green painting by the window, so the rabbit could see the yellow sun. "Good night, rabbit," she whispered. "Sleep on your green hill."

Elena was at Grandma's house. She could smell warm cookies. The cookie jar sat up high on a shelf. Elena wanted one very much.

She reached up. She reached and reached. The jar was too high. "Grandma, can you help me, please?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "What a nice way to ask," said Grandma. She lifted the jar down.

Elena hugged the jar. But her hands slipped. The lid fell and rolled under the chair. "Sorry, Grandma," said Elena. Grandma knelt down with her. "That is okay. Let us look together." They peeked under the chair. There was the lid! Elena picked it up. Grandma gave her a warm cookie. "Thank you, Grandma," said Elena.

Later it was time to swim. Grandpa blew fresh air into her swim ring. The water was cool on her toes. Elena splashed and laughed. The sun went down. "It is getting late," said Grandma. Elena climbed out. Grandma wrapped her in a big soft towel. "That cookie fell because my hands were slippery," said Elena. Grandma laughed and hugged her close. "More cookies tomorrow," she said.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. The sun was bright now. "Are we at Grandma's yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "We get there later."

Kinsley looked out the window. A big truck went by. Then it was gone. "Now the truck is gone," said Kinsley. She held her book on her lap. It was the book Grandma read to her yesterday. Yesterday was the day before today.

"Will Grandma give me a peach?" asked Kinsley. "Tomorrow we can pick peaches," said Mama. "Today we just ride in the car." Kinsley watched the trees. She climbed her feet up onto the seat edge. The trees went by, one, two, three.

The car turned a corner. Grandma's house came into view. "We are here now!" said Kinsley. Grandma stood by the door. She held out a peach. It was big and juicy. "I got here because the car drove and drove," said Kinsley. She took a big bite.

Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose ran and ran. Grandma gave him a big cup of water.

"I want to play," said Henry. He got up to run. His legs felt slow and wobbly. He sat back down on the soft couch. He drank more water. He drank the whole cup.

The sky outside was cloudy. Henry watched the clouds go by. He napped under a warm blanket. He woke up and drank more water. Then he blew his nose into a soft tissue.

Grandma went to the store. She came back with soup. Henry ate it all up. His nose did not run so much now. His legs did not feel wobbly.

"Can I play now?" Henry asked. Grandma smiled. "Just a little," she said. Henry walked to the toy box. He picked up his red truck. He rolled it slow and easy on the floor. Then he took a big drink of water and rolled the truck again.

Jules had a cold. His nose was red. His voice had gone away. When he tried to talk, only a tiny sound came out. Jules wanted to say "more toast, please." But no words came.

Mom gave him warm water with honey. Jules took the spoon and did a slow dig into the honey jar. The honey dripped into his cup. It was sweet and warm. "Rest your voice," said Mom. "It will come back."

Jules closed his mouth. He kept it closed like a little door. He drank his warm water. He watched Dad cut an apple. He waited. He looked at the clock. The big hand moved a little bit. Then Jules tried again. "More toast, please," he said. His voice was back! Mom clapped her hands.

Then Dad opened his mouth to cheer. Nothing came out. Dad had caught the cold too. Dad pointed at the honey jar. Jules picked up the spoon and did a slow dig for Dad. "Now you wait," said Jules.

Harper ran to the fence. A white sheep stood on the other side. "Hello, sheep!" she called. The sheep turned its head.

Grandpa gave Harper a small job. "Find five ways to meet the sheep," he said. Harper wanted a prize, so she began.

First she peeked through the fence. "I used my eyes," she said. Then the sheep said, "Baa!" Harper laughed. "My ears heard that!" She touched the wool. It was soft and warm. "That was my hands." Grandpa held out hay. The sheep ate it fast. "It smells good," said Harper, "my nose knows!" Then Grandpa gave her cool water. "My tongue tastes that. That is five!"

Grandpa clapped. He picked her up high. "Eyes, ears, hands, nose, tongue," said Harper. The sheep went "Baa!" one more time.

In the morning, Layla ran to Grandma's kitchen. The bread was baking. Layla smelled it with her nose. "Grandma, what part do I use to smell?" she asked. "Your nose," said Grandma. Layla laughed. "One! My nose smells the bread."

Grandma gave her a warm slice. Layla touched it with her fingers. "Two! My fingers feel the warm bread." She took a little bite. "Three! My tongue tastes it. Yum." The kitchen window was open. A bird sang outside. "Four! My ears hear the bird," said Layla.

Then she saw her favorite cup on the shelf. "Five! My eyes see my cup." Grandma clapped. "You named all five senses." Layla counted them on her fingers. "Nose, fingers, tongue, ears, eyes. That is five." She put her hands on her cheeks. "The bird sings because the sun is up," she said. Grandma kissed her head.

Matthew got to daycare and saw the play kitchen. It had a little pot and little cups. His friend Emma held a baby doll. The doll was crying, Emma said. Matthew wanted to help the baby.

Emma said the baby was hungry. Matthew looked in the pot. It was empty. So he found some round blocks. He dropped them in. "Soup," he said. He stirred it with a big spoon. He made the spoon go round and round. Then he held it up to the doll's mouth. Emma made eating sounds. "Mmm," said the baby.

The crying stopped. Emma smiled a big smile. Matthew said, "The baby stopped crying because I fed her soup." The teacher gave him a coin for the pretend store. Matthew made the coin go into a tall tower of cups. "One coin, one cake," he said. The teacher bought a pretend cake.

Then Emma handed Matthew the doll. "Your turn to be the dad," she said. Matthew remembered how his own dad patted his back. He patted the doll, soft and slow. The doll went to sleep. "Shh," whispered Matthew.

Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a cold. His nose was red. His sock was warm and cozy on his feet.

Mama brought him a cup of water. "Drink a little," she said. Arthur took a sip. Then he took another sip. "My cough went away," he said. "Why did it go away?" Was it because of the water?

Mama tucked a blanket around him. Arthur yawned a big yawn. His eyes felt heavy, like rocks. He let his head rest on the soft pillow. Soon he was asleep. He slept and slept.

When Arthur woke up, he sat up tall. He sniffed with his nose. It was clear now! "Mama, I slept, and now I am better," he said. Mama smiled and gave him an orange. Arthur took a bite. "Ooh, sour!" he said. He made a funny face. Then he wiggled his sock toes and laughed.

"Can we sleep again tomorrow?" he asked.

Oliver was at Grandpa's house. The big game was on TV. Everyone sat on the big couch. Aunt May sat on the arm of the couch. Uncle Ben sat there too. The arm was full.

Oliver had no seat. He wanted to see the TV. Dad said, "The game will not start yet. We can wait." So Oliver waited. He walked around the room. He found a small stool. He carried it to the couch. He set it down in front of Dad. He sat on it.

The game began. The crowd on TV got loud. Everyone cheered. Oliver could see the whole TV now. "My stool made me tall," said Oliver. Grandpa laughed. Then the team scored, and Grandma hugged the lamp by mistake. "That is Grandma's seat," said Oliver, and he patted the stool.

Today was Victor's birthday. There were balloons on the door. There was paper on the table with bears on it. Grandma came. Mia came too.

Mom set down a big cake. The cake had three candles. "Why three?" asked Victor. "You are three!" said Mom.

Victor took a big breath. He blew and blew. The candles went out. The room got dark for a second. "The candles went out because I blew!" said Victor.

"Make a wish and choose your first piece," said Dad. Victor chose the piece with a bear on it. It was chocolate. It was so good.

Then everyone sang. The singing was very loud. It was not scary at all. It was fun.

Victil clapped and clapped. "Next year I will be four," he said. "Will there be four candles?" "Yes!" said Mia.

Brielle stood at school with a red beanbag. Her teacher, a kind woman, put a hoop on the floor. "Throw it in," said the woman. Brielle threw it very hard. The beanbag flew over the hoop. It landed far away.

Brielle got it back. She tried again, very hard. Over the hoop it went again. She sat down. "Too far," she said.

Then she looked at the hoop. It was close. She threw the beanbag soft and low. It went in! "Soft throw goes in," said Brielle. The woman clapped.

Next came a big ball. A boy named Sam rolled it to her. Brielle held out one hand. The big ball hit her hand and bounced off. It rolled into the block tower. The tower fell down. Sam looked angry. His face was red and his mouth turned down.

"I can fix it," said Brielle. She helped Sam build the tower again. Block by block, up it went. Sam smiled. Then the woman said, "Two hands for a big ball." Brielle held out both hands. Sam rolled the ball. She held it with both hands. She caught it! "Both hands hold the big ball," said Brielle.

Sam rolled it again. Brielle caught it once more. Then she rolled it back, soft and low.

Natalie was four. She played soccer at the big park. Her team was called the Red Apples. On game day, every player got a red shirt to wear.

One day, Natalie did not wear her red shirt. She wore her blue shirt. She ran onto the grass. She kicked the ball. Then a boy took the ball away from her. Another girl took it too. Natalie stopped and frowned. There were so many kids. She could not tell who was on her team.

A shy boy named Sam tugged her hand. He pointed at his own red shirt. Then he pointed at the red shirts near the goal. Natalie looked down at her blue shirt. Then she looked at the red shirts. She saw it. The kids in red passed to each other. The kids in blue passed to each other. "The shirt shows the team," she said.

Coach Maya had the extra red shirt. Natalie put it on. She ran back out. Sam passed the ball to her. Natalie kicked it, kick, kick, kick. A little ant crawled by her shoe. She stepped over it and kept running. Then she kicked the ball into the net. Goal!

The Red Apples all jumped up and down. Sam gave Natalie a big hug. "Red shirts stick together," said Natalie. She ran back to the middle of the field, ready for the next kick.

Maya stood in the school hallway. Her hand held Papa's hand tight. The hallway was long and empty. Maya did not know where to put her bag.

Papa walked with her to the wall. There were little doors with names. Maya saw an M. She looked closer. It said MAYA. "That is my name," she said. She hung her bag on the hook. The hook caught the strap and held it. "My name shows my spot," said Maya.

One shoe felt bumpy. Maya took it off. Sand fell out on the floor. The sand came from the beach yesterday. It fell out because the shoe was full of sand. Maya tipped the other shoe too. More sand fell out. A teacher came with a small broom. "I will sweep it," she said. "Then come paint with us, Maya." Maya smiled and took Papa's hand one more time. Papa kissed her head. Then Maya ran to the paint table.

Natalie wanted to paint a green frog at daycare. But she looked and looked. There was no green paint. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. No green.

Natalie was playing doctor with Sam before snack. She made Sam's teddy bear all better. Then she came back to the paint. She still wanted her frog. She asked, "Where can green come from?" The sun did not shine through the window. It was a rainy day. So the paints were all hers to try.

She put yellow paint on her brush. She added blue paint. She mixed it with her stick. It made a big messy blob. The blob turned green! "Yellow and blue make green!" said Natalie. She painted a big green frog. Then she painted one for Sam's teddy bear, too. The teddy bear doctor now had a frog.

Jack stood at the big window. He counted the planes. "One plane, two planes, three," he said. "Grandpa is on plane three." Grandma held his hand. Plane three landed. The door opened. Out came Grandpa with one big suitcase. "Grandpa!" Jack yelled. Grandpa hugged him soft and long.

At home, Grandpa opened the big suitcase. "I will stay for a whole week," he said. He put his shirts in the drawer. He put his socks in the drawer too. Jack watched. "Why do the clothes go in the drawer?" he asked. "A week is a long time," said Grandpa. "The drawer is my little home now."

Jack saw a small ant on the floor. "Look, Grandpa!" he said. "I like ants," said Grandpa. "I will watch it with you." They sat down together. Jack counted the ant's little legs. "One, two, three, four, five, six," he said. Grandpa smiled. Jack was young, and the week was just beginning. Grandpa said, "Now show me your toys."

Wesley went to the pet store with his dad. He saw a tall cage with a little brown rabbit inside. "I want that one," said Wesley. Dad smiled and said yes.

At home, Wesley put the rabbit in his new cage. But the rabbit hid in the corner. Wesley clapped his hands. "Come out!" he called. The rabbit hid deeper. Wesley felt a big worry in his tummy. "Dad, he doesn't like me."

"Let's be very quiet," said Dad. "New pets need calm." So they sat still. The room got quiet. Then the rabbit hopped out. It found a carrot and began to eat.

Wesley whispered, "He came out because we got quiet." The rabbit ate the carrot in a big circle. Wesley giggled softly. Dad put an arm around him. The rabbit hopped near Wesley's hand, warm and soft, and stayed.

Mateo went to the library with his mama. He wanted to find a book all by himself. But he could not read the letters yet.

A girl sat at a small table. She patted the chair next to her. "Come look," she said. She opened a thick book full of letters.

"B is for bear," the girl said. "B says buh. Bear starts with buh." Mateo looked at the big letter B. He said, "Buh, buh, bear." He said it again, slow. "Buh."

Then he stood up. He walked past the shelves. He looked at book after book. He saw a B on a red cover. "Buh," he said. "Bear book?" He opened it. Yes! It was about bears.

"I found it because B says buh," Mateo told the girl. She smiled and patted the page. "Read it with me," she said.

Mateo sat down, nice and slow. He put his hand flat on the B. "Buh, buh, bear," he said, one more time.

Violet went to the library with Grandma. She wanted a book about a red boat. She looked on the shelf where boats might hide.

The librarian gave her a card. "You can take books home," the librarian said. Violet picked a book with a boat on the front. The front cover had words on it. Grandma read them out loud. "Sail Away, Little Boat," Grandma said. "The words tell us the name!"

Violet opened the book. She turned the pages one by one. First the front, then the middle, then the back. Each page had more words. Grandma pointed at them. "These words say what the boat does," Grandma said. Violet touched the letters with her finger. The boat in the picture sailed on blue water.

At home, Violet read the book every night. She wanted to keep it forever. "Can this book stay with me always?" she asked. Grandma shook her head gently. "It has to go back. Other kids want to read it too." Violet felt a little sad. Grandma hugged her. "We can borrow it again another day."

On return day, Violet held the book tight. Then she put it in the return box. The book slid down with a soft thump. The librarian smiled. "Now another child can read about the boat," she said. Violet stood tall. "Because I gave it back!" she said. Grandma took her hand. "Let's pick a new book," said Grandma. Violet ran to the shelf.

Wesley came to school early. The room was quiet. Then his nose wiggled. Something smelled sweet. Wesley wanted to know what it was.

He looked with his eyes. He saw blocks and wood trucks. No cookies anywhere. He listened with his ears. He heard a little hum. It came from the kitchen. Wesley ran to Miss Jo. "Can my nose find the cookies?" he asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Yes. Your nose smells them. Let's walk." They walked and the smell got bigger. The hum got bigger too.

Miss Jo opened the oven door. Cookies! The hum was the oven, because the oven was hot. "The oven made them," Wesley said. He touched one cookie. It was warm on his fingers. He took a bite. Sweet on his tongue! "I found them with my nose!" he shouted. Miss Jo laughed and held his hand. "Eat up, Wesley. You have two more."

Sienna sat in the car. Her brown bear was gone. "Oh no," she said. "I can't find Bear!"

Daddy was in the driver's seat. "Where did you see Bear last?" he asked.

"I had Bear at home," said Sienna. "I hugged Bear in the house." She thought hard. "Then I got in the car. Bear was in my hand!"

Daddy smiled. "Then Bear is still close by. Things don't jump far. Look near your seat."

Sienna looked down. She looked under her legs. No Bear. She bent over and peeked under the seat. It was dark in there. She could not see.

"There is a little lamp in the door," said Daddy. He clicked it on. A warm light glowed.

Sienna peeked again. There was Bear! Bear had slipped out of her hand. Bear had fallen down, under the seat. "I dropped Bear, so Bear went down there!" said Sienna.

She pulled Bear out and hugged him tight. She kissed his brown nose. "Thank you, Daddy," she said. "Thank you, little lamp."

Daddy drove home. Sienna held Bear all the way. "Now we look under the seat first," she said.

Grandma's house smelled like fried potatoes. It was Hanukkah, and Thomas got to help light the menorah.

"Pick a candle," said Grandpa. Thomas picked the blue one. He put it in the very last slot. "We light the new candle first," said Grandpa. Thomas held the little helper candle. He touched it to his blue candle. The flame popped up bright.

Then Grandpa lit the other candles from his blue flame. One by one they glowed. Thomas watched. "The new candle helped all the rest!" he said. "It did," said Grandpa. "Yours started it."

After that they ate hot latkes. Thomas wished for more applesauce. "Too late," said Aunt Jo, holding up the empty bowl. "You ate it all, silly." Thomas laughed and licked his fork. Outside the window, snow fell on the quiet street.

"Same time tomorrow," said Grandpa. Thomas clapped his hands.

Stella looked out the window. The sky had been stormy all night. Now the backyard was white. No school today! It was a snow day.

Stella put on her boots. She ran outside. The snow was deep and soft. She touched it with her mittens. It was very cold. She made a big snowball. Then she had a silly idea. Her toy cow was inside, waiting on the porch. "Mr. Cow needs a snow hat," she said. She put the snowball on the cow's head. The cow wore a white hat. Stella laughed and laughed.

Then she wanted to keep the snowball forever. She carried it inside. She set it on the table. She went to find Dad. They came back with cocoa. The snowball was gone! There was only a wet puddle. "The house is warm," said Stella. "Warm makes snow melt." Dad nodded. Stella tipped the puddle out the door. "Bye bye, snow. Come back tonight!"

Theodore stood in the gym at school. He wanted to throw the beanbag into the hoop. The hoop lay flat on the floor. He threw hard. The beanbag hit the hoop and bounced out. "Oh no," said Theodore. Miss Dot was near him. She fixed his red hat so he could see. "Try again," she said. Theodore threw soft this time. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed in the hoop and stayed. "I threw soft, so it stayed in!" said Theodore. Next Miss Dot rolled him the big ball. He used one hand. The ball spun past his fingers. He tried both hands. The ball came right into them. "Both hands catch the big ball!" he said. Then they sat and ate crunchy crackers together.

Axel wanted to paint a green frog. He looked in his paint box. He found red paint. He found blue paint. He found yellow paint. No green paint at all.

Axel sat down. He put some blue paint on his paper. He put some yellow paint next to it. He mixed them with his brush. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," said Axel.

Now he could paint his frog. He painted a big green frog on the paper. Then he painted a red apple for the frog. He painted a blue pond, too. The frog looked happy next to the pond.

Axel wanted to build a home for the frog. He took different paper and folded it. He made a little green house. He put the frog picture inside. "Nice home, frog," said Axel. He held it up to show Mom. Mom smiled and clapped her hands.

Chloe went to the store with Dad. She wanted to buy a green apple for Grandma. Green was Grandma's favorite color.

Chloe looked in the fruit bin. She saw red apples. She saw yellow apples. But no green apples. Chloe felt sad. Then she saw a big sign. It said "Paint Sale." Buckets of paint sat on a shelf. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint.

Chloe had an idea. She picked up a brush. She dipped it in yellow paint. Then she dipped it in blue paint. She painted a paper apple. The apple turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," said Chloe. A store man smiled and gave her a green pig toy. It swung on a string. Chloe put the toy in the basket. It made the basket heavy, so Dad carried it.

At home, Grandma bit a yellow apple. She held the green painting up high. "My favorite," she said.

Nathan went to the park with Dad. There was a little fish stand by the pond. Nathan picked one small goldfish. "My first pet!" he said. He held the bag tight so it would not slip.

At home, Nathan gave the fish lots and lots of food. The next morning, the water looked cloudy. "Oh no," said Nathan. The fish swam slowly near the top. Nathan helped Dad clean the bowl. They put in fresh, clear water. Dad said to feed just one small pinch. Nathan gave one pinch, no more.

The next day, the water stayed clear. "Too much food made the water dirty," said Nathan. "Now I know." The goldfish swam fast and happy in its clean, shiny bowl. "Good morning, baby fish," said Nathan.

Charles ran to the little table. Today he would write his name! He picked up a pencil. He held it near the top, like a stick. The pencil slipped. His letter C came out wobbly and small.

His teacher sat next to him. She showed him her own hand. She held the pencil low, near the tip. Her fingers were snug and cozy, like a foot in a shoe. Charles tried it. He pinched the pencil near the point. He drew a big C. Then an H. Then A, R, L, E, S.

"Look!" he shouted. "I wrote Charles!" The letters stood in a row on the paper. He jumped up and waved it high. "I'm writing it again!"

Elijah got a small kitten from the vet. Her name was Pip. At home, Pip ran under the couch. She would not come out. Elijah peeked under. "Why are you hiding?" he asked.

He waited and watched. Maybe she was scared? The house was big and new to her. So Elijah sat very still. He put out a little food. He talked soft and slow. "It's okay, Pip."

Soon a small paw came out. Then Pip came out too. She ate the food. Her tummy got round. "You were scared because everything was new," Elijah said. "Now you know me."

The next day Pip was not grumpy anymore. She walked right up to Elijah. "Do you want to play?" he asked. Pip purred very loud.

Rosalie sat at Grandma's house. It was Hanukkah. Daddy called everyone to the table.

Grandma lit the candles. "One, two, three, four," Rosalie counted. The flames were little and bright. "I want to blow them out," said Rosalie. "Like my birthday!" Grandma shook her head. "No, we watch them. We let them burn."

Rosalie waited. The candles got shorter and shorter. Where did the wax go? Did the fire eat it? Then one flame went out by itself. Pop, it was gone. Then another one. Soon all the candles were dark, all on their own.

"They went out!" said Rosalie. "Why, Grandma?" "They are short candles," said Grandma. "They burn down, and then the light is done." Rosalie spun her dreidel. It went round and round like a wheel. "I did not have to blow," she said. "The little candles did it themselves."

Austin went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big orange carrot on the shelf. It looked like a magic wand from his storybook. Austin reached up high on his toes. His fingers touched the shelf. Then his hand bumped a bag of frozen peas. The bag fell down with a thump. Peas rolled all over the floor like little green marbles.

"Sorry," said Austin to the peas. A store lady came to help. "Can you help us, please?" asked Mama. The lady smiled and picked up the bag. Austin helped too. He put the peas back one by one.

Then Austin held his carrot up like a wand. "Zap!" he said. The lady laughed. "Thank you," said Austin to her. "Thank you for helping."

At home, Mama cooked the carrot. Austin took a bite. It was sweet. "The peas fell because I bumped them," said Austin. "And the lady helped because we asked!" Mama kissed his head. Austin waved his carrot wand one more time. "Zap!"

It was a stormy night outside. Rain tapped on the window. Inside, it was warm and bright. Tonight Madeline's family would light the Hanukkah candles.

Papa put the menorah on the table. Madeline held the little candles in her hand. "I want to light them," she said. "You can hold the helper candle," said Papa. "It is called the shamash." The shamash was the tallest candle. It stood up higher than all the rest.

Madeline touched the shamash to a small candle. The small candle began to glow. Then the flame jumped to the next candle, and the next. "The tall candle lit them all," Madeline said. "One candle can share its fire." Grandma smiled. She gave Madeline a warm pancake. Madeline took a big bite and counted the lights. Outside, the storm kept on. Inside, eight little flames danced.

Mia was thirsty. She wanted cold water from the fridge. But her cup was up on the big shelf.

"Too big for me," she said. She looked around the kitchen. She found a small stool. The small stool made her tall. She reached and reached. Then she got her cup down. "One cup," she said. "Two hands. Three steps back."

She filled her cup at the sink. The water ran fast. It splashed and jumped. "Fast water makes a mess," said Mia. So she turned the tap a little. Now the water ran slow. Slow water filled the cup, drip by drip.

Her mama was making soup. The pot was hot. Mia saw steam rise up. She did not touch it. The fridge was cold. Her water was cold too.

"Why is the water cold, Mama?" she asked.
"Because it lived in the fridge," said Mama.

Mia took a big sip. Then a small sip. She put her cup down on the table, and the table had one wet ring on it.

Scarlett loved art time at school. Today she wanted to paint a frog. But there was no green paint on the tray. "Where is green?" she asked her teacher. "Look at the paint cups and see," said Ms. Lee.

Scarlett looked. She saw red paint. She saw yellow paint. She saw blue paint. No green anywhere. She patted the tray with her hand. It felt cool and smooth. She sniffed the cups. They smelled like paint, not like green.

Her friend Tomo sat next to her. He was painting a red fire truck. "I want green for my frog," Scarlett said. Tomo dipped his brush in yellow. Then he dipped it in blue. He made a mark on his paper. The mark turned green!

Scarlett opened her eyes wide. "Yellow and blue make green!" she said. She dipped her brush in yellow. She dipped it in blue too. She made a big wet dot. The dot was green, just like Tomo's. She had found out how to make her favorite color.

She painted her frog. It was green all over. She painted a green leaf next to it. Then she made a sign for her picture. She wrote her name on it in red. Ms. Lee hung the frog on the wall. "Look at my green frog!" Scarlett said. Tomo clapped for her.

Zoe rode in the car with Dad. The road was long. The sky was cloudy. They were going to the hospital. Mama was there with a new baby.

Zoe held her soft bear. She let the bear hide under her coat. "Shh," she said. "The baby is little."

They found Mama's room. Mama held a tiny baby. He had small hands and small feet. "This is Ben," said Mama. "He is your brother."

Then Ben began to cry. He cried and cried. Zoe felt sad. "Why is he sad?" she asked.

"Listen," said Mama. "He is hungry. Babies cry when they need something." Mama fed Ben some milk. He stopped crying. He made small sounds.

Zoe looked at Ben. "He cries because he is hungry," she said. "Now he is happy."

Later Ben cried again. Zoe said, "He needs something!" Mama picked him up. Ben hid his face in Mama's neck. Then he went to sleep.

Zoe patted his back, soft and slow. "Night night, Ben," she whispered.

Elena sat on her bed. The curtain moved. The wind made it go puff, puff. It was windy outside today.

The curtain went flap, flap, fast. Elena felt scared. She pulled the blanket up. Then she saw the tree by the window. The wind was moving the tree. The tree moved the curtain. She peeked out. "The wind did it," she said. She was not scared now.

Eena wanted to play. She sent her paper boat across the rug. "Boat, go to the pond," she said. The blue rug was the pond. The boat slid and stopped. Then it fell over. Elena felt angry. She stamped her foot.

She took a big breath, slow and long. Her body felt calm. She tried again, gently. This time the boat slid all the way. It sat on the blue pond. "You did it!" said Elena. She jumped up and down. Her teddy fell off the bed with a soft thump. Elena hugged him tight. "We are happy," she said. The curtain went puff, puff, slow now. Elena yawned. She sent the boat one more time, very softly, and closed her eyes.

Mason was at Grandma's house. Grandma gave him a big pencil and paper. "Write your name," she said. Mason grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. The pencil slipped. His M looked like a squiggly worm. Grandma laughed. "Try pinching it like a crab," she said. "Nip, nip!" Mason pinched the pencil with two fingers. The pencil stopped slipping. "My fingers turn it now," Mason said. He turned the pencil to make a big M. Grandma's cat jumped on the table. "Are you afraid of my cat?" asked Grandma. "No, I like her," said Mason. "But is she afraid of my M?" "Look, she is sleeping," said Grandma. Mason wrote his name. M, A, S, O, N. He counted the letters. One, two, three, four, five. Mason held up the paper. "Five letters, Grandma! All mine!"

Owen got to the playground early. The sun was warm on his face. Only one other kid was there, a girl with red boots.

Owen wanted to go down the big slide. He climbed one step. Then he stopped. His tummy felt funny. His legs felt wobbly. He was scared. "Why is my tummy jumpy?" he asked himself. He puffed a slow breath out, like blowing out a candle. He climbed another step. He puffed again. The jumpy feeling got smaller and smaller. At the top, he sat down and slid. "Wee!" His tummy felt light now, in a good way. He was excited.

The girl in red boots was building a sand tower. It fell down with a soft plop. Her lip wobbled. She was sad. Owen sat by her on the sand, which was soft like a pillow. They built the tower again, one handful at a time. It stood up tall. The girl laughed. Owen clapped his hands. "You did it!" he said. "Our tower is tall because we built it slow," said the girl. Owen slid down the big slide one more time, all by himself.

Matteo stood at the edge of the pool. The water looked big and blue. "I want to swim," he said. Mom held his hands in the water. Matteo's legs hung down. He did not move at all. "Kick your legs," Mom said. Matteo kicked. Splash, splash, splash! His legs made white bubbles. Now he moved! He moved all the way to the red ball. "I moved because I kicked," he said.

Mom let go of one hand. Matteo kicked again. Splash, splash, splash! He moved faster now. "Look at me!" he did shout to Dad. Dad laughed and clapped. Then Matteo stopped kicking. His legs went still. He stopped moving, too. The water held him like a thick blanket, but he did not go anywhere. He began to sink down a little. Mom lifted him up. "Kick again," she said softly. Matteo kicked. Up he came, and off he went. Splash, splash, splash!

A girl next to them was holding the wall. She looked scared. Her legs were still. "Kick your legs," Matteo said to her. "Then you move." The girl kicked. She moved! "I can swim!" she shouted. Matteo smiled a big smile. He turned and kicked toward the red ball again. Splash, splash, splash! "Wait for me!" he called to the ball.

Layla woke up in her big girl bed. "I am awake!" she said. Her tummy made a little growl. She ran to find Mama.

"Can I have toast?" she asked. Mama laughed. "Toast first, then we play." Layla ate her toast. She ate it all up, even the crust.

Then Layla saw snow out the window. "Snow! I want snow!" She grabbed her boots. She pushed her bare feet in. The boots would not go on. She pushed and pushed. Her toes said no.

Mama sat down next to her. "Try something else," said Mama. Layla looked at her feet. She looked at her socks on the floor. She put a sock on one foot. The sock made her foot small and smooth. The boot slid right on!

"Socks first, boots second," said Layla. "The sock makes my foot slippery!" Mama giggled. "You found it out all by yourself." Layla put on the other sock. She put on the other boot. She stomped like a bear.

Outside, the snow was cold and soft. Layla's heart felt like a drum. "Mama!" she called. "Look at me! I got dressed!" She made one big stomp in the snow. Her boot left a bear print.

Evan wanted the big yellow truck. It had a digger on the front. It could dig deep, deep holes.

But Sam had the truck. Sam was digging in the sand. Evan grabbed the truck. Sam held on tight. The truck did not move.

Teacher Mia came over. She held up one hand. "One more minute, Sam. Then it is Evan's turn," she said. Sam dug one more hole. Then he gave Evan the truck.

Evan dug a big hole. He looked at Sam. Sam looked sad. Evan gave the truck back. "Your turn," said Evan.

Sam smiled. He dug and dug. Then he gave the truck to Evan again. Back and forth it went. Evan thought about that. Did the truck feel bigger when they shared it? It looked like more truck somehow. Two boys, one truck, and so many holes in the sand.

At clean-up time, the bell rang. Everyone put the toys in the red box. Evan put the truck in last. The lid closed with a click.

Wyatt wanted a cup of water at school. Miss Kim had a big jug. "The water is cold," she said. Wyatt put his hand near it. Brrr, it was cold!

At snack time, Wyatt got hot cocoa in a big cup. He blew on it. He waited. It stayed hot. He waited more. Still hot. Wyatt had a want: he wanted to drink it now.

Then Wyatt saw a little cup on the shelf. He poured some cocoa into the little cup. The little cup was small. He blew once. He took a tiny sip. It was not too hot! The small cup made the cocoa cool fast. The big cup cooled slow.

Wyatt smiled. "Small cup, fast cool," he said. His friend Mia had a big cup too. Her face looked sad. "Too hot," she said. Wyatt poured her a little cup too. Mia blew once and drank it all. "Yum," she said. "Thank you, Wyatt." Then they went to build a tall tower of blocks.

Alice wanted to make pancakes. She wanted to make them all by herself.

First, Dad helped her wash her hands. Then she got to bathe the blueberries in a bowl of water. The little berries splashed and bobbed. "Clean berries, clean berries," she sang.

Alice poured the batter. Dad poured a square of butter into the pan. The butter went sizzle, sizzle. Then Alice dropped a big spoon of batter into the pan.

She waited. She waited. Nothing happened. "Why is it still runny?" she asked. Dad tapped the pan handle. "Look at the top," he said. Little bubbles popped up, pop, pop, pop. "The bubbles say it is ready," said Dad. Alice flipped the pancake. It turned golden brown. The first pancake was hers.

Then the dog ran in. He sat by the stove and licked his lips. Alice laughed. "No pancakes for dogs," she said. The dog put his paw on her slipper and did not move.

"Fine," said Alice. "One blueberry." The dog ate it in one gulp.

Nathan held his black teddy bear. His brother Sam held the tickets. The whole family was going on a trip, far from home.

"Wave one, wave two, wave three," said Nathan. The ferry went up and down. The waves made the boat rock. "The big wave pushed us," said Nathan.

Then Nathan went outside with Dad. The wind was strong. It blew Nathan's hat right off his head. "The boat goes fast, so the wind comes," said Nathan. Dad nodded and held Nathan's hand tight.

A seagull flew by. It landed on the rail near Sam. Sam had a biscuit in his hand. The seagull wanted it.

"Look out," said Nathan. Sam shared a little piece. The seagull ate it fast.

That night, Nathan dreamed about the big waves and the little white bird.

Leon wanted to feed his teddy bear breakfast. He looked in the toy box. The toy box had cars and blocks and balls. "Those are toys," said Leon. "Teddy can't eat toys."

So Leon followed his mom to the kitchen. The kitchen had a fruit bowl. It held a fresh banana and a red apple. "Teddy can eat food," said Leon. "Fruit is food!"

Then Leon heard a bark at the door. It was his dog, Biscuit. Biscuit did not eat fruit. Biscuit ate food from his own bowl. Leon put dog food in Biscuit's bowl.

But wait. Teddy was gone! Leon looked under the table. There sat Biscuit, and on his back rode teddy, like a cowboy on a horse.

"Woof!" said Biscuit. "Giddy up!" said Leon. "The bear rides the dog!"

Lea sat on the city bus with her mama. She held a new library card in her hand. She held a big red book, too. It was a book about a cat.

On the way home, Lea hugged the book. "This book is mine now," she said. "I want to keep it forever."

"You can keep it for a while," said Mama. "But we take it back on Friday. Then other kids can read it too."

Lea felt sad. She did not want to give the cat book back.

On Friday, they rode the bus again. Snowy windows made everything white outside. Lea put the book in the return box. It slid down with a soft thump.

Then a small girl ran up. She took the cat book off the shelf. She smiled big.

"That girl has the book because I brought it back," said Lea.

"Yes," said Mama. "And we can borrow it again."

Lea picked a new book. She sat close to Mama on the bus. "Let's read it at home," she said.

Rose wanted her red crayon. It was not in the box. "Where did it go?" she said.

Rose looked with her eyes. She saw the cat, the rug, and the table. No crayon. Then she heard a little sound with her ears. Tap, tap. It came from under the sofa. Rose got down on her knees. She touched the soft rug with her hands. She smelled something sweet near the sofa. It smelled like apples.

"Mom, come here!" said Rose. Mom lifted the sofa cover. There was the red crayon next to an old apple. "The apple rolled here," said Rose. "That is why my crayon hid!"

Rose licked her lips and smiled. "I found it with my eyes and my ears and my hands and my nose." She sat by the window and began to color. Outside the sky was cloudy, but her picture was all red.

Felix went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about a black cat. He could not find one.

Felix looked on a shelf. He saw books about cows. He saw books about pigs. "Those are animals," he said. He kept looking. He saw books about trucks and balls. "Those are toys," he said. He saw books about apples and bread. "Those are foods," he said.

A girl named Mia was there too. She dropped her books. Felix helped her pick them up. "Thank you," said Mia. She held up a book. It had a black cat on the front.

"That is my cat book," said Felix. "Can you show me where you found it?"

"It was with the animal books," said Mia. She put her head next to the cow books. "Cats and cows live together there."

Felix found the cat shelf. The cat book was big. He sat down with mama. Mama read it to him. Felix patted the black cat on the page. "Home now," he said. "Cats go with animals."

Charlie ran into the backyard. He held a small box. Inside was his very first pet. A bunny named Flop!

Charlie set the box down. Flop hopped out. Flop sniffed the grass. Then Flop began to chew it.

"Mom, come see!" Charlie called. Mom came fast. She smiled at Flop.

"Thirsty bunnies need water," Mom said. "Can you fill this bowl?"

Charlie filled the bowl at the tap. He set it by the grass. Flop hopped over. Flop drank and drank.

Charlie clapped his hands. "Flop drinks because I filled the bowl!" he said.

Mom held up her phone. "Smile!" she said. Click! The phone took a picture.

Now the yard had a fence, too. "The fence keeps Flop safe," said Mom.

Flop munched a green leaf. Charlie sat down close. He watched his bunny eat. "Good boy, Flop," Charlie whispered. "Tomorrow I will fill your bowl again."

Hunter wanted to help Dad in the backyard. Dad was cooking on the grill. Hunter stood next to Dad, like a big boy. "I stay close to you," Hunter said. Dad smiled.

The grill was hot. Hunter put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot!" he said, and pulled his hand back fast. Dad gave him a block of ice from the cooler instead. "Cold," Hunter said. He held the ice in his little hand. The ice felt good and smooth. A drop fell on his shoe and made a messy wet spot.

Hunter saw a stick on the ground. It was long and pointy. He did not touch it. "Pointy sticks can poke," he said. Then he smelled the hot dogs cooking. Dad put one on Hunter's plate. Hunter sat on the step and took a big bite. "The grill was hot because of the fire," Hunter said. Dad laughed. "That's right, big helper."

Sienna had to get a shot today. She waited in a small room with her mom. "Will it hurt?" Sienna asked. "Just a quick pinch," Mom said. "I will hold your hand."

The nurse came in with a tiny bandage. Sienna made her arm very stiff. She held it tight like a brick. The nurse said, "Let your arm go soft, like a noodle." Sienna let it flop down. The nurse wiped her arm with a cool cotton ball. Then the shot came. It was one small pinch, and it was done. "My soft arm made it quick," Sienna said. "Tight makes it slow. Soft makes it fast."

The sky outside looked stormy. But inside the ice cream shop it was warm. Sienna picked pink ice cream with a flower made of candy on top. Mom took a big lick of hers. "My arm is all better," Sienna said. She waved her sticker at the lady behind the counter.

Leo ran to the play corner at school. Today it was a pretend house! There was a little stove and a small bed. On the bed sat a baby doll. The doll was crying. "Waa, waa," said Mia, making the doll's voice. "The baby is hungry!"

"Baby needs a bottle," said Mia. But there was no bottle anywhere. Leo looked in the box. One pot, two cups, three spoons, no bottle. Leo wanted to help so much. Then he saw a yellow block. The block was long like a bottle. He held it to the doll's mouth. "Here, baby, drink," he said.

The doll got quiet. "The baby thinks the block is a bottle!" said Leo. Mia clapped her hands. "You fed her!" she said. "Now it is my turn," said Mia. She took the block and patted the doll's back. One pat, two pats, three pats. The baby went to sleep in the small bed.

Then Sam ran over. "Can I play?" he asked. "You can be the big sister," said Mia. "Big sisters help." Sam picked up the pot. He stirred one, two, three times. "Dinner is ready!" he said.

Leo smiled big. "The baby slept because I fed her," he said. "And the bottle was just a block!" He ran to get a cup. Maybe the cup could be a phone. He put it to his ear. "Ring, ring! Hello, this is Leo's house!"

James ran into writing club with a big smile. He wanted to write his name all by himself. His teacher, Miss Kim, gave him a fat pencil and some paper.

James grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The J came out all wobbly. The A looked like a little squiggle. "Oh no," said James. "My letters are messy."

Miss Kim sat next to him. "Try this," she said. She showed him how to pinch the pencil with two fingers. Thumb on one side. First finger on the other. The pencil sat on his middle finger like a little rest. James tried it. "It feels like I am holding a pet," he said. "Soft and gentle."

He pinched. He wrote a J. It popped right onto the paper, nice and straight! "Look!" said James. "The J is good!" He wrote A, then M, then E, then S. The A stood tall. The S curled just right. He was so excited that he jumped up.

"My paper is full of my name!" said James. "The letters are neat because I pinch, not squeeze!" Miss Kim clapped. James wrote his name one more time, slow and proud, and held the paper up high.

Kayden ran to the kitchen table. His lunch was there. A warm bun and a red apple.

"Mama, I want to eat now!" he said.

"Not yet," said Mama. "Your hands have germs on them. First we wash with soap. We wash for twenty seconds. Count with me."

Kayden stood at the sink. Mama put soap on his hands. He rubbed them together. Bubbles grew and grew.

They counted, "One, two, three..." all the way to twenty. The bubbles went down the fall of warm water. Splash, splash, gone.

Kayden looked at his hands. Were the germs gone too? He could not see germs. But Mama said twenty seconds was long enough to wash them away.

Mama gave him a dry towel. Kayden patted his hands. Then he held his apple. "My hands are clean now," he said.

He took a big, happy bite.

The next day, Kayden ran to the sink all by himself. "One, two, three..." he counted. He washed and washed. Twenty seconds, all done. Then he ran to the table for his snack.

"Did you use soap?" Mama asked.

"Yes! Twenty seconds," said Kayden. He held up his hands to show her. They were wet and shiny. Mama smiled and gave him the dry towel.

Kayden planted a big kiss on his clean hand. "Bye bye, germs," he said.

Wyatt had three little seeds. He wanted to grow carrots. He put one seed on top of the dirt. He pushed the other seeds down into the dirt. Then he gave them water from a spoon.

Every day Wyatt looked at his garden. "Will my seeds wake up?" he asked. Soon two little green leaves popped up. Then two more. But the spot with the seed on top stayed bare. "Why is that spot empty?" Wyatt wondered.

A bird hopped down. The bird began to chew the seed lying on top. Chew, chew, gone! Wyatt's mouth fell open. "The bird ate it!" he said. "The dirt hid my other seeds. That is why they are safe."

The leaves grew tall and straight. They grew and grew. At last, Wyatt pulled one up. A fat orange carrot hung from the leaves! He washed it with the hose. He took a big bite. "My carrot grew because the dirt kept it," he said. "And I gave it water every day too." He ran to show his mom, carrot held high.

Amira ran to the window at school. She saw dark clouds. Then she heard a big boom. The boom was loud. The loud boom made Amira feel scared. Her tummy felt tight.

Her friend Ben fell down by the blocks. He cried big tears. Falling down made Ben feel sad. Amira patted his back. "It is okay," she said.

Then Miss Kim held up a red kite. "We will fly it outside after the rain," she said. Amira jumped up and down. The kite made her feel excited. Her heart went fast, like a drum.

Outside, the sun came back. Amira flew the red kite high. A bird flew by with twigs in its beak. It was making a nest in the big tree. "The bird is happy too," said Amira. Ben smiled and held her hand.

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She ran to the block corner. So many blocks! She grabbed a circle block first. She stacked it on a square block. Roll! The circle block wobbled and rolled away. "Oh no!" said Lillian. The silly snake had no floor now.

Lillian picked up the circle block again. She pushed it on the rug. It rolled far, far away. Then she pushed a square block. It did not roll. It sat still. "The circle rolls because it is round!" said Lillian. "The square has flat sides. It stays!"

She stacked square blocks for the floor. She added rectangle blocks for the walls. She put triangle blocks on top, like a roof. The house stood tall. Lillian put the snake inside. Then she grabbed orange crayons to color a door. "Knock knock!" she said. "Who is there? A snake in a square house!"

Owen steps into the waiting room. He holds Mama's hand. There are chairs and a fish tank. One fish is orange. Owen waits and watches the fish swim.

A nurse calls his name. Owen needs a shot today. He wants to be big and brave. He steps into the little room and sits on Mama's lap. The nurse cleans his arm with a cold wet wipe. Owen shivers. "Why is it cold?" he asks. "To make my arm super clean," he says to himself.

Then Mama gives him a big hug. Her arms squeeze his arm tight. The nurse counts, "One, two, three." The quick pinch comes. But it feels small, so small! Owen looks down. It is all done. "The hug squeezed my arm," Owen says. "So the pinch felt little!" The nurse puts a nice round bandage on his arm. Owen steps out and waves to the orange fish. "Goodbye, fish," he says.

Lena wanted new stickers. Yesterday, Mom had said, "Tomorrow we go to the store." Lena woke up early. Was it tomorrow now? She looked out the window. The sun was up. A loud bird sang by her bed.

"Mom, is it tomorrow?" Lena asked. Mom smiled. "Yesterday we said tomorrow. Now it is today. Today is the day we go." Lena clapped her hands. Sleep had turned tomorrow into today! "So tonight I sleep again?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "And later, tomorrow comes back."

Lena picked her shoes. She put them on now, not later. At the store she found star stickers. She held them tight. "Thank you, today," Lena whispered. At bedtime she looked at her stickers. Tonight was for sleeping. Tomorrow was for more. "Goodnight, tomorrow," she said. She turned off the light.

Athena wanted to play at the park. But the sky looked gray. Dark clouds sat over the swings.

"Mama, is it going to rain?" she asked.

"Maybe," said Mama. "Feel the wind. It is windy today."

The wind blew hard. It took Athena's hat right off. The hat flew over the brown grass. Athena ran and caught it. "The wind pushed my hat," she said. "Because it is windy."

Mama opened her bag. She pulled out rain boots. "Put these on. If it rains, your shoes stay dry." Athena pushed her feet into the boots. Then the rain came. Drip, drip, drip. Athena looked down. Her boots were dry! "My feet are dry," she said. "Because I have my boots."

Mama held out a warm coat. Athena zipped it up. The rain made little sounds on her hood. Tappity tap. It sounded like tiny drums.

When the rain stopped, the sun came out. "Look, it is sunny now," said Athena. The sun helped a puddle grow smaller and smaller. Athena stomped in it with her boots. Splash! Her feet were still dry. "Sunny days and rainy days are both fun," said Athena.

Mama laughed. "Yes. And hot cocoa waits at home." They walked home together, hand in hand, boots still warm and dry.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two, three," she said. She tapped a pea each time. Then she stopped. What came next? She peeked at her big brother, Ben. "I forgot the next one," she said. She looked upset.

"You can start at one again," said Ben. "Songs go back to the start." Aubrey took a breath. "One, two, three, four, five." The words came out in a row. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She had counted all her peas.

Then her cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. It made a little river. "Oh no," said Aubrey. Ben grabbed a towel. He wiped the river away. "The milk spilled because the cup tipped," said Aubrey. Ben smiled. "That's right. Let's move your cup away from your elbow."

Aubrey moved the cup. Then she ate one pea. "Nine left!" she said. "Nine, eight, seven." Ben laughed and clapped. Aubrey popped another pea in her mouth. "Six!"

Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had her big letter book. Sunlight poured in the window onto the pages. Charlie pointed at a letter. "B," she said. Then she saw another letter. "B," she said again. But Mama shook her head. "That one is D," said Mama. Charlie frowned. The b and the d looked like twins to her. She felt worried. "Too many letters look the same," she said.

Mama sat down close beside her. "Look with your eyes," said Mama. Charlie looked hard at the b. The stick came first, then the bump. She looked at the d. The bump came first, then the stick. Charlie said "b" and made the b sound, buh. She said "d" and made the d sound, duh. "They are not the same!" she said. "The stick and the bump take turns!" She read the whole page with no mistakes. A feather from her pillow floated onto her lap. Charlie giggled. "My pillow is happy," she said. Mama gave her a kiss on her head. "My stinky little toes need a bath after this," Mama teased. Charlie laughed and hugged her book.

Ava went on a trip with Mom and Dad. Grandma came too. They drove a long way to the beach. "Why is the car ride so long?" Ava asked. "Because Grandma's house is far from the sand," Mom said. Ava looked out the window. She saw no sand, only trees.

At the beach, Ava wanted her yellow duck. It was not in her bag. "Why can't I get my duck?" she asked. "Because home is far away," Grandma said. "We can't drive back for one toy." Ava felt like crying a little. Grandma held her hand.

Then Grandma found a red ball. She put it in the water. The ball did not sink. It float-ed on top. "Look, it can float," Grandma said. Ava patted the water. The ball bobbed up and down. Ava laughed. Her trip was short on toys but big on fun. Grandma sat close by her on the warm sand.

Ivy got a little blue card. It was her very own library card. Mom said, "You can pick one book." Ivy walked slowly along the shelves. She found a book about a worm in a garden. The worm had a dry leaf for a bed. "This one," said Ivy.

At the desk, the lady stamped the book. "Bring it back soon," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Ivy held the book tight all the way home.

At home, Ivy read the worm book three times. She did not want to give it back. "I want to keep it forever," she said. But Mom said, "It has to go back, so other kids can read it too." So they took it back. Then Ivy saw a boy pick the worm book off the shelf. He sat down and opened it. He smiled. "He likes my worm book," said Ivy. Then she walked to the shelves to find a new one.

Raphael stood in the pool changing room. The floor was cool under his toes. The air smelled like soap and water. Dad was there, zipping up the swim bag.

"Look at my arm bands," said Raphael. One band was big and soft. One band was small and floppy. He pulled the floppy one on. It slid right down to his hand. Plop. It fell off on the wet floor. Raphael picked it up.

"Why did it fall off?" he asked. Dad smiled. "It has no air inside. We must blow it up." Dad blew and blew. The band grew fat and tight. Now it stayed on Raphael's arm. It would not slide at all.

"Water game time!" said Raphael. He held Dad's hand. They walked to the pool. The water was blue and shiny. Raphael splashed his feet at the edge. Dad held him close.

"You are safe with me," said Dad. Raphael kicked his legs. The tight bands made his arms float up high. He laughed out loud.

"Now I can swim," said Raphael. "Look at me go!"

Sofia had a big red bag. She wanted to put her name on it. Her mom gave her sticker letters.

Sofia held up the letter S. "S says sss," she said. She put it on the bag. Then she held the letter O. "O says ah," she said. That went on next.

The letter F was tricky. Sofia looked at it. "Does F say buh?" she asked. She said buh, buh, buh. Then she said fff, fff, fff. Her lips bit her lip a little. "No, not buh," she said. "F says fff." She put the F on the bag.

She went slow. She stopped to look at each letter. One letter at a time.

At last the bag said SOFIA. Sofia smiled. "S, O, F, I, A," she read. Then she said each sound too. "Sss, ah, fff, ih, ah. Sofia!"

Mom clapped. Sofia hugged the big red bag.

Aaron stood in the pool changing room. His swim bag was open. He could not find his goggles. "Where did they go?" he asked. Dad looked in the big red bag. Then Dad looked in Aaron's shoe. There they were. Aaron put the goggles on. They felt tight, but good.

A lady had painted a huge house on the wall of the changing room. Aaron looked at it while Dad zipped up his suit. "Why do I need goggles?" Aaron asked. "Let's find out," said Dad. He held Aaron's hand and they walked to the pool.

First Aaron put his face in the water with no goggles. His eyes felt funny and he sat up fast. Then he put his face in with the goggles on. The water stayed out. He could see the blue tiles at the bottom. "I can see because the goggles keep the water away!" said Aaron. Dad smiled and held him close. "Now let's swim to the wall," said Dad. Aaron kicked his legs and off he went.

Liam woke up and ran to the window. He looked outside. The sun was out. "Sunny today!" he said. He put on his sun hat and went out to play.

Then the wind came. The wind blew his hat right off. The hat flew across the grass. Liam ran after it. "Why did my hat fly away?" he asked. He picked it up and held it tight. "The wind pushed it. Wind is strong." The wind made the tree leaves dance too.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip on Liam's nose. He ran inside fast. Mom gave him a raincoat and boots. Now he could jump in the puddles. After playing, he came in for warm juice. Mom dried his hair so it stood up straight. Liam laughed and took a big sip.

Sara took her orange cat toy to the playground. She wanted to play house. But she had no house!

First she found a big box. "This is my house," she said. Next she found a leaf. "This is my plate." Last she found a stick. "This is my spoon." One box, one leaf, one spoon. Now her house was ready.

Baby cat was hungry. Sara scooped sand with the spoon. She held it to the toy's soft mouth. "Eat, baby," she said. Then the wind blew. The leaf plate flew away! Sara looked around. Why did it fly? The wind did it, she thought. Wind makes light things fly.

She picked up the leaf and put a small stone on it. The wind blew again. This time the leaf stayed. "Heavy things stay put," said Sara. She patted baby cat. "Time for sleep." She drew a picture in the sand with her finger. It was a bed for baby cat. "Goodnight, house," Sara whispered.

Emilia went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a sleepy bear. She loved it. She hugged it. "I want to keep this book forever," she said.

Dad shook his head. "We take it home now. We bring it back another day." Emilia held the book tight. She did not want to let go. Her foot gave the floor a little kick. Thump. Thump.

Dad helped her count. "One week, then we bring it back," he said. Emilia counted too. "One week," she said.

At home, Emilia read the book. She opened the front first. The words told her what to say. She read it one time, two times, three times.

On the big day, Emilia held the book in both hands. She put it on the library desk. A boy picked it up next. "Now he can read it," Emilia said. She smiled and went to find a new book.

Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. "I will make soup!" she said. She put a red pot on the stove. But the stove had no knobs today. Miss Kim had taken them off to wash.

Amelia peeked into the toy box. No knobs there either. How would her soup cook?

Then she saw Ben. Ben held a teddy bear. Ben wrapped the teddy in a small blanket. "The teddy is cold," said Ben. He patted the teddy's arm. "Sleep now."

Amelia had an idea. She did not need a knob. She could pretend! She turned her hand round and round in the air. "Click!" she said. "The stove is on now!"

Ben ran over. "Soup! My teddy is hungry." Amelia filled a bowl with pretend soup. Ben held it to the teddy's mouth.

"The teddy ate it all because I pretended the stove was on," said Amelia. "Now I will make tea!" She turned her hand in the air again. "Click!"

Clara wants to build a big tower at school. She gets the big blocks first. Big blocks go on the bottom. Then she adds the small blocks on top. The tower grows tall, tall, tall.

Tom runs by fast. His feet go boom, boom, boom on the floor. The big tower wiggles. It falls down with a crash. Clara says, "Running fast made it fall." Tom says, "Sorry. That was naughty of me." He helps sweep up the blocks with his hands.

The teacher gives them warm milk and a cold apple. "Ouch, hot!" says Clara, and blows on her cup. She waits a bit. Now the milk is just right. Tom eats his cold apple. It goes crunch.

Tom walks slow, slow, slow back to the blocks. His feet go tip, tip, tip. Clara stacks the blocks again. Big on the bottom. Small on top. The tower stands tall and still. Clara laughs. "Slow feet keep my tower up!" Tom smiles and claps.

Alexander sat in the music room. A big drum sat in front of him. It had a picture of a pig on the side. His sweater was itchy, so he tugged the sleeve up.

Alexander hit the drum with his hand. Boooom. The sound was low and slow. He wanted a big, bouncy sound. He hit it again. Boooom. Still low.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Try this," she said. She pulled the drum skin tight with her hand. "Now tap it."

Alexander tapped the tight skin. Bim! The sound was high and quick. He tapped again. Bim, bim, bim!

"The tight skin makes a fast sound," Alexander said. "The loose skin makes a slow sound."

"That's right," said Miss Rosa.

Alexander pulled the skin tight and played a fast song. Then he let go and played a slow song. Booom, bim, bim, booom. The pig on the drum looked like it was dancing.

"I did it," said Alexander. He patted the pig and played one more song.

Jake wanted to know his five senses. Mom said, "You can learn them right here." Jake looked at the sun in the backyard. It was too bright. "My eyes see the sun," Jake said. "My eyes are for seeing!" He ran to the rose bush. He sniffed a red rose. "My nose smells," Jake said. "My nose is for smelling!" A bee buzzed by. Jake heard the buzz. "My ears are for hearing," Jake said. Then a leaf fell on his head. He touched it with his hand. "My hand is for touching," Jake said. "But what is left?" Jake asked. Mom handed him a sweet strawberry. Jake took a bite. "Yum! My mouth is for tasting!" he said. Mom smiled. "You did it. All five!" Jake counted them on his fingers. He wiped strawberry juice off his chin. "That was nice," Jake said. "Can we do it again tomorrow?" Mom laughed. "Yes, we can."

Matthew went to the store with Dad. He wanted to make a fruit salad. He needed apples for it.

Dad held up a big red apple. "How many do we need?" he asked.

"Ten apples!" said Matthew. "One, two, three, four, five." He put apples in the bag one by one.

"Is that ten yet?" Matthew asked himself. He looked into the bag and counted again. "No. One, two, three, four, five. Only five." Five was not ten. He needed more apples.

So he kept going. He put in more apples, one at a time. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Now the bag was full.

"I counted more, so now I have more," said Matthew. "Five was too little. Ten is just right!"

At the checkout, a warm lamp glowed above the fruit. Matthew held the bag against his chest. "Ten apples," he said. "Can we make the salad now?"

Aurora sat on the big clean couch. Everyone had come to watch the game. Uncle Max brought a bag of popcorn. Dad turned on the TV. But the screen stayed dark.

"TV needs the little box," said Aurora. She pointed at the remote. It was under the popcorn bag. Dad picked it up. He pushed the red button. The screen lit up. The game came on. Everyone clapped.

At half time, Mom went to stir the soup. Aurora smelled it from the couch. The pot was too big for the little stove burner, so Mom moved it to the big one. Then the soup began to bubble. "The big burner is hot enough," Aurora said. Uncle Max laughed and gave her a handful of popcorn. She ate it slowly and watched the players run.

Elijah found a bowl of sticky notes on the table. Each note had one big letter on it. There was an A and an M and a B.

Elijah wanted to write his mama's name. But he did not know which letters to pick. He picked the B first. He said its sound, "buh." Banana starts with B. Mama does not.

Then he picked the M. He said its sound, "mmm." The sound tickled his lips. Mama starts with "mmm!" He stuck the M on the wall.

Next he picked the A. He said, "ah." Apple starts with A. Mama starts with "ah" too. He stuck the A next to the M. Then he stuck up another M and another A, because he needed two of each.

Elijah pointed at the letters. "M, ah, M, ah," he said slowly. Then he said it fast. "Mama!"

Mama came to the wall. She gave him a soft hug. "My name!" she said.

"Yes," said Elijah. "The M makes my lips tickle. So I found it fast."

He stuck one more note on the wall. It was the letter E. "E is for Elijah," he said. "My turn now."

Ellie went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a bunny. She looked at the shelf. The books were all mixed up.

Ellie found a book about cars. "That is not a bunny," she said. She found a book about apples. "Apples are food. Bunnies are animals." She put it back. She found a book about teddy bears. "Bears are toys. Toy bears, toy trains, toy blocks. But I want an animal."

Ellie looked at the pictures on each book. Cars had wheels. Food was good to eat. Toys were for playing. Animals had fur and feet. Then she saw long ears on a cover. She opened the book. A bunny hopped in the pictures.

"The bunny is an animal, like a cat and a dog!" said Ellie. Dad smiled. "You found it. Books go in the right spot when we look."

Ellie sat on the big pillow by the window. She got sleepy as Dad read. One bunny, two bunnies, three baby bunnies in the book. Ellie closed her eyes just a little. "Read the hopping part again," she said.

Ella sat on her bed with her library book. She wanted to keep it forever. It had a picture of a big cloudy sky on the front.

She looked at the front cover. It had little words on it. "Mom, what do the words say?" she asked. Mom said, "They say The Cloudy Day. Words on books tell you things." Ella turned the pages one by one, front to back. "Is this how we read?" she asked. "Yes, from the front to the back," said Mom.

Eella brushed her hand over the smooth page. She saw paint spots on the corner. "Oh no," she said. She wanted to fix them. She tried to rub the paint off. It stayed. She waited and looked again. Then Mom said, "Tomorrow the book goes back. Other kids get to read it too." Ella held the book close. "Can we get it again?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, we can borrow it again." Ella turned to the last page. "The end," she read out loud.

Maeva held a small clay lamp. It had one little flame. The flame was for Diwali, the festival of lights.

A big wind came. It blew the flame out. The lamp went dark. "Why did it go out?" asked Maeva. "The wind blew it," she said. Papa lit it again with a match.

Maeva walked slow. She cupped her hands around the flame. The wind could not reach it now. The flame stayed on. It did not go out.

People smiled at her lamp. Grandma gave her a sweet in a bowl. Maeva ate it with a spoon. The sweet was warm and soft.

Her shoe began to slip off. She stopped and pulled it back on. Papa waited for her. He held her hand so she would not fall.

At home they set the lamp by the door. "Why does it go there?" Maeva asked. "To light the way," said Papa. The little flame glowed and glowed. Maeva waved to it. "Good night, little light," she said.

Luka sat on the park bench with his big sister, Mia. He wanted to win the game she played at school. "You name a sense and a body part," Mia said. "Then you get a gold star." Luka had no gold stars yet.

A dog ran by. "Woof, woof!" Luka put his hands over his ears. "My ears hear the dog!" Mia smiled and clapped. "Yes! Hearing uses your ears. One star for you."

Luka saw a tiny bug on a leaf. He pointed at it. "My eyes see the bug!" Mia clapped again. "Seeing uses your eyes. Two stars!"

Then Luka picked a red flower. He sniffed it with his nose. "My nose smells the flower! The rain made it smell good. That is why it smells so sweet." Mia laughed. "Three stars! Smelling uses your nose."

Next, Mia gave him a sweet berry. Luka began to chew. "Yum! My mouth tastes it!" Then he touched the wet slide. "My hands feel it! Hands are for touching!" Mia jumped up. "Five stars, Luka!"

Luka held up his hand and wiggled all five fingers. "Five senses, five stars!" he said.

Athena went to the park with her red ball. The ball was round and bouncy. She kicked it near a big tree. Then the ball rolled down the hill. It rolled right into the pond. Splash!

Athena stood at the water. "My ball!" she said. She could not reach it. Then she saw the ball sit on top of the water. "The ball floats," she said. It floated because it was light and full of air. A duck swam past. The duck pushed the ball with its beak. The ball came closer and closer.

Athena picked up a little stick. She held it out. The duck nudged the ball again. Athena grabbed her ball. "Thank you, duck," she said. She sat under the tree and ate a round apple. She dropped a piece of crust in the water. The duck ate it up. "Ducks like food, not toys," Athena said. The duck gave a happy quack.

Abigail sat at the little table. She wanted to draw on the tablet. She pressed the round button once. The screen stayed black. She pressed it again. Still black. She frowned.

Then she held the button down. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen lit up. It was bright and round like a moon. "It needed a long press," said Abigail. "A little tap does not work."

She found the drawing app and drew a tree. She drew one root, then two roots. She drew a bird ready to fly. "Time to put it away," said Teacher Jo.

Abigail pressed the button again. She held it down. The screen went dark. She set the tablet on the shelf, flat and safe.

"Look, Teacher Jo," she said. "I can do it all by myself."

Penelope loved to color at daycare. She colored a big red cat. Then she colored her own hands red, too.

"Look, red hands!" said her friend Milo. He laughed. Red paint was on his nose, too.

The teacher rang the snack bell. Penelope reached for a cracker. The cracker turned red where her fingers touched it. "Oh no," she said. "My hands make the cracker red!"

The kind teacher took her to the little sink. Warm water ran over Penelope's hands. The soap made bubbles. She rubbed and rubbed. The red went down the drain. Her hands were clean now.

Penelope picked up a new cracker. It stayed plain and crunchy. "Wet hands get clean," she said. Then she ate it all up.

After snack came a nap. Penelope lay on her mat and hugged her red cat picture. "Sleep now," she whispered. She closed her eyes, and the room went quiet.

At the end of the day, Mommy helped her put on her coat. "One arm, then the other arm," said Mommy. Penelope pulled the zipper up all by herself. "I did it!" she said. Mommy kissed her red-cat picture.

Charlie stood at the gate of the school playground. Her tummy felt jumpy. She did not know anyone yet. A boy ran past her without saying hello.

Her teacher gave her a sticker for her shirt. It said Charlie in big red letters. "Now your name can talk for you," said the teacher. A girl came near the slide. She looked at the sticker. "Hi, Charlie," the girl said. "My name is Mia." The sticker told Mia her name! That is why the boy ran past. He could not read her mind, only her shirt.

Charlie and Mia dug in the sandbox together. They found a pink worm. It wiggled and made them laugh. "Silly worm," said Charlie. Their ice pops began to melt in the sun, so they sat in the shade. Charlie licked hers slowly. Mia waited for her too. "See you tomorrow," said Mia.

Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. He hoped she would love it.

"I will paint her green frog," said Felix. But there was no green paint. Not one drop.

Felix looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. He saw blue paint. No green. He felt a little scared. Then Miss Ada said, "Try mixing two colors."

Felix dipped his brush in yellow. He dipped his brush in blue. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned green! It bubbled like a magic potion.

"Yellow and blue make green!" said Felix. He painted a big green frog. Then he mixed red and yellow. Swish, swish. That made orange, like a little sunset in his cup.

Yellow and blue make green. Yellow and blue make green. Felix said it two times, like a song.

At home, Felix gave Grandma the picture. "A green frog!" said Grandma. "And I made the green myself," said Felix. "Blue went in, yellow went in, and poof! Green came out."

Grandma kissed his head. Then they hung the frog on the fridge, right next to the orange sunset.

Ava sat in her car seat. Her tummy made a little growl. "I want a snack," she said. Mom handed her the snack bag from the front seat. Ava looked inside. She saw a red apple. She saw a cheese stick. Then she saw a banana. She picked up the banana. It felt hard and light. She peeled it a little. There was no fruit inside. It was yellow plastic all the way. It was her toy banana from the play kitchen! "Silly me," said Ava. "Toys are not food." She put it back in her bag. Then she took the apple. It was cold and sweet. She ate it slowly. "The apple is real food," she said. "It makes my tummy quiet." Mom smiled at the red light. The car went over a small bump. Ava held up the toy banana. "You sleep in my toy box," she told it. Then she looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. "That is an animal," said Ava. "It eats real food too."

Gianna stood at the big airport window. A plane came in. Was Grandma on that one? Gianna had a question. She asked it out loud. "Is Grandma here now?"

Mom said, "Soon. Watch the door."

A man pulled a little bag. The bag rolled behind him. Why did it roll? Gianna looked down. The bag had wheels! Wheels make bags roll.

Then the door opened. Grandma! She pulled a big, big bag. It rolled too. Gianna laughed.

"Why is your bag so big?" she asked.

"I stay for a whole week," said Grandma. "Seven days. Seven sleeps."

Gianna counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven sleeps!

"That's a lot of clothes," said Gianna.

"It is," said Grandma. "And I packed my fishing pole. We will fish at the pond."

"Fish? Like the fish in my book?"

"Just like that. Real ones. We will catch one, and then we will let it go."

Gianna jumped up and down. She pulled the big bag a little bit. It rolled beside her.

The sky outside turned dark. The clouds looked big and mean. Would the plane go away?

"No rain yet," said Mom. "Run fast!"

They ran to the car. Seven sleeps, seven days. Gianna said it all the way home.

Grandma said, "And one fish."

Elizabeth stood by the cubbies at school. Her coat was on. But the zipper would not zip up. She pulled and pulled. Nothing happened.

Teacher Sam waited by the door. He did not rush her. Elizabeth sat down on the little bench. She looked at her zipper. She saw the two sides at the bottom. They were apart. She pushed one side down into the little slot. It made a small click. Then she pulled the zipper tab up. The zipper teeth came together, one by one. All the way to the top!

"Look! The zipper goes up when the bottom is in," Elizabeth said. Teacher Sam smiled. "Yes, it does," he said. Elizabeth laughed and ran to the puzzle table. She was fast. Her coat stayed warm and closed all morning.

Madelyn woke up with a big wish. She wished for her red apple in the blue bowl. She ran to the kitchen. "Apple, apple," she sang. But her hands were all sticky. Why were they sticky? She had eaten jam at breakfast. Jam on her hands made them sticky.

Mommy said, "Sticky hands need a bath." Madelyn looked at the water. She patted it with one finger. Bubbles went up, up, up. Mommy washed her hands and the sticky went away. "The water took the jam off," said Madelyn. "Because I washed!"

After the bath, Madelyn needed to get dressed. She picked her wild shirt with tigers on it. She pulled it on all by herself. Her hair was wet. Wet hair, dry shirt. She felt warm and clean.

Then came her apple, washed and shiny. She took a big bite. Crunch! Madelyn smiled and said, "I washed my hands, so now my apple is clean to eat." She ate it all up, down to the little brown seed.

Henri ran into Grandpa's house. "The baby is here!" he shouted. "My sister is here!" Grandpa smiled big. The baby lay in a soft blanket. Henri had a toy worm in his pocket. He wanted Baby May to hold it. He put the worm in her little hand. The worm slid right off. It fell on the floor. Henri tried again. It fell again. "She won't hold it," said Henri.

Grandpa did not say a word. He just tapped Henri's hand. Henri looked at his own finger. He put his finger in the baby's palm. May squeezed it! She held on tight! "She likes my finger!" Henri laughed. "Babies can hold fingers, not worms." Grandpa brought cold juice and frozen strawberries. They sat by the baby.

Then May made a funny face. She let go of Henri's finger. She grabbed Grandpa's big thumb instead. Henri followed it all the way to her cheek. "She chose you, Grandpa!" said Henri. Grandpa winked. "Now give her the worm," he said. Henri laid the worm on her tummy. May held her own hands on top of it. "She did it her own way!" said Henri.

Mateo sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint a house for his teacher's new baby. He poured some purple paint into his cup. The paint went plop, plop.

First he painted a big square. It had four sides, all the same. The square fell over in his mind. "A house needs a roof," said Mateo. A square roof would not fit. Then he saw it. He turned his brush and made a triangle. The triangle had three sides. It sat right on top of the square. "It fits!" said Mateo. The triangle roof worked because it was pointy on top and flat on the bottom.

Next he painted a purple door. It was a rectangle. It was tall like him. He made one window shaped like a circle. The circle was round like a ball. It rolled nowhere, it just stayed round.

His friend Lily looked over. "My roof fell off," she said. Mateo held up his brush. "Make a triangle," he said. "Three sides. Flat on the bottom." Lily tried it. Her triangle roof sat on top of her square. It did not fall. "It fits!" said Lily. Mateo gave her a big smile. He painted a tiny circle baby inside the house. The teacher clapped her hands. "Two houses," she said. "And one small baby." Mateo dipped his brush in purple one more time.

Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. The wind blew hard. It blew his hat right off his head. The hat flew up, up, up. "Oh no," said Harrison. "My hat went away!" He ran and got his sweet blue hat. He held it with both hands.

Then rain began to fall. Pit, pat, pit, pat. Big Mama opened her umbrella. Harrison stood under it too. The rain tapped on top. "Why do we need the umbrella?" he asked. "The rain is wet," said Mama. "It keeps us dry." The rain made little drops on the tip of his shoe. One drop sat on his toe through the hole in his sock.

The rain stopped. The sun came out. It was warm on his face. Harrison took off his mittens. "My hands are hot in the sun," he said. "The wind needs mittens. The sun does not." He put them in his pocket.

The bus came at last. Harrison climbed up one big step. "The wind blew my hat, so I hold it tight," he told the bus driver. The driver smiled. Harrison sat down by the window, hat on his lap.
