Henri sat in the big salon chair. He held his doll, Pip. Today Henri would get his very first haircut. The chair felt tall. His feet did not touch the floor.

The hairdresser, Mia, put a soft cape on him. "Snip, snip," went her scissors. Henri shut his eyes tight. Then he opened one eye. Little bits of hair fell on the cape. They fell on his arm too. It did not hurt at all. Henri looked at Pip. "Hair has no hurt in it," he said. "That is why the scissors are okay."

Mia smiled. "That's right." A bit of hair fell on Pip's head. Henri laughed. "Pip looks silly with hair!" He brushed it off. Then a little pile spilled onto the floor, soft as snow.

Mia gave him a mirror. Henri saw his short hair. "I like it," he said. He hugged Pip tight.

Leah turned three today. There was a party in the backyard. Balloons sat near the fence. Grandpa set a cake on the table.

Leah wanted to blow out the candle. She took a big breath. She blew. The flame stayed on. She blew again. The flame still stayed on.

"Try once more," said Mama. Leah stood near the cake. She blew slow and long. The candle went out. Everyone clapped.

"One big breath," Leah said. "One big breath makes it go out."

Then she hopped on one foot. She hopped again. The candle was out because of her big breath. The party went on. Leah ate cake with her friends.

"Happy birthday, Leah," said Grandpa.

Beatrice went to the store with Dad. She wanted milk. But the milk was gone from the little shelf. "Where is the milk?" she asked. Dad said, "Maybe a big box in the back."

They walked to the back. Beatrice saw a big door. It was the cold room. Dad opened it. Cold air came out fast. Beatrice shivered. Brrr! She saw little milk jugs and big milk jugs. The big ones were up high. The little ones were down low.

Beatrice took a little jug. It was very cold. She held it with two hands. Then they passed the bakery. The bread there was hot. "The cold room made the milk cold," Beatrice said. "This hot oven makes the bread hot!" Dad smiled. "That is the answer," he said. "You found it all by yourself." Beatrice laughed. "Cold and hot are opposites. But my tummy likes them both!" At home, Dad poured warm milk in her cup. Beatrice took a big sip.

Sofia wanted to play the guessing game. But she did not know the rules yet. "What if I get it wrong?" she asked. Mama sat close and held her hand. "We learn it together," said Mama.

Mama held up a lemon. "Close your eyes. Now smell." Sofia sniffed with her nose. "It smells sour!" she said. "Your nose knows," said Mama. Next came a bell. It rang, and Sofia heard it fast with her ears. Then Mama let her touch a soft blanket. "My hands feel it!" said Sofia. Mama gave her a sweet berry. Sofia tasted it with her tongue. At last Sofia opened her eyes and looked at the moon in the window. "My eyes see the moon!" she said.

"Now it is your turn," said Mama. "Show me all five." Sofia pointed to her eyes, her ears, her nose, her tongue, and her hands. "Five!" she counted. Mama clapped. Sofia turned around and around, laughing. Then she sat on Mama's lap, warm and safe, and looked at the moon one more time. "Good night, moon," said Sofia.

Grayson ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. His teacher had put a new sign on the wall. "Today the sign says sunny," said Grayson. He clapped his hands. Now he could dress the big teddy bear for outside.

But which clothes? Grayson picked snow boots and a thick coat. "Too hot," said his friend Mia. She pointed at the window. The sun was bright. The sky was all blue and warm. Grayson touched the coat. It was heavy and hot in his hand. Then he got it. Snowy days need warm coats. Sunny days do not.

So Grayson found a little sun hat and cool shorts. He glued a paper sun onto the bear's shirt. "Perfect," said Mia. Outside, the sun felt warm on Grayson's arms.

A shy girl named Ruby peeked at the bear. "Can I hold it?" she asked. Grayson smiled big. "Yes! The bear loves the sun." Then they ran together into the bright, warm yard.

Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread. She reached far across the table. Her elbow bumped her cup. Milk spilled onto Dad's hat, the one he had set on his chair.

"Sorry, Dad," said Wren. Dad got a towel and wiped the hat. "That's okay," he said.

Wren tried again. "Bread," she said. Dad just looked at her. Then Mom smiled. "Try the nice word," Mom said. Wren said, "Bread, please." Dad passed the bread right away. The word worked!

Wren took a bite. Then she pushed her chair back and slid down. "My feet are stuck," she said. "Can you help me, please?" Dad helped her sit up tall.

"Thank you, Dad," said Wren. Dad kissed her head. Wren ate the bread. The lazy cat slept under her chair and did not help at all.

Livia could not find Bunny. Bunny was her best toy. "Where are you?" she called.

She peeked under the bed. No Bunny. She peeked in the toy box. No Bunny. "Think, Livia," she said. "Where did I go today?"

Livia had played outside. She had played with paint. She had eaten a snack. She put her hands on her cheeks. "I will go back to each place," she said. "Toys do not walk. Bunny stays where I put Bunny down."

First she went outside. Bunny was not far, by the big tree. No Bunny there. Then she came back in. She peeked at the paint table. No Bunny. But she saw something. A small pink color on the floor. It was a paint dot. It made a little line.

Livia followed the paint dots. Dot, dot, dot. They went past the chair. They went by the sofa. They stopped at the laundry basket. Livia peeked inside. There was Bunny! Bunny had paint on one ear. Bunny had been washing!

"Mom!" Livia called. "I found Bunny!" Mom came fast and smiled. "Bunny has paint on his ear," said Mom. "Let's wash him nice and clean." Livia washed Bunny's ear with a soft cloth.

Then Livia hugged Bunny tight. "No more painting with you," she whispered. Bunny's ear was clean and soft again.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna counted on her fingers. "Seven days," she said. "Seven sleeps, Grandma!"

Sienna wanted to paint a picture with Grandma on the very first morning. But Grandma sat on the couch. Her eyes were droopy. "Not yet, little one," Grandma said.

Sienna looked at the big clock on the wall. It was morning, but Grandma was sleepy. "Why are you sleepy, Grandma?" she asked. "You slept last night."

Grandma smiled. "My home is far away. I sat on a train for many hours. Long rides make me tired."

Sienna thought about that. The train ride made Grandma tired. That was why. So Grandma needed more sleep first.

Sienna got a soft blanket. She tucked it around Grandma. "Sleep now," she whispered. "Paint later." Grandma closed her eyes.

The clock ticked and ticked. At lunch time, Grandma woke up. "I feel much better now," she said.

They sat at the kitchen table. Sienna painted a red apple. Grandma painted a yellow sun. The paint smelled like rain and flowers.

"See, Grandma," said Sienna. "You slept, and now you are not tired anymore."

Grandma laughed and kissed her head. "You are my smart helper."

There were still six sleeps left. "Tomorrow," said Sienna, "we paint a big blue cat."

Emilia wanted toast with butter. Mama gave her a small knife. The butter was cold and hard. Emilia pushed it on the toast. The toast tore. A little hole showed.

"Try the soft butter," said Mama. The soft butter sat in a small dish by the warm toaster. Emilia dipped her knife. She spread it slow. The butter went on smooth. "Soft butter does not tear the toast," said Emilia.

Next came the milk. Emilia held the jug up high. Milk splashed on the table. A tiny ant came to look at the little puddle. "Hello, ant," said Emilia. She did not talk to it for long. She had work to do.

She set the cup on the table. She poured slow and low, close to the cup. The milk went in. Not one drop fell. She poured the last bit. The cup was full.

Emilia sat down. She bit her smooth, buttery toast. She drank her milk. The ant waved its legs and crawled away.

Anthony rides the big city bus. He holds his bunny in his lap. Then the bus bumps. Anthony holds on to the seat. Where did bunny go?

Anthony looks down. He looks under the seat. No bunny. He looks by his feet. No bunny. Then he thinks, "The bus went bump. Maybe bunny fell." He bends down low. He peeks under the seat again, way in the back. There is bunny! It is a soft little nest under the seat, and bunny sits in it.

Anthony pulls bunny out. "The bus went bump, so you fell," he says. "That is true." He hugs bunny tight. A kind lady smiles at him. "Your bunny is dirty," she says. Anthony wipes bunny's face with his sleeve. Now bunny is clean. The bus stops, and Anthony waves to the lady. "Bye bye! We found our nest!"

Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist. "First time," said Mama. Florence looked out the window. She saw a fish shop go by. Big fish, little fish, all on ice.

The bus stopped and stopped. "Are we near?" asked Florence. "Not yet," said Mama. "We wait." Florence waited. She counted the buttons on her coat. One, two, three.

At last the bus stopped near a little office. A man in a blue shirt smiled. "Hello, Florence. I am the dentist." He had a small mirror on a stick. "Open your mouth big and wide," he said. "Then I can see your back teeth."

Florence closed her mouth. Then she opened it a little. Then she opened it very wide. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see all your teeth now," he said. "Let's count them." He counted one by one. Then he put some tooth paste on a little brush. It tickled. It tasted like strawberries.

Florence sat up. "My teeth are clean," she said. The dentist gave her a sticker with a fish on it. Florence put it near her heart. "Open wide again," she said, "so you can see my sticker."

Leah ran to the swings. But a line of kids stood there. Four kids, then five kids. Leah got in the line too.

"I want to swing now," she said.

"Wait for your turn," said a big boy. "Let's count."

He clapped his hands. "One, two, three." The kids sang with him. "Four, five, six." Leah sang too. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!"

The first boy hopped off his swing. Then a girl. One kid went each time they counted to ten.

Leah watched and watched. At last she was at the front. One, two, three, four, five. Her turn came fast!

She swung up high. Her hands held the clean, cold chain. She laughed.

Then she saw a small boy behind her, waiting in the line. He looked sad.

Leah counted with him. "One, two, three." She swung and counted. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

She jumped off. "Your turn now," she said.

The boy smiled a big, happy smile. "One, two, three!" he sang, pumping his legs.

Arthur ran to Grandpa's garden. "I want big carrots!" he said. Grandpa gave him tiny seeds. Arthur made a little hole in the middle of the dirt. He dropped three seeds in. Then he covered them up.

Every day Arthur looked. Nothing grew. Arthur forgot to give the seeds water! Grandpa filled a small can. Arthur poured water on the dirt. "Drink, seeds, drink!" he said.

The next morning was very cold. The water in the can went freeze, hard as ice! But the dirt was soft. Two little green leaves popped up. Arthur jumped up and down. "The water made them grow!" he said.

Grandpa smiled. Soon the leaves grew tall. Under the dirt, a yellow carrot got fat. Arthur pulled it out. "My carrot! I grew it!"

Grandma was coming to stay! She would sleep in Juliette's room for seven whole days. Juliette counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven! "Grandma needs a bed," said Mama. "Can you help make it?" Yes! Juliette could help!

They went to the big market to get things. Juliette waved at the apple man. She waved at the bread lady. Everyone knew Grandma was coming! "Grandma likes tea," said Mama. "But her tea mug stayed at her own house." Oh no. Grandma would have no mug for seven whole days!

Juliette looked and looked. A red mug. A green mug. Then she saw it. A tiny blue mug with a duck on it. "This one!" she said. It was little, just like Grandma's hands. It fit right inside her own fingers. She held it up high. "Grandma's mug!"

At home, Juliette made the bed. She put a soft blanket on it. She put the duck mug by the lamp. Grandma's hat sat on the chair, waiting too. Then the door opened. Grandma was here! She picked up the little mug. "A duck for my tea!" said Grandma. "I am sorry I left my mug home. But this one is better." Juliette clapped and clapped. Seven days of tea with Grandma! Juliette poured the very first cup.

Owen ran to the park with his red ball. He felt so excited. His tummy felt like bouncing.

Then a big dog ran up. The dog barked very loud. Owen felt scared. He hid behind a tree. His hands shook. Why was the dog barking? Owen peeked out. The dog was looking at his ball, not at him. Maybe the dog was angry because the ball went into her yard! Owen threw the ball far. The dog ran and got it. Then the dog wagged her tail. She was happy now. Owen laughed. "The dog was loud because she wanted my ball," he said.

A girl came by. Her name was Mia. She was crying. Her ice cream had fallen. Drip, drip, on the ground. Now it was smelly too, because a goose came to bite it. Owen gave Mia his ball to hold. She stopped crying. She smiled. Owen felt warm inside. "Want to play?" said Mia. Owen threw the ball high, and they both ran after it.

Penelope walked into her classroom. The sun sat low in the window. Yesterday she found a red leaf at the park. It was big and shiny. She wanted to show it to her friend Sam today. She looked in her bag. The leaf was not there. The leaf was still at home, on top of her table.

"Where is your leaf?" asked Sam. "It is at home," said Penelope. "I found it yesterday. But yesterday is all done. I cannot go back and get it now." Her tummy felt a little tight. Then she had an idea. "Tomorrow I will bring it," she said. "Tomorrow is the day after today. First we sleep, then it comes."

All day they painted pictures. Later, the teacher rang the bell. "The day went fast," said Penelope. She walked to the door with Sam. "Tonight I will put the leaf in my bag," she said. "Then tomorrow it will be here." Sam smiled. "I will wait for it," she said.

Jasmine had a library book about rainbows. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight.

"Can this book stay with me always?" she asked.

Mom shook her head. "The library book must go back on Friday. Other kids will read it too."

Jasmine pouted. Then she had an idea. "Can I draw my own rainbow book?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "That one is yours to keep."

Jasmine took paper and crayons. She drew a big rainbow. She drew a small rainbow. She asked Mom to write the words. Mom wrote "Rainbow" on the first page. Jasmine pointed at the letters.

"Those are real words?" she asked.

"They are true words," said Mom. "Books start at the front. We read this way."

Jasmine turned the pages one by one, front to back. Then she put her book under her pillow.

"Friday can come now," she said.

Henry sat at the little red table. He wanted to paint a big orange pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

His teacher pointed to the cups. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. Henry said them too. "Red, yellow, blue." He touched each cup. "One, two, three."

He looked at the red cup. He looked at the yellow cup. He put his brush in the red. Dab. Then he put it in the yellow. Dab. He stirred on the white paper. The paint turned orange!

Henry laughed. "Red and yellow make orange!" he said.

His friend Mia looked sad. She wanted green for her frog. Henry showed her the blue cup. Then the yellow cup. "Blue and yellow make green," he said.

Mia dabbed blue. Then yellow. Green! Her frog got a big green back.

The brush tickled Henry's fingers with paint. He made a small orange pillow for his pumpkin to sit on. Mia made a green lily pad.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Henry. "Mix, mix, mix!"

"More pumpkins!" said Mia. Henry dipped his brush in the red again.

Max ran to the red truck. Ben grabbed it too. "My turn!" said Max. He pulled. Ben pulled. The truck fell on the floor. A wheel came off.

Max picked up the wheel. He tried to put it back on. It would not go on. Teacher Mia sat with them. She held up her hand. "Let's count to twenty," she said. "Ben goes first. Then Max."

Ben drove the truck around the rug. Max counted. He counted to twenty twice. Then Ben put the truck in Max's hands. Max drove it fast, past the blocks and past the pillow corner.

A small spider came out from under the truck. "It's tickly!" said Max. "My sock feels itchy." He laughed and wiggled his foot. "Ben, look!" he said. "Trucks carry spiders!"

Camille put on her warm blanket cape. She ran to the ice rink with Dad. The ice was all white and shiny. Kids were playing on the soft mats by the boards.

Dad put a hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in!" Camille threw it high. It went way over the hoop. She threw it fast. It went far away. "Why does it keep missing?" she asked. She looked at the hoop. It was close. She tried one more time, soft and slow. The beanbag went up and sank right into the hoop. "It was too hard!" she said. "Soft works!" Dad clapped.

Then Dad rolled her a big red ball. Camille held out one hand. The ball hit her fingers and bounced off. She held out both hands. The big ball landed right in them. "Two hands catch the big ball!" she said. Dad threw it again. She caught it again. The zamboni drove past on the ice. "Look, pretty lights!" she said. "Throw it high, Dad!"

Jasmine wanted to cool her teddy bear. He was hot from sitting in the sun. She got two ice cubes. One was big. One was small. She put them on teddy's tummy. She tickled teddy with a string to make him laugh. Then she looked. The small ice cube was gone. The big ice cube was still there. It melted slow, not fast. Jasmine licked the big ice cube. It was cold and a bit sour, like lemon water. "The small one melted fast," she said. "The big one melts slow." She got more big ice cubes. She put them on teddy one by one. Soon teddy's tummy was cool. "There," said Jasmine. "Big ice, slow melt. You feel better now." Teddy sat up, and she hugged him.</think>Jasmine wanted to cool her teddy bear. He was hot from sitting by the sunny window. She went to the freezer. She got two ice cubes. One was big. One was small. She put them both on teddy's tummy. She waited. She licked a popsicle while she waited. It was cold and sour, like lemon. Then she looked down. The small ice cube was gone. The big ice cube was still there. "The small one melted fast," said Jasmine. "The big one melts slow." She got another big ice cube and put it on teddy. She tied a string around teddy's paw to make it look like a bandage. Soon his tummy was cool and his paw looked fixed. "Big ice stays longer," she said. She hugged teddy tight. "Now you are not hot."

Quinn stood at the pet store. She held a little box with holes. Inside was her new bunny, Pip.

"Is Pip sad in the box?" Quinn asked. "He is not sad," said Dad. "He is shy. New homes feel big to bunnies."

At home, Quinn put the box on the floor. She opened the lid. Pip did not hop out. He just sat still. Quinn waited. Then she put a small carrot near the door. Pip sniffed it. His nose went wiggle, wiggle. Then he hopped out!

"He came out because of the carrot," Quinn said. "Smells help him feel safe." Dad smiled. "Yes. Bunnies follow their noses."

Pip hopped to his water bowl. He drank a little sip. Quinn sat very still on the floor. "I will not grab you," she said softly. Pip hopped close to her shoe. His ears touched her sock.

Quinn reached out one gentle hand. Pip sniffed her fingers. Then he settled down in a soft warm ball. Dad put a blanket by the bowl. "This is his spot," Dad said.

Quinn watched her bunny sleep. "Good night, Pip," she said. "This is your home now."

Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels.

"I am hungry," said Felix. Mom reached back her hand. In the bag were a banana, a small toy duck, and some crackers. Felix picked up the duck. He put it near his mouth. Then he shook his head. "No," said Felix. "Ducks are toys. Toys do not go in my tummy."

"Smart boy," said Mom. Felix counted what he could eat. "One, banana. Two, crackers. Banana is food. Crackers are food." He peeled the banana. It smelled sweet. He took a big bite.

Outside the window, Felix saw cows. "One cow, two cows, three cows!" he said. "Cows are animals." Then Felix saw something in the road. "Stop, Mom! Dog!" Mom stopped the car. The dog ran safely across. Felix waved his banana at the window. "Bye, dog! I leave some crackers for you!" Mom put two crackers on the grass by the fence.

The car went on. The wheels went bump, bump. Felix found a surprise in his pocket. It was a little toy car! "A toy!" he said. "Not food. Just for playing." He made the toy car zoom on his knee. Then he ate his crackers, one crunch at a time.

Alice ran to the big slide. But her friend Sam was there first. Sam stood at the top and would not come down. "We can count and take turns," said Alice. "How does counting help?" asked Sam. "We count to ten, then we swap." Alice began. "One, two, three." Sam listened from the top. "Four, five, six." Alice kept going, slow and steady. "Seven, eight, nine." Sam slid down with a little bump in the sand. "Ten!" said Alice. Now it was her turn. She climbed up and slid down fast. The slide felt cool, not slimy like the pond rocks at home. They counted to ten again and again, back and forth, all morning. "Counting is like a dream," said Sam happily. Alice laughed and began again: "One, two, three."

Hayden went to the library with his mom. It was cloudy outside. Inside, the lights felt warm.

Hayden wanted the big red book about a cat. It was on a high shelf. He reached and reached. He could not get it.

"Help, please," he said to the librarian. She smiled. "Of course," she said. She got the cat book down.

Hayden hugged the book. "Thank you," he said.

He sat at the little table. One book, two books, three books. He counted his stack. Then his elbow bumped a cup. The cup tipped over. Water ran across the table.

"Sorry," Hayden said to the librarian. "It fell because my elbow hit it," he said.

She helped him cover the wet spot with a towel. Then she handed him something small. It was a cat sticker.

"For me?" asked Hayden.

The librarian nodded. "For saying please and thank you and sorry."

Hayden put the sticker on his shirt. It was a tiny orange cat. He grinned all the way home.

Brooks had a cough. It kept him awake at night. Mom said, "We will go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy, Brooks sat in the cart. He saw tall shelves. He saw boxes and bottles. Mom found the honey. She showed the jar to Brooks. "Honey can help your throat," she said.

At home, Mom gave Brooks a small spoon of honey. It was sweet and slow in his mouth. He swallowed it. The scratchy feeling got quiet. That night, Brooks coughed less. He slept in his warm bed. In the morning he said, "Mom, the honey made my cough stop." Mom smiled and put the jar back on the shelf. "One more spoon for breakfast," she said. Brooks ran to the kitchen table.

Louis stood at the little table in cooking class. Today he would make toast and pour milk. His heart went bump, bump. He wanted to do it all by himself.

First the toast. Louis pushed the butter with his knife. The butter would not spread. It tore a hole in the toast. "Try small bits of soft butter," said Miss Ana. Louis took a tiny bit and rubbed it on. It went on smooth. "Small bits work," said Louis.

Next the milk. Louis held the jug far above the cup. Milk splashed out. It ran onto the table. A drop began to chase his friend Mia's plate. Louis moved the jug down low, close to the cup. He tipped it slow. The milk went in. Not one drop fell.

"Look, Miss Ana," said Louis. He lifted his cup up high. "I did it, all by myself!"

Connor was in his playroom. His hands were dirty from the sand table. He wanted his big red truck to zoom fast down the ramp. It went slow. Too slow. Connor let go again. Slow, slow, slow. He began to wonder why.

Then he tried his small blue car. It went fast. Very, very fast. It zoomed right past the truck. The big truck was heavy. The small car was light. "That is why!" said Connor. "Big goes slow. Small goes fast."

Next to the ramp was his toy kettle. It had warm water inside. Connor touched it. Hot. He dipped his dirty truck in cold water from his cup. The cup felt cold. "Hot cup, cold cup," he said. He washed the truck until it was clean.

Connor held the car up high. "Want to zoom again?" he asked. The little car zoomed down the ramp and bumped right into the big, clean truck.

Asher ran to the park with Mama. He wanted to play on the slide. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Asher held her hand.

Near the slide, there was a big grill. Smoke came up from it. Asher pointed. "Hot," said Mama. She held her hand near, not on it. Asher put his hand near too. He felt the warm air. He pulled his hand back. "The grill is hot because of the fire," he said. "I will not touch it."

Asher slid down the slide. Then he slid down again. He got thirsty. Mama said, "Let us bring your cup." Asher drank his juice. It was cold. "Cold juice, hot grill," he said. Mama laughed.

Then a little dog came by. It had Asher's red ball in its mouth! "Woof," said the dog. It dropped the ball at Asher's feet. Asher was happy. "Thank you, dog," he said. He threw the ball, and the dog ran after it.

Isaiah sat in his big car seat. He held a small cup of ice. Mom said, "Hold it tight. We will drive fast now." The sun came in the window. It was hot on his hands. Isaiah looked down. His ice was getting small and wet. Drip, drip, on his pants. "Mom, why is my ice melting?" he asked. "Because the sun is hot," Mom said. "Ice melts in hot places." Isaiah thought hard. He saw the little window by the vent. Cold air blew out of it. He moved his cup to the cold spot. He held it there. Soon the ice stopped dripping. It stayed big and cold. "The cold air wins!" Isaiah said. Mom smiled. Then Dad said, "Uh oh. Now we drive slow. Red light." The car stopped. Isaiah giggled and licked his ice. "Slow is good," he said. "Slow helps me eat it all."

Raphael went to the dentist. He wanted a sticker at the end. The friendly dentist said, "Open wide!" Raphael opened his mouth. Then it was time for a snack. Raphael ran to the table and grabbed an apple.

The dentist said, "Wait! Wash your hands first." Raphael put his hands under the water. "Too fast," said the dentist. "Use soap. Wash for twenty seconds. Sing happy birthday two times." Raphael rubbed the soap on his palms. He sang the song. In the middle of the song, he saw bubbles cover his hands. When the song ended, the bubbles were gone. His hands were clean and shiny.

Raphael ate his apple. "The soap got the germs off," he said. "That is why I wash!" He did not skip the sink after the toilet either. The dentist gave him a big sticker. "Two hands clean," said Raphael, holding it up.

Eva climbed the school bus. She held the rail with both hands. Her mommy had pinned a pink tag on her coat. The tag had her name on it. "I can write my name," Eva said. "But Mommy wrote it for me."

She sat by the window. The bus was big and yellow. One driver. Two big mirrors. Three rows of seats. Eva looked out. She saw a red nose on a clown poster. She saw trees going by, one, two, three.

The bus stopped. Eva looked at her pink tag. Then she looked out the window. There was a sign. It said her school's name, just like her tag said her name. The bus stops at the school with my name on it, she thought. A teacher with a smile came up the steps. She looked at Eva's tag. "Hello, Eva," the teacher said.

The door opened with a whoosh. Eva took the teacher's hand. One step. Two steps. Three steps down. On the ground lay a small pink flower. It had fallen out of a girl's basket. Eva picked it up and put it in her pocket. Then she walked through the big door.

Arlo wants to make a paper garden. He cuts out one sun, two clouds, and three red flowers.

He puts a flower on the paper. He tips the paper up. The flower slides off. "Guess it wants to fall," he says. Why does it fall?

Mama hands him a glue stick. Arlo rubs it on the back of a flower. The glue feels cool and slippery. He presses the flower down. He counts, "One flower, two flowers, three flowers." He tips the paper again. The flowers stay!

"So the glue was wet," Arlo says. "Now it is dry. Dry glue holds the flowers."

He adds the sun and the clouds. He tips the paper way up high. Nothing falls. "My garden stays," he says. "One sun, two clouds, three flowers. All stuck!"

Arlo runs to the window. "Look, Mama! My garden is on the wall!"

Avery sat at the paint table. Her class had a goldfish. It was the class pet. The fish swam in slow circles. "Hello, fish," said Avery.

Avery wanted to paint the fish. She had yellow paint. She had blue paint too. But the fish was green.

She painted with yellow. The fish looked wrong. Then a drip fell. Blue paint spilled into the yellow. The colors moved together. The puddle turned green.

Avery looked and looked. "Blue and yellow make green," she said. She dabbed her brush in the new green. She painted the fish carefully, slow and small.

The teacher leaned down. "That looks just like him," she said.

Avery held up her paper next to the bowl. Green fish, green paint. The fish blew a tiny bubble.

Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her mama gave her a hug. Then her mama waved and went down the hall.

Elizabeth held her new backpack. She looked around the room. There were little red hooks on the wall. Each hook had a name on it. She saw a hook with "Elizabeth" on it. She hung her backpack on that hook. She hung her coat there too.

At play time, Elizabeth made a picture. She used the glue bottle. A drop of glue got on her fingers. "Oooh, it feels slimy," she said. She rubbed her fingers together. The glue got sticky and stringy.

Her teacher brought a wet cloth. "This will help," she said. Elizabeth wiped her hands. The sticky glue came off. "The water took the glue away," Elizabeth said. "Thank you," she said to her teacher.

When it was time to go home, Elizabeth looked at the wall. She found the hook with her name. Her coat was right there. "The name tells me where my things go," she said. She pulled up her zipper all by herself. Then she ran to the door to find her mama.

Beau sat in his big car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. It was windy outside. The trees waved their leaves. Beau's tummy made a growl. "I want a snack!" he said.

Mom said, "Look in your bag." Beau dug in the bag. He pulled out a toy car. Vroom! But a toy car is not a snack. He pulled out his teddy bear. He hugged the teddy. But a teddy is not a snack either. Then he found his book. He looked at the picture of a duck. But a book is not a snack! Beau dug deeper. His hand found something yellow. It was a banana! A banana is a food. Beau peeled it all by himself. He took a big bite. Yum! His tummy went quiet.

The car stopped at a red light. Beau had to wait. He waved his banana at Mom. Mom smiled and said, "One more bite, and then we are home." Beau took the biggest bite of all.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Myles took her to the park. It was spring, and the flowers were out.

"Look at the ducks," said Myles. "Look, look, look!" Grandma looked and laughed. They ran to the swings. They ran to the slide. They ran to the big tree.

Then Grandma sat down on a bench. Her eyes went closed. Myles pulled her hand. "Swing more!" But Grandma did not move. She was asleep. Grandmas get tired when they run, because their legs are old and slow. Myles saw this all by himself.

"Grandma needs a rest," he said. He sat by her feet. A duck came near. "Shh," said Myles. "Grandma needs a rest."

Soon Grandma opened her eyes. "Did I miss the ducks?" she asked. "You missed three ducks," said Myles. Grandma laughed and laughed. Then she stood up, took his hand, and said, "Show me all three."

Nora was at Ben's house. Ben had a tablet. Nora wanted to draw on it. But the screen was dark. She tapped it. Nothing happened. Why was it dark?

"Try the little round button," said Ben. Nora pressed the round button at the side. Click. The screen lit up! It was bright and full of colors. "The button made it wake up," said Nora. She found the drawing app. It was the square with a paintbrush. She tapped it and drew a messy purple cat with six legs.

Then Mom called them for a snack. Nora put the tablet on the shelf, next to a big red book. "I press the button again later," she said.

After snack, she pressed the round button. Click. And there was her purple cat, still on the screen, waiting for her. "It remembers my cat," said Nora. She added one more leg.

Paisley saw a big blue bus at the park. It was a bookmobile! Books sat on little shelves inside. Paisley wanted a book about a red fire truck.

A lady in the bus smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" she asked. Paisley jumped up and down. "Yes! Yes! Yes!" she said.

The card felt rough on one side. Paisley held it tight. The lady found the fire truck book. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back next week so other kids can read it too."

Paisley stopped jumping. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Then she saw a boy at the shelf. He was looking for a truck book too. There were no more truck books. The boy looked sad. The boy was sad because the book was in Paisley's hands.

Paisley looked at her card. She looked at the boy. "You can read it after me," she said. "I will bring it back fast, fast, fast."

Paisley walked home with Mama. She hugged the book all the way. Every night they read about the red fire truck. The good feeling grew and grew.

On the last day, Paisley walked back to the bus. She gave the book to the boy. He sat down right away to read. "My turn next time!" said Paisley, waving her rough little card.

Lennon went to the big cultural center with Mama and Nana. There was a party for Diwali. Music played. Little lamps glowed everywhere.

Lennon ran to the door. But a kind man stood there. He pointed down at his feet. He had no shoes on! "We take our shoes off here," said Mama. "That is why everyone is barefoot." Lennon looked down. Her shoes were on. That was wrong!

Mama helped her pull them off. Then Mama sent Lennon to put them in a shoe box by the wall. Lennon placed them in, so they would not get lost. Nana held her hand. They walked in together.

The floor was cool and smooth under Lennon's toes. She sat by the lamps. "Shoes off, then we go in," she said. Mama smiled and gave her a little lamp to hold.

Lucy ran to the park with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. "It is sunny today," she said. Dad spread a blanket on the grass. Lucy took off her shoes. The grass tickled her toes.

Then the wind came. It blew and blew. Lucy's hat flew off her head. "My hat!" she cried. The wind pushed it under a bush. Lucy ran to get it. Dirt was on the brim. Dad helped her brush it off. "The wind took my hat because it was loose," Lucy said. Dad nodded. "So we will tie it tight." He tied the strap under her chin. The wind blew again. The hat stayed on Lucy's head.

"Now I can keep my hat," Lucy said. She felt the warm sun again. A kind lady on the next blanket smiled at her. "Hold on tight," the lady said. Lucy laughed and held her hat with both hands.

Hailey sat in the cafe with Mom. Mom gave her a pencil and a paper menu. "Can you write your name?" Mom asked. Hailey wanted to write it so much. She grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out wiggly and ugly. The H looked like a squished bug.

Mom took Hailey's little hand. She set the pencil on Hailey's middle finger. Then Mom helped her pinch the top with her thumb and one finger. "Try now," Mom said softly. Hailey pinched and squeezed. The pencil felt steady, like a paint brush in her hand.

She drew one line down. Then another line down. Then a line across. It was an H! Hailey laughed. "The pencil stays still when I pinch it," she said. She drew a big A next. The waitress came by and clapped. Mom gave the paper a kiss and put it in her bag. "The best H I ever saw," said Mom. Hailey pinched the pencil again and wrote one more A.

Lily sat in the computer lab at school. In front of her was a tablet. It was dark and still. She wanted to draw a cat on it. But first she had to turn it on.

Lily found the small round button on the side. She pushed it. She waited. She counted, "One, two, three." Then the screen lit up. "The button makes it turn on!" said Lily. On the screen was a row of little pictures. One, two, three, four, five. She looked for the drawing app.

She tapped the picture with the crayon. The app opened. Lily drew a purple cat with a straight tail. She drew one ear, two ears, three whiskers. Then the teacher said it was time to go.

Lily moved her finger across the screen. The cat was gone. She pressed the button again and held it. "One, two, three." The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, straight in a line with the others.

"I pressed it, and it slept," said Lily.

Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted apples for snack. But how many apples should they get? Mom did not say. "Can you count them?" asked Mom. Sarah held up her hands. She did not guess. She knew the counting song. "One, two, three," she said, touching each apple. "Four, five, six, seven." The apples were red and round. One apple had a triangle sticker on it. "That sticker is cute," said Sarah. She kept going. "Eight, nine, ten." The words came out in the same order as her song. Ten came last, every time. "Did I count right?" she asked. "Yes! Ten apples," said Mom. "Ten apples because the song goes one to ten, and then it stops." Mom put the apples in a bag. The bag went in the cart. Sarah held the bag all the way to the car. "One bag," she said. "Ten apples."

Ibrahim sat in his big car seat. They were going to Grandpa's house. The sun came up early, and the road was bright.

Ibrahim dropped his toy car. It fell under the seat. He could not reach it. "Mama, can you help me, please?" he asked. Mama reached back and got it. "Thank you, Mama," said Ibrahim. She smiled at him in the mirror.

Then they stopped for apples. Papa gave one to Ibrahim. But Ibrahim squeezed it too hard, and it rolled onto Mama's lap. "Sorry, Mama," he said. Mama wiped her dress. "That is okay," she said. Then they crossed a big bridge. Water ran under it. "That is a river," said Ibrahim. "Can we pass it soon?" Papa drove on and on.

After the bridge, Mama gave Ibrahim his apple again. It tasted sweet. "The apple rolled because I held it too hard," said Ibrahim. He held it soft this time. "Good hands," said Mama. Ibrahim took a big, happy bite.

Lydia stood on the grass by the baseball diamond. She had a purple beanbag and a big red ball. Papa put a hoop on the ground.

"Throw the beanbag in," said Papa.

Lydia threw it. The beanbag went far left. It landed in the grass.

"Not yet," said Lydia.

She brought the beanbag back. She looked at the hoop. She threw again, slow and soft. This time the beanbag dropped in.

"Slow and soft," said Lydia. "It goes in when I throw soft."

Papa clapped. Then he picked up the big red ball.

"Now catch," he said. "Hold out both hands."

Lydia held out one hand. Papa rolled the ball. It bumped her hand and rolled away.

"Not yet," said Lydia.

She brought the ball back. This time she held out both hands. She made a big bowl with them. Papa rolled the ball again. It rolled right into her hands.

"Both hands catch the ball!" said Lydia.

"Both hands," said Papa. "Big ball, big hands."

They sat on the bench. Papa gave Lydia a purple card with a star on it.

"You get a star," said Papa.

Lydia held the card up high. "My star," she said. "My big hands, too."

Charlie wanted to wear her bear pajamas to bed. But she could not find them anywhere.

"Where did they go?" she asked. "Did they run away?"

"No," said Dad with a smile. "Look in the laundry basket."

There they were. The pajamas were wet. Charlie had splashed in her bath, and now the pajamas had fallen in the puddle on the floor. "Wet pajamas got wet because of my bath water," said Charlie. "That is why!"

Dad laughed. "You are a smart detective."

They hung the pajamas on the radiator. Dad said they would be dry by morning, because warm air dries wet things. Charlie put on her bunny pajamas instead. They were soft and warm.

Before bed, Charlie ate a banana and brushed her teeth. Dad tucked her in.

"Will my bear pajamas be dry for school?" Charlie asked.

"Yes, after the warm air bakes them dry all night," said Dad.

Charlie hugged her bunny pajamas. "Good night, bunnies. The radiator is baking my bears."

Addison went to the library with her dad. She wanted to build with the big blocks. The blocks sat in a red bin.

She stacked a square block on top. It sat still. Then she tried to stack a circle block. The circle rolled away. It rolled under the chair. "Come back!" said Addison. She got on her knees. She reached under the chair. Her dad laughed. "That circle is fast," he said.

Addison put the circle on the rug. She pushed it. It rolled again. She put a square on the rug. She pushed it. The square just slid. It did not roll. She scratched her head. "The circle rolls because it is round," she said. "The square has flat sides. Flat sides stop it."

She stacked squares and triangles and rectangles. They all sat still. At the top she put one circle. It wobbled. It rolled off and bonked her toe. "Ow! Silly circle," she said. Her dad kissed her toe. Then he read her a story about a mean dragon who could not roll down a hill. "He is too square," said Addison. Her dad laughed and laughed. She pushed the circle one more time, and it rolled all the way to the story door.

James wanted to paint a big green tree. The teacher let him pick a paint pot. But the green pot was frozen. It had been outside in the cold all night. James tapped the pot. The paint would not move. "We can let it warm up," said Miss Kim. James waited. He looked out the window. The tree was still green. The pot was still hard.

Then James saw the blue pot. He saw the yellow pot too. He put blue on his brush. He put yellow on top. He stirred them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," said James. "That is the name of my new color. Tree green." Miss Kim smiled. James painted his tree, slow and careful, from the brown pot to the green leaves. "Look at my tree," he said.

Athena stood in the kitchen with her family. She wanted to help make breakfast.

Daddy poured big pancakes. Athena poured one small pancake. "Mine is small like a coin," she said. The pan was hot, so the pancakes sizzled fast. Athena wanted her small pancake to be a magic cake for the moon.

But the small pancake cooked fast. The big pancakes cooked slow. Athena watched her coin pancake. It turned brown quickly. "Oh no!" she cried. Her magic cake was too dark.

Daddy smiled. "Small things cook fast," he said. "Big things cook slow." Athena thought about this. Then she made a new plan. She made a big pancake, as big as a plate. It cooked slowly, slowly. It stayed golden and perfect.

Athena put the big pancake on a cold plate from the fridge. The plate felt cold on her fingers. "Moon cake!" she said. Her curly hair bounced as she jumped. Daddy took a bite. "Best moon cake ever," he said. Athena giggled and poured more batter.

Beatrice loved the doll corner at school. Today she found three baby dolls in the basket. One baby, two babies, three babies. She picked up the smallest one.

"You are crying," said Beatrice. The baby was really just quiet plastic. But her friend Milo sat nearby. He was the daddy in their pretend house. "The baby is hungry," said Milo. Beatrice looked around. There was no real food.

Then she had an idea. She took a small red block. She held it like a bottle. "Here, baby, here is your milk." She tipped the block to the baby's mouth. She made a tiny slurp sound, "slurp, slurp, slurp." Milo clapped his hands. The baby was all better now.

"She stopped crying because I fed her," said Beatrice. "Hungry babies cry. Full babies sleep." She laid the baby on a scarf for a blanket. She had to bend down low to tuck it in. She patted the baby's back, one pat, two pats, three pats.

Then Milo brought a toy phone. "Ring, ring! The doctor is here!" Beatrice grabbed it. "Hello, Doctor Beatrice speaking." The baby needed one more check-up. She pressed a finger on the baby's chest. "Beep! All healthy!" Milo laughed so big.

At tidy-up time, Beatrice put the babies back in the basket. One baby, two babies, three babies. She was happy. "Same game tomorrow?" asked Milo. Beatrice nodded. "Bring the phone," she said.

Milo ran to the bunny cage. He wanted to hold Snowy today.

"Snowy had a turn yesterday," said Miss Kim. She was a kind woman with a soft voice. "Amy held him yesterday. Today is Tom's turn. Tomorrow you can hold him."

Milo frowned. He did not want tomorrow. He wanted now.

"It is not tomorrow now," said Tom. Tom held Snowy gently.

Milo waited. He fixed his loose shoe lace. He drew a bunny. He paid careful attention when Miss Kim read a story. The story was long.

The bell rang. Mom came to get Milo.

"Did you hold the bunny?" Mom asked.

"Not yet," said Milo. "I get my turn tomorrow."

He slept. Then the sun came up. Milo put on his shoes fast.

"Is it tomorrow now?" he asked Mom.

Mom smiled. "Yes. Now eat your breakfast."

At school, Milo held Snowy. Snowy was warm and soft.

"Tomorrow turned into today," said Milo.

Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her big brother. Now she had to stay home.

Lillian wanted to play. She picked up her toy plane. She ran down the hall. But her nose was stuffy. Her legs felt slow. She sat on the floor and sighed.

Mom made her a warm drink. Mom tucked her into bed with her plane. Lillian slept and slept. When she woke up, her nose was better. Her legs felt fast again.

Lillian ran to Mom. "Mom, my cold is almost gone!" she said. She held up her plane. "I slept, and now I feel good."

Mom smiled. "Yes, my sweet girl."

Lillian threw the plane across the room. It flew in a big loop. She ran and caught it. Her nose did not run anymore. She laughed and threw it again.

"Again!" said Lillian. "Watch me catch it!"

James went to the bank with Mom. Outside it was cold and windy. James did not want to be cold.

"Time for your coat," said Mom. "I can do it," said James. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in fast. The other arm hid. He wiggled and wiggled. At last the arm popped out. The coat was on!

Now came the zipper. James pulled it up. But it would not zip. It just slid and slid. Why would it not go? James looked down. The zipper had two sides. One side was up high. One side was down low. They were not together.

James touched the little slider at the bottom. What if the two sides had to meet there first? He pushed both sides down. He pushed them into the slider. Click. He pulled the zipper up. Zip! It went all the way to his chin. "The two parts touch at the bottom," said James. "Then it zips!"

Mom smiled. "What a good zipper job," she said. James saw a picture on the wall. It had a snowman in a coat. "His coat zips too," said James. He patted his own chest and walked out the door.

Mohamed went to the market with Dad. He held a big red bag. "We need eggs," said Dad. "We need milk," said Mohamed. "Pancakes for dinner tonight!"

A fly buzzed near the apples. It did a little loop. "Silly fly," laughed Mohamed. "No pancakes for you."

At home, Mohamed helped cook. Dad let him stir. The batter was lumpy. Mohamed stirred more. The lumps went away because he stirred. "Look, Dad! Smooth now!"

Then Dad tapped the shelf. A hook was loose. He got his hammer. Tap, tap, tap. "All fixed," said Dad. "Now the pan can hang."

Mohamed poured batter into the hot pan. It sizzled. It smelled sweet and warm. Dad flipped one pancake high. It flew up, up, up. Then it landed right in the pan.

"Again!" laughed Mohamed.

The pancakes stacked up on a big plate. Mama and Baby Amina came to the table. Mohamed gave everyone two pancakes. He ate his bite and grinned.

"Best pancakes ever," said Mama.

Mohamed licked syrup off his thumb. "Tomorrow we flip three!"

Rosalie rode in the car a long, long way. "We are far from home," she said. Her feet felt the warm sand. "This beach is not cold like winter," she said. Winter at home made her wear boots. Here she wore tiny flip flops.

Rosalie found a tiny white shell. She put it in her pocket. Then she splashed in the sea. Her swimsuit got all wet. She sat down on the hot sand. The sun shone and shone. Soon her swimsuit was dry!

"Why is it dry?" she wondered. The sun did it. The wet went away because the sun was hot. She asked, "Did the sun drink my water?"

Then Mama's phone made a sound. It was Grandma! Rosalie got to call out, "Hello, Grandma! The sun dried my suit!" The waves said swoosh, swoosh.

Kai was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a gift for him. It was a little red drum. In the corner, gold fish did swim in a bowl. Grandma turned on a song.

Kai clapped. His claps were too fast. The drum went boom, boom, boom. "Too fast," said Grandma. She clapped slow and steady, like a big clock. Tick, tock, tick, tock. Kai watched. Then he tried. He clapped when Grandma clapped. Now his claps fit the song.

Then Grandma sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She sang it slow. Kai listened. He sang the next words by himself. He did not forget them. "How I wonder what you are," he sang, and clapped on each beat. The naughty cat jumped up and tapped the drum with her paw. Boom. "The cat can clap too!" said Kai.

Jaxon stayed at Grandma's house. He wanted to wear his dinosaur socks. Grandma said, "Bath time first." Jaxon was shy about the big tub. He knocked on the side with his knuckles. It sounded like a drum. Then he climbed in. The warm water made him smile. He made a line of bubbles along his arm, all the way to his elbow.

After the bath, Grandma gave him a soft towel. She hung the wet towel on the line outside the window. Then Jaxon tried to put on his dinosaur socks. They stuck on his toes. He pulled and pulled. The socks would not go on. "My feet are still wet," Jaxon said. "Wet feet make socks stick." Grandma smiled. "Dry them first," she said.

She patted his toes with the towel until they were dry and warm. The socks slid right on. Jaxon looked down at the dinosaurs. They looked like they were dancing on his feet. Grandma handed him his cup of milk. "Socks on fast now," said Jaxon. "Because my feet are dry." He took a big sip and wiggled his toes.

Jake went to the library with his mom. Story time was about bees. Jake wanted the big bee puppet more than anything. He reached for it fast.

But a girl named Mia had it first. She hugged the bee and made it buzz. Jake froze. His hand stopped in the air. Then he said, "Can I have a turn next?" Mia nodded and kept buzzing. After one song, she held out the bee. "Your turn," she said.

Jake made the bee fly to the moon. Then a boy asked, "My turn?" Jake passed the bee right over. The teacher clapped. "We all share, so we all get turns," she said. At the end, the library got messy with pillows everywhere. Jake helped stack them in a tall tower. "Goodbye, bee," he whispered, and the bee seemed to wink.

Isla went to the pharmacy with Dad. There was a little sink by the counter. Isla wanted a snack from her bag. "First, hands," said Dad.

Isla turned on the water. She put soap on her hands. She rubbed and rubbed. It was hard to know when to stop. Then a song came from a toy fox on the shelf. Isla began to sing along. She washed her hands the whole song. "All clean!" she said.

The pharmacist smiled and gave her a sticker. It was a little fox with bubbles. Later, Isla used the toilet. She ran back and sang her song again while she washed. Then she ate her snack. The crackers tasted good. "Clean hands," said Isla, holding up her sticker.

Eli sat on his bed. He had a new book from the library. It had a red cover and a picture of a frog. On the back was a big pot. The frog wanted to jump into the pot.

Eli opened the book. He saw little marks on the page. "Those are words," he said. The words sat under the pictures. His mom read them out loud. The marks told what the frog did. First the frog hops. Then the frog jumps into the pot. The words said so. The pictures did not say it. The words did.

Eli turned the pages one by one. He started at the front. He went to the back. The last page showed the frog sleeping. Eli patted the cover. "My book," he said. He put it under his pillow.

The next morning, Mom held out a bag. "We take the book back today," she said. Eli shook his head. He held the book tight. At the library, a girl stood by the desk. She was waiting. She pointed at the red cover. "I want the frog book next," she said. Eli looked at her. He looked at his book. He gave it to the librarian. She put a card in it. "You can borrow it again," she said. Eli jumped once, soft, on the library floor. The girl sat down with the book. She opened the front page first.

Eleanor woke up on her birthday. She was four today! Mom said, "Your cake has four candles now. You are one year older, so we add one candle."

Grandma and Grandpa came. Ben from next door came too. Everyone sang the birthday song. Eleanor clapped her hands.

Then the candles. Four little flames stood on the cake. "Make a wish," said Mom. "Then blow." Eleanor took a big breath. She blew hard. The flames went out. All four! Smoke curled up like little strings.

"Why did they go out?" asked Ben.

"Because I blew on them," said Eleanor. "Air makes the fire stop."

Then Grandpa rolled the cake to her on a little cart with one wobbly wheel. Eleanor cut the first slice. It was chocolate, her favorite.

"Look how strong I am," she said, lifting the big piece. "I am four now."

Leah held her doll tight. Mom said, "Let's find milk!" Leah loved the store. It was so big! She was so small.

First they went fast. The cart went zoom! Then they went slow. Slow by the apples, red and round. "Big apple," said Leah. She picked a small one too. "Small apple!" The small one fit in her hand.

Then they came to the cold door. Leah touched the glass. Brrr! It was cold in there. The milk felt cold, like ice, almost frozen. Then they walked past the bread. The oven was hot. Leah felt warm air on her face. "Hot!" she said.

Leah got one apple at snack time. She bit it. "Mom!" she whispered. "My small apple is all gone!" Mom smiled. "You ate it up, Leah." Leah hugged her doll. "More store tomorrow?"

Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a green frog. He looked in the paint cup. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was no green paint. "Oh no," said Miles.

A dog barked outside the window. Bark, bark. Miles looked up, then looked down again. He touched his own nose. He had a dot of yellow paint on his nose. He dipped his brush in yellow. Then he dipped it in blue. He stirred the paint round and round. The brush made him feel dizzy, so he stopped. The paint turned green. He stirred once more. Yellow and blue made green. "Yellow and blue make green," said Miles. He said it again. "Yellow and blue make green."

Miles painted a big green frog. The frog sat on a green leaf. His teacher walked by and smiled. "What a green frog," she said. Miles held up his brush. "I made the green myself," he said. The dog barked one more time outside. Bark, bark. Miles painted a little black dog next to his frog.

Xavier went to the grocery store with Mama. He reached for his soft bunny. Bunny was not in his pocket.

"Oh no," said Xavier. "Where is bunny?"

Mama smiled. "Think, Xavier. Where did you see bunny last?"

Xavier thought hard. "The lunch aisle! Bunny saw the bread."

They walked back to the lunch aisle. They looked by the bread. They looked by the apples. No bunny.

"Let us look again," said Mama.

They looked down low, near the floor. There was bunny! Bunny sat under the shelf, next to a big can of soup.

"Found you!" said Xavier. He hugged his soft bunny tight.

"Bunny likes soup," said Mama with a laugh.

"No, Mama," said Xavier. "Bunny fell down. The shelf is tall and bunny is small."

Mama laughed again. "You speak the truth, little one."

Xavier put bunny back in his pocket. He patted it two times. "Stay put, bunny. Stay put."

At home, they ate lunch together. Bunny sat on the table too, right next to the bread.

Kinsley went to Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Baby Rose. "Baby Rose is crying," said Mia. The doll made a crying sound.

"We need to help her," said Kinsley. Mia made a bottle for the baby. Kinsley patted her back. But Baby Rose still cried. Kinsley looked all around. Then she saw it. The baby's blanket had fallen on the floor. She peeked under the small quilt top. The baby had no blanket on. "The baby is cold," said Kinsley. "She cries because she is cold."

Kinsley picked up the blanket. It had some lint on it. She helped clean it off with her hand. Then she tucked it around Baby Rose, right up to her chin. Mia turned off the crying sound. Baby Rose was quiet now. "She feels better," said Mia.

Then Mia brought a tiny pot and a tiny hat. "Baby Rose needs clothes for the cold day," she said. Kinsley put the hat on the baby's head. The play kitchen door was open, so Kinsley shut it. "Now the kitchen is warm too," she said. Mia smiled and rocked Baby Rose in her arms. "Time for sleep, baby," said Mia. Kinsley sang a little song, very soft. Baby Rose's eyes closed.

Julia stood on a small stool in the kitchen. She wanted warm milk in her cup. Mom was right there, making bread.

"The pot is hot," Mom said. "Wait a bit."

Julia touched the cold counter instead. Cold felt nice on her fingers. She looked at the big pot on the stove. Then she looked at her small cup. The big pot held lots of milk. Her small cup held just a little.

Mom poured the milk fast into the cup. It sloshed out! "Too fast makes a mess," Mom said. She wiped it up with a gray cloth. Then she poured again, slow and easy. This time not one drop fell.

Julia touched the side of the cup. "Still too hot," she said. Mom put the cup in cold water. The cold water took the heat away.

Julia touched it again. "Now it's just right!" She drank it all up.

Mom smiled. "You waited so well." Julia stood up tall and put her cup in the sink. Mom gave her a warm hug.

The gray cat walked in and rubbed Julia's back. Julia giggled. "The cat wants warm milk too," she said.

Nova sat at the little red table in art class. She wanted to paint a cow in green grass. But the green paint cup was empty. Nova looked and looked. No green anywhere.

Then she saw Sam by the shelf. Sam had a big cup of blue paint. "Can I have some blue?" Nova asked. Sam poured a little blue into her cup. "Thank you," said Nova. The teacher gave her a cup of yellow paint too, because Nova had asked so kindly.

Nova dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred on her paper. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," Nova said out loud. She painted the grass high and high. Then she painted her cow standing in it. Sam leaned over to see. "Nice cow," he said. Nova smiled and painted one yellow flower too.

Charles went to book club with his mama. He wore his bear sweater. The sweater was itchy. He pulled his sleeve up and down.

The teacher held up a letter. "This is S," she said. Charles knew that one. "S goes sssss," he said, like a snake. All the kids laughed and hissed too. Ssss, ssss, ssss.

Then the teacher held up M. Charles did not know M. He frowned. Then he pressed his lips together and said, "Mmmmm." The letter looked like two bumps. It sounded like yum. "M is for my itchy sweater," Charles said. "Mmm, mmm, mmm!"

He tried B. "Buh, buh, buh," he said. "B is for bear!" He counted the letters he knew. One, S. Two, M. Three, B. Three letters!

His mama helped him take off the sweater. "Too itchy?" she asked. "Yes," said Charles. "But my ears are not itchy. My ears know three letters now." He patted his own ear and giggled.

Raphael ran into the doctor's office with his old toy truck. He could not wait!

A nurse said, "Time to check your eyes." Raphael looked with his eyes. He saw a big red E on the wall. Then the nurse said, "Now we check your ears." Raphael heard a beep with his ears. Beep! Beep!

The doctor came in. She said, "Smell this, taste this, touch this." Raphael smelled a sweet orange with his nose. He tasted a sour drop with his tongue. He touched a cold truck wheel with his fingers. "My eyes see, my ears hear, my nose smells, my tongue tastes, my fingers touch!" said Raphael. "Five things my body can do!"

The doctor laughed. "You got it!" Raphael drove his old truck all the way to the door. "My eyes see the door," he said. "Bye, truck! We come back soon!"

Kai stood in the garage with Dad. Dad played a song on his old radio. The song had a steady beat. Boom, boom, boom.

Kai wanted to sing along. But he did not know the words yet. He clapped too fast, like he was chasing the song. His claps ran ahead of the beat. "Too fast!" he laughed. His hands felt tired.

"Try one clap for each boom," said Dad. He tapped his foot. Boom, boom, boom. Kai watched Dad's foot. He waited for a tap. Then he clapped. Clap. Clap. Clap. "My claps go with the booms now!" said Kai. "The song goes slow, so I go slow."

Then Dad sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" two times. Kai listened with his ears and his eyes shut. On the third time, Kai opened his mouth. The words came out all by themselves. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" He sang the whole song from memory. Dad gave him a big hug. Kai felt warm like toast.

Then the radio stopped. The garage went quiet and still, like a frozen puddle. But Kai kept singing anyway. "How I wonder what you are!" Dad clapped the beat for him, boom, boom, boom, all the way to the end.

Amelia looked out the window. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on her swing. No school today! It was a snow day at home.

Amelia ran to the back door. She opened it and stepped out. The snow felt cold on her hands. Her fingers hurt. She ran back inside. "Mommy, my hands are cold!"

Mommy gave her big red mittens. Mommy gave her a warm coat and a hat. "Now you can play," Mommy said.

Amelia went out again. This time her hands stayed warm. "The mittens keep my hands warm," she said. She patted the snow. She made a small snowball. Her hands were still warm!

A little bird sat on the fence. It looked cold. Amelia put some seeds on the snow. "Here, bird," she said. The bird flew down to eat.

From next door, she heard a loud sound. A train went by the houses. It sounded far away in the quiet snow. Amelia waved at it.

The snow looked pretty in the sun. It shone like sugar. Amelia made footprints all over the yard. Mommy called, "Cocoa time!"

Amelia ran inside. She held the warm cup with her mittens still on. "Warm hands, warm tummy," she said, and took a big sip.

Mateo jumped into the family car. "Where is Bunny?" he asked. Bunny was gone. "I want Bunny now!"

"Let's look," said Mama. Mateo peeked under the seat. He found a cookie. He found one shoe. No Bunny. "Bunny is not here," he said. "Bunny is all alone somewhere."

"Think," said Mama. "Where did you play with Bunny last?" Mateo scratched his hair. Then his eyes got big. "The toy store! I put Bunny on the shelf while we looked!" The shelf had lots of toys. Maybe Bunny was still there.

They drove fast, fast, fast. Mateo looked out the window the whole way. "Hurry, Mama, hurry!" he said. The store man smiled. "We do not sell bunnies like that," he said. "But we kept one safe for you." He held out Bunny!

Mateo hugged Bunny tight. "Bunny was on the shelf," he said. "That is where I left him!" He buckled Bunny in beside him. "You sit with me now," he said. "No more shelf for you, Bunny. Home we go!"

Luke went to the mall with Dad. Luke was getting his first haircut. The chair was big and tall. Luke had to sit up high. Dad helped him climb in.

The hair lady put a cape on Luke. It snapped shut at his neck. Then she began to cut. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Luke looked at his lap. The hair did not touch his pants. Why not? He asked himself. The cape was the reason. The hair fell on the cape and slid off. "The hair slides down because the cape is smooth," Luke said out loud.

The hair lady put her scissors on the counter. There was a low shelf there. A magnet sat on the shelf. Her clips stuck to the magnet. They did not fall off. Luke watched them click together. "Can I bring one clip home?" Luke asked. "No, but you can hold it," she said.

Luke held the clip near the magnet. It jumped right onto it. The magnet pulled it fast. Luke laughed. Then Dad lifted him down. Luke looked in the mirror. His hair was short now. He touched his head with both hands. "Look, Dad, all gone!"

Ava sat at the big table. There was a yellow pencil by her hand. Her teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. "Today we write our names," she said.

Ava grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The A came out fat and wobbly. It looked like a sleepy bee had walked across the paper. "Silly A," said Ava. Tom laughed next to her. "Mine looks like a snake," he said.

Miss Kim showed a trick. She put her thumb and one finger at the pencil tip. Then she tucked the pencil under her other fingers. Ava tried it. She pinched the tip, just like that. Her hand did not slip. She drew a straight line, then a line that leaned. "It's an A!" said Ava. She drew more. V. A. Again and again.

"Why is it easy now?" Tom asked. Ava held up the pencil. "Because my fingers lock it right here," she said. She pinched the tip tight and tapped it. "Now my letters can't run away."

Tom leaned over. "Can you write my name too?" Ava giggled. "T is easy. T is just a stick with a hat." She pressed her pencil down and began the first line.

Harper held her mama's hand. The door said DENTIST. Harper did not want to go in.

A kind lady with gray hair smiled. "Hello, Harper," she said. "Come sit in my big chair."

The chair went up. The chair went back. Harper lay down like a sleepy mouse. "Why does the chair go back?" she asked.

"So I can see your teeth," the lady said. "Teeth hide in the back."

The lady held a little mirror. "Let's count your teeth," she said. "One, two, three." She touched each tooth softly. Harper counted too. "Four, five, six." They counted all the way to twenty.

Then the lady made the teeth clean. The brush was small and round. It tickled a little. Harper giggled.

The chair went up again. Harper looked in a mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white.

"I know why the chair goes back," Harper told Mama. "It goes back so the light can see my teeth. And the brush makes them clean."

"Twenty clean teeth," said the lady. "See you soon, Harper."

Matteo went to the park with his bucket. He wanted to find five pretty things for Grandma.

His eyes saw a red leaf. He picked it up. His ears heard a bird sing. He listened and listened.

Then he found something soft. It was a fuzzy feather. He touched it with his fingers. His nose smelled something sweet. It came from a flower. He took one careful sniff. He put the flower in his bucket too.

"Four things," said Matteo. "I need one more."

His friend Mia came by. She held out a small berry. "Taste this," she said. "My mom says it is a sweet berry." Matteo tasted it with his tongue. It was sweet!

"Thank you, Mia," he said. "You helped me find five."

He counted his treasures. "My eyes, my ears, my fingers, my nose and my tongue helped me today. Five helpers for five things!"

He ran home with his bucket.

Levi got new blocks at school. He wanted to build a house for his toy animal. A big house, fast!

He stacked a circle block on the bottom. It rolled! The whole tower fell down. "Oh no!" said Levi. He tried again. The circle rolled again.

Then Levi saw a square block. It had flat sides. He put the square on the bottom. It did not roll. It stayed right there! Levi stacked a triangle on top for the roof. He used two rectangles for the walls. The tower stood tall.

"Look, teacher!" Levi called. "The square stays because it is flat. The circle rolls because it is round!" He put his animal inside the house. "You can stay here," he said. The animal fit just right.

Elizabeth went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to see the ducks. Grandma held her hand. "Stay close to me," said Grandma.

Elizabeth saw a big metal bench in the sun. She put her hand near it. The bench was very hot! She pulled her hand back fast. "Ouch," she said. The bench sat in the sun all morning. That was why it was hot. Grandma put her hand on the shady part. The shady part was cool. Elizabeth touched the shady part too. "Cool," she said.

Then Elizabeth saw something shiny by the path. It was a piece of broken glass. She wanted to touch it. But glass with sharp edges can cut. She did not touch it. She pointed and said, "Grandma, look!" Grandma picked it up with a gentle hand and put it in a bag. "Good looking, Elizabeth," said Grandma.

The ducks were by the pond. Elizabeth stayed right by Grandma. She dropped little crumbs one at a time. A duck came close and ate one. Elizabeth laughed. "The duck likes my crumbs," she said.

Thomas walked into the grocery store with his mom. It was cold outside, so he wore his red coat. But the coat was open, and Thomas felt chilly in the frozen food aisle.

"Try to zip it yourself," said Mom. Thomas pulled the zipper. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no zip. Thomas looked down. He saw the problem. His shirt was stuck in the zipper. The shirt was in the way, so the zipper could not close.

Thomas pulled the shirt out of the way. Then he pushed the little tab up, slowly. Zzzzzip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. "My shirt was in the line of the zipper," said Thomas. "Now it is not!"

"That is a neat zip," said Mom. Thomas smiled. At the checkout line, he unzipped his coat by himself too. Then he zipped it again, just to practice. "I can do it," said Thomas. "All by myself!"

Jacob sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to see Dr. Amy, but the door was closed. "Close your eyes," said Mom. Jacob closed them. Now he could not see the door at all. "My eyes make seeing work," said Jacob.

Dr. Amy came in. She had a picture of a river on her coat. Jacob saw the blue water. He heard her say hello with his ears. He touched her cold stethoscope with his fingers. Then Dr. Amy held up a jar. "Smell this," she said. Jacob's nose smelled oranges. He remembered oranges at Grandma's house.

At the end, Dr. Amy gave Jacob a little cup. His tongue tasted sweet juice. "Now my tummy will not feel weak," said Jacob. He held Mom's hand tight all the way home.

Aubrey found a book at daycare. It had a dog on the front. The cover said DOG in big letters. Aubrey could see the word DOG matched the picture. "That word says dog," she said.

Miss Amy came over. "These books are from the library," she said. "We borrowed them. On Friday we take them all back."

Aubrey held the dog book tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

"No, sweetie," said Miss Amy. "Other kids want to read it too. That is why we bring it back."

Aubrey had a question. "Can I get it again after?"

"Yes," said Miss Amy. "You can borrow it lots of times."

Aubrey opened the book. She started at the front. She peeked at the dog on each page. She turned page after page until she got to the end.

A boy named Sam sat next to her. He looked sad. He did not have a book.

Aubrey handed him the dog book. "You can read it after me," she said. "Then we give it back on Friday. Then other kids read it too."

Sam smiled. He opened the front cover. He pointed at the word DOG. "This part says dog," he said.

"That's right," said Aubrey. Then she peeked over his shoulder at the pictures.

Ella wants to play house at daycare. But the baby doll has a scratch on its arm. "Oh no," says Ella. "The baby is hurt."

Ella holds the doll close. "Who will fix you?" she asks. Teacher Mia comes over. She is kind and warm. "You can fix the baby," she says.

Ella puts a soft bandage on the scratch. Then she wraps the doll in a small blanket. The doll stops looking hurt. Ella rocks it and sings, "Hush, little baby."

Tom wants to play too. He pretends to be the dog. He says, "Woof!" Ella laughs. Now they have a pretend house together.

"The baby feels better now," Ella says. "It feels better because I fixed the scratch." Teacher Mia smiles and sits right beside her. Ella gives the baby doll a big hug.

Nora looked out the big window. "Rain today!" she said. Raindrops went tap, tap, tap. Nora put on her rain boots. She held her umbrella up high.

Mama said, "Look at the sky now." The rain had stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny! "No rain boots in the sun," said Nora. She took them off. She put on her orange hat instead. "Sunny means hat!" said Nora.

Then the wind blew. Whoosh went the trees. Nora's hat flew off her head! She ran and ran. She caught her orange hat. Windy means hold on tight, she thought. She held it with both hands.

Nora sat down to paint a picture. She painted a turtle. She painted rain and sun and wind. "My turtle needs a hat too," said Nora. She painted a tiny orange hat on the turtle. "There!" said Nora. "Now my turtle is ready for sun, rain, and wind!"

Isaiah sat on the rug in the living room. Uncle Ben held his phone up high. The big game was on the TV too. Isaiah had a loose tooth in his mouth. He wiggled it with his finger.

On the phone, the ball began to spin through the air. Then everyone shouted. Isaiah's mouth fell wide open. "It went in! We won!" He jumped up and down. His loose tooth did not fall out. It just wiggled some more.

But the TV still showed the ball in the air. Isaiah frowned. "Did I miss it?" he asked. He looked at the phone. Then he looked at the TV. The phone showed it first. The TV was slow. He waited and watched. The ball spun again on the big screen. Then the TV crowd shouted too. "It happens twice!" Isaiah said. He clapped with everyone. Dad lifted him up onto the couch, and Isaiah sat safe between Dad and Grandma.

Max went to Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big pink shell. "Put it to your ear," said Grandpa. Max listened. He heard a whoosh sound. "It sounds like the ocean!" said Max. His ears did that.

Grandpa said, "Let's play the sense game. I will hide something." Grandpa put a cookie in a box. Max could not see it. "My eyes miss it," said Max. He shook the box and heard a little rattle. His ears helped. He opened the box and smelled the cookie. His nose knew! Then he touched it. It was bumpy. His hands told him. Then he took a bite. Yum! His tongue did that.

"Five senses," said Max. "Ears, eyes, nose, hands, tongue."

"You are so brave to try with your eyes shut," said Grandpa. "Can ears really hear a snack?" Max laughed. "Yes! Ears hear the rattle!" Grandpa gave him one more cookie for winning the game.

Ivy walked home with a small box. Inside was her first pet, a bunny named Pip. The snow fell on the street. Ivy held the box with both hands.

At home, Ivy put Pip on the floor. Pip sat very still. His nose did not move. Ivy wondered why. She looked at Pip. Then she looked at her own hand. It held a little carrot.

"Are you hungry?" she asked. Pip's nose began to wiggle. He hopped to the carrot. He ate it all up.

Ivy clapped. "The carrot made you hop!" she said. Now she knew. A bunny eats, then a bunny plays. So every morning, Ivy gave Pip his food first. Then Pip would hop and jump all day.

One day, Pip would not eat his carrot. Ivy looked in his bowl. The water was empty. She filled it up. Pip drank and drank. Then he ate his carrot. "Water first, food next," said Ivy. She patted his soft ears with her little hand.

Arya went to the library for song time. She wanted to sing her counting song. But the numbers fell out of her head!

She tried. "One, two, um, seven?"

The boy next to her laughed. "Seven comes after six, silly!"

Arya looked at the bookshelf. The librarian let her touch the spines. One book, two books, three books. She patted them like drums. Four, five, six. Then seven came right after six! Eight, nine, ten sat at the top of the shelf.

"Now I know," Arya said. "The numbers go in a line. They wait for turns!"

After songs, Dad gave her a salty cracker. Arya counted her bites. "One, two, three!" Then it was all gone.

"Ten more songs," said Arya, holding up just three fingers.

Rosalie stood by the big pool. The water smelled like sun and clean towels. Today was her first swim team meet. Her tummy felt flippy.

"Rosalie, you go second," said Coach Amy. "Wait for Ben to touch the wall. Then you jump in." Rosalie watched the light sparkle on the water. The whistle blew. Ben swam fast. His arms splashed. Rosalie got so excited. She jumped in too soon!

The coach held up a flat red sign. "Oh no," Rosalie said. "We have to start over. Why?" She watched the other team swim. Then she saw it. Ben had not touched the wall yet. The wall was like a tag in tag. You have to tag the wall first, then your friend can go. "I went before the tag," Rosalie said softly.

The team tried again. This time Rosalie waited. Ben slapped the wall. His hand made a clapping sound. Then Rosalie jumped. She kicked and kicked. Her team clapped for her at the end. "We did it!" Rosalie laughed. "The wall is the tag!"

Ali stood in the backyard with Dad. Mom was inside with the new baby. Ali held his toy truck. He felt worried. "Will the baby take my toys?" he asked. Dad smiled. "Babies are too little for trucks," he said. "The baby cannot play yet. But you can hold her hand."

They went inside. Mom put the baby in Ali's arms. Ali sat very still. The baby was small and warm. Ali put his finger near her hand. The baby grabbed it. She held on tight! "She likes me," Ali said. "She is holding my finger."

Then the baby made a little sound. Her eyes closed. "She went to sleep," said Mom. "Babies sleep a lot." Ali sat and did not move his hand. He did not want to lose her grip. Dad sat close by. The baby held on, and Ali held on too.

Anthony sat in the car with Dad. "We will meet Maria," said Dad. "She cuts hair in her salon." The salon was a little shop with a big window. Maria had a chair just for kids. It looked like a small red car with a steering wheel. Anthony sat in the car chair and held the wheel.

Maria snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some bits went down Anthony's collar. They stuck to his neck. They tickled and made him squirm. Maria laughed a kind laugh. She used a soft, poofy brush. She brushed his neck, and all the itchy bits fell away. Anthony patted his neck. "The hair bits made me itchy," he said. "The brush made the itchy stop."

Then Maria held up a mirror. Anthony saw a boy with short, neat hair. Was that really him? "That boy looks pretty sharp," said Dad. Anthony grinned at the mirror boy. The mirror boy grinned right back. Then Anthony turned the steering wheel and said, "Beep, beep! Let's go home!"

Riley went to the vet with Dad. They picked up a small pet snake. His name was Pip.

At home, Riley gave Pip fresh water. The next day, the water looked cloudy. Pip hid in his little house. He would not come out. Riley put a pinky mouse in his home. Pip did not eat it. Riley waited. She waited all day. Still, Pip stayed inside.
