Riley looked at the cloudy water. "The water is old," she said. She took the bowl out. She washed it with warm water. She filled it with clean water. She set it back in, nice and slow. Then she sorted the pinky mice and put one by the bowl. Pip came out. He drank and drank. Then he ate his mouse.

"The clean water helped," Riley said. She smiled at Pip. "I will change your water every day."

Elena went to the park with her mama. She wanted to draw with her new chalk on the sidewalk. The sun was hot on the ground. "The chalk is too hot," Elena said. She put it in the shade. She waited and waited.

Then Elena touched the chalk again. "Now it is cold," she said. The big tree made the shade. The shade made the chalk cold. Elena smiled. She began to draw a big cat. She drew a small cat too.

A dog ran by, very fast. A turtle walked by, very slow. Elena drew a fast dog. She drew a slow turtle. "What is your cat's name?" mama asked. "Cat," said Elena. She drew and drew until the sun went down. "Time to go, Elena," said mama. Elena picked up her cold chalk. "Bye bye, park," she said.

Jasmine ran to the sandbox with her bunny. She wanted to play house. But bunny was cold. The wind blew hard.

Jasmine saw Ben by the slide. He had a friendly face. He was wrapping his truck in a scarf. "My truck is a baby," said Ben. "Babies need warm blankets." Jasmine looked at her bunny. Bunny was a baby too. Babies need warm things.

She found a leaf and a big red cup. She put the leaf in the cup. Then she put bunny on the leaf. She mixed sand and water in a pot. It became a smooth grey cake. "Time for dinner, baby bunny," she said. Bunny sat by the pretend stove.

Ben came over with his truck baby. The truck baby ate sand cake too. "Our babies are warm now," said Jasmine. "Because we wrapped them up." The wind kept blowing. But the babies slept snug in the cup and the scarf. Jasmine patted bunny on the head. "Goodnight, baby," she whispered.

Declan wanted to wash his toy truck. The truck was covered in paint from art time. Red paint, blue paint, and sticky paint too. So Declan ran to the bathroom. He stood on his little stool by the sink.

First, he turned one tap. The water felt cold. Brrr, cold like ice. Then he turned the other tap. The water got warm, then hot. Declan pulled his hand back fast. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He turned the hot tap back, just a tiny bit. Now the water was warm and nice. Why did the water change? Because that tap was the hot one. He knew it now.

He soaped the truck and rubbed the paint off. Bubbles grew big and shiny. They smelled like lemons. Then he saw something. A small silver razor sat by the sink. Dad's razor. It looked shiny and new. Could he touch it? Declan looked at it. It was sharp, like a tiny knife. He kept his hands in the warm water instead.

"Mama, come see!" he called. He liked to stay close to Mama in the bathroom. Mama came and stood by the door. Then, surprise! The toy truck was not alone. A tiny shy frog sat on the soap dish. "Hello, frog," said Declan. "Do you like warm water too?"

Emile sat on the cold floor at daycare. He found a box of wooden blocks. He wished to build a tall, tall tower. He put a circle block on the bottom. He put a square block on top.

The tower wobbled. Then it fell over. The circle block rolled away across the rug. "Oh no," said Emile. He picked up the circle block. It rolled again, right out of his hand.

Emile looked at the blocks. He put a square block on the bottom. Squares had flat sides. Flat sides did not roll. He put another square on top. Then a rectangle. Then a triangle, like a little roof.

"Look, Miss Ana!" said Emile. "My tower stands up!"

"It stands because the bottom does not roll," said Miss Ana.

Emile nodded. "Circles roll. Squars stay still." He placed his shoe next to the tower. "My shoe is flat too. It helps the tower stand." The tower stood tall and still, all through play time.

Billie went to the playground after school. Her grandma came too. The sun was big and bright. Some slides sat in the sun. Some slides sat in the shade.

Billie wanted to go down the big slide. She put her hand on it first. The slide was very hot. She pulled her hand back fast. "The sun made it hot," she said. Then she saw the little slide under the tree. She touched it. That one was cool. "The tree made shade," she said. So she slid down the cool slide, again and again.

Near the fence, Billie saw a shiny can on the ground. She wanted to pick it up. Then she remembered. "I don't touch cans," she said. "They are not mine." She looked for grandma instead. Grandma sat on a lazy old bench under the tree. Billie held her hand the whole way home. "Stay close," said grandma. And Billie did.

Matteo sat in his car seat. "Let's count red cars!" said Dad. "We need ten." Matteo loved red cars. He wanted to find them all.

"One, two, three," said Matteo. A red car went by. "Five!" he shouted. Dad laughed. "Five is old news. One comes after three. Try again, big guy." Matteo frowned. Then he sang his counting song in his head, the one his teacher sang at school. "One, two, three, four, five!" The words came out in the right order, like steps on stairs. Each word had its own place.

Another red car drove past. "Six!" yelled Matteo. Then seven, then eight, then nine. One more red car came around the bend. Matteo bounced in his seat. "Ten! Ten red cars!" He clapped his hands. "The song helped me! The numbers go in a line!" Dad beeped the horn twice. "You did it, Matteo. Now let's count blue trucks!"

Eloise sat in the big red seat. Her favorite team was on the field. Dad was next to her. Grandma was next to Dad. Uncle Ben was next to Grandma. One, two, three, four people in a row.

Eloise wanted to tell Dad something. She saw a player drop the ball. She opened her mouth to speak. Then the crowd jumped up. Everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" The noise was like thunder. Dad could not hear her at all.

So Eloise waited. The players lined up. The crowd sat down. The stadium got quiet.

"Now," said Eloise. "The crowd sat down. That is why it is quiet now."

Dad laughed and clapped. "You cleaned your cup and your ears too," he said.

Eloise smiled. The loud game felt like a dream. "One, two, three," she said. "Watch with me."

Ruby sat at the little red table. On it lay a shiny string of beads. Her teacher, Miss Pam, had a question.

"Ruby, which string has more beads? This one, or that one?"

Ruby wanted to be right. She lifted the shiny string. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." The last bead was blue. "Five," she said. "Five beads."

Then Ruby had a worry. What if she counted the blue one first? Would it be different? She asked herself, "What will I get?"

She counted again. She started at the blue bead this time. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five.

"It is five both ways," Ruby said. She counted the other string. It had four beads. "This one has more. This one has five."

Miss Pam smiled. "Good counting, Ruby."

Ruby held up the shiny string. "Five," she said. "Five both ways."

Lea was going on a trip with her family. They packed a big bag. They drove a long, long way. Then they came to a beach. It was not like home. The sand was different. The water went on and on.

Lea had her rubber duck from her house in her hand. "Duck wants to swim," she said. She put the duck in the sea. The duck did not sink. It sat on top of the water. "Look, it floats!" said Lea.

Her brother Tom pushed the duck down. The duck popped back up. It went bloop! Lea laughed. "Silly duck," she said. She pushed it down too. Bloop! Up it came again. "It floats because it is full of air," said Lea. She squeezed the duck. It squeaked in her hand.

"Air inside, up it goes," said Tom. They played until the sun went low. Lea held her duck tight. "You can sleep in a different house tonight," she told it. The duck squeaked all the way up the beach.

Athena sat at the big piano. Her teacher, Miss Kim, stood beside her. Athena wanted to play the rain song. She hit the keys very fast. Boom, boom, boom! The sound was so big.

"Why is it so loud?" Athena asked.

Miss Kim did not say. She just smiled. Athena tried again. This time she pressed the keys slowly and gently. Tip, tip, tip. The sound was tiny, like soft rain.

"Slow fingers make soft sound," said Athena. She pressed slow again. Tip, tip, tip. It worked! She made a stormy part with fast, hard fingers. Boom! Then a quiet part with slow fingers. Tip, tip, tip.

Miss Kim showed Athena a picture of rain clouds. Athena played along with it. Fast for the storm. Slow for the little drops.

At the end, Athena gave Miss Kim a hug. "Thank you," she said. Then she played the rain song one more time, tip, tip, boom!

Nolan went to the community garden with Grandma. He held a little bag of carrot seeds. The seeds were tiny and smooth. Nolan rubbed them between his fingers.

He dug a small hole. He put the seeds in. He patted the dirt down. Then he ran to the pond with his small red cup. He filled it up. He poured water on the dirt.

"Will the seeds grow today?" he asked. "No," said Grandma. "First they drink the water. Then little green tops pop up."

Every day Nolan filled his cup at the pond. Every day he watered his seeds. One morning he saw something green. "The water made them grow!" said Nolan. He jumped up and down. A tiny green top was peeking out of the dirt.

Theodore ran to the farmers' market with Mama. He held her hand the whole way. The market was big and loud and full of colors.

"I will cook for the family," said Theodore. "I will make butter!" He found a farmer with white cream in a jar. "Can I buy it? Please?" He paid with his own coins. He was so proud.

At home, Theodore poured the cream into a little jar. He put the lid on tight. He knocked on the lid two times, like a little drum. Then he shook the jar. He shook it fast. He shook it slow. He shook it and shook it.

At first the cream just sloshed. Theodore kept shaking. Then something changed. The sloshing stopped. Something hard was bumping inside the jar. He opened the lid and looked. A yellow lump sat in thin white milk. "Mama! Papa! Come see!" he called. "I shook the cream, and it turned into butter!" He shook it, and that made it happen.

Papa warmed a pan. Theodore spread his butter on hot toast. The butter melted right away, all shiny. He cut the toast into a lion shape. The lion had a buttery mane.

"Theodore made this!" said Papa, taking a big bite.

"More shaking tomorrow!" said Theodore, and he shook the empty jar one more time.

Lucy woke up and saw white. Snow had come in the night. No school today. Mom said, "It is a snow day." Lucy put on her red boots. She tried to lock the door behind her, but her mittens were too big. Mom helped with the lock, and they laughed.

They went to the big hill. Lucy sat on her sled. Mom gave one little push. The sled went fast, so fast. Lucy rolled into the soft snow. A small brown leaf sat on top of the snow. Lucy picked it up. It looked funny with little white dots on it.

Lucy looked at the leaf. "The snow fell on you," she said. She looked at the hill. "The hill is fast because the snow is on it." She climbed up again, holding the leaf. "Ready, Mom!"

Maverick sat at the little blue table. He was making a lion. He glued on the mane. He glued on the eyes. He glued on the long paper tail.

Then Maverick wanted more glue. He squeezed the bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. One dot, two dots, three dots, four dots. The glue made a big wet puddle.

"Uh oh," said Maverick. "Why is my lion bumpy?" He looked closely. He touched the paper. It was soft and soggy. "Too much glue," he said. "The wet glue made my paper wrinkle."

His friend Nia sat next to him. She held out her glue stick. "You can use mine," she said. "It makes small dots." Nia was kind to share.

Maverick took the glue stick. He made one small dot. Then one more. The new paper tail stayed flat. He stuck it on the lion.

"Thank you, Nia," said Maverick. He held up his lion. The long tail swung back and forth. "Roar!" said Maverick, and Nia laughed and roared too.

Brielle stood in the sunny backyard. She had a red beanbag and a big blue ball. She wanted to toss the beanbag into the hoop.

"One, two, three, throw!" she said. The beanbag flew up. It came down in the grass. Not in the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle. She tried again. "One, two, three, throw!" This time she threw it softly. The beanbag went up. It went down. It landed right in the hoop. Brielle jumped. "Soft hands, soft throw!" she said. She clapped and clapped.

Then Papa rolled the big blue ball to her. Brielle held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. It rolled under the bush. "Come back, ball!" she said. Papa rolled it again. This time Brielle held out both hands. She opened them wide, like a big bowl. The ball came. The ball landed. She caught it with both hands!

"I caught it! I caught it!" said Brielle. The wind began to blow her hair. Papa laughed at the sound of her happy squeal. "Again!" said Brielle. "One, two, three, roll!" Papa bent down and rolled the ball back across the grass.

Claire stood at the front door. She wanted to sail her little red boat in a puddle. But where was a puddle? Yesterday it was rainy. Big puddles had filled the street. Claire had worn her yellow raincoat and boots.

Today the sun was bright. Claire looked down. The puddles were gone. The raincoat was too hot, so she took it off. "The sun made the water melt away," she said. "That is why the puddle is gone."

Then the wind blew. It pushed her hair all around. It was windy too. Claire held her boat tight.

Her brother Sam came to the door. He had no hat. His ears looked cold. Claire ran and got his blue hat. "Here, Sam," she said. "The wind is strong."

Sam put on the hat. Then they saw white dots falling. Snow! It fell on the boat and did not melt.

Claire opened the door wide. "Snow boat race!" she shouted.

Layla ran to the toy corner. The big red truck was there. She wanted it so much.

But Ben had the truck first. He was pushing it up a hill of blocks. Layla reached out her hand to grab it. Then she stopped. She saw the teacher's sand timer on the shelf. The teacher had shown them how it works. You flip it over, and the sand falls down. When all the sand is gone, the turn is done.

Layla asked, "Can I have the next turn?" Ben said, "Okay." He flipped the timer. Layla sat down on the rug to wait. The sand fell slow, little by little. She counted the grains she could see.

At last the sand stopped. "Your turn now," said Ben. He handed her the truck. Layla pushed it fast across the rug. She grinned and said, "The sand said it is my turn!"

Ibrahim went to the park with Mama. He had his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. At the slide, he put the car down. Then he ran to the swings. When he came back, the car was gone.

"Where is my car?" he asked. He looked by the slide. No car. He looked in the sandbox. No car. Mama said, "Try to remember. Where did you play last?" Ibrahim thought hard. "The slide," he said. "I put it down there."

The winter wind blew cold on his face. The leaves on the ground moved. They moved all together, in one way. Then Ibrahim saw it. The wind had pushed his car. It had rolled under the bench!

He got down on his knees. His hand touched something smooth and cold. It was the blue car. "The wind moved it!" he said. "The wind made it roll under here."

Mama smiled and helped him up. "Good looking, Ibrahim," she said. He held the car tight in his warm hand. "You stay with me now," he told it. The wind blew again. Ibrahim laughed, and put the car in his pocket, all safe.

Leah sat on the big soft rug in the living room. Daddy's tablet lay on the table. It was dark and still. Leah wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped again. Still nothing. Then she found the little button on the side. She held the button down with her finger. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen grew bright. "The button makes it wake up," said Leah. She asked herself, "Now what?" The little picture of a crayon sat in the corner. She touched it. The drawing app opened.

Leah drew a big orange cat. She held the tablet with both hands while she drew. After a while, the tablet felt a little hot near the bottom. "Time to stop," said Daddy with a smile. Leah pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She carried the tablet to the shelf and set it down, just like Daddy showed her.

"It sleeps now, like I sleep in my bed," said Leah. Daddy laughed softly. "Yes, it rests till tomorrow." Leah patted the dark screen. "Night night, tablet."

Theo put on his favorite shirt. It had a yellow duck on the front. He was going to the music room at the community center.

A big rainbow xylophone sat on the table. Theo wanted to play his song. He hit the bars fast, all over. The sounds went boom, boom, boom. It did not sound like a song. It sounded like big feet stomping.

Theo stopped and looked at the bars. He tapped a long bar. It made a low sound. He tapped a short bar. It made a high sound. He tapped the short bars, one, two, three. Ding, ding, ding. "The small ones go up high," Theo said.

He played the short bars again, slow this time. Ding, ding, ding. The lady next to him clapped her hands. Theo patted his duck shirt. Then he played his high song one more time.

Isabelle went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. It was a rainy day, so her shoes were wet and muddy. Outside the big hall, everyone was taking off their shoes. Isabelle saw lots of shoes in little rows. She held Mama's hand tight. "Why do the shoes come off?" she asked. Mama said, "You will see."

Isabelle pulled off her boots. She put them in a row next to Papa's shoes. Then she walked inside. The floor was warm and soft on her feet. She looked back at the door. A man with muddy boots came in without taking them off. His boots made brown marks on the clean floor. A lady wiped the marks with a cloth.

"That is why," said Isabelle. "Shoes off, floor stays clean." Mama smiled and picked her up. There were candles and flowers everywhere. Grandma was there too. She had a cough, and Mama gave her some medicine with water. After, Grandma took Isabelle to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat," she said. Isabelle liked the warm water. It was like a little bath for her hands. Then they sat down together, and Isabelle ate a sweet, round piece of fruit. "Mmm," she said. "More, please."

David put on his little apron. Today he would bake fox cookies for his family. The teacher, Miss Ana, stood close by his side.

"Let's read the recipe together," said Miss Ana. David read the picture list. Flour, butter, honey. He mixed everything in a big bowl. The dough felt soft and squishy. David pressed the fox cookie cutter down. Out came a fox shape, one, two, three.

He licked his finger. "The honey is so sweet," he said. Then he put the fox cookies on a tray. Miss Ana slid the tray into the warm oven. David waited and watched through the glass.

The soft dough changed. It got firm and a little brown. "The hot oven makes it hard," David said. Miss Ana smiled and nodded.

Soon the cookies came out. They were crisp foxes, ready for Mom and Dad. David put them in his little box. He held Miss Ana's hand all the way to the car.

Florence went to the hospital with her dad. Her mum had a new baby. "A baby brother," said Dad. "His name is Sam."

Florence held up her picture. "I draw a dog for Sam," she said. But Sam did not look. Florence waved. Sam did not look. "Did I do it wrong?" she asked.

Dad said, "Try again. Come close." Florence leaned in near Sam's face. She held her soft toy mouse. Sam opened his eyes. Sam looked and looked. "Babies see things best close up," said Mum. "So that is why," said Florence. "Babies see close up."

Sam made a small sound. It was like a tiny cat. Florence sang softly. Sam moved his hand. Florence touched one little finger. "Hello, Sam," she said. "This is my mouse."

Ali ran into the big kitchen. Snow was falling outside the window. "Today I help!" he said.

Nana gave him warm toast. The butter was cold and hard. Ali pushed it. It would not spread. The toast tore. Then Nana set the toast near the warm stove. Ali tried again. The butter was soft now. It spread all over. "Soft butter goes on easy!" said Ali.

Next came the milk. Ali held the little cup with two hands. He tipped the jug fast. Milk splashed out. "Too fast," said Ali. He tipped it slow, just a little. The milk went in. Not one drop fell. "Slow pour, no spill!" said Ali. He looked at his cute cup, so full and white. Ali took a big drink. "More toast, please!"

Eva went to the library with her dad. She saw a book about a red dragon. Eva loved dragons. She grabbed it fast.

A girl sat at a little table. She was reading a book. She held it up. "See? You start here," the girl said. She pointed to the front. She turned the pages one by one. Eva looked at her own book. Little marks ran across every page. "The marks talk," the girl said. "Dad reads them to me." Eva pressed her ear to the page. The page was quiet. But when Dad read it, the dragon roared. The marks really did talk!

Eva held the dragon book tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Dad shook his head. "We take it home for a while. Then we bring it back. Other kids read it too." Eva frowned. Then she thought of the girl. The girl might want the dragon book next. "Okay," Eva said. "But I get the last hug." She hugged the dragon one time. Then she put it in Dad's bag. "Bye, dragon," she whispered. "Roar for the next kid."

Leah hurried to the play corner at school. Her baby doll was in the crib. Her friend Max said, "The baby is crying. She is hungry." Leah looked for a bottle. She could not find one. The bottle was lost.

Then Leah saw a small yellow bucket. It was hard and shiny. She tipped it upside down. It looked just like a bottle! Leah held it to the baby's mouth. "Drink your milk," she said softly. Max tapped the bucket with his hand. "More milk, baby," he said. The baby drank and drank. Soon Leah laid her down in the crib. She covered her with a small cloth blanket.

Max clapped his hands. "The baby stopped crying because you fed her," he said. Leah smiled and patted the doll's head. "Sleep now, baby," she whispered.

Everly was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Everly wanted to hold the baby. But Mom said, "Not yet. The baby needs to eat first."

The baby was hungry. She cried and cried. Everly covered her ears. "Why is she so loud?" asked Everly. Grandma was cooking soup at the stove. "Babies cry when they need something," said Grandma. "This baby needs milk."

Mom sat in the big chair. She fed the baby milk. The baby drank. The crying stopped. Everly listened. The house was quiet now. "She cried because she was hungry," said Everly. "Now her tummy is full."

The soup was too hot. Grandma blew on it. "We will let it cool," she said. Everly waited at the table. Then Mom said, "Now you can sit by the baby." Everly sat very still. She touched the baby's tiny hand. The baby held on tight. Everly smiled and whispered, "Hello, baby sister."

Nova ran to the block corner at daycare. She was excited to build a tall tower.

Her friend Leo was there first. Nova grabbed a red block. Leo yelled and pushed the blocks down. Now Leo looked angry. His face was red and tight.

Nova felt scared. She ran to Teacher Mia. "Leo pushed the blocks," she said. "I am afraid of him."

Teacher Mia held her hand. "Stay here with me," she said. "Let us look at Leo."

Leo sat on the floor now. He cried big tears. His face was sad.

"His blocks fell down," said Nova. "That is why he is mad."

Teacher Mia nodded. Nova picked up one block. She gave it to Leo. Leo wiped his eyes and smiled.

"Want to build with me?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Nova. They stacked blocks high, high, high.

Mason saw his toy lion up on the big shelf. He wanted it so much. He reached up. His hand was too small. The lion did not move.

Mason tried to shake the shelf a little. The lion still did not come down. He felt like crying. Then Dad walked in. "Dad, please help," Mason said. Dad smiled. "Of course! You asked so nicely." Dad lifted the lion down.

"Thank you, Dad," said Mason. He hugged his lion tight. Then he ran fast, and he bumped into Dad's leg. "Sorry, Dad," said Mason. Dad gave him a kiss on the head. "That's okay," said Dad.

Mason sat on the soft rug. He held his lion. "I said please," Mason said. "Then you helped me." Dad sat down too. "That's right," said Dad. Mason made the lion shake its mane. "Roar," said Mason softly. Dad laughed. Mason laughed too. The lion got a big goodnight hug.

Weston ran to the play kitchen at daycare. He wanted his apple for snack time. But there were lots of apples there. Some were toys. One was real.

Miss Ana said, "Snack time soon, Weston." Weston picked up a red apple. He squeezed it. It was hard and light. He put it down. He picked up another one. This one was heavy. He held it close to his nose. It smelled sweet. The toy apples had no smell at all.

"You found the real one," said Miss Ana. "The hard ones are toys. Toys are for pretend food. The heavy one is real. Real food smells good."

Weston smiled. He took his real apple to the little table. It was sticky from his friend's honey at breakfast, so Miss Ana washed it with warm water.

Then Weston took a big bite. "Crunch!" he said. Miss Ana laughed and sat down next to him.

Violet ran to the swings. Her dad sat on the bench nearby. But the big swing was taken. A boy was on it.

Violet wanted that swing. She grabbed the chain. The boy yelled, "Hey!" Violet stepped back. Her shoes felt itchy and she wiggled her toes.

"Say sorry," said the boy's grandma. Violet looked down. "Sorry," she said quietly. The boy said, "It's okay." Then his grandma helped him off the swing.

The swing was free now. Violet climbed on. "Dad, please push me!" she called. Dad came and pushed. Up went Violet, high like a bird.

"Thank you, Dad!" she shouted. Dad laughed. "You said the magic word," he said. Violet kicked her feet. "Please gets pushes!" she said. Dad pushed her again, and the swing went zip through the air.

Sienna was going on a big trip. She rode the train with Mama and Papa. The train went chug, chug, chug. Sienna counted what she saw out the window. "One cow. Two trees. Three little houses."

Then Sienna reached for her bunny. Her bunny was her best friend. He was not in her arms. He was not in her lap. Sienna looked and looked. "Where is Bunny?"

Sienna thought hard. She remembered her bed. She remembered her warm blanket. "I left Bunny on my bed," she said. "That is why he is not here. He is not here because I left him at home." A big tear rolled down her cheek. Mama gave her a soft hug.

Papa opened the window a tiny bit. Fresh air came in. It smelled like grass and rain. Sienna held her little chocolate egg. She held it too long in her warm hand. The chocolate began to melt. Sticky, drippy chocolate! Mama laughed and wiped her fingers with a napkin.

Then came a small surprise. Sienna opened her small pink backpack for a fresh tissue. Something soft was inside. It was Bunny! Mama had tucked him in at the door. "You packed me, Mama!" Sienna said. She hugged Bunny tight all the way to Grandma's house.

Aaron was at Grandma's house. On the table was a library book. It had a bear on the cover. It was Aaron's favorite book.

Aaron opened the book. The pages had little marks on them. Grandma pointed at the marks. "Those marks are words," she said. "Words tell the story." Grandma held the book. She turned the pages one by one. She started at the front. She read to the back. Aaron listened to every page.

"I want to keep this book forever," Aaron said. Grandma shook her head. "The library lets us borrow it," she said. "We take it home, but we bring it back by Friday. Other people want to read it too." Aaron felt sad. He held the book tight. "What if someone else takes my bear book?" he asked. Grandma sat close to him. "We can borrow it again," she said. "The library will not say no."

So they read the book one more time. Then it was Friday. "We must hurry," said Grandma. "School is over and the library closes soon." They drove to the library together. Aaron put the book in the return box all by himself. He saw a girl pick it up right away. She hugged it and smiled.

"Grandma, the girl has my book because I gave it back," Aaron said. Grandma took his hand. "And next week, it can be yours again." Aaron smiled big. "Words tell the story," he said. "And books go front to back." Grandma laughed and hugged him. "Let's pick a new one to take home," she said.

Willow sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "What will happen there?" she asked. "The dentist will look at your teeth," said Mom. "She has a little mirror. It lifts up high, so she can see the top teeth."

Willow held her toy cat. "The mirror will not fit in my mouth," she said. "My mouth is small." Mom smiled. "Open your mouth wide. Then it fits."

At the dentist, a kind lady said, "Open wide." Willow opened her mouth wide. The little mirror went in. "I can see your teeth," said the dentist. Willow did not fall off the chair. She sat very still.

"My mouth was small," said Willow. "Then I made it big. The mirror went in because I opened wide." Mom hugged her. "That was smart thinking," said Mom. The dentist gave Willow a sticker. Willow held it up all the way home.

Joshua sat at the craft table at summer camp. He wore his big yellow hat. The sun was high in the sky outside. Today he was making a paper sun with long yellow rays.

Joshua put glue on a ray. He stuck it on right away. Then he held the paper up. The ray slid down and fell off. "Oh no," said Joshua. His friend Mia looked over. "My ray fell too," she said.

Joshua touched the glue. It was wet and sticky. He pressed the ray on again. This time he counted slowly. One, two, three. He kept his hands still. He watched the glue. It began to dry. He let go. The ray stayed!

"The glue was wet," Joshua said. "Wet glue slides. Dry glue sticks."

Outside, the campers began to sing. Joshua sang too. He held his paper sun up high, and all the rays stayed on.

Gabriella went to Mia's house. Mia had a big blue blanket on the floor. "This is the sea," said Mia. "My doll will swim in it." The doll jumped in and slid under the blanket.

Gabriella wanted her bear to swim too. But her bear was scared. He sat on the edge and did not move. "He needs a boat," said Gabriella. She found a shoebox. Now the bear had a boat. He sailed right across the blue blanket sea.

Then Mia's doll got cold. "Her skin is cold from the water," said Gabriella. She wrapped the doll in a sock. The doll got warm and cozy. A spotted cat puppet came to check on them. He was the sea doctor.

Mia yawned. "The sea is sleepy now," she said. The blanket waves went flat and still. "Night night, sea," said Gabriella. She patted the blanket three times.

Asher went to the store with Mama. In his bag was a library book about soft kittens. "Mine," said Asher. "I will keep it forever."

At the store, Asher saw signs. One sign said MILK. "Mama, that word says milk!" "Yes," said Mama. "Words tell us things." The book had words too. Asher turned the pages, one, two, three, four. The story went from the front to the back. He read it that way, front to back.

But Asher had a plan. He would hide the book under his coat. Then the library could not take it back. He tucked it in. He zipped up. Then he heard a small sound. "Meow," said the book. Asher laughed. "Silly book, you cannot meow!"

Mama smiled. "We take the book back on library day," she said. "Other kids read it too." So Asher gave the book a hug. He held it soft and close. "One more read," he said. "Front to back. Then you go home to your friends."

At bedtime, Asher turned the pages. One, two, three. The soft kitten found her mama at the end. "Good for you," said Asher. He patted the cover and said, "Library day is soon. But you are my friend first."

The book went into the bag all by itself, and Asher waved. "Bye bye, little meow."

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor skip, skip, skipped to the door to meet her. Grandma had a big suitcase and a tiny pillow in her bag.

On Monday, Grandma fell asleep in the middle of the day. She slept in the chair by the swing. "Grandma, why are you sleepy?" Eleanor asked. "It is not even night!"

Grandma yawned. "I flew on a plane for a long, long time," she said. Eleanor wondered about that. Did the plane make Grandma tired?

On Tuesday, Grandma napped again. On Wednesday, she napped just a little bit. By Friday, Grandma was awake all day. Eleanor clapped her hands. "Grandma, you are fixed!" Grandma laughed and picked her up for a big hug.

Cooper sat at the little blue table. He was making a sun with yellow paper. He picked up the glue bottle. He squeezed and squeezed. Glue went everywhere. His paper got very wet. The soft yellow paper tore a little bit. Cooper made a sad face.

His teacher brought a small glass of water for his hands. Cooper dipped his fingers in. The room was noisy with kids cutting and pasting. Then Cooper got a new piece of paper. This time he made one small dot of glue. He pressed on a yellow circle. It stayed on. It did not tear. Cooper pushed it again. It still stayed.

"The big glue made the paper tear," Cooper said. "Little glue makes it stay." He held up his sun. It shined all yellow and whole. "Look, teacher! I fixed it with a tiny dot!"

Raphael stood by the big window at the community centre. Snack time was coming. Two bowls of crackers sat on the table. Miss Maya said, "Can you tell me which bowl has more?"

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Then he counted the second bowl from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He frowned. Did counting from the other end change things? He counted the first bowl again, starting from the other side. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Still seven!

"Miss Maya, I got seven both times," he said. "It is seven, whichever cracker I count first." Miss Maya smiled and gave the bigger bowl to the twins. They were extra hungry today.

One cracker was broken in half. Raphael ate it first. Then his ice pop began to melt in the sun, so he drank it from the bowl like juice.

Nolan woke up from his sleep at Grandma's house. Today was a big day. He was getting his very first haircut!

Grandma held his hand. They walked to the salon down the street. They passed the playground on the way. "I can play after," said Nolan.

The hairdresser had a shiny spray bottle. She squirted water on Nolan's hair. Squirt, squirt! His hair was wet now. The wet hair stuck together in little points. The scissors went snip, snip. The wet pieces fell down like tiny dark rain. They stuck to the cape and made it not clean.

Nolan watched in the mirror. He touched his dry hair at home sometimes. Dry hair puffed up and flew away. Wet hair stayed on the cape in little lines.

"Look," said Nolan. "The water makes my hair stick. That is why it falls down!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "Wet hair is easy to cut."

Soon the haircut was done. Nolan jumped off the chair. "Playground time!" he said.

Grandma laughed. They ran out the door, hand in hand.

Eliana sat on the rug in the living room. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Aunt Jo sat on the couch with a bowl of popcorn. The big game was on TV. Everyone wore blue shirts.

Then Eliana saw a bright spot on the screen. The sun was on the TV. She could not see the ball. The bright spot hid it. "I can't see," said Grandpa. He leaned to one side. Aunt Jo leaned too.

Eliana looked at the window. The sun came from there. She stood up. She took the curtain in her little hands. She pulled it across. The curtain slid shut. Now the window was closed. The bright spot went away. The screen was clear and dark. "There is no sun now," said Eliana. "The sun made the spot." Grandpa clapped. On the TV, a player kicked the ball into the net. The crowd went loud. Everyone jumped up. Eliana hugged the popcorn bowl. "We did it," she said.

Kai sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But where was the green paint? He looked in the cup. He looked in the box. No green. "That's bad," said Kai.

His teacher Miss Ana said, "What colors do you see?" Kai looked hard. "Red. Blue. Yellow." He touched the yellow cup. It felt cool and slippery. He touched the blue cup too.

Then Kai had an idea. What if yellow and blue mixed together? He zipped his brush into the yellow paint. He zipped it again into the blue paint. Swish, swish, round and round on the paper. The paint made a new color. It was green!

"Look, look!" said Kai. "Yellow and blue make green! That is why there was no green cup." He painted a fat green frog with big eyes. Outside, the summer sun came in the window. It warmed his hand. "Miss Ana," he asked, "what does red and yellow make?"

Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. The soup was warm. Grandma began to pour the milk.

Then everyone stopped. Nobody ate. Emile looked around. Why was the food just sitting there?

"Hold my hand," said Grandma. Emile held her hand. Cousin Lou held his other hand. Everyone at the table made one big circle with their hands.

Then everyone said the blessing together. "Thank you for our food." Emile did not know the words yet. He opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His cheeks went pink.

"Just hum," said Lou with a grin. "Nobody can tell."

So Emile hummed. He hummed very loud. He sounded like a little bee.

Grandma laughed. "Now we eat!" she said. Because the blessing was done, everyone picked up a spoon at last.

After lunch, Emile found Grandma's big sun hat. He put it on. "Thank you for our food," he said to the hat.

"That's it!" said Grandma. "Say it two more times before dinner. Then it will stick like glue."

Emile said it to the hat. He said it to the cat. The cat walked away.

At dinner, everyone held hands again. This time Emile knew just what to do. He held on tight and said, "Thank you for our food."

Lou clapped. Grandma kissed his head. Then everyone picked up a spoon at the very same time.

Sienna ran to the table. Lunch was ready! Her hands were dirty from the sandbox.

"Hands first," said Mama. "Wash with soap."

Sienna looked at her hands. Sand was on them. Yucky germs were on them too. Germs were too far away to see, but they were there.

She pushed the bench to the sink. She turned on the water. She pumped the soap. Bubbles! Big white bubbles!

"Now we count," said Mama. "Count to twenty."

"One, two, three," said Sienna. She rubbed and rubbed. "Four, five, six."

"Sing the happy song," said Mama.

Sienna sang. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" The bubbles grew and grew. "Eleven, twelve!"

She washed the backs of her hands. She washed between her fingers. "Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!"

Rinse, rinse. The bubbles ran down. "Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!"

Mama gave her the towel. Sienna looked at her hands. Clean! Pink and shiny clean!

Sienna lifted her sandwich up high. She took a big bite.

"Mama!" she said. "Soap makes germs go away. That is why we wash!"

Then she looked at the towel. A tiny ladybug sat on it!

"Hello, ladybug," said Sienna. "Did you wash your hands too?"

Asher sat in the big chair. It was his first haircut! The barber put a cape on him. The cape went snap, snap, snap.

The barber cut with his scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. "Look, look!" said Asher. The hairs landed on the cape. They did not fall on his shirt.

The cape caught them! The hairs sat on the cape because it was big and wide.

"Now you get a sticker," said the barber. He put it in Asher's hand. Asher held it tight so he would not miss it.

Asher jumped down from the big chair. "I got a haircut!" he said. "My hairs fell on my cape!" He ran to show his mom the sticker.

Beatrice ran to the block corner at school. She saw the big red robot toy. Tom was holding it. Beatrice wanted it too.

"Give it!" said Beatrice. She pulled the robot. Tom pulled back. The robot fell on the floor. It made a loud crash. Now nobody had the robot.

Miss Kay knelt down. "We take turns," she said. "Tom, you play first. Then Beatrice." Tom set a timer on the shelf. When it rang, it was Beatrice's turn.

Beatrice held the robot. Tom waited, but his lip looked sad. Beatrice looked at him. "You can push the button," she said. Tom pushed the button. The robot blinked. "Nice robot!" said Tom. Beatrice waved the robot's arm. "Beep beep!" she said.

Then the timer rang again. Tom got his turn. Beatrice waited. The timer made turns fair. Nobody had to pull. Nobody had to cry.

"Your turn, my turn," said Beatrice. "That is how it works." Tom smiled and pushed the button again.

Brielle sat in her reading nook. She wanted to spell her name. But the letters looked like squiggly lines to her. She felt mad. She threw her sock on the floor.

Mama sat down next to her. She pointed to the first letter. "This is B," Mama said. "It says buh. Listen. Buh, buh, Brielle."

Brielle tapped the letter. "Buh," she said. Then she looked at her book. "Buh, bear!" The bear on the page started with B too.

She looked at the sock on the floor. "Suh, sock!" she said. S made the suh sound. She laughed and picked it up.

Brielle traced B with her finger. Slow, then fast. Then she said, "B-R-I-E-L-L-E. That is me!"

She hugged her book tight and read the letters again, all by herself.

Kayden wanted his red plane. It was not in the toy box. "Where is it?" he asked. Mom sat next to him. "Think about yesterday," she said. Kayden thought. Yesterday he flew the plane in the yard. He left it by the big tree. "I remember now!" he said.

They went outside together. The plane was wet. Yesterday the rain came after Kayden went inside. The rain made the plane wet. "The rain fell on it," said Kayden. "That is why it is wet." Mom smiled and nodded.

Kayden began to cry a little. "Is my plane broken?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "We will dry it now. Later it will be dry and shiny." They wiped the plane with a soft towel. They put it by the sunny window.

"Now we wait," said Mom. "Tomorrow it will be all dry." Kayden held the plane up to the light. "Fly tomorrow," he told it. Mom laughed and kissed his head.

Elizabeth lived on a farm with her grandpa. Today Grandpa had a game. "Can you find your five senses?" he asked.

Elizabeth held up one finger. "Eyes see!" she said. She saw a black cow in the field. Two fingers. "Ears hear!" The cow said moo. That was three? No, two. She laughed at herself.

Three fingers. "Nose smells!" She sniffed the cow. "Phew!" said Grandpa, and they both giggled.

Four fingers. "Tongue tastes!" Grandpa gave her a sweet red apple from a basket.

One finger was left. Elizabeth looked at it. What did hands do? She patted the cow. The cow was soft and warm. "Hands feel!" she shouted. "The cow feels soft because I touch it!"

"Five senses, five fingers," said Grandpa. "Now let's go bathe that smelly cow."

The cow ran the other way. "Moo!" said the cow.

Sadie sat on a small log at summer camp. It was time for lunch. The counselor said, "Wash your hands first."

Sadie ran to the water pump. She got her hands wet. She rubbed on soap. Then she rinsed fast and ran back.

"Too fast," said the counselor. "Germs need twenty seconds with soap."

Sadie did not know what twenty seconds was. The counselor said, "Sing the happy birthday song twice. That is twenty seconds."

At snack time, Sadie tried it. She got her hands wet. She put on soap. She sang the song one time. She kept rubbing. She sang it again. Bubbles sat on her fingers like small clouds.

After the toilet, Sadie sang too. She counted the songs, not just splashes.

Later, Sadie looked at her clean hands. "The song makes the germs sleep," she said, and took a big bite of her apple.

Ryan was at summer camp. Lunch was coming. His tummy felt hungry for sandwiches.

A man named Sam stood by a big sink. "Come wash your hands," Sam said. Ryan ran over. He got soap on his hands. He rinsed it off fast. Then he grabbed a sandwich.

Then Ryan looked at his hands. He saw dirt on them still. He put the sandwich down. "Yuck," he said. "My hands still have dirt."

"Try again," said Sam. "Count with me." Sam rubbed his hands with soap. He counted to twenty. "One, two, three..." Ryan rubbed his hands too. The soap got bubbly. They counted all the way to twenty.

Ryan rinsed the bubbles off. He looked close. The dirt was gone! "The soap needed more time," Ryan said.

A girl named Mia could not reach the soap. Ryan got a small stool for her. "Thank you," said Mia. "That was polite," said Sam.

Then Ryan sat down and ate his sandwich. It tasted good. After lunch he had to use the toilet. When he came out, he went right back to the sink. He counted to twenty again.

"Twenty seconds," said Ryan, holding up his clean hands. "Now I can play."

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. It was yellow and shiny. It smelled like fresh wood.

"I will write my name!" said Lucas. He grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The line came out fat and wobbly. It did not look like a letter at all. "Oh no," said Lucas. "My L looks like a worm."

Mama sat down next to him. She picked up her own pencil. She held it with just three fingers, pinched near the tip, like a little crab claw. Lucas watched. He tried it too. Pinch, pinch. He made a skinny little line down. Then a little line across. "One, two, an L!" shouted Lucas.

"Now the U," said Mama. Lucas drew one big curve. "U!" he said. Then C, then A, then S. "L, U, C, A, S," he counted out loud. He looked at the paper. There it was. His name. Five letters, all in a row. "I pinch, and the letters come out beautiful!" said Lucas.

"You wrote your own name," said Mama. "We will hang it up for everyone to see. Daddy will read it after he comes home." Lucas clapped his hands. "My letters live on the paper now!" he said. He tapped the L one more time. "Hello, L."

Bennett went to the park with a cold popsicle. It was a hot day. The sun made everything warm.

Bennett saw a big tree. It made a big shadow. He also saw a small flower. It made a small shadow. Bennett held his popsicle up to the sun. Drip, drip! The red juice ran down his hand. "Oh no," said Bennett. "The sun is hot. My popsicle is melting fast."

Bennett ran slow, then fast. He stood in the big shadow under the tree. The shadow was cool. His popsicle stayed cold. "Look, Mom! The shadow helps!" He licked it with a straight, happy face. A little child ran by and pointed. A squirrel sat in the tree, holding a nut like a tiny popsicle. Bennett waved at it. "Hi, squirrel! This is my shady spot."

Addison sat on the bottom step at Grandma's house. She wanted the big red ball. Cousin Max had the big red ball. He bounced it high. Addison watched. Her bottom stayed on the step.

Grandma came out with two cups of juice. "One for Max," she said. "One for Addison. We take turns with the ball too." Max stopped bouncing. He rolled the ball to Addison. Addison hugged it. Then she rolled it back. Max laughed. They sent the ball back and forth. It went to Max, then to Addison, then to Max again.

Grandma put cookies on a plate. "Share them," she said. Addison took one cookie. She gave the plate to Max. Max took one cookie too. The cookies were tasty. Addison said, "When we take turns, we both get to play." Then she rolled the ball one more time. Max caught it.

Josephine was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Josephine wanted to draw on it, but she did not know how to start it. "What if I break it?" she asked.

Mia's mom smiled. "You will not break it," she said. "Just try."

Josephine put one finger on the round button. She held it and counted. One, two, three. The screen lit up! "The button makes it turn on," Josephine said. "I held it, so it woke up."

Next, Mia showed her the little paint picture. Josephine tapped it with her finger. The drawing app opened. She picked a thin brush and drew a big yellow sun. She drew a red cat, too. "My cat!" she said. "I win, I made a cat!"

Then it was time for a snack. "Do I just leave it here?" Josephine asked. "No," said Mia. "We put it away." Josephine tapped the button once, quick and light. The screen went to sleep. She set the tablet on the shelf, safe and flat.

"You did it all by yourself," said Mia's mom. Josephine sat down at the table. She took a warm cookie in her hand. The tablet rested quietly on the shelf, waiting for the next picture.

Weston ran to the big tree in the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. It was not in the toy box. Where could it be? A noisy crow sat in the tree. "Caw, caw!" it called.

Weston looked under the green grass. No ball. He looked by the blue water bowl. No ball. Then he saw something in the tree. Was it a red apple? No. It was his ball! The crow had put it on a branch. Why? The crow liked bright red things. "The crow took my red ball because it is red," Weston said.

Weston put his yellow truck on the grass. The crow flew down. It picked up the yellow truck! Weston laughed and grabbed his red ball. He hugged it tight. "Thank you, noisy bird!" he called.

Sophie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. She reached with her fork. She reached with her hand. The basket was too far.

Daddy was cutting carrots now. He said, "I will pass the bread later, when I sit down."

Sophie waited. She watched the carrots go round and round. She looked at the flower in the jar. It was the last flower from yesterday. It had been closed this morning. Now it was open wide.

Sophie looked again at the basket. Daddy sat down. He passed her the bread.

"I waited and now I have it," Sophie said. She took a big bite. "Tomorrow can we have bread again?"

"Yes," said Daddy. "First we eat today's bread."

Sophie smiled and reached for the butter.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil and paper. He wanted to write his name.

He held the pencil in his fist. He made a mark. It was a big blob. "Oh no," said Jackson. "I miss the lines."

Mom sat down next to him. She picked up her own pencil. She held it with her fingers, near the tip. Jackson watched. He tried it too. He pinched the pencil like Mom.

"Now my hand can see where to go," said Jackson. The pencil made a nice straight line. He drew a big J. Then a small a. The J looked pointy, like a hook on a door.

Jackson wrote more letters. He missed the c and made it look like a wet worm. He laughed and tried again. This time the c curled just right.

"Look, Mom! Jackson!" he said. His name sat on the paper. Mom clapped her hands. Jackson drew one more J, just for fun.

Grandma came to stay at Sienna's house. "How long?" Sienna asked. "Seven sleeps," said Grandma. Sienna counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven sleeps was a whole week!

Grandma would sleep on a big air bed in Sienna's room. They pumped it up together. Then they read a story. Then they slept.

In the morning, the bed was flat! Grandma was on the floor. "Oh no," said Grandma. Sienna looked all around the bed. She found the little plug. It was not pushed in! "The plug came out," said Sienna. "That is why the bed went flat." They pushed the plug in tight. They pumped the bed up again. It stayed big and bouncy all night. Sienna jumped on it once, just to check. "Seven sleeps," she said, "and a bouncy bed too!"

Arlo ran to the big slide. But the slide was snowy. The snow was soft and white. Arlo touched it with his mittens. It was cold.

"Mom, the slide is all snowy," said Arlo. Mom sat on the bench. "The sun is out now," she said. "Let us wait and watch."

Arlo waited. He grabbed a stick and drew in the snow. He made a circle. He made a line. Then he looked up. The sun was warm on his face. The white snow on the slide was getting small. It dripped, drip, drip, down the legs.

"The sun makes the snow melt," said Arlo. "The snow is little now." He put his hand on the slide. It was just a bit wet. He waited some more. At last the slide was clear. Arlo climbed up, whoosh, down he went! He went down three more times.

On the walk home, Mom said, "Yesterday the snow came. Today the sun melted it." Arlo smiled. "Tomorrow at school I will draw the slide at my desk," he said. "I will draw the drip, drip, drip."

Matteo went to the temple with his Papa. It was a special day. After the songs, everyone sat down for bread and soup at long tables.

Papa held out his hand. "We say the blessing first," he said. Matteo took Papa's hand. He took Nana's hand too. Everyone at the table held hands. Then they all said the words together. "Thank you for our food. Amen."

Matteo did not know the words yet. So he just listened. Then he saw the bread. It looked warm and good. He reached for it with his free hand. His elbow bumped his cup. Water splashed onto the cloth.

Nana helped him wipe it up. "Wait for the Amen," she said softly. "Then we eat."

Matteo waited. He held hands. He listened to the words. One, two, three, then "Amen." Now everyone picked up bread at the same time. Matteo took a big bite. It was warm and good.

After the meal, Matteo drew with a crayon. He drew the long table and all the hands. "Amen means go," he told Papa. "When we say it, we eat." Papa smiled. "You are a lucky boy," he said. "You learned our blessing today." Matteo put his crayon down and said, "Amen."

Maverick went to the garden with his grandma. He had four little seeds in his hand. One seed, two seeds, three seeds, four. He made a hole and dropped them in. He patted the soft dirt down.

The sun was hot that day. Maverick slipped off his shoe and sat on a piece of wood to rest. He looked at his dirt. "Where are my plants?" he asked. Every day he came back. Every day he saw only dirt.

Then one morning, four little green leaves popped up. But by noon, they were droopy and sad. Maverick touched the dirt. It was dry. He ran to the tap and filled his small can. He poured the water on the leaves. The next day, the leaves stood up tall. "The plants droop because the dirt is dry," Maverick said. So he watered them every day, one can, two cans, and soon he counted four fat carrots.

Eliana went to the store with Grandma. She wanted to pick apples for a snack. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Eliana held the cart with one hand.

They walked past the bakery. Something smelled warm and sweet. Eliana saw big bread rolls on a shiny tray. She reached up her hand. "Oven," said Grandma. "Hot, hot, hot." Eliana put her hand back down. A man with a kind face touched the tray with a long silver tool. The bread went in a bag. Nobody touched the bread with bare hands.

"We count one, two, three," said Grandma. They counted apples into a bag. One, two, three red apples. Then Eliana saw something under a case. It was a small knife, shiny and sharp. "That one, I do not touch," said Eliana. Grandma nodded. A worker came and picked it up with gloves.

At the cold case, Eliana put her palm on the glass. It felt icy. "Cold glass," she said. "The bread tray is hot. The glass is cold." Grandma smiled. "That is right," she said.

At the checkout, Eliana waited for her turn. She waited and waited, slow and calm. Then the kind man from the bakery waved. "Apples for you?" he asked. Eliana held up the bag. "One, two, three," she said. She squeezed Grandma's hand, and they walked out the door together.

Emilia went to the park with Dad. It was a beautiful summer day. She stood by the gate and looked around.

"Where is the ice cream truck?" she asked.

"It came yesterday," said Dad. "Yesterday is gone. Today the truck comes later."

Emilia frowned. She wanted ice cream now. "Can we make it come now?"

"We cannot," said Dad. "But we can play first. Later comes after."

Emilia went on the swing. She slid down the slide. Then she heard a little song. Ding, ding! The truck was here!

"The truck came later!" she said. "Later comes after I play."

"Yes," said Dad. "You played, and then later came."

Emilia got a cold strawberry ice cream. She took one big lick. It dripped down her hand because the sun was hot.

"The sun makes it melt!" she said. "So I eat it now, not later."

Dad laughed. Emilia took another bite. "Tomorrow we come back," she said. "And later, the truck comes again."

Grayson walked on the nature trail with Dad. He saw a purple flower. "Can you smell it?" asked Dad. Grayson sniffed with his nose. "My nose smells it," he said. He picked up a pine cone. His hands could feel the bumpy parts. "My hands touch it," he said.

Then a bird sang in a tree. Grayson heard the song with his ears. A butterfly landed near his shoe. He saw its wings with his eyes. Dad gave him a red apple from the bag. Grayson took a bite. "My mouth tastes it," he said. "Yum."

Then Dad held up one hand. "Tell me all five," he said. Grayson counted his fingers. "Nose, hands, ears, eyes, mouth." Dad smiled and nodded. Grayson ate the rest of the apple. "I can tell them all," he said.

Hannah sat on the big train seat. She was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. Hannah had her toy pig with her. She put the pig on the seat next to her. "Stay there, pig," she said.

The train went around a bend. The seat tipped a little bit. The pig slid down. Plonk! The pig fell on the floor. Hannah bent down and picked him up. She put him back on the seat. The train went around another bend. The pig slid again. Plonk! Down he went.

Hannah sat very still and thought. She looked at the pig. She looked at the bend out the window. "The train turns," said Hannah. "The pig slides because the train turns." She tried one more time. She put the pig on her lap instead. She held him with her two hands. The train turned again. The pig did not fall. He sat snug and warm.

"You stay with me now," said Hannah. The pig looked at her with his same little smile. Outside, the trees went by, green and fast. Hannah held her pig all the way.

Lydia stood in the reading corner. She wanted the bunny book. She wanted it forever.

A librarian gave her a card. It was red and little. "Your very own card," the librarian said. Lydia clapped her hands. The card said her name.

The librarian put the bunny book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "But you must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Lydia hugged the bag. "Mine forever," she whispered.

At home, Lydia read the bunny book. She read it at lunch. She read it to her teddy bear. She sang a little song about bunnies. "Hop, hop, hop," she sang.

Then Mommy said, "The book goes back tomorrow. A boy named Sam wants it next."

Lydia frowned. "I love this bunny."

"Sam loves bunnies too," said Mommy.

Lydia thought. The book made Sam happy. The book made her happy too. One bunny book, two happy kids.

The next day, Lydia walked back to the library. She gave the book to the librarian. "Here," she said. "For Sam."

Then she found a new book. A puppy book. She held it up high.

"Can I take this one home?" she asked. "And bring it back after?"

Show and Tell day was here. Weston's teacher put a big box on the floor. "Help me sort it," she said. There were three bins. One bin was for animals. One bin was for toys. One bin was for foods. Weston wanted to fill them all, but the box was very full.

Weston picked up a toy duck. "A duck is an animal," he said. He put it in the animal bin. Then the class bunny, Snowy, hopped by. Snowy nibbled the toy duck. Then Snowy hopped to the food bin and nibbled a carrot. Weston watched. "The toy duck is not food," he said. "Snowy will not eat it."

Weston picked up the toy duck again. He squeezed it. It squeaked. He did not feed it. It did not hop. "It is a toy," he said. "Snowy is the animal. Snowy eats. The duck just squeaks." He put the toy duck in the toy bin. Everyone clapped.

Then Weston heard a funny sound. He stopped to listen. Squeak, squeak! A real duck was at the window. "A duck at school!" said Weston. His teacher laughed. "That one is an animal," she said. "It can go in no bin. It will walk to the pond."

Sofia went to the library with Grandma. There was a shape rug by the bookshelf. It had a red circle and a blue square.

Sofia wanted to build a tower. She put a circle block on top. The circle block rolled away. It rolled under the chair. "Why did it roll?" Sofia asked. Grandma picked up the block. "The circle is round," she said. "Round things roll."

So Sofia tried a square block. The square had flat sides. It sat still. She put a triangle on top. It sat still too. She put a rectangle on the bottom. The tower stood up tall.

A little boy watched her. He clapped his hands. "Do it again!" he said. Sofia gave him a square block. He put it on the tower.

Then they sang a little song. "Round ones roll, flat ones stay," they sang. One of Sofia's shoes was loose. She sat down and pulled it tight. Then she put one more block on top, very slowly, and the tower stayed.

Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She wanted a cookie for dessert. "Cookies are for later," said Mom. "Now we eat dinner." Eleanor looked at her peas. She ate one spoonful. Then she ate another.

"After dinner, will it be tomorrow?" asked Eleanor. Mom shook her head. "Tomorrow comes after a whole sleep," said Mom. Eleanor thought about that. Yesterday she had slept. Yesterday she had played in the rain. Today was a new day, and today she had peas.

Eleanor kept eating. She took her time. One pea, then another. She did not rush. Mom folded her napkin and waited. Dad folded his napkin too. The table was quiet and warm.

At last the bowl was empty. Eleanor held it up. "All gone!" she said. "Is it later now?" Mom smiled. "Yes. It is later now." Mom put one cookie on the table. Eleanor took a big bite.

"I know why I got the cookie," said Eleanor. "I ate my peas first. The cookie came after." Mom nodded. Eleanor looked out the window. "Tomorrow I will eat my peas too. Then tomorrow will be a cookie day." She patted her full tummy. "But now it is now, and I have my cookie."

Madeline went to the park with Papa. She wanted to fold a green boat. But green paper was all gone at home.

"I have yellow paper," said Papa. "I have blue paper too."

Madeline sat on the swing. Papa pushed her high. She went up, up, up. Then she came down and got to work.

She took the yellow paper. She rubbed her blue chalk all over it. One, two, three strokes. Then more. The yellow turned funny. She looked close. It was green!

"Blue on yellow makes green," said Madeline.

She folded the paper. Fold, fold, fold. The boat had a pointy top. It was a green boat at last.

Now she needed water. The park had a little puddle by the slide. Madeline carried her boat over. She set it down. The boat floated!

"Look, Papa, look!" she said.

Papa clapped. Then Madeline made another one. Yellow paper, blue chalk. One, two, three strokes. Green again! Blue on yellow makes green.

She folded the second boat too. Two green boats sat on the puddle. They bumped side to side.

"Hello, boats!" said Madeline. She waved her hand up high.

Rowan put on his red shirt. His team all wore red shirts. Red shirt number one, red shirt number two, red shirt number three. Rowan was number four. His big sister clapped from the bench.

The game was long. Rowan got the ball. He threw it very hard. It hit the rim and bounced off. He got the ball again. He threw it hard again. It bounced off again.

"Why does the ball jump off?" he asked himself. "Because I throw too hard." So Rowan did not throw this time. He saw Ben near the hoop. Ben had his hands up. Rowan passed the ball soft and low. Ben caught it. Ben put it in the hoop. Swish.

The red shirts ran to Rowan. They patted his back. After the game, Rowan was tired. He went home and told his sister about the basket. Then he got to sleep early, still smiling, holding his ball.

Kinsley held her toy pig. She was at the mall with Daddy. They were a little late for her first haircut.

"Haircut for Kinsley!" said Rosa the hair lady.

Kinsley sat in the big chair. It went up, up, up. Rosa picked up the scissors.

"No, no!" said Kinsley. "My hair is dry! Scissors can not cut dry hair."

Rosa smiled. She sprayed water. Pssh, pssh, pssh. Kinsley's hair got wet.

"Wet hair!" said Kinsley. "Now the scissors can cut it."

Snip, snip, snip. One curl fell. Two curls fell. Three curls fell onto her toy pig.

"The pig has hair too!" said Kinsley. "Silly pig."

Rosa held up the mirror. Kinsley saw a big girl with short curls.

"Hello, big girl!" said Kinsley. "Snip, snip!"

Hunter ran into the big hall. There were balloons on every chair. There was a table with a cake. Grandma put candles on the cake. Hunter counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four," he said. "Four candles because I am four," said Hunter.

But the candles were thin and tall. They wobbled. Hunter did not want them to fall. He was careful. He touched one candle, very soft, to make it straight. It stood up tall. "There," said Hunter. "Now it will not fall."

A big box sat by the door. A white feather was tied to the bow. Hunter touched the feather with one finger. It was soft and light. He gave the box a little push. The feather went up in the air. It came down slow. Hunter laughed.

Then everyone sang the birthday song. Dad said, "Make a wish, Hunter." Hunter blew at the candles. Out went one, two, three, four. All the lights were gone from the cake. Hunter clapped his hands. "I blew, and they went out!" he said. Grandma cut the cake into pieces for everyone.

Alexander dug little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed in each hole. Then he patted the dirt down, pat, pat. The sun felt warm on his hat.

He planted two rows of seeds. He watered the first row with his small blue can. Then he heard his swing creak in the wind. He ran to the swing and swung high, back and forth. He forgot to water the second row.

Every morning Alexander looked at his garden. Little green leaves came up in the first row. Tiny leaves, like baby hands. The second row stayed bare and brown. "Oh," said Alexander. "My seeds grew because I gave them water." So he got the can and watered the second row too.

Soon leaves came up there also. Alexander licked a drip of water off his tongue and smiled. Then a fat worm popped out of the dirt, waving hello.

Iris spilled her milk on the floor. It made a big white puddle. "Oh no," she said.

Iris wanted to wipe it up. She looked for a cloth. She found her teddy bear instead. She touched it. It was soft, not for wiping. She put teddy down gently. Then she found her toy robot. It was hard and shiny. Not for wiping either. She put the robot down too.

Then Iris saw the bread on the table. Food was not for wiping. At last she found a small towel. She wiped the milk. The puddle went away. The floor was dry and clean.

Iris patted her teddy bear. "Teddy is a toy," she said. "Milk is a food. The towel did the job."

Then the phone rang. Iris heard Grandpa's voice. "Hello, my little one!" said Grandpa. Iris smiled and hugged her teddy tight.

Alexis ran to the park with his cozy red jacket on. The jacket was soft like a bear hug. He was so excited to see the ducks.

At the pond, Alexis began to count the ducks. "One, two, three," he said. Then a big dog barked. Bark, bark! Alexis felt scared. He hid behind a tree. The dog ran past with a boy chasing it. The boy looked angry. "Come back, dog!" the boy shouted.

Then the dog stopped. The boy sat down on the grass. He looked sad. A tear rolled down his cheek. Alexis peeked out from the tree.

Alexis walked over slowly. He smiled a big smile. "Hi," he said. "Want to see the ducks?" The boy looked up. He saw Alexis smiling. Then he smiled too. They counted the ducks together. "One, two, three, four!"

Later they sat on a bench. Alexis's mom gave them a plate with crackers. The boys shared every cracker.

"Smiling made you happy," Alexis said. The boy nodded. Then they both giggled, loud like the ducks.

Norah stood at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. Only red, blue and yellow cups sat there. The wet paint smelled stinky, like old socks. Norah felt worried.

She asked her teacher, "How can I paint a frog with no green?" Her teacher smiled. "Try mixing two colors." Norah paid attention to the cups. She picked yellow. Then she picked blue. She dipped her brush in both. The colors swirled together on the paper. They made green! "Blue and yellow make green," Norah said. "That is why my frog can be green."

Her teacher hung the painting on the board with a big red magnet. The frog looked happy. "Ribbit," said Norah.

Theodore ran to art class. He wanted to paint a house. First he drew a big square. The square had four sides. It was the house body. Then he drew a rectangle door. The rectangle was tall like him.

Now he needed a roof. He cut a square paper and put it on top. It would not fit. It slid off, plop, into the paint bucket. "Oh no!" said Theodore.

Then he saw the orange paper. It was a triangle. It had three pointy sides. He put the triangle on top. It fit just right, like a hat!

"The square slid because it was too flat," said Theodore. "The triangle has points!"

He painted a tiny yellow sun, a round circle in the sky. "C-I-R!" he tried to spell. His teacher laughed. Theodore laughed too. "House done!"

William sat on the clean bench in the backyard. He had a little seed in his hand. "What can I do with my seed?" he asked. "You can plant it," said Grandma.

William dug a small hole. He put the seed in. He patted the dirt down. Now he had to wait.

While he waited, he used his ears. He heard a bird sing. Then he used his eyes. He saw the bird hop. His nose smelled the flowers. His tongue tasted cold water. His fingers felt the soft dirt.

"Five senses," said William. "Ears, eyes, nose, tongue, fingers."

Days went by. Then a green sprout came up. It grew because the seed had water and sun. William sat and watched it grow a little more each day.

"Hello, little sprout," he said. "I will wait for you."

Myles sat at the little blue table. He was making a cat. The cat had a paper face and a furry grey tail. The furry tail was soft like a kitten.

Myles wanted the tail to hang down. It would swing when he moved the paper. He put glue on the tail. Then he put on more glue. Then even more glue, all shiny and white.

He held the cat up. Drip, drip. The wet glue ran down. The soggy paper got soft. The heavy tail pulled the paper down. Plop. The tail fell right off and landed on the table. Why did it fall? Was it too wet? Was it too heavy?

Myles got a new tail. This time he made one small dot of glue. He pressed it and counted slowly, one, two, three, four, five. He held the cat up and gave it a little shake. The tail stayed on. It swung back and forth, back and forth.

"Look, Teacher Maya," said Myles. "One dot of glue. Now my cat can swing her tail."

Jake sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny. Today he would get a shot. He did not want a shot.

Mom held his hand. "A shot takes one second," she said. "Let's count it. One, two, three, done!" The nurse came in with a small tray. She had a cute bandage with a yellow duck on it. She put it next to a little fork-shaped pin, a toy prize for brave kids.

"My arm is tight," Jake said. He squeezed it into a ball. The nurse shook her head. "A tight arm hurts more. A soft arm hurts less." Jake let his arm go soft, like a sleepy cat. He asked, "Will it hurt a lot?" Mom said, "A tiny poke, then we get ice cream."

"One, two, three," they all counted. The nurse said, "All done!" Jake blinked. It was over that fast. "My arm was soft, so it hurt less," Jake said. The nurse smiled. "That's right. You did it yourself."

She put the duck bandage on his arm. Jake got the little fork prize too. At home, Jake used his new fork to feed himself dinner. He took one bite, then two bites, then three. "Mom, can we count my ice cream too?" he asked. Mom laughed and scooped a big bowl.

Athena went to the store with Dad. Today was a big day. Tomorrow was Grandma's birthday. Athena wanted to buy a pink hat for her. "Show me the hats," she said to Dad.

There were red hats and blue hats. There were no pink hats. A lady in the store said, "The pink hats were here yesterday. They are all gone now." Athena felt sad. "But tomorrow is her birthday," she said. "I need it today."

Dad said, "We can come back later. The bus comes at two o'clock." Athena waited by the door. She watched the big clock on the wall. The hands moved slow, slow, slow.

Then a box came off a truck. The lady opened it. Pink hats! New hats for today. "The truck brings new things," Athena said. "Yesterday the hats were gone. Now there are more." She picked the best pink hat.

The bus came at two o'clock. Athena held the hat box on her lap. "Tomorrow Grandma will smile," she said. Dad smiled too.

Lennon went to the library with Dad. She saw a tablet on the little table. She wanted to draw a cloud.
She tapped the screen. Nothing happened. She tapped again. Nothing. The boy next to her was noisy, but the tablet stayed dark.
The librarian knelt down beside her. "Try this button," she said. She pointed to the side. Lennon pushed the button and held it. The screen lit up! "It turns on because I hold it," Lennon said. Dad smiled.
Lennon found the drawing app. She drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a sun for the boy, because he looked sad. He smiled and held it gently.
The librarian said it was time to put the tablet away. Lennon pushed the button and held it again. The screen went dark. She set it down softly on the table.
"Bye bye, cloud," said Lennon.

Rowan sat at the dinner table. He took a big bite of warm rice. His tummy felt happy.

Rowan had a problem. He wanted to play outside after dinner. "No outside," said Mama. "It is almost bedtime." Rowan looked down. Why did bedtime come so fast?

Then Rowan took a sip of warm milk. It felt warm in his tummy. He yawned a big yawn. Why was he so sleepy? He drank more milk. He yawned again. "Warm milk makes me sleepy," he said. The warm milk made his eyes blink slow.

After dinner, Mama ran a bath. The water was warm and bubbly. Rowan patted the bubbles with his hand. Pop, pop, pop! He patted them some more. The warm water made him feel even sleepier.

Mama helped him put on his soft pajamas. One sock, then the other sock. His feet were warm now. Rowan yawned one more yawn.

He did not go outside. He went to bed instead. "Warm milk, warm bath, warm socks," said Rowan. "All warm things. All sleepy things." He hugged his bear and closed his eyes. Outside could wait for morning.

Ayla went to the park with her doll, Pip. Ayla wanted to play house. She found a big flat rock. "This is our house," she said.

Pip needed a bed. Ayla made a bed from leaves. The leaves were soft. The bed was cozy. But Pip had no blanket. Ayla looked around. She found a big green leaf. She put it on top. "Sleep now, Pip," she said. Pip lay very still.

Then Ayla wanted to feed Pip. She had no spoon. She looked down. She picked up a little stick. The stick was not a spoon. But she held it like a spoon. "Here comes food!" she said. She tapped the stick on a bottle cap. Tink, tink. "Pip, the stick is a spoon because we say it is!" Ayla laughed. Pip said nothing. Dolls are quiet like that.

Grandma sat on a bench nearby. "Is Pip eating well?" asked Grandma. Ayla nodded. "Yes. She ate three leaves." Then the big green leaf blew off the bed. The wind took it! "Oh no!" said Ayla. "Pip is cold because the wind took her blanket." She ran and got two leaves this time. She put one under and one on top. "Now you are cozy twice, Pip." Grandma clapped her hands. "Best house in the park," she said.

Asher stood at the school gate. His mama held his hand. The gate was big and green. Asher did not want to let go.

"You can wave to me," said Mama. "I will wave back." Asher let go of her hand. He waved. Mama waved back, big and wide. Then she stood by the fence and waited.

Asher had an apple in his bag. It came from the farm at home. His hands were slippery from the rain, so the apple slipped out. It rolled on the wet ground. It rolled right to a girl with red boots.

She picked it up. She looked at his name tag. Everyone at school had a name tag on their shirt today. "Here is your apple, Asher," she said. Asher looked down. His name was right there on his chest!

"You know my name," he said. "Yes," said the girl. "Your tag tells me." She pointed to her own tag. "I am Nia. Want to walk in together?"

Asher took his apple. He took Nina's hand too. He turned and gave Mama one more wave. Then the two friends walked through the big green gate.

"Nia!" called a small voice. A boy was crying by the wall. His tag had flipped over, so nobody could read his name.

Nia turned it right side up. "Hello, Tom," she said. Tom wiped his eyes and smiled. "Come with us," said Asher. "We all have names now."

Charlie wanted the blue truck. But her cousin Sam had it. Sam pushed the truck. Vroom, vroom.

"Can I have a turn?" Charlie asked.

Sam held the truck tight. He shook his head. Charlie felt like crying. But then she had an idea.

"Sam, you take a turn. Then I take a turn," she said. "That is fair."

Sam thought. Then he smiled. "One, two, three," he counted. He pushed the truck. Then he gave it to Charlie. She pushed it. Vroom, vroom.

"Your turn is short," said Sam.

"Why is it short?" Charlie asked herself. She looked at the clock. "Because my turn is one minute. Then I leave the truck for you."

They took turns all morning. Soon it was lunch. Mom called, "Wash your hands first!" Charlie did. Sam did too. That was a rule at the table, and Mom said rules keep everyone safe and happy.

Sam put a carrot on Charlie's plate. "I share with you," he said. It looked funny sticking up like a little tree. Charlie laughed and took a big bite.

"More turns after lunch?" asked Charlie.

"Yes," said Sam. "You go first."

Zoey sat on the rug at school. Miss Kim put out letter cards. "Find the B," said Miss Kim. Zoey picked up a card. It said D. "Oops," said Zoey. B and D looked the same to her.

Her friend Ben showed her his card. "This is B," he said. "B has two bumps." Zoey looked hard. She turned her card. "My D has one bump," she said. "One bump, one bump," she said again. Now she could see it.

Miss Kim asked, "What sound does B make?" Ben said, "Buh, buh, bus!" Zoey clapped. She found a new B card. "Buh, buh, bear!" she said. Ben gave her a high five.

At play time, Zoey drew a beautiful sweater on paper. She made a big B on it. "B is for sweater bumps," she laughed. Then she drew fish. "They swim fast," she said. She looked at the word fish. "F! Fuh, fuh, fish!" said Zoey.

Willow could not find her bunny. She looked under the table. No bunny. She looked in her toy box. No bunny. Then Willow thought about her day. Bunny was with her at snack time. The snack was a banana, and banana gets sticky on soft toys.

Willow went to the kitchen. She looked at the chair where she sat. There was her bag on the chair. She opened the bag. Bunny was inside! Willow lifted Bunny out and gave it a hug. Bunny felt sticky and a bit yucky. "Bunny needs a wash," said Willow.

Mama helped fill the sink with warm bubbles. Willow gave Bunny a gentle scrub. The cat came to scratch at the door, so Willow let her in to watch. Soon Bunny was clean and soft. Willow sniffed her. "All clean," said Willow, and she held Bunny tight.
