Blake stood in the huge hallway. It was her first day of school. She held her red backpack tight. Her tummy felt funny. She wanted to find her classroom, but the door was gone. "Where did my room go?" she asked.

Then she saw a picture of a dog. It hung right by Room Four. "The dog shows my room!" she said. Yesterday, her teacher had let her hang it there. That was why the dog looked familiar. The picture was there so Blake could find her way.

A boy stood by the wall. He looked lost too. "March with me," Blake said. She lifted her knees up high. The boy laughed and marched too. They found Room Four together. The door opened, and the teacher smiled. "Good morning, Blake," she said. "Good morning," said Blake, and she waved the boy in first.

Wren got her pretty red coat. She wanted to zip it all by herself. Mom was busy making lunch in the kitchen.

Wren pushed the zipper up. But the zipper did not move. She tried again. Still no move. She looked down at her coat. The zipper pull was up high, not down at the bottom. She remembered Mom putting it at the bottom first.

Wren pulled the slider all the way down. She held the two sides of her coat together. Then she pushed the pull up, slow and slow. The zipper moved. It went up, up, up to her chin.

"Look, Mom! I did it all by myself!" said Wren. Mom smiled and clapped. "The zipper starts at the bottom," said Wren. Then she ran to wash her hands for lunch.

Victor sat at the little table in the school library. He had a big red pencil. He wanted to write his name. He made squiggly marks. They did not look like letters at all.

Victor held the pencil in his whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. He felt sad. He looked at his hand. Then he saw his friend Mia. She held her pencil with just three fingers. She pinched it near the tip, like a little bird beak. Her letters came out neat.

Victor tried it. He pinched the pencil with his thumb and two fingers. He pressed down. The pencil did what he wanted. The V came out. The I came out. The C came out. "Look, look!" said Victor. "My fingers pinch, so my pencil goes straight!"

Miss Ada smiled. "That is your name, Victor. Now let's go wash our hands for snack." Victor looked at his paper. V-I-C-T-O-R. All the letters were there. Writing letters was fun now. He held up his paper. "Read it," he said. "Read my name!"

Charles went to the art studio. He wanted to make a shiny picture. He got paper and a glue stick. He also got a jar of sparkles.

Charles drew a big sun with the glue. Then he poured sparkles on top. The sparkles fell off. They did not stick. Charles tried again. He drew the sun once more. He poured more sparkles. They fell off again.

A girl at the next table was painting. She dipped her brush. She let the paint drip onto her paper. Charles watched the paint. It was shiny and it stayed on. The paint was sticky like honey. "The paint sticks," said Charles. "My dry glue does not stick."

So Charles got a brush and some paint too. He mixed yellow paint with a little red. Now it looked just like a sun. He painted it on his paper. The paint went on slow and wet. Charles waited. He waited a little more. The paint began to dry. It stayed on the paper. It was shiny in the sun.

Charles held up his picture. "Look, it sticks now!" he said. The sparkles sat on the table. His shiny sun glowed in his hands.

Addison sat with her family at a restaurant. A big screen hung on the wall. A game was on. Everyone was cheering for the red team.

"Root for the red team with us," said Dad. Addison clapped her hands. She watched the screen. A player kicked the ball into the net. Then the score on the screen changed. The big number went up. The restaurant got very loud with happy sounds.

Addison watched some more. A player kicked the ball again. It missed the net. The score did not change. Addison stood up on her chair. "The number only goes up when the ball goes in," she said. Mom smiled and nodded.

Then a red player ran fast. She kicked the ball. It went in. "Watch the score!" Addison said. The number went up. Everyone filled the restaurant with cheers. Addison drank her smooth juice and clapped. The red team was winning now. "The ball went in," said Addison. "That is why the number is bigger."

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to make a house. He had paper shapes in a box.

"One square, two squares, three squares," he said. He glued the brown square on the paper. "The square is the house," he said. Now he needed a roof. He picked a circle. He put it on top. The circle wobbled and slid off. He put it on again. It slid off again.

Ibrahim picked up a triangle. It had three straight sides. He put it on top of the square. It sat flat and did not fall. "The circle fell because it was round," Ibrahim said. "The triangle stays because it is flat on the bottom."

His friend Maya yelled, "My roof fell too!" She held a circle in her hand. Ibrahim gave her a triangle. "Try this one," he said. She put it on her house. It stayed.

Then Maya gave Ibrahim a spoon. He used it to spread the glue. He pressed on one triangle, one square, one rectangle door, and one circle sun.

"Look at my house!" Ibrahim said.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Nice roof," she said.

John was at Grandma's house. He wanted to play outside. It was cold, so he had to wear his coat. "I can do it myself," John said.

He pushed his arms in the sleeves. Then he grabbed the zipper pull and pulled it up. But the zipper did not move. John pulled again. The zipper still did not move. "Silly zipper!" he said. Grandma laughed a little. "Try looking at the bottom," she said.

John looked down. There was a little metal pin sticking out at the bottom. The other side had a little slot. John pushed the pin into the slot. It clicked in. Then he pulled the zipper pull up. Zip! It went all the way to his chin. "The pin has to go in the hole first," John said. "That's why it was stuck!"

"Smart boy," said Grandma. They went outside to the garden. A frog sat by the pond. It made a loud jump into the water. Splash! "Take that, cold day!" said John, and he zipped his coat up even more.

Lena wanted to draw a cat at school. But the paper box was empty. No paper left.

Teacher Sam showed her the tablet. "Hold this button," he said. "Count one, two, three." Lena held the button. One, two, three. The screen grew bright. A yellow cat picture shone on it.

Lena tapped the drawing app. It was a little brush with rainbow colors. She drew a big yellow cat with long whiskers. Then Tom came over. He looked sad. His phone was dark, and he did not know why. "Hold the button and count," said Lena. Tom held it. One, two, three. His screen lit up too. "The button makes it wake up!" said Lena.

Then it was cleanup time. Lena pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She carried the tablet with two hands. She set it in its box, all tidy. Teacher Sam smiled. "You put it away so well," he said. Lena clapped her hands. "I can do it all by myself," she said.

Paint day was here at last. Charlotte wanted to paint a green tree. But there was no green paint. There was red, yellow, and blue.

A boy named Sam sat next to her. "No green," he said. He helped her open the little paint cups. The school dog, Bingo, barked one happy bark at the smell of paint.

"What will make green?" Charlotte asked herself. She put yellow on her brush. Then she put blue on top. She mixed them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," she said.

She painted a big green tree. Sam mixed red and yellow. His paint turned orange. He painted a fox. Charlotte hung her tree on the wall. "Look, green," she said, and smiled.

Jasper woke up in his bedroom. He wanted his blue sock. "I had it yesterday," he said. Yesterday was the day before today. The sock was not on his foot now.

Jasper looked under the bed. No sock. He looked on the rug. No sock. He looked in his toy box. No sock. "One bed, one rug, one box," he said. "Still no sock."

Mama came in. "I put your socks in the wash yesterday," she said. "Sorry, Jasper. The wash takes time. It is going now. It will be done later." Jasper put on his yellow socks today. "The blue socks come back later," he said. "Then I will wear them tomorrow." He kept his shoes by the door. Later could wait. Mama smiled and said, "Let's go eat."

Oliver sat at the camp craft table. He was making a paper lion. He wanted it for his grandma.

First he cut the mane. Then he cut the face. Now he needed to glue them together.

Oliver squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. A big puddle came out. The paper got wet and soft. It wrinkled up like a raisin.

"Oh no," said Oliver. "Why did my paper get bumpy?"

He looked at the glue bottle. Then he looked at the puddle. Too much glue made the paper soggy. That was why.

His friend Mia sat next to him. Her paper was flat and smooth. She used tiny dots of glue. One dot here. One dot there.

Oliver asked, "Can I try small dots too?"

"Yes," said Mia. She pushed the glue bottle toward him.

Oliver took a fresh paper lion face. He made one small dot. He made another small dot. He pressed the mane down. The paper stayed smooth.

Then he set his lion in the sun by the window. Soon the glue was dry. The lion felt firm and crisp.

The teacher came by. "What a big lion! Look, it has a curly tail."

Oliver turned the lion over. He had not glued a tail at all. But there one was, drawn in orange crayon. Mia had drawn it for him while he was not looking.

Oliver smiled. "My lion is done," he said. "And it is flat!"

Brielle stood in the reading corner. The rug was soft under her toes. A shelf of books stood by the window.

"Today you get a library card," Mom said. Brielle put her hand in Mom's hand. They walked to the big desk. The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave Brielle a small card. It had Brielle's own name on it.

"Pick one book," said Mom. Brielle looked a long time. She picked a book about a red truck. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

"You can take it home," said the lady. "But you must bring it back." Brielle held the book tight. "Then someone else can read it too," said Mom.

At home, Brielle read the truck book three times. She put it by her bed. Each night she read it again.

Then the day came. Mom said, "It is time." Brielle carried the book back to the library. She gave it to the lady. The lady put it on the shelf.

Brielle looked at the shelf. A boy was reaching for the truck book. "He can read it now," Brielle said. "Because I brought it back."

Then she picked a new book about the moon. "This one," she said.

Aiden ran to the park. The sun did shine on the slide. He felt so excited. His tummy jumped like a little hop.

Then Aiden saw a boy cry by the swing. The boy was sad. His ice cream had fallen down. It fell because the cone was too wobbly. "It fell," said the boy. Aiden looked at the ground. He saw the pink ice cream by his shoe.

Then a big dog ran up fast. The boy hid behind the bench. He was scared. But the dog just sniffed the ice cream and wagged his tail. The dog wanted the ice cream, not the boy. The boy came out from the bench. He laughed a little.

Aiden got mad one time too. A girl took the far swing, the one he liked. His face got hot. Then he took a big breath, like blowing out a candle. His hot feeling got small. The girl smiled and said, "You can have a turn next." Aiden felt happy inside. He watched the chickens peck far across the grass. "The dog came for the ice cream," Aiden said. "Not for us."

Matteo wants the cookies. Teacher Rosa hid them somewhere at daycare. "Can I find them?" he asks. "Yes, use your body," she says.

First he closes his eyes. He sees nothing. He opens his eyes. Now he sees the red shelf. "My eyes see the shelf. No cookies there."

Then he hears a sound. His ears hear it. Tap, tap. It is friend Mia with a spoon. No cookies there, either.

Matteo uses his nose. He sniffs near the big hill of blocks. Nothing. He sniffs near the toy box. Nothing. He sniffs by the little door. Mmm, sweet! "My nose smells cookies!" He follows his nose. The smell gets big. It leads him to the kitchen corner.

He touches the tin with his hands. It is warm. "Warm cookies!" He licks one crumb with his tongue. Sweet, so sweet.

The milk is hot, so he does not sip it. "Hot milk can burn my tongue," he says. He waits a short time. Then he sips. "Yum. My nose found them because cookies smell sweet!"

Beatrice woke up on a sleepy morning at Grandma's house. She saw a big piano in the corner. Grandma smiled and said, "You can try it."

Beatrice sat on the bench. She touched one key very softly. The piano made a tiny sound. "Why so small?" she asked. She pressed the key again, this time with her whole hand. The sound grew big and warm. "I pressed hard, so it sings big," she said.

Grandma played one, two, three notes. Beatrice played one, two, three notes too. Then she tapped a key so gently that it made almost no sound at all. "I touched it light, so it sleeps," she said.

Then a small surprise came. Beatrice held down one key and tapped another. The first sound kept ringing, long after her finger flew away. She counted the rings in the quiet room. One, two, three, four. "The sound stays if I hold it," she whispered.

Grandma sat beside her. "Play with me," she said. Beatrice pressed the keys, soft and loud, loud and soft. Outside, a bird began to sing along. Beatrice laughed and played one more note.

Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She had a new pencil and empty paper. "I want to write my name," she said. But the pencil kept slipping. Her letters came out wiggly and wrong. Why did the pencil slip?

Lily held the pencil in her whole fist. That was the problem! She looked at Grandma's hand. Grandma pinched the pencil with two fingers, like picking up a tiny seed. Lily tried it. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and one finger. The pencil sat snug, like a little stick resting on a branch. It did not slip at all.

Lily wrote a big L. Then i, l, and y. "Lily!" she said. "That's me!" She drew a picture of her street next to it. Grandma clapped her hands.

Henri was awake early. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shirt. He packed his toy car in his little bag. "You will find your name there," Mama said.

At school, Henri saw small doors on the wall. Each door had a name. He looked and looked. Then he saw a red triangle. His name was on the red triangle. He hung his bag under it. The toy car went in too.

A boy chased a ball near the toys. Henri chased it too. They laughed. The teacher looked at the red triangle. "Henri," she said, "your bag is safe there." Henri smiled. The door held his bag because it had his name. He waved to Mama. "My name stays here," he said.

Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find the ducks by the pond. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Josephine held Grandma's hand.

Near the pond, there was a small fire. A man was cooking on it. The fire was orange and jumpy. Was it hot or cold? Josephine wanted to poke it with a stick. She begged, "One little touch, Grandma?"

Grandma pulled her back. "No touching the fire," she said. Then she held Josephine's hand near the warm air above it. Not on it, just near it. "Ooh, warm," said Josephine. The fire made heat. Heat could hurt her skin.

A kind man by the fire gave her a warm bun instead. Josephine blew on it. She took a tiny bite. Yum.

Then she saw the ducks. She stayed close to Grandma all the way to the water. The fire is hot, she thought, so I don't touch it. The bun was warm, so she could eat it slow.

"I found the ducks, Grandma!" she said.

Elias sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse held up a small bandage. It had little bears on it.

"Will the shot hurt?" Elias asked. He looked at his dad. Dad smiled and held his hand.

"Your arm got tight," the nurse said. "Can you make it soft, like a sleepy cat?" Elias took a big breath. He let his arm go loose and soft. The nurse said, "All done!" It was over before he could count to three.

The shot was fast because his arm was soft. His tight arm made it slow. His soft arm made it quick. Elias thought about that all the way to the ice cream shop.

At the shop, Dad got him a strawberry cone. Elias sat at the small table. He wiggled his fingers and looked at his arm. There was the bear bandage.

"Why does my arm have a bandage?" Elias asked. He answered himself. "The nurse put it there. It stays because it is sticky." He tapped it. It stayed on. It stayed because it was sticky.

Dad laughed. "You are a good noticer, Elias." Elias licked his ice cream. Then he asked, "Can cats get shots too?" Dad said, "Yes, cats get shots too. Maybe they make their arms soft as well." Elias took one more big lick and smiled.

Raphael ran into Grandpa's garage. "I want to make a rocket!" he said. Grandpa smiled and got out the paper and glue.

Raphael squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out in a big puddle. It felt cold and squishy on his finger. He stuck the paper fins on the rocket. Then he picked it up to fly it. The fins slid right off! "Oh no!" said Raphael. The paper was all wet and floppy.

"The glue is still wet," said Grandpa. "Wet glue is slippery." Raphael put the rocket down on the table. He watched and waited. He wiggled his toes. He hummed a rocket song. Finally the glue felt dry and sticky. He picked up the rocket and tapped a fin. It stayed on!

"Zoom, zoom!" said Raphael. He flew the rocket all around the kitchen. "My dad will see it tomorrow!" he said. Grandpa laughed. "I think he will love it," said Grandpa. Raphael gave him a big hug. "Thank you, Grandpa," he said. Then he flew the rocket to the moon, twice.

Anthony sat in a big chair at the restaurant. A giant screen glowed on the wall. It showed a big game. Mom, Dad, and Uncle Ben were there too.

The crowd on the screen waved and jumped. Then a player kicked the ball into the net. Everyone in the restaurant jumped up. They made a big noise! Anthony covered his ears. It was very loud.

Anthony watched some more. The players ran and ran. He saw the ball go close to the net again. Uh oh. Anthony put his hands on his ears first. Then the ball went in! The noise came again, loud and happy.

"The noise comes when the ball goes in," Anthony said. "The goal makes them cheer!" Uncle Ben laughed. "You are a smart one, Anthony!" Anthony smiled and clapped. Then he sent a fry flying across the table with his spoon. Dad caught it and ate it. "Another one!" Dad said, opening his mouth.

Willow brought a big red bag to school. Inside were her show-and-tell things. But the bag fell over and everything rolled out on the rug.

"Oh no," said Willow. "My things are all mixed up."

Her teacher knelt down beside her. "Let's look together," she said.

Willow picked up a carrot, an apple, and a banana. She put them in one pile. "These are foods," she said. "We can eat them."

Then she picked up a ball, a teddy bear, and a toy truck. She put them in a second pile. "These are toys," she said. "We play with them."

A small wooden cow lay by her shoe. Willow looked at it. It went in the toys pile too, because it was a toy, not a real animal.

"You learn fast," said her teacher.

Willow smiled. The same red bag held her things again, all neat and sorted. She zipped it up.

Sofia stood on her stool in the kitchen. She wanted to make her own breakfast. "Can I do it today?" she asked. Mama smiled and put the toast on a plate. The toast was still warm. Sofia picked up the butter knife.

She tried to spread the butter. On cold bread, the butter would have torn it. But the warm toast made the butter soft. The butter went on smooth, like paint. "It glides!" said Sofia. "The warm toast makes it soft!" She looked at her bread. The butter made it shiny. It was a real breakfast, made by her.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the big cup in one hand and poured. The milk splashed out. A puddle grew on the table. "Too fast," she said. She put the cup down on the table. She stood still. She paid close attention to the milk. She poured slowly, slowly. This time not one drop spilled.

Sofia took a big bite of toast. "Mama, does the milk pay attention too?" she asked. Mama laughed. "I think it does, when you go slow." Sofia looked at the white color of the milk in her cup. She clapped her hands.

Anthony looked out the window. The sky was dark and white at the same time. Snow was falling on the grass. No school today! Anthony jumped up and down. "Snow day!" he shouted.

Mom helped him get dressed. One hat. Two mittens. Two boots. One big coat. Anthony counted them all. Then he ran outside. The snow went squeak, squeak under his boots. He made a big snowman with a carrot nose.

Anthony wanted to show Dad the snowman. So he brought a snowball inside. He set it on the table. "Look, Dad!" he said. But then they ate lunch. When Anthony came back, the snowball was gone. There was only a wet spot. "The house is warm," Anthony said. "Warm makes snow melt." He said it again, slowly. "Warm makes snow melt!"

Just then the sun came out. It shined through the window. It hit a piece of ice on the porch. A little rainbow danced on the wall. Anthony pointed at it. "One snowball melted," he said. "One rainbow stayed!"

Myles went to Dad's office after school. He wanted to draw a cat for Mom. Dad gave him a tablet.

Myles tapped the small button. The screen stayed dark. He tapped it again. Still dark. Then Dad held Myles' finger on the button. They counted together, "One, two, three." The screen lit up! "You have to hold it," Myles said. He found the drawing app and drew a fat orange cat.

Later Myles got tired. His eyes felt sleepy. He looked out at the busy street below. "Time to put it away," said Dad. Myles pressed the button until the screen went dark. Then he helped Dad fold the soft blanket. "I did it all by myself," Myles said. Dad smiled and gave him a big hug.

Liam was three today. His party was at the big park. There was cake and balloons. There was even a little farm near the pond.

"Look, ducks!" said Liam. He got some bread. He helped feed the ducks. The ducks came close. They ate the bread fast.

Then Mom called, "Cake time!" Everyone sat on the grass. The cake had three candles. The candles were lit. The little flames wiggled.

"Make a wish," said Dad. Liam squeezed his eyes shut. He wished for a red bike. Then he took a big breath. He blew and blew. The candles went out. All three!

"Is my wish true now?" Liam asked.

"Blowing out the candles is the trick," said his big sister, Maya. "You did it all by yourself!"

Maya tried to blow her party horn. It made a silly sound. She laughed and fell over in the grass.

"Happy birthday, Liam!" said Maya, still laughing.

Ayla got a drum from the shop. It had a case with a zipper. She pulled the zipper down. Out came two drum sticks.

In the band room, Ayla held the sticks. She tapped the drum. The sound was tiny. "Why is it so small?" she asked. Her teacher said, "Try again. Take your time."

Ayla tapped once more. Still tiny. She looked at her sticks. They were all crooked. She made them straight. She tapped again. Boom! A big sound came out.

"Ooh," said Ayla. "My sticks were crooked. Now they are straight. The sound is big!" She tapped slowly. Boom. Boom. Boom.

"Can I do it again?" she asked. "Yes," said her teacher. Ayla sat tall and tapped. Boom. Boom. The drum sang.

Daniel sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "Where is the sun?" he asked. It was dark now. Mom said, "The sun went to sleep. It will come back tomorrow." Yesterday the sun was up. Today the sun went down. Tomorrow the sun would come back again. One day, then one day, then one day. Daniel counted on his fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. Three fingers!

Daniel pulled his doll close. "Dolly, the sun is lost," he said. Mom smiled. "No, it is not lost. It is sleeping. Later the sky will be light." Daniel watched the dark road. The car lights made big circles. Then the moon came up. Big and white. "Look!" said Daniel. "The moon is awake now!"

Daniel rubbed his eyes. "Why is the moon out?" he asked. He thought and thought. "The moon is out because the sun went down," he said. Mom said, "Yes, that is right!" The car went bump, bump, bump. Daniel held his doll. Soon he would be home. Then he would sleep. Later it would be morning. And tomorrow, the sun would come back. Daniel waved at the moon. "Bye bye, moon. See you tomorrow!"

Felix wanted a cheese sandwich. Mom put it on the plate. "First, wash your hands," said Mom. Felix looked at his hands. They looked clean. But he had played on the floor. He had petted the dog.

"I wonder if my hands are stinky," said Felix. He sniffed them. "Yes! Stinky dog hands." He ran to the sink. Mom gave him soap. He rubbed the soap all over. Bubbles grew on his fingers.

"Now we wait," said Mom. "We sing the hand song. It is twenty seconds long." They sang together. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Felix kept rubbing while he sang. The bubbles popped one by one.

"Why do we sing?" Felix asked. "The song is twenty seconds," said Mom. "The soap needs time. Twenty seconds makes the germs go away." The song ended. Felix rinsed his hands. The water carried the bubbles down the drain. His hands smelled like apples now. He held them up to Mom's nose.

"Smell!"

"Not stinky anymore," said Mom. Felix sat down and took a big bite of his sandwich.

Chloe wanted to go outside. It was cold. She put her arms in her coat. Then she pulled the zipper. The zipper did not move. Chloe looked down. The zipper ends were apart.

She tried again, slow this time. She put the two ends together. Click. They stuck. She held the bottom with one hand. With her other hand, she pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up to her chin.

"Look, Mommy! I did it!" said Chloe.

Mommy smiled. "Your coat is on. Your zipper is up. Now we can go."

Chloe ran to the door. Outside, the wind was wild. It blew the leaves across the wood pile. Chloe held her coat tight. "My zipper keeps me warm," she said. Then she jumped in a leaf.

Ellie went to the pet store with Dad. She saw a small brown hamster. "I want that one," she said. "Can I hold him now?"

Dad shook his head. "New hamsters need to go home first," he said. "Then we wait."

Ellie took the hamster home in a little box. She put him in his cage. She wanted to play. She put her hand in. The hamster ran into his little house and hid.

"Did I do something bad?" Ellie asked.

"You were too fast," said Dad. "He hides because everything is new."

Ellie felt sorry. She sat down on the floor. She did not move. She waited and waited.

The hamster peeked out. He turned his tiny head. He sniffed the air. Then he walked to his food bowl and ate a seed.

Ellie watched him, very still. "I will wait every day," she said. "Then you will like your new playground."

The hamster stuffed one more seed in his cheeks.

Leon had three little paint pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. The blue pot had a picture of waves. Mom said, "This blue is called ocean blue." Leon liked the ocean blue best.

Leon wanted to paint a green frog. But he had no green paint. He looked in his pots. Red, yellow, ocean blue. No green. Leon felt sorry for the frog with no paint. Then Leon had an idea.

He dripped ocean blue into a cup. He dripped yellow in too. He mixed it with his brush. Round and round. The paint turned green! Leon said, "Blue and yellow make green." He said it again. "Blue and yellow make green!"

Leon painted the frog green. Then he washed his brush in the water tub. The brush was heavy with paint. It sank down, down to the bottom. Leon pulled it up and laughed. He held it up to the sun. "My green frog," said Leon. "One, two, green."

It was Ellie's birthday. A big paper sign would hang on the wall. Papa held it up high. "I can't reach," said Papa. Ellie got the little chair. Now the sign could hang just right.

The friends came in. Mama put down cupcakes. But one candle was lost! Ellie looked under the table. She found it by the owl toy. The owl was sitting on the candle. "Silly owl," said Ellie. The owl seemed to wink.

Mama said, "How many candles now?" Ellie counted. "One, two, three!" Three candles, because she was three years old. Grandpa blew one out. "Hey!" said Ellie. He laughed. She blew out two. Papa clapped and clapped. Ellie took a big bite of cupcake. Frosting was all over her nose. "One, two, three kisses," said Mama. She counted them out loud.

Lucy went to the park with her red balloon. A little boy sat near the sandbox. His ice cream had fallen in the sand. His eyes were wet. His mouth turned down. He looked sad.

Lucy wanted to help. She held out her balloon. "Do you want to hold it?" she asked. The boy shook his head. He was still sad. Lucy waited. She sat down near him. She waited some more.

Then a big dog ran by, barking loud. The boy grabbed Lucy's hand. His eyes got wide. He was scared. Lucy was scared too. She squeezed his hand softly. They sat very still. The dog ran past. It did not stop. The boy looked at Lucy. "The dog is gone," he said. His mouth turned up a little.

Lucy had an idea. She gave the boy a big hug. She held on and counted, one, two, three. When she let go, the boy was smiling. "Hugs make sad go small," said Lucy. Then the sky changed color. Pink and orange clouds! Both kids pointed up. "Wow!" they said at the very same time.

The boy's mom came back with a new ice cream. He took a bite and laughed. Lucy waved her balloon high. "Best park day," she said.

Everly sat in the big red seat. Grandma had brought her to the concert hall. On the stage, a lady began to play a song. It was "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Everly loved that song.

Everly wanted to clap along. She clapped very fast, clap clap clap clap. But her hands did not match the song. The song went slow, like a walk. Her claps went fast, like a run. "Hmm," said Everly. She put her hands in her lap and listened.

Then she tried a new game. She waited for the big notes. Boom, boom, boom. Each big note got one clap. Clap. Clap. Clap. Now her hands fit the song. "The claps go slow because the song goes slow," Everly said. Grandma smiled and clapped too.

Then Everly took a breath. She wanted to sing the words all by herself. She closed her eyes and thought hard. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The words came out. "How I wonder what you are." She did not stop. She keep singing, word after word, all the way to the end. "Up above the world so high." The last line came out big and clear.

After the song, Grandma gave her a pretzel. Everly bit it. It was salty and warm. The lady on stage bowed, and Everly clapped slow and steady, one clap for each big note, all the way to the end.

Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He wanted to write his name all by himself. He held the pencil in his whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. The N looked like a wide squiggle. His friend Sam had a small hat on his head to look like a writer. Nathan looked at Miss Jo's hand. She held her pencil with two fingers, like a little bird beak. Nathan tried it. He picked up his pencil the same way. Now his hand could move! He drew a straight line down. Then another line. The letter N looked like a real N. "Why is it easy now?" Nathan asked. "Because my fingers can hold it like a bird beak," he said. Miss Jo smiled wide. His pencil did not sink in his grip. Nathan wrote N, A, T, H, A, N. Sam clapped for him.

Margot sat on the floor. The big game was on TV. Grandma sat in the big chair. Uncle Sam sat on the couch. The cat sat on the rug. The cat was too lazy to move.

The team ran fast. Everyone jumped up. "Hooray!" they shouted. Margot could not see the TV. Grandma's legs were in the way. Margot asked, "Why can't I see?" She answered herself. "Everyone is standing up!"

So Margot hurried to get her little chair. She climbed up on it. Now she was tall too. Now she could see the TV just fine.

The team scored again. Everyone jumped up again. Margot stood on her chair too. She could still see! "I can see, I can see!" she said.

Grandma smiled and held her hand. The cat went back to sleep.

Jordan planted a tiny seed in the school garden. He made a deep hole with his finger. He dropped the seed in and patted the soil. Every day he ran to the garden to look. Nothing came up. His friend Mia had little green leaves already.

Teacher Kim sat with the children in a circle. "Let us share our garden news," she said kindly. Jordan said, "My seed is asleep." Then he watched Mia water her pot. She gave it water every day. Jordan had not given his seed any water at all.

So Jordan filled a small blue can. He poured the water on his dirt, slow and gentle. He did it the next day too. On the third morning, a green tip poked up. Jordan clapped his hands. "The water helped my seed wake up!" he said.

Ethan had a library book. It was about a big brown dog. The dog liked to bark at the mail truck. Ethan loved that book. He read it every night.

Tonight was bedtime. Ethan held the book tight. "I want to keep it," he said. "It is mine."

Dad shook his head. "The book has to go back," he said. "Wednesday is the day. Other kids want to read about the dog too."

Ethan turned the pages. He opened the front cover. He saw words there. "What does this say?" he asked.

Dad read the words out loud. They said who borrowed the book before. Ethan turned to the last page. He saw words there too. Words could tell him things!

At the library, Ethan gave the book to a lady. She typed on her computer. The computer made a little beep.

Then Ethan found a long, long book about trucks. "Can I take this one home?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "And when Wednesday comes, we bring it back. That is why the beep tells us the day."

Ethan held the new book. He read it front to back, just like the dog book.

"The book went back," he said, "so the beep can stop. And now I have a truck book!"

At bedtime, Ethan turned page after page. The last page had a big red truck on it. "Goodnight, truck," Ethan whispered.

Isla wants to sing the counting song at school. But she does not know all the words yet.

At circle time, Miss Rosa sings, "One, two, three." The children clap. Isla claps too. Then the song goes on. "Four, five, six." Isla hears her friend Tom sing it. She hums the tune but her mouth stays quiet. She is scared she will say the wrong words.

At play time, Isla pretends she is a farmer. She counts her toy cows. "One, two," she says. Then she stops. Tom sits next to her. He counts the rest with her. "Three, four, five." The cows are far across the rug. They walk the cows back. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten cows in the barn!

The next day, Miss Rosa starts the song. Isla takes a big breath. She sings, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the words come out in the right order. The singing helped her remember.

Miss Rosa smiles. "Sing it again," she says. Isla sings, and Tom sings too.

Levi loved the dress-up corner at school. Today he wanted to be a chef. He put on the big white hat and the red apron. "I will cook soup!" he said.

But first he had to find his shoes. The class was going outside. Levi looked under the table. He found one shoe. He found one sock. Where was the other sock? The sock was wet! It had fallen in the water table. Levi laughed. "My sock went swimming!" he said.

Miss Kim was gentle with the wet sock. She helped him lift it out of the water. She gave him a dry sock from his bag. Levi pulled it on. It felt warm and soft on his toes. Then his shoes went on fast. He gave Miss Kim a big hug. "Dry socks make shoes happy," Levi said. Then he ran outside to play.

Jack ran to the red slide at the park. A girl was already at the ladder. Her name was Mia. Jack stopped and waited.

"Can I go too?" he asked. Mia nodded. "You go first. Then me," she said. So Mia went down the slide. Then Jack had his turn. It was fast and fun. Then Mia had another turn. Then Jack did too. They took turns, one by one.

Then Jack saw a round ball under the bench. He picked it up. A small boy ran over. He looked sad. "That is my ball," the boy said. Jack gave it back. "You can play too," said the boy. So all three played catch in the soft green grass. Jack had a bite of his apple. He opened his mouth for one big bite. Then he chose to share his apple too. He cut it with his fingers into little pieces.

"Next time, you go first," Jack told the boy. The boy smiled big.

Beau sat on the big stage. His teacher gave him a drum. He wanted to play the loud part in the song. He hit the drum very hard. The sound was too big and mixed up, like a puzzle with lost pieces.

The teacher put a card on the floor. "Can you read this card?" she asked. It said, "Tap soft." Beau tapped soft. The drum made a small, round sound. It fit the song just right.

"That is true," Beau said. "I tap soft, and the sound is soft." He tapped soft all the way to the end. The other kids clapped. Beau looked down at his drumstick. He gave it a tiny kiss, like a goodnight. "Good drum," he whispered.

Declan sat in his car seat. The sun shone on his knee through the window. The knee got hot. Declan pulled his knee away. It felt better in the shade.

"Hot," said Declan. "The sun made it hot."

Mom smiled from the front seat. "Good thinking," she said. Declan tried again. He put his hand in the sun. It was hot too. He moved his hand into the shade. Now it was cool.

They stopped at the gas station. Declan wanted to look around. He held Mom's hand tight. His shoe did not slip on the wet floor. Near the pump there was a big sign with a flame on it. Declan pointed. "Hot," he said. "Do not touch."

"You are right," said Mom. They walked back to the car. The fresh air felt cool on Declan's face. He climbed into his seat all by himself.

"Big boy," said Mom. She buckled him in. Declan waved at the sun through the window. "You are hot," he said. "I sit in the shade." The car drove home. Declan smiled at his cool, shady knee.

Arlo put on his red shirt. Today was a big game in the backyard. His team was the Red Robots.

Arlo ran to kick the ball. The sun was in his eyes. He could not see the ball. He kicked and missed. "Why can't I see?" he asked. "The sun is too bright."

Dad blew the whistle. It was time for half. That means the teams switch sides. The Red Robots ran to the other end.

Arlo looked up. No sun in his eyes now! "Where did the sun go?" he asked. "It is still there. We just face the other way." Arlo kicked the ball. He saw it go in the goal. Hooray!

At snack time, Arlo got orange slices. He began to eat one. It was sweet and juicy. "We switched sides and the sun went away," said Arlo. "Switch sides, sun goes away. Switch sides, sun goes away."

He kicked the ball again. Goal!

Levi's bear was cold. His bear had no blanket at all.

"I will play house," said Levi. He got a small towel. He wrapped the towel around bear. Bear was warm now. But bear was still hungry. Levi made a pretend cake from a block. He put the block on a little plate. "Here is cake, bear," he said. Bear could not eat. Bears are toys. They do not open their mouths. Levi thought hard.

"What if I eat for bear?" he asked. "Yes! I can pretend for him." So Levi made a pretend bite. "Crunchy," he said, laughing. Bear was fed. Then Levi remembered one more thing. Babies need songs at night. He sang a soft song to bear. He rocked him in his arms. Mom came in to watch.

"You take good care of bear," she said. "He is my baby," said Levi. He laid bear down. "Night night, baby bear."

Jack ran up the steps with a big smile. He held a small cage. Inside was a white bird. "My first pet!" Jack said. Mom put the cage on the table. "Let's give her a name," she said. Jack clapped his hands. "Snow!" he said.

Jack wanted Snow to play right away. He banged on the cage. "Come out, Snow!" he said. Snow jumped to the back of the cage. She hid in the corner. She did not eat her seeds. Jack asked, "Why won't she play?" Mom said, "Watch her."

Jack sat very still. He made his voice small and soft. Snow peeked out. She hopped down. She pecked at her seeds. One white feather fell to the cage floor. Jack picked it up. "Snow is not scared now," he said.

The next morning, Snow chirped loud at Jack. She begged for more seeds with her beak open. Jack laughed and filled her cup. Then he held the feather up to the window. "Look, Snow," he said. "You can see the whole sky!"

Milan loved the play kitchen at school. Yesterday he cooked a red soup with a wooden carrot. He wanted to cook again today. But when he got to the kitchen, Sam was there. Sam was cooking a big pot now.

"Can I cook too?" asked Milan.

"Not now," said Miss Ada. "You can cook later, after Sam."

Milan waited. He watched Sam stir. The sun made a bright spot on the floor. Milan put his coin in the waiting jar. Each waiting child put one coin in. Sam put in three coins yesterday. Three coins meant a long turn.

Milan put in one coin. One coin meant a short wait. He sat down and watched the bright sun spot. He counted to ten. Then Sam was done.

"Now?" asked Milan.

"Now," said Miss Ada.

Milan cooked his soup. He stirred and stirred. "Today I waited," he said. "Tomorrow I will bring more coins. More coins, more cooking."

Jaxson woke up in his warm bed. The sun was on his wall. He wanted his blue socks. He looked under the bed. One sock was there. One sock was not.

Jaxson looked in his toy box. No sock. He looked in the closet. No sock. Then he saw mud on the floor. Little muddy footprints. One, two, three steps. They went to the door.

Jaxson followed the prints. The girl next door was outside. Her name was Mia. She had his sock on her hand, like a puppet. "It fell out the window," she said. Jaxson laughed. The sock was dirty.

Mama put the sock in the wash. It spun around and around. Then it hung on the line. The wind made it dance. Jaxson counted his socks on the line. One, two. Now he had two clean socks again.

At bath time, Jaxson washed his feet well. He did not want dirty feet again. He put on his pajamas. They were soft and warm. He left one sock out for Mia. "For your puppet hand," he said.

Zoe and her family drove to a big park. Their car had four wheels. The wheels went round and round. Zoe held her juice box.

The car turned. The juice tipped. "It fell because the car turned," said Zoe. Daddy laughed. "That's right," he said. "I will go slow now."

Then Zoe looked in her lap. Her teddy was not there. She looked on the floor. No teddy. Her eyes got big. "I want teddy," she said.

Mommy reached back. She opened the big bag. She opened the little bag too. Then she held up teddy. "Teddy was packed away," said Mommy. "We brought him from home."

Zoe hugged teddy tight. She gave him a sip spot on her lap. An ugly bug walked by the window. Zoe did not mind it now.

The car stopped. Daddy opened the door. Trees and birds were everywhere. Zoe held Mommy's hand and stepped out.

"Home is far, but teddy is here," said Zoe.

Charlie went to the basketball court with her dad. She had a red beanbag and one big blue ball. "I want to get the beanbag in the hoop," she said. She threw it up. The beanbag hit the hoop and fell down.

Charlie tried again. She threw it far, far up. It went over the hoop. Then she threw it soft and low. It went under. She sat down on the long bench. "I will try one more time," she said. She looked at the hoop. She held the beanbag tight and threw it just over the front of the hoop. The beanbag went in! "One in the hoop," said Charlie. "One happy girl!"

Then Dad rolled the big blue ball to her. Charlie held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. "Ow," she said softly. Dad rolled it again. This time Charlie put out both hands. She pulled them in close to her chest. The ball stuck to her like a magnet! "I caught it!" she said. "Two hands catch the big ball. Two hands!"

Dad clapped. Charlie patted the ball like a good friend. "One beanbag, one ball, one hoop," she said. "Now I know just what to do."

Lincoln ran to the school garden. He had three little seeds in his hand. "Today we plant carrots!" he said.

His teacher gave him a cup of water. Lincoln poured it on the dirt. Then he pushed each seed down. He patted the soil on top. "Grow, grow, grow," he whispered.

The next day, Lincoln brought his lunch. He had salty soup in a thermos. He did not want the rest. "The plants can drink it," he said. He poured the salty soup on his dirt.

Two days later, his friend Maya yelled, "Look! My seed is up!" Lincoln looked at his dirt. Nothing was there. Tiny green leaves were not poking out. His seed was not growing. It was a puzzle. "Why is my seed not up?" he asked. He looked and looked.

Then Lincoln saw the wet spot. It smelled like soup. "Oh no. The soup was too salty," he said. "Salty water makes seeds not grow. Water is what they need." Maya nodded. "Plain water," she said.

Lincoln got the hose. He washed the salty soup away. He watered his spot with clean water. Every day he came back. On day four, he saw a fat pink worm crawl by. Then, right next to the worm, a tiny green tip pushed up out of the soil.

"My carrot is coming!" Lincoln shouted. He jumped up and down. Maya clapped. The worm wiggled back into the dirt.

Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was ready. Nora reached for a crunchy carrot.

"Stop," said Grandma. "First we wash hands. Soap takes twenty seconds."

Nora made a face. "That is too long!" Twenty seconds felt big to her.

"We can sing while we wash," said Grandma. "The happy song, all the way through."

Grandma turned on the water. She made soap bubbles on Nora's hands. They sang together. Nora rubbed and rubbed. The song ended. The water turned gray. The bubbles slid down the drain.

Nora looked at the water. "The dirt went away," she said. "The soap pushed it off!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "That is the answer."

Nora marched to the table with clean hands. She took a big bite of the carrot. It went crunch.

After lunch, Nora used the toilet. Then she ran to Grandma. "Soap time!" she said. "Twenty seconds, all by myself."

Grandma smiled and helped her reach the soap.

Emmett woke up from his nap. He smelled something sweet. "Cookies!" he said. But where were they?

He used his eyes to look. He saw a big bowl on the table. He saw flour on the floor. Mom came in with a broom. She began to sweep the flour away. "You have a cookie nose," Mom laughed. "It sniffed them out!"

Emmett heard a click. His ears heard it! The click came from the oven. "Is that the oven, Mom?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "The oven is hot. Hot ovens make cookies bake."

One, two, three, four, five, Emmett counted. He counted his eyes. He counted his ears. He counted his nose. "That is three helpers," he said. "My nose helped most today. My nose found the cookies!" Mom laughed so hard her hair went wild.

Then the timer rang. Ding! Emmett touched the cookie with one little finger. It was warm. He took a bite. Yum! Sweet and gooey. "My tongue likes cookies best," he said. "My tongue wins!"

Mom handed him milk. Emmett held up his cookie and said, "Best nose day ever." Then he took another big bite.

Riley was at Grandma's house. She wanted a snack. "Count ten crackers," said Grandma. "Then you can eat them." Riley began to count. "One, two, three." Then she stopped. What came next? She could not remember.

Grandma hummed a counting song while she folded a blanket. "One, two, three, four, five," sang Grandma. The kitchen was quiet, so Riley heard every word. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Grandma. Riley clapped. The song had shown her the next words!

Riley counted again, like a song. "One, two, three, four, five. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten crackers sat on the plate. But the tenth cracker looked funny. It had little ears! "Grandma, a cracker has ears!" Grandma laughed. It was a dry piece of bread shaped like a bunny. Riley took a big bite of the bunny cracker anyway. "Ten tastes better," she said.

Leah was at the beach with her mom. There was a little pool next to the sand. Leah wanted to swim in it. She held the wall and kicked her legs. But when she let go, she sank down fast.

Then Leah watched a big girl in the pool. The girl put her face in the water. She blew little bubbles out of her mouth. Leah tried it too. She put her face in and blew bubbles. Her body popped up like a ball! "Why do I float now?" Leah asked. Mom smiled. "Because you let your air out slow," she said. Leah blew more bubbles and floated all the way to the steps.

After the pool, they went to bathe in the warm sea. Leah washed off the sand. Then they sat on a towel and ate a big piece of cake. Some sand got on it. "It's crunchy," Leah said with a giggle. Mom laughed and gave her a new piece. Leah ate it all up and looked at the pool. "Bubbles tomorrow," she said.

Hazel stood in the backyard with her dragon. The dragon was green and small. He was a toy, not an animal. But Hazel pretended he was real.

"Dragon, you must be hungry," she said. She ran inside and got a cracker. Crackers are food. Real things eat food. She held the cracker up to the dragon's mouth. The cracker just sat there. It did not get smaller. The dragon did not eat.

Then she heard a sound behind her. It was a small bark. Her dog Biscuit ran up on four straight legs. He sniffed the cracker. He ate it in one bite. Biscuit was an animal, and animals eat food.

"So that is why," said Hazel. "Biscuit is real. Dragons are pretend." She patted Biscutt on his head. Then she held her dragon up high and whispered, "You can eat pretend crackers." She picked up a little stone and set it near the dragon's mouth. "There," she said. "All gone, little dragon."

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood still in the kitchen. "Why is it dark?" he asked. "The power went out," said Mama. "No power means no lights."

Mama found the flashlight. She clicked it on. A big circle of light fell on the floor. Jules made his hands into a shape in the light. The shape looked like a bunny. Jules watered his little plant by the window, and the light helped him see the pot.

Jules wanted cold milk. He went to the fridge. "Can I leave the door open?" he asked. "No," said Mama. "The cold will run away." Jules closed the door fast. He waited. The fridge stayed cold inside because the door was shut.

Later, the lights came back on. The lamp glowed warm and yellow. "The power came back!" said Jules. "That is true," said Mama. She smiled. Jules looked at his bunny shape on the wall. It was gone now. But he could still see the little plant by the window. Its green leaf was standing up tall. Jules gave the leaf one soft pat. "Goodnight, plant," he said.

Jordan ran to the art table at daycare. His teacher had put out big paper and glue. "Today we make snow pictures," she said. Jordan loved winter. Snow pictures were good.

Jordan squeezed lots and lots of glue. He stuck on cotton balls. They looked like soft white snow. But the glue was wet and shiny. "Can I take it home now?" he asked. "Not yet," said his teacher. "Wet glue drips. It has to dry first."

Jordan looked at the shelf. Yesterday's pictures were stacked there in a pile. He touched one. It was dry! "Where did the wet glue go?" he wondered. The picture from yesterday was dry because it had a whole night to sit. Maybe his picture needed a night too.

Jordan put his picture on the shelf. He added it to the top of the stack. "Now I wait," he said. "Later it will be dry." After nap time, he touched it. Still a little wet. So he waited more.

The next day, Jordan ran to the shelf. He touched his picture. Dry! The cotton balls did not move at all. "It dried up overnight," he said. "Yesterday it was wet. Today it is dry!" He carried it to his cubby. "Tomorrow I take it home," he said, "when Mama comes to get me."

Oliver walked home with a small puppy. The puppy was brown and soft. Oliver held the box very carefully. "Your name is Max," he said.

At home, Oliver wanted to play. He banged his drum. Max ran under the chair. Max would not come out. Oliver stopped the drum. Then Max came out slowly. "The loud drum scared you," Oliver said. "Loud sounds made you hide." Oliver sat on the floor. He was very quiet. Max walked to him and licked his hand.

"Good boy," Oliver said softly. He gave Max a nice soft blanket. He gave Max a bone to chew. Max chewed the bone and wagged his tail. Oliver petted him gently, so he would not hurt him. "I will keep the house quiet," Oliver said. Max fell asleep on Oliver's lap.

Florence ran to the block corner at school. Today she would build a nest for the toy bird. It had to be round and safe. "Watch out," said her friend Ben. "You must pay attention to the blocks you pick."

Florence picked the circle blocks first. She stacked them high. But the top circle wobbled. Then it rolled off! It rolled right across the rug. "Oh no," said Florence. "The circle rolled because it is round."

So she tried the square blocks next. She stacked them one, two, three. The squares did not roll. They had flat sides and stayed still. Florence put two triangle blocks on top, like a little roof. She made a round circle rug inside. Then she set the toy bird down in its nest. "Your nest is safe now," she said. The bird sat still and did not roll one bit.

Charlie woke up and peeked out the window. Snow was on the street. Snow was on the cars. No school today! It was a snow day.

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his warm coat. His mama pulled his hat down over one ear, then the other. Charlie went outside. He made three snowballs. He put them in his red bucket.

Then Charlie carried the bucket inside. He set it by the door. He wanted to save the snowballs for later.

Charlie played with his trucks. He played a long time. Then he came back to peek in the bucket. The bucket was empty! There was only water inside.

"Where did my snowballs go?" said Charlie.

The house was warm. Warm makes snow melt. The snowballs melted because the house was warm.

"I know," said Charlie. "Snow stays outside."

He went back out and made three new snowballs. "You stay here," he told them. "Outside is cold. Outside is just right."

Carter sat on the soft rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Mom was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too. Everyone wore different shirts. Carter's shirt was blue. Uncle Ben's shirt was green.

The team ran with the ball. Everyone jumped up. "Go, go, go!" they shouted. Carter clapped his hands too. But the room got very loud. Carter could not hear the man on TV. He could not hear the whistle. He tugged Uncle Ben's sleeve. "Too loud," he said. Uncle Ben nodded. "Let's cheer with our hands," he said. So they all clapped softly. Then Carter could hear the whistle. "When we yell, the TV is hard to hear," Carter said. "When we clap, I can hear it."

The clock on the wall showed it was almost snack time. Mom brought apple slices. Carter held one up to Uncle Ben. "Thank you," said Uncle Ben, and he took a big bite. The team scored. Everyone clapped, soft and happy. Carter heard the whistle one more time.

Jasper wanted to play a new game with Mama. "Name your five senses," said Mama. Jasper did not know them yet. He wanted to do it well.

Mama held up a bright yellow lemon. "Tell me one sense." Jasper sniffed it. "My nose smells it!" "Yes," said Mama. "Smelling uses your nose."

Next, Mama rang a little bell. Ding, ding. Jasper pointed to his ears. "My ears hear it!" Then Mama let him taste the lemon. Jasper made a funny face. "My tongue tastes it. Sour!" Mama laughed with him.

Jasper looked at his hands. He touched the swing in the hallway. It was smooth and cold. "My hands feel it!" "Yes," said Mama. "Touching uses your hands."

"One more," said Jasper. He looked all around. "My eyes see you, Mama!" "All five," said Mama. She clapped.

Just then the swing bumped his leg by itself. Jasper blinked. "My eyes see that, and my hands feel it too!" he said. "Two senses at once, Mama!"

Ruby wants the big bear sticker. But first, the doctor has to do a checkup.

"Look here," says the doctor. He holds up a little picture. Ruby looks with her eyes. She sees a red bird! "Now be very quiet," he says. He puts a small tube near her ears. Ruby hears a tick tick tick inside. "That is your heart," says the doctor. "It goes thump!"

Then Ruby smells something sweet. It is the sticker sheet! She sniffs with her nose. "Yum, like strawberries," she says. The doctor laughs. "Stickers are not for eating. You taste with your tongue, and this is paper." Ruby sticks out her tongue to show him. "Say ahh," says the doctor. She says ahh.

Last, the doctor touches her neck with soft fingers. "Your neck holds your head up," he says. Ruby touches her neck too. Then the doctor says, "You did it! All done." Ruby picks the bear sticker. She holds it tight. "My heart went thump because I was so happy," she says.

Joseph was awake early for school. He ran to the window. It was sunny outside. "Short sleeves today," he said. But then the wind came. The tree bent over. The leaves flew up high. Joseph could not reach the big branch, but the wind could.

At school, Miss Kim said, "Time to go out." Joseph put on his sun hat. Outside, the wind pulled it off his head. It rolled far away. His friend Ana ran to get it. "Thank you, Ana," said Joseph. Then he looked around. Maya wore a hood. Ben wore a warm cap. Their hats stayed on.

Joseph had an idea. He pulled his hood up over his ears. The wind blew and blew. The hood did not move. "The wind took my hat," he said, "but it can't take my hood." At pick-up time, Joseph ran to his family. "Mom! The wind was strong today. My hood won."

Zoe sat in the waiting room. She was going to get a shot today. Her tummy felt jumpy. She skipped all around her mom's chair, then sat down again. On the table was a special book about a bunny. Zoe touched the smooth pages. It smelled like paper and soap.

The nurse came in. "Sit very still," she said kindly. Zoe held her arm out. It wiggled like jelly. "If my arm wiggles, the shot is harder," Zoe said. So she pressed her arm flat on the table. She looked at the bunny book. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Zoe felt one tiny pinch, quick as a kiss.

The nurse put a soft bandage on. It had a star on it. "Now you can go to your dance class," Mom said. Zoe held her star arm up high. "Look what I got!" she said.

Xavier wanted to draw a big sun. Miss Amy had a tablet for him. But first the screen was black. "Press the little round button," said Miss Amy. Xavier pressed it. The screen lit up! "I did it," he said.

His fingers were sticky from jam at snack time. He tapped the green dot. Nothing happened. The green dot would not move. Miss Amy helped him wash his hands. Now his fingers were clean. He tapped the green dot again. The drawing app opened! "My hands were sticky," said Xavier. "Now they are clean, so it works."

He drew a big yellow sun. He drew red rays too. Miss Amy gave him a word for it. "Sun," said Xavier, and smiled.

Then it was time for lunch. Xavier pressed the round button. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, all by himself. "Bye bye, sun," he said. He waved at the tablet on the shelf.

Arya went to the library with Grandma. She wanted a book about spring. "Where is the spring book?" she asked. Grandma said, "Let's look on the shelf."

On the floor, a baby dropped a red ball. The ball was a circle. It began to spin. Then it rolled far, far away. The baby's lip went wobbly. Arya ran to get the ball. She gave it back. The baby smiled.

At the table, there were shape blocks. Arya picked a triangle block. It had three sharp corners. She pushed it on the table. It would not roll. She picked the circle block. It spun and rolled off the table. "The circle rolls," said Arya. "The corners stop it."

Then Arya looked at the books. Every book was a rectangle, with four flat sides. Rectangles do not roll. That is why books can sit on the shelf. Arya found a green book with flowers on it. "Spring!" she said. Grandma opened it. "My favorite season," said Grandma. Arya sat close and turned the first page.

Mohamed sat in his car seat. The sun was hot on his arm. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He moved his arm into the shade. The shade felt cool. "The sun makes it hot," he said. "The shade makes it cool."

"Papa, what is that?" Mohamed asked. He pointed at the cup holder. A cup of tea sat there. Steam went up, up, up. "Is it hot like the sun?" "Yes," said Papa. "Very hot. We do not touch it." Mohamed put his hands on his lap. He kept them far away from the cup.

They stopped at a big shop. Papa got out. Mohamed wanted to follow. But he waited and held the door. "Stay close to Papa," Mama said. Mohamed took Papa's hand. The parking lot was big and empty. "Where do we walk?" he asked. "Right beside you," said Papa. They walked in together, hand in hand.

Charles wanted to make a picture. He had orange paper and yellow paper. He wanted to glue them together. "Will the glue hold it?" he wondered.

He put glue on the orange paper. He stuck the yellow paper on top. He held it up. The yellow paper fell off! Charles looked at his hands. The glue was still wet and slippery. Hmm. Wet glue does not stick.

"I will wait," said Charles. He set his picture on the table. Then he went to eat his lunch. He had a sandwich and milk.

After lunch, Charles came back. He peeked at his picture. He touched the glue with one finger. The glue was dry now! He picked up the paper and shook it. The yellow paper stayed on. It did not fall.

"Dry glue sticks," said Charles. "Wet glue does not." He hung his picture on the wall.

Elias sat in a big chair at the mall. It was his first haircut. He put his toy car in his pocket. The hair lady put a soft cape on him.

Snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape, not on Elias. "The hair falls on the cape," said Elias. "The cape catches it." He watched the bits pile up. Then the hair lady brushed them all off. "All done," she said, smiling.

Elias got down and looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I like it," he said. Then they walked past the pretzel shop. "They cook the pretzels here," said Mom. "Can I smell them?" asked Elias. He sniffed the warm, sweet air. Mom bought him a pretzel and a juicy red apple. Elias held his toy car in one hand. He took a big bite of the pretzel. "Yum," he said.

Mohamed wanted to play house with his bear. But the bear had a small wet spot on its tummy. "Why are you wet, bear?" he asked. Then he saw the answer. His water cup was tipped over. "You are wet because the cup spilled," he said.

Mohamed put the bear in the sun by the window. "The sun is hot," he said. "It will make you dry." The shadow of the curtain moved off the bear. Now the sun could touch it. Mohamed waited. He patted the bear. "Almost dry, almost dry," he said.

Soon the bear was warm and dry. Mohamed hugged it tight. "Now we can play house," he said. He gave the bear a pretend meal of blocks. "Eat your rice, baby," he said. The bear sat in the little chair, warm in the sun.

Arnaud loves the class robot. Yesterday the robot was loud. It rolled on the floor and sang songs. But today the robot is quiet. It sits still in the corner. Arnaud taps its head. Nothing happens.

"Why is it so quiet?" he asks his friend Maya. Maya looks at the robot. She opens a little door on its back. "Look," she says. "The battery is empty."

Arnaud wants to fill it up now. He takes the little plug. He pushes it into the wall. A small light turns red. "Now we wait," says Maya. "The battery fills slowly."

They eat snack. They play outside. Later they come back. The light is green now. Arnaud presses the button. The robot rolls out and sings its loud song again.

"It works now because the battery is full," Arnaud says. He claps his hands. "Tomorrow we will let it sing all day!"

Isaiah stood in the school library. He wanted a book about a ball. But he did not know where to look. The shelves had so many books. He felt like crying a little.

Ms. Rosa knelt down beside him. "What do you want, Isaiah?" she asked.

"I want a ball book," he said. "I can't find one."

"Listen to the first sound in ball," said Ms. Rosa. "Buh, buh, ball."

Isaiah said it too. "Buh, buh, ball." Then he looked at the letters. He saw a big black B. "B!" he said. "B says buh!"

He ran to the B shelf. He pulled out a book with a ball on the cover. "This one starts with B," he said. "It says buh, like ball!"

Ms. Rosa smiled. "You found it all by yourself."

Isaiah sat on the soft rug. He hugged his book tight.

"Read it to me," he said.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. Mom was there too. She had a big soft bag. In the bag was a small bundle. The bundle was Bennett's new baby sister. Her name was Ruth.

"Can we play ball?" Bennett asked. "Shh," said Mom. "Ruth is asleep." Bennett felt sad. He wanted to play with her now.

He waited. Ruth slept. He waited some more. Ruth slept some more. Grandma said, "Tiny babies sleep almost all day. They grow while they sleep." Bennett watched Ruth's little belly go up and down. Up and down, slow and slow.

So Bennett made a card. He used a pencil to draw Ruth. He drew one baby, two small hands, three little toes. Then he helped Grandma cut out a red paper heart. Snip, snip, snip. He waited some more.

At last Ruth woke up. She made a small sound. Mom put her on the blanket. Bennett held out his finger, very slow, very soft. Ruth's tiny hand grabbed it. She held on tight. "She likes me," said Bennett. "She held my finger because I waited."

Emmett sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself. "One, two, three, six," he said. That did not sound right. Daddy smiled and began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Emmett listened. The words always came in the same order. He tapped each pea and tried again. "One, two, three, four, five." So far, so good.

Mommy made a rainbow of fruit on his plate. Strawberries came first, then oranges, then bananas. "Can I teach the rainbow to count too?" Emmett asked. He pointed at each color. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All ten! He jumped in his chair. Then Daddy put one more pea on the plate. Emmett pointed at it. He knew no word for it. He got mad and stamped his foot. "There is no more counting!"

Daddy laughed softly. "After ten comes eleven," he said. Emmett tapped the new pea. "Eleven!" He said it two more times. Then he ate the rainbow, strawberry by strawberry.

James sat in the playroom. He had a big pile of blocks. He wanted a tall, tall tower. First he made the bottom row. Then he stacked the blocks up, up, up. The tower got tall. Then it fell over with a crash.

James wanted to know how many blocks he had. He pointed at them. "One, two, five, nine," he said. That did not sound right. His big sister Mia came in. She patted his head. "Want to try a puzzle too?" she asked. She showed him a number puzzle with ten pieces.

Mia sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." James listened. The words came in the same order every time. That was the trick! He tapped each block as he sang. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten blocks!" said James. "The words go in a row, like the puzzle pieces." Mia smiled. He stacked the tower again, quick and careful. It stood tall. "One, two, three," he sang all the way to the top.

Aurora stood by the school gate. She held Grandma's hand tight. "I see Mommy soon," she said. Then a big bus went by. It ran through a puddle. Splat! Water hit Aurora's shoes. Her socks got wet. They felt cold and squishy.

"Oh no," said Aurora. "My socks are all wet." Grandma knelt down. "We can fix that," she said. She took Aurora to her cubby inside. There was a small bag inside. It had clean dry socks. Grandma helped Aurora pull off the wet socks. She hung them on her arm. "See," said Grandma. "Wet socks stay wet on your feet. Off your feet, they can dry."

Aurora put on the dry socks. They were soft and warm. Then Mommy came through the door. "My Aurora!" said Mommy. She gave her a big hug. Mommy touched the wet socks on Grandma's arm. "These need a bath and the sun," said Mommy. "Then they will be thick and fluffy again."

At home, Mommy dropped the socks into the tub. Aurora watched them swim like two little fish. "The water made them wet," said Aurora. "Now the sun will make them dry." Mommy smiled and kissed her head. "That's right," said Mommy. "Snack time now." They went to the kitchen together, hand in hand.

Carter went to the store with his mom. He wanted to pick apples for lunch. "Stay close to me," said Mom. Carter skipped beside the cart.

Then Carter saw a squishy orange. He reached for it. It sat on a high shelf with a big red sign. A man in a tall hat said, "Careful. That shelf keeps food hot. Touching hot food can hurt." Carter pulled his hand back fast. He looked at the steam rising up.

Carter saw the cold case next. His apple waited there, shiny and cool. He picked one up with two hands. "This one is cold," said Carter. "Hot things steam. Cold things feel like my fridge at home." Mom smiled. "Good thinking, Carter." They skipped to the checkout with one red apple.

Josephine sat at the little red table. She wanted to paint a frog. But there was no green paint.

She looked in the cup. She had yellow paint. Ben next to her had blue paint. "Can you share?" she asked. Ben poured some blue into her cup. It dripped, plop, plop.

Josephine stirred with her brush. Round and round she went. The yellow and blue mixed together. Now the paint was green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said.

She painted a big green frog. It had bumpy feet and a wide mouth. Ben clapped his hands. "Nice frog!"

Then Ben spilled his water. His paper got all wet. Josephine did not want to be mean. She gave him some of her paper. She gave him a hug too.

"Paint with me," she said. And they both painted green frogs.

Nova held a paper lantern. It was red with a gold fish on it. The morning had been long, and now it was dark. Papa lit the little candle inside. The lantern glowed warm and soft.

A big wind came. The candle went out. Nova felt sad, but she held still. Papa lit it again. The wind came back. The candle went out again.

Nova thought and thought. She put her hands around the candle. The wind could not get in. The flame grew small, then tall. It stayed lit!

"My hands stopped the wind," Nova said. "The wind made it go out. My hands made it stay."

Papa smiled and held his hands around his flame too.

They waited with all the other families. One by one, the lanterns rose up into the sky. Nova let go of hers. It floated high, a little star going up and up.

"Look, Papa! It flies because the fire makes warm air. Warm air goes up!"

The lantern grew smaller and smaller. Somewhere far above, it blinked once, like a wink.

Nova went to the big hall with Grandma. There was a long wooden table. Many people sat down to eat. Nova saw a box on the table. It was a present for Mr. Bean, because it was his birthday.

Before eating, everyone held hands. Grandma held Nova's hand. "We say thank you first," said Grandma. Nova did not know the words. She looked down and waited.

Grandma began. "Thank you for this food." Nova listened to each word. Then she said the next words in a small voice. "Thank you for our friends." Everyone smiled. Nova squeezed Grandma's hand. Grandma squeezed back.

The food was warm and good. Mr. Bean opened his present. It was a wooden spoon. Nova held hands again at the end. "Thank you for this day," she said, all by herself.

Everett was four years old today. Grandma's house was full of balloons. Everyone came in cars. They did not drive home yet. They stayed for the party.

The cake came out. Everett looked at it. "Where are my candles?" he asked. "I need four candles. I am four today." Grandma handed him the box. He took out one candle. He put it in the cake. Then he counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." There were four candles now.

Everett took a big breath. He blew. The flames did not go out. He was not mad. He waited a moment. Then he took a bigger breath. He blew again. All four candles went dark at once. Everyone clapped. "The candles went out because I blew hard," Everett said. Grandma cut the cake.

Elijah stood by the blocks at school. He wanted to line up first for snack time. But he did not know if he was first.

Miss Ada began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Elijah clapped along. He loved this song. He sang it in the car. He sang it in the bath. The words always came in the same order. After five came six, then seven, then eight, then nine, then ten.

Miss Ada pointed to the children at the door. "One," she said to Mia. "Two," she said to Sam. Elijah froze, very still, and waited. "Three," she said, and her finger touched Elijah. "Three! That is me!" he said. He bounced on his toes.

After snack, Elijah found a tiny horse on the rug. He held it up. "One horse," he said. Then he found a cow. "One horse, two cow," he sang. Sam laughed. "Cow comes after horse now," Sam said. Elijah giggled and hugged the tiny horse. "Ten more friends," he said, and pointed at the toy basket.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. It was pancake morning. Grandma said, "You can be the cook today." Bennett stood on his little stool. He was a big kid now.

First he cracked two eggs. A tiny piece of shell fell in. He fished it out with his finger. Then Grandma helped him measure the flour, the milk, and the sugar. Bennett stirred and stirred. He turned around fast to get the spoon. Now he felt dizzy. He held the counter and stood still. The room stopped spinning.

Then Grandma handed him a small spoon of baking powder. "Watch this," she said. She dropped a bit into a cup of warm water. It fizzed and bubbled up. Bennett's eyes went wide. "It woke up!" he said.

They mixed it into the batter. Grandma poured circles into the hot pan. Little holes popped up all over the pancakes. "The bubbles did that," Bennett said. "The bubbles come because of the baking powder." Grandma smiled and flipped one high.

The family ate the pancakes together. They were tall and soft and fluffy. Papa put honey on his. Bennett bit into his warm pancake. It smelled like sweet mornings. He licked syrup off his thumb and said, "I want to cook tomorrow too."

Audrey ran into the pharmacy with Mama. Today was shot day! She loved the little bandages they gave after.

"Your turn," said the nurse. Audrey climbed up on the chair. She squeezed her arm into a tight ball. "Ow!" said Audrey. The shot hurt a lot on a tight arm.

"Try making your arm soft," said the nurse. "Like cooked noodles." Audrey let her arm go loose. It hung down like a wet noodle. The nurse poured a drop of medicine into the tiny needle. "Ready?"

"Ready!" said Audrey. She took a deep breath. Poke! It was done. "That one was small!" said Audrey. "My arm was soft, so it did not hurt much."

"You got it," said the nurse. She put on a bandage with a cat on it. Audrey held it up high. "Look, Mama! Noodle arms win!" Mama laughed and picked her up. On the way out, Audrey waved her cat bandage at the whole store.

Peylon sat at the big table. Grandma put out paper and glue. Peyton wanted to make a sun. She squeezed the glue bottle hard. Glue came out in a big puddle. She stuck on a yellow circle. Grandma went to the next room to find scissors. Peyton waited.

The paper felt wet. The sun slid to the edge. Then it fell off onto the floor. Peyton picked it up. She looked at the glue puddle. "Too much glue," she said. "It made the paper all wet."

Grandma came back. She fished a small cotton ball out of the craft box. "Try this," she said. Peyton dipped it in the glue. She made one little dot. She stuck the sun back on. This time it stayed. Grandma gave her a fresh sheet of paper too. Peyton made one dot, then another. "Little dots work," she said. Grandma smiled and put her hand on Peyton's head.

Jaxson sat at the dinner table. His doll sat in the chair next to him. Papa put a big bowl of soup on the table. Steam went up, up, up.

"Hot!" said Papa. "Wait a bit."

But Jaxson was excited. He grabbed the spoon fast. He sipped the soup. "Ow! Hot!" Jaxson made a grumpy face. His eyes got wet and sad. He put the spoon down. Why did the hot soup hurt him? Then he saw the steam dance over the bowl. Where the steam danced, the soup was still hot. He blew on the spoon. He blew and blew. The steam went away. He sipped again. Warm, not hot. Yum!

"Jaxson blew, so the soup got cool," he said.

Papa smiled. "Yes! Good blowing."

Jaxson fed a tiny sip to his doll. "Warm soup, doll."

He took another big sip and smiled.

Rowan went to the cultural center with Mama and Dadu. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights. Long tables held many little clay lamps called diyas.

Rowan got to light one. Dadu held his hand steady. The little flame grew tall. Rowan smiled and smiled. Then the flame got small. Then it went out. "Oh no," said Rowan. "My lamp is broken."

Dadu shook his head. "Look inside," she said. Rowan peeked at his diya. The oil was all gone. The wick had nothing to drink. Dadu took a small bottle of oil. She poured some in. The wack soaked it up like a sponge. Rowan touched the stick again with the match. This time the flame stayed.

"The lamp went out because the oil ran out," said Rowan. Dadu laughed and hugged him. Then something surprising happened. All around the room, the big lights turned off. Hundreds of little flames filled the dark. Rowan's lamp was one of them. Mama lifted him up so he could see. "So many lights," said Rowan. "And mine is right there."

Connor ran to the playground. He wanted the red swing. But a girl was on it already. She swung up high.

Connor stopped and watched. He did not push. He did not yell. He waited. His shoes made a little line in the wood chips. The sun was warm on his head.

"Can I have a turn too?" Connor asked.

"Yes. You can come next," said the girl. "We can count to ten."

They counted together. "One, two, three." The swing went slow. "Ten!" The girl jumped off. Connor sat down on the red swing. It was hard at first. He pulled his legs in. Then he kicked out. He went up and up.

"Look at me!" he called.

Then a small boy came and stood by the swing. He waited just like Connor had waited.

"Your turn comes after me," said Connor. "We count to ten. That way it is fair for everyone."

"Can I count too?" asked the small boy.

"Yes," said Connor. "Count with me. One, two, three."

The swing went high. "Nine, ten!" Connor jumped down and held the swing still. "Here you go. Your turn now."

Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her team wore red shirts today. Grandpa waved from the bench. A gray squirrel sat by his shoe.

Sophie kicked the ball. A girl in a blue shirt ran to her. Sophie kicked the ball away. The coach blew a soft whistle.

"Why did you kick it away?" the coach asked.

Sophie pointed at the blue shirt. "You are not red," she said. "I pass to red."

The girl smiled. "I am on the other team today," she said. "Next time I will wear red too, if I join your team."

Sophie looked around. All her friends had red shirts. Ben had red. Mia had red. The ball came to Sophie. She kicked it to Mia. Mia kicked it in the goal!

Sophie jumped up and down. She wanted to cry, but happy tears. Grandpa hugged her tight. The gray squirrel clapped its little paws.

"Red is my team," Sophie said. "I always pass to red."
