Olivier was at the doctor's office. He was not late. Mama said, "Good, we are early." Olivier wanted the plane sticker on the wall. The doctor kept it high up.

First the doctor said, "Close your eyes." Olivier closed his eyes. Then he could not see the plane sticker. He opened his eyes. Now he saw it again. "My eyes see it," he said.

Next the doctor held a little bell. She rang it by his ear. Ding! Olivier heard it. "My ear heard that," he said. The doctor laughed.

Then the doctor held a sticker near his nose. Olivier sniffed. It smelled like nothing. "Stickers have no smell," he said. The doctor said, "That is right."

Then it was time for the taste test. The doctor gave him a little cup. Olivier tasted it. It was sweet juice. "My tongue tastes it," he said.

Last, the doctor let him touch the plane sticker. It was smooth and shiny. "Can I keep it?" Olivier asked. The doctor said, "Yes. You were so good."

Olivier drew a picture on the paper table cover. He drew a big plane. Then he put his new sticker next to it.

Zayn stood on the ferry with his dad. They were going to see Grandma. The wind stirred Zayn's hair. The boat went up and down on the waves. The car deck below smelled stinky, so they stayed up top.

Zayn had a bun in his hand. He wanted to save it for Grandma. But a little bit fell out of his fingers. It dropped down, down, into the water. A big white seagull swooped down and ate it. Then another seagull came. Then three more. Zayn looked at them. "The birds come because my bun fell," he said. Dad smiled and nodded.

So Zayn broke off one small piece. He dropped it on purpose. The seagulls came again, fast as a flash. Zayn laughed and clapped. He kept the big piece of his bun safe in his pocket. In his other pocket was an apple seed. He would plant it in Grandma's garden.

The ferry came to the other side. Zayn held Dad's hand and walked down the ramp. Grandma was waving by the gate. "I saved you a bite," Zayn said, "but the seagulls got the rest."

Hannah stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. She had a small beanbag in her hand.

Hannah threw the beanbag. It hit the edge of the hoop. Then it rolled away. "Why did it fall out?" she asked. She looked at her hands. "My hands went down too fast." She tried again. This time she held her hands up and let go slowly. The beanbag flew up and dropped right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Hannah.

Then her teacher rolled her a big ball. Hannah reached out with one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. Her friend Sam said, "Use two hands!" Hannah held out both hands. The big ball came again. Both hands caught it and hugged it tight. Hannah laughed. "Two hands are better than one!" she said. She threw the ball back to Sam.

Asher sat at the craft table at the library. Miss Jo gave him white paper and a white crayon. "Draw a rainbow," she said. Asher drew a big rainbow. But he could not see it. The white crayon on white paper was invisible.

Asher felt sad. "My rainbow is lost," he said. The girl next to him was painting with bright colors. Asher's tummy was hungry, but he wanted his rainbow first. Miss Jo gave him a brush and blue paint. "Try this," she said.

Asher painted over the whole paper. The blue stuck to the paper. But the paint slid off his rainbow lines. His rainbow popped out, bright and shiny. "The paint won't sit on my crayon!" Asher said. The crayon kept the paint away.

The girl next to him smiled. "Do one for me," she said. Asher drew a big sun with the white crayon. He painted over it with red. The sun came out too. Then they shared crackers from Miss Jo's bowl. Asher took two, and gave one to his new friend.

William sat in his car seat. He held his toy car and his red apple. His tummy felt empty. He wanted a snack now.

"Beep, beep," said the toy car. William drove it up his arm. Then the apple slipped. The apple did fall down, down to the floor. William reached and reached. It was too far. Now he had no snack, and his tummy growled.

"We will stop soon," said Mama. "Look at the farm." William looked out the window. One cow, two cows, three cows! One cow, two cows, three cows! The big cows ate green grass. William waved at them.

The car stopped at a little farm stand. There was a long wooden table. On the table sat milk, apples, and bread. "The milk is from the cows," said the farmer. William looked at the cows. Then he looked at the milk. "The cow makes my milk!" he said.

Mama bought a cold apple for William. His old blanket was in the bag, and it felt itchy on his legs, so he pushed it away. He bit the apple. Crunch! It was sweet. "The apple grows on a tree," said Mama. William looked up. He saw red apples in the green tree.

"One apple, two apples, three apples!" said William. Mama smiled. "Crunch," went William again.

Evelyn was at the big park. She could not find her blue bunny. "Where did Bunny go?" she said. Her tummy felt tight, like a rock. Mama knelt down beside her.

"We can look for Bunny," said Mama. "Let's go the same way we walked." So they walked back. Evelyn counted the spots. "One, the gate. Two, the swings. Three, the sand." At the sand box, no Bunny. Evelyn looked and looked.

Then she saw something. Bunny did not stay on the swing. It fell because the swing was moving. So Bunny fell off, down into the soft sand below. Evelyn dug with her hands. Her fingers touched something soft. It was Bunny! "The swing pushed Bunny off," Evelyn said. "That is why it fell!"

Evelyn picked up Bunny and hugged her. "I found you," she said. Now Evelyn would carry Bunny in her little bag. Then Bunny could not fall again. "Good idea," said Mama. Evelyn smiled big. "One, two, three," she said. "Three spots, and Bunny in spot three!" She gave Bunny one more squeeze and ran to the swings.

Jayden turned four today. His family had a party at the park. There was cake, juice and balloons. Mom set the cake down. Jayden counted the candles. "One, two, three, four." He asked Mom, "Why four candles?" Mom said, "You are four, so we put in four." He smiled big.

Grandma held up paper letters. "Can you spell your name, Jayden?" He did it slow. "J, A, Y, D, E, N." Grandma taped the letters to the table. Then the wind came. The wind blew out two candles. Jayden asked, "Who blew them out?" Dad said, "The wind did. The wind can blow out candles too." So Jayden covered the candles with his hands. Mom lit the two candles again. They stayed lit.

Everyone sang the birthday song. Jayden made a wish. He took a big breath and blew. All four candles went out at the same time. His friends clapped. Then a small surprise ran up. It was the park duck. It sat right by the cake. "Hello, duck," Jayden said. "You cannot eat my cake." He gave it a little bread bit instead.

Peyton ran to the park. She wanted to find the ice cream truck. Where was it?

Peyton closed her eyes. She could not see the truck. But she could hear it! Her ears heard a little bell. Ding, ding, ding! "The truck is coming!" she said. She used her ears.

Peyton's nose sniffed the air. Her nose smelled something sweet. It smelled like vanilla! She opened her eyes. Now her eyes could see the big white truck. It was by the black fence at the end of the yard. She ran and ran.

Peyton held the cold cone with her hands. Her hands felt the cold. She took a lick. Her tongue tasted the sweet, sweet cream. "Yum!" said Peyton. "My ears found it first!" The bell rang again. Ding, ding, ding!

Maeva went to the store with Dad. The store had food, toys, and a little book corner. Maeva saw a book with a fish on it. The fish could swim in deep blue water. She opened the book. There were little marks on every page. "What are these little marks?" she wondered. Dad said, "Those are words. Words tell you things." Maeva turned the pages one by one. Front to back. Page one, page two, page three. Then she got to the end. The fish went deep down and hid. "I want to keep this book forever," said Maeva. Dad shook his head. "This book is from the library. We borrow it. We take it home, then bring it back. Other kids read it too." A big clock ticked on the wall. "The clock tells us when to bring it back," said Dad. Maeva held the book tight. She looked at the fish one more time. "Okay," she said. "But can we read it at home first?"

Athena ran to her cubby at daycare. Her bunny was not there. Bunny was her favorite toy. She looked in the coat pile. No bunny. She looked under the snack table. No bunny.

Teacher Sam knelt down beside her. "Where did you play last?" he asked. Athena thought hard. "The sand table," she said. "First I played there. Then we went outside." So she went back to the sand table. She dug with both hands. Sand went everywhere. Still no bunny.

Then Athena looked at her shoes. They were full of sand. "I put on my boots to go outside," she said. "I had to cut my playing short for winter." Outside, the snow was crunchy under her feet. She walked in her old boot prints. Step by step. Crunch, crunch. Then she saw it. Bunny's ear was sticking out of a snow pile by the sleds.

"Bunny!" said Athena. She hugged him tight. Teacher Sam smiled. "You found him by going back where you were." Athena nodded. "Bunny fell in the snow when I built the pile." She put bunny in her pocket. Then she ran back inside to show her friends.

Isaiah held Mama's hand at the store. "We need apples," said Mama. "And we must not forget the juice."

Isaiah loved the store. The aisles were so long! First they passed the toy aisle. He saw a red truck and a fuzzy bear. Then they passed the fish tank. Little fish swam round and round. "Fish are animals," said Isaiah. "Yes," said Mama. "Fish are animals that swim."

At last they found the apples. Isaiah picked one up. It was round like a ball. He put it on the edge of the cart. The apple rolled! It rolled because it was round. Round things roll! The apple dropped down, down, down.

Mama caught it. She laughed and laughed. "Round apples need the bag," she said. Isaiah put the apple in the bag. It could not roll there. Then Mama held up the juice. "We did not forget!" Isaiah clapped his hands. "Apples, juice, fish, and my truck!" said Isaiah. "Best store day ever!"

Grandma came to stay at Amira's house. "How long is a week?" Amira asked. Grandma said, "Seven sleeps." So every morning, Amira dropped a stone in a jar. One stone, two stones, three stones. "Each sleep makes one stone," she said. That was the rule.

Amira wanted Grandma to sleep well. She gave her a soft blanket to keep her warm. But at night, Amira heard a bump. Grandma could not sleep. "Was the blanket too small?" Amira wondered. No, Grandma had bumped her toe on the dark path to the bathroom.

So Amira found her toy sheep. It was white and soft. She set the sheep by the bathroom door. "Now you can see where to walk," she said. Grandma patted the sheep. That night there was no bump. The little sheep glowed in the dark, and the path was clear.

Four stones, five stones, six stones, seven stones. The jar was full. Grandma gave Amira a big hug. "You kept me warm and safe all week," she said. Amira held up the sheep and smiled. "The sheep did it too."

Leah sat in her car seat. The car went fast, then it went slow. "One red car. Two blue cars. Three trucks," she said.

She wanted her water bottle. It was in the deep pocket by the door. She could not reach it. "Daddy, please help me," she said. Daddy reached back and got it. "Thank you," said Leah.

Then the car had to swing around a big corner. The bottle tipped over. Water dripped on the seat. "Oh no," said Leah. "The bottle fell because the car went around the corner." Daddy said, "Sorry, Leah. I will go slower." He found a towel and wiped the seat.

Then Daddy told her a joke. "What does a car say? Beep beep!" Leah laughed and laughed. "Tell it again, please," she said. Daddy smiled and started the joke one more time.

Owen wanted the red truck at daycare. Ben had it. Owen grabbed it. Ben cried loud.

Miss Amy came over. She sat down by Owen. "Try asking," she said. Owen looked at the truck. "Can I have the truck, please?" he asked. Ben sniffed. "Okay. After I do one more beep."

Owen waited. He counted the beeps. One, two, three. Ben held out the truck. "Thank you," said Owen. It was windy outside the window. The tree tapped the glass, tap, tap. Owen pushed the truck on the rug. It bumped Ben's foot. "Sorry, Ben," said Owen. "It's okay," said Ben.

Then Owen could not find the truck ramp. He looked under the table. He looked in the box. He whispered to Miss Amy, "Can you help me?" She found the ramp behind the shelf. Owen pushed the truck down, down, down. "It goes fast because the ramp is tall!" said Owen.

Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp made a warm circle of light. Mama put down a bowl of soup. "Today we have soup," said Mama. "Yesterday we had pasta. Tomorrow we will have spaghetti." Sophia looked at her bowl. "I want spaghetti now," she said. "Spaghetti comes later," said Mama. "First soup, then spaghetti."

Sophia did not want to wait. She turned her spoon around and around. She shook her spoon and the soup went drip, drip, drip. One drop, two drops, three drops. The table got messy. Mama gave her a cloth. Sophia wiped one drop, two drops, three drops. The table was clean now.

"I want tomorrow now," said Sophia. Mama smiled. "Tomorrow comes after we sleep. Yesterday we had pasta. Do you remember?" Sophia thought. Yes, she remembered the pasta. It was gone. "Pasta was yesterday," said Sophia. "Soup is today." "That's right," said Mama. Sophia ate her soup, one spoon, two spoops, three spoons.

The bowl was empty. "Now soup is done," said Sophia. "Now it is spaghetti time," said Mama. She set down a plate of spaghetti. "Later came!" said Sophia. She lifted her fork and twirled the noodles around and around.

Olivia wants to paint a cat. But her cat is orange. She has no orange paint. She has red, yellow, and blue.

"Red, yellow, blue," she says. She taps each wooden cup. Those are her three paints. None of them is orange.

She stops. She has a question. Can two paints make a new paint? She dips her brush in red. She dips it in yellow too. She stirs them on her plate.

The paint turns orange! Olivia jumps up. "Red and yellow make orange!" she shouts. Now she can paint her cat.

She paints a big orange cat. Then she wonders about blue. She mixes red and blue next. The new paint is purple! "Wow," she whispers. Purple was hiding in her cups all along.

She runs to find her cat. "Look!" she says. The real cat sniffs the painting. Then he rubs his head on it. "You like orange too," Olivia says. She holds up her purple brush. "Next, I paint you a purple hat!"

Mya sat on the playroom floor. She had ten red blocks. She wanted to build one big tower.

"Mom, come see my tower!" she called. Mom was feeding the baby. "One minute," said Mom. Mya counted her blocks to see how many she had. "One, two, three, five, eight," she said. She looked at the blocks left in the pile. Her count did not use them all up. Something was wrong.

Mya frowned. She tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." This time she tapped one block for each word. Every block got a word. No block was left out. "The numbers go in a row," she said. "They have a job. Each one taps one block." She remembered a song at school. It went the same way every time, one to ten.

Mom came in with the baby. "Show me," said Mom. Mya stacked and counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The tower stood tall. The baby clapped her hands. "Look, baby," said Mya. "You can like my tower. It has ten blocks. Ten is lucky today."

Blake's bear was sick. He had a tummy ache from too many pretend cookies. "I will be the doctor," Blake said. She put a bandage on his tummy. She gave him pretend soup in a small cup.

Next, her bunny was hungry. Blake fed her a carrot that was really an old sock. Bunny chewed and chewed. Then Bunny felt much better.

"Now my job is done," said Doctor Blake. But then she heard a tiny sound. Peep, peep! She looked under her bed. Her doll was hiding there. "You need a house," said Blake. She made a house from a big box. She planted a feather in a cup to be a tree for the yard. The doll moved in and smiled.

Blake clapped her hands. "When I take care of you, you get happy," she said. Then the bear, the bunny and the doll all sat down with her for one more pretend cookie.

Leon was at Grandma's house. It was a snowy day. Big white flakes fell past the window.

"I will make pancakes for everyone," said Leon. Grandma stood close by. Leon mixed flour, milk and one egg. He poured a pancake into the pan. It made a happy sizzling noise.

But the pancake stayed flat and thin. It looked like a little snowy plate. Leon frowned. "Why won't it get big?" he asked. Grandma showed him the baking soda box, still on the shelf. "We forgot this," she said.

Leon added the baking soda to the bowl. He poured a new pancake. It sizzled again. Then it puffed up, big and fat! "It got big because of the baking soda," said Leon. Grandma smiled.

The family ate the big pancakes. Daddy ate four. "Leon made these," said Grandma. Leon held his warm plate and grinned.

Gabriel went to the park with Dad. The pond was still and quiet. Two ducks swam by and began to fish in the water. Dad put a big hoop on the grass. He gave Gabriel a small red beanbag.

"Throw it in," said Dad. Gabriel threw the beanbag very hard. It flew over the hoop and landed in the grass. He tried again, hard and fast. It bounced off the rim. Then Gabriel tried a slow, soft toss, low and easy. The beanbag went up and dropped right into the hoop.

"I threw it slow and it went in!" said Gabriel. Dad clapped. Next Dad rolled him a big blue ball. Gabriel held out one hand. The ball hit his fingers and fell. Dad rolled it again. This time Gabriel held out both hands, open wide. The ball landed right in them. He caught it!

"You used two hands," said Dad. Gabriel laughed. "One hand was silly," he said. He hugged the big ball. The sun made a bright window of light on the path. Gabriel walked home holding his ball all the way.

Wyatt wanted to find ten bugs for his jar. He only found one small brown bug on the porch. He sat down and felt sad. Then he heard Mom singing in the kitchen. She was counting spoonfuls of flour. "One, two, three," she sang. Wyatt tapped his knees. The words went in order, and they never stopped. So he started to sing too. "One, two, three, four," he sang. He walked to the garden. "Five, six, seven." He looked under a leaf. Two green bugs sat there! "Eight, nine." He peeked at a rock. A tiny red bug crawled past. "Ten!" said Wyatt. He had ten bugs now. "The song helped me look slow," he said. Mom came out and smiled. "Can I see your jar?" she asked. Wyatt held it up so she could see every small bug. "Ten friends," he said.

Elizabeth had a toy bunny. She held it in her arms. "Bunny is hungry," she said. Elizabeth found a little carrot in the kitchen. It was a food, and foods are for eating. She put the carrot up to the bunny's mouth. The carrot just sat there. The bunny did not chew. The carrot did not get smaller.

Elizabeth tried again. She made munching sounds. "Bunny, eat!" she said. The carrot still did not go away. Her big brother Sam came in. He held their real cat, Max. Sam put a bit of fish on the floor. Max bent his head. Max chewed and chewed. The fish was gone.

Elizabeth looked at Max. Then she looked at her toy bunny. "Toys do not eat," she said. "Real animals eat." Sam smiled. "That's right," he said. "Your bunny is soft and quiet. Max is soft too, but Max has a tummy."

Elizabeth gave her toy bunny a gentle hug. She gave the bunny a kiss on its little nose. Then she looked out the window at the street. A real dog was walking by with its owner. "That dog eats too," said Elizabeth. "One day Max can have more fish," said Sam. Max licked his lips and purred very loud.

Paisley held her baby doll at school. The baby was hungry, but the bottle was lost. Paisley looked in the toy box. She looked under the little table. No bottle anywhere.

Then she saw a small yellow block. She held it to the baby's mouth. "Here is your milk," she said. The block was not a bottle. But in pretend play, it could be one. Tom saw her and grinned. He picked up a block too. "My baby wants milk too!" he said.

Next they made a road on the carpet for the pretend car. Tom drove the car. "A stinky skunk is on the road!" he cried. Paisley dug in the toy box. She pulled out a spoon. "Use this shovel," she said. "Dig him out of the way." The car zoomed past. The babies drank their milk. "All better," said Paisley.

Riley sat at the little blue table. Teacher Sam put out letter cards. Riley wanted to find the R card, because R is for Riley.

She picked up a card. It had two bumps and one stick. She turned it around. She turned it again. The card looked the same both ways. Riley put it down and waited. She looked some more.

Then she picked up the R card. It had one bump and two sticks. When she turned it around, it did not look the same anymore. "This one turns different," said Riley. Teacher Sam smiled. Riley held up the R. "R goes rrr," she said, like a big cat.

At dinner time, Riley found the R on her milk carton. She turned it around. It still said R. "R goes rrr," she told her milk. Then she took a big drink.

David stood by the gate. His green hat was on his head. He waited for his mom. "Mom!" he called. She came with a big bag.

David wanted to go to the park. But his shoes made a squish sound. He had stepped in a puddle at school. His socks were wet. His toes felt cold. Mom sat down on the bench. She took out dry socks from the bag. She pulled off the wet socks. She put the dry socks on his feet. "Warm now," said David. "The wet socks made my toes cold. Dry socks make them warm."

Then Mom gave him a banana. She used a small knife to cut it into pieces. David ate them all up. He drank his water. He was not hungry anymore.

They walked to the park. David ran in the sand. He went down the slide. "We will go home soon," said Mom. "Then a warm bath. Then pajamas. Then bed." David slid down one more time. "Again!" he said. Mom smiled and held out her hand.

Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the red jello. Mom said, "Not now. Later, after your peas."

Sadie looked at her plate. The peas were still there. "Is it later now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mom. "Now you eat. Later comes after now."

Sadie ate one pea. Then two. Then three. "Now?" she asked.

"Keep going," said Mom.

Sadie talked about her day while she ate. "Today I played in the sand. Yesterday I played in the rain. Tomorrow I want to paint with the color blue."

Mom smiled. "That sounds fun."

Sadie ate the last pea. The plate was empty. "Mom! Now it is later! The peas are gone, so it is jello time."

Mom put the red jello on the table. Sadie took a big bite. "Yummy," she said. "After now comes later. And after today comes tomorrow!"

Charlie ran to the little table. Today he would write his name! Miss Mia put down a fat pencil.

Charlie grabbed it with his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The pencil slid away. The letter C looked all wobbly, like a yucky worm.

"Try again," said Miss Mia. "Lay the pencil on your hand."

Charlie laid the pencil on his fingers. He pinched it with two fingers, like a little crab. Pinch, pinch, rest! He lifted his hand and put it back down. Pinch, pinch, rest!

Now the pencil stood up tall. Charlie drew the C. Then H. Then A. "C, H, A!" he shouted.

"You did it!" said Miss Mia. "Now keep going."

Charlie went on. R, L, I, E. The letters marched across the paper like cars on a road. Straight ones, round ones, all of them neat.

Charlie held up the paper. "My name! Look, my name!"

Miss Mia clapped. Charlie grinned and traced it again, pinch, pinch, rest.

Jayden was at Grandma's house. He wanted to build a picture of the garden. He found Grandma's paint pots on the big table.

"One red, one blue, one yellow," he said. He counted them again. "But no green." The grass in Grandma's garden was green. His picture needed green. Now he had a problem.

He painted a red flower. He painted a yellow sun. Then he tried the grass. He put blue on the plate. He put yellow next to it. He mixed them with his brush.

The paint turned green. "It made green," Jayden said. "Blue and yellow make green."

Grandma came to look. "That is nice green grass," she said.

"Not bad," said Jayden. He painted the long, long grass. It was green all the way to the fence.

"More blue," he said. He dipped his brush again.

Amira wanted to set the table. Mama gave her a stack of cups. "We need six cups," said Mama.

Amira put out cups. She counted them. "One, two, three, five, six." She scratched her head. The cups looked wrong. There were only five on the table.

Papa came in. He was hungry and tired. "Can I have a cup of water?" he asked.

Amira counted again. She pointed at each cup. "One, two, three, four, five." One cup was missing! The counting words had to go in a row. If she jumped from three to five, the count got mixed up.

Amira got one more cup. She touched each one as she said the words. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Now there were six cups, just like Mama said.

Papa drank his water. "Thank you, Amira," he said. "This helps me a lot."

Amira smiled. Then she sang her new song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Mama clapped, and the whole kitchen felt warm.

Aurora sat at the dinner table. In the middle of her plate was warm soup. She was hungry, but she felt grumpy. "What is this soup?" she asked. Her grandma said, "Use your nose and find out." Aurora sniffed with her nose. "Mmm, it smells like carrots!" Then she touched the bowl with one finger. It was hot, so she pulled her hand back fast. Her ears heard the soup bubble. Her eyes saw orange dots floating on top. She took a little sip. "I can taste it!" she said. Then she held her nose closed and sipped again. Now she could not taste the carrots at all. "Why?" she wondered. She let go of her nose. The carrot taste came back. "My nose helps my tongue!" she said. She painted a big smile on her face with her spoon.

Mason lost his monkey. His soft, spotted monkey was gone.

"I want my monkey," said Mason. "Where can he be?"

Grandma said, "Think. Where did you play last?"

Mason played in the blanket fort. He crawled in. "Not here." He looked under the big chair. "Not here." He peeked behind the couch. "Not here." That was one, two, three places.

Then Mason stopped. He thought hard. "I was playing before my nap. I had my monkey then. I dropped him. So he is near my nap spot!"

Mason ran to the little bed. He looked down. There was a spotted paw! Under the blanket corner!

"My monkey! You were hiding near my bed," said Mason.

He hugged his monkey tight. "Found you, monkey. Found you."

Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find her own book. But she could not read yet. The letters looked like little squiggles.

Dad gave her a clue. He said, "Your name starts with B." Brooklyn looked at the shelves. She looked and looked. There was a red letter on a book. It had two bumps and one tummy. Dad said, "That is B. It says buh."

Brooklyn put her finger on the B. "Buh, buh, Brooklyn," she said. The letter B was at the front of her name! Now she knew one letter all by herself.

She found more books with B. Each one had the two-bump letter. "Buh," she said each time. Dad smiled and nodded.

One book had a picture of a rubber duck. The duck sat in a bath. Brooklyn hugged the book. "B is for bath," she said. Dad said, "Yes! Buh, bath."

The sun did shine in the window. It made the B on her book glow. Brooklyn carried the book to the desk. She gave the librarian her card.

"Buh, buh, Brooklyn," she said, very proud.

The librarian clapped softly. "Your B book," she said.

Brooklyn held the book tight all the way home.

Emile found a thick book at school. It was about big red trucks. He loved it. He wanted to keep it forever. He put it in his bag. Then Miss Ana held up a small paper flag. The flag was stuck in the book Emile took. "Whose book is this?" she asked. Emile gave it back. He saw words on the flag. "What do the words say?" he asked. Miss Ana pointed to each word. Emile followed her finger. The words said take it home, bring it back. "So the book can go home with me?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "But you must bring it back. Other friends want to read it too." Emile hugged the book. He read page one first. Then page two, all the way to the end. "I will bring it back," he said. On Friday, he put the book in the box. His friend Tom took it next. Emile waved goodbye to the trucks.

Ava sat at the dinner table. Rain tapped on the window. "It is a stormy night," said Mama. Ava drank her milk. "Milk comes from a cow," said Ava. The dog sat by her chair. He looked up with big eyes. "You beg for my carrots," said Ava. She gave him one little piece.

After dinner, it was bath time. Ava wanted to keep her socks on. She stepped into the tub. Splash! Her socks got all wet. "Oh!" said Ava. She pulled them off. They dripped in her hands. "Socks get wet in the bath," she said. "Why is that?" Then she touched the water with her toes. Warm! The wet socks went in the basket.

Mama dried her with a big towel. Ava put on soft pajamas. She brushed her teeth and climbed into bed. "Did you like the warm bath?" asked Mama. "Yes," said Ava. "But no socks next time."

Blake was at Mia's house. Mia's mama put on a song. The song had a beat. Boom, boom, boom.

"Clap like this," said Mia. She clapped on the boom. Blake clapped too fast. She clapped all over. The beat got lost.

"Listen first," said Mia. "Then clap."

Blake sat very still. She heard the boom, boom, boom. She clapped on each boom. Clap, clap, clap. It matched!

"I did it!" said Blake. "The claps go on the boom!"

"Now sing with me," said Mia. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star."

Blake knew that one! She sang the words from her head. She did not lose them. It was easy!

Then Mia's mama brought a surprise. A soap that smelled like strawberries! "Wash hands, then snack," she said.

The song played again. Blake clapped and sang at the same time. "Again!" she shouted. "Again, again!"

Grandpa had a book on the table. Felix picked it up. The cover said a word. "What does it say?" he asked. "It says Dinosaur," said Grandpa. Felix looked at the letters. "Can I spell it?" he asked. He pointed at each letter. D, I, N, O, S, A, U, R. Grandpa smiled.

Felix opened the front of the book. He turned the pages one by one. The pictures came in order. First the egg. Then the big dinosaur. The last page showed the moon.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Felix. Grandpa shook his head. "It is from the library. We take it back on Thursday. Then other kids can read it too." Felix held the book tight. Then he had an idea. He got a pencil and paper. "I will spell dinosaur myself," he said. The parrot in the cage was noisy, but Felix kept writing. "D, I, N, O," he said. At last he drew a big green dinosaur under the letters. "Now I have my own book," he said. "And on Thursday, the library gets yours."

Florence went to the library with her dad. She saw a book about a small gray mouse. "I want this one," she said. The cover felt smooth. The pages made a soft swish when she turned them.

Florence opened the book. She saw little black marks on every page. "Dad, what are those?" she asked. "Those are words," he said. "They tell the story." Florence pointed at the marks. She turned pages from the front to the back. "The mouse moved to a big red barn!" she said. She could follow the mouse all the way.

At the desk, a kind lady put the book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back when you are done. Then other kids can read it too." Florence hugged the bag tight.

At home, Florence read the book four times. Then she read it again. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

The next day, they went back to the library. Florence gave the book to the lady. A boy was waiting there. He smiled and took the mouse book. Florence watched him hold it. "He gets to read about the mouse now," she said. She moved to the shelf and picked a new book. This one had a bear on it. "This one is special too," she said.

Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big ball of yellow dough. He wanted to make a bear. He patted the dough flat. He rolled little balls for ears. He pushed them on the head. One ear fell off. He pushed it on again. This time it stayed.

The bear had sleepy eyes. Hudson gave him a soft blanket of blue paper. "Now you can sleep," Hudson said. The bear sat still under the paper.

Hudson licked a bit of dough off his finger. He made a face. It was salty! "Mom, the dough is salty," he said. Mom smiled. "We put salt in it," she said. Hudson looked at his bear. "You are made of salt," he whispered. He patted the bear's head gently and tucked the paper in tight.

Avery went to the store with Dad. She wanted the red balloon by the door. But another girl was there. The girl was holding the last red balloon.

Avery felt her eyes get hot. "Dad, can I take it?" she asked.

"No," said Dad. "She had it first. She gets her turn. Then we can ask for the next one."

Avery waited. She watched the girl's mom pay. The girl let go of the balloon string and the balloon began to dance near the ceiling fan. It bobbed up and down.

Then a store man came with a whole box. "More red ones," he said. He gave one to Avery. It had a sharp point at the knot, so Dad tied the string twice.

"Why did she get one first?" Avery asked.

Dad said, "Because she was first in line."

Avery nodded. "First in line goes first," she said.

At the car, she held the string tight. Her red balloon bobbed beside her all the way home. "My turn came," she said.

Wyatt ran to the freezer aisle. It was cold in there! His coat was in the cart. "I will put it on all by myself," he said. He pushed his arms in fast. One sleeve was wrong. His arm was stuck behind his back! He wiggled and giggled and pulled it out. Then the arm slid in the right way.

Now the zipper. Wyatt pulled it up. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no zipper! Then he looked down. The zipper side was not in the little slot at the bottom. He pushed it in. Click! It was in. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It worked! "I did it, Mama!" he said.

Wyatt jumped and his tag bounced like a feather. "The zipper only works when it starts in the slot!" he said. He unzipped it. He zipped it again. "Let's go find the ice cream," he said, and he marched to the freezer door.

Miles was four years old today. His party was at the big park. Grandma put the cake on the table. The cake had four little candles. All his friends ran over to see.

"Wait!" said Grandma. "The candles are still lit."

Miles looked. The four little flames were still dancing. Grandpa held his hand. "Blow with me," said Grandpa. Miles took a big breath. He blew hard. The flames went out. Thin smoke curled up.

"Why do we blow them out?" asked Miles.

"So the wax won't drip on the cake," said Grandpa with a smile.

Then Mom called, "Ice cream first!" Miles saw the ice cream tub. It sat in the sun. It was soft and wet at the edges. "The sun is melting it!" said Miles. "The sun makes it melt because it is hot."

"That's right," said Mom. "So we eat it fast."

Everyone got a bowl. Miles licked his spoon. The cold ice cream tasted sweet. His dog, Biscuit, sat by his feet and begged for a taste. Miles giggled and patted his head. Then Mom cut the cake into pieces. Miles took the biggest one. "Happy birthday to me!" he said.

Maeve sat on the grass with Dad. The sports field was big and green. People sat all around on blankets. Maeve had a little flag with a sun on it.

She held the flag up high. "I can see the game," she said. Then a man behind them said, "Oh. I cannot see now." Maeve turned around. Her flag was in front of his face. The flag was high. His eyes were low. That was why he could not see.

Maeve pulled the flag down. The man smiled. "Thank you," he said. "Now I can see the players."

A player kicked the ball. The ball went into the net. The net moved. The referee blew his whistle. Everyone stood up and cheered. Maeve clapped and jumped. Her tummy felt happy and jumpy inside.

After the game, Maeve skipped to the car. She held her flag down low. "The flag is for later," she said. Dad laughed and took her hand.

Madelyn went to the library with her dad. It was a bright morning. Story time was in the big room. Madelyn wanted to sing the counting song with the other kids. But she did not know all the words. Her tummy felt wobbly. "I might get it wrong," she whispered. Dad held her hand. "Let's listen first," he said.

The teacher sang, "One, two, three, four, five." She clapped on each word. Then she sang, "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Madelyn listened hard. The words were like a train. Each word sat in its own spot. First came one, then two, then three. They never hid. They always marched in the same order.

The teacher sang it again. Madelyn clapped and sang too. "One, two, three, four, five." Her voice was not alone. The whole room sang with her. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She got every word right.

The song stopped, and Madelyn laughed. "The numbers always go in a row," she told Dad. "So I can remember them." Dad gave her a hug. Then they picked three books to take home. "One, two, three," Madelyn counted, all by herself.

Charlotte went to the store with Dad. They needed apples for pizza night. Dad said, "We need red apples too."

Charlotte saw the apples. Some were red. Some were yellow. Some were green. Her baby brother Sam pointed at a green apple. He wanted it.

A lady was giving out little apple pieces to try. Charlotte tried a green piece. Her mouth went tight and sour! "Yuck," she said. Then she tried a red piece. It was sweet. Charlotte looked at Sam. She said, "Green is sour, Sam. Red is sweet." She put red apples in the bag. She picked one small red apple just for Sam.

At home, Dad put hot pizza on the table. Red apple slices sat in a bowl. Sam held his little red apple. He took a big bite and smiled. Charlotte gave him a hug. Dad said, "Good picking, Charlotte." Charlotte bit her hot pizza slice and smiled too. "Red apples for Sam," she said.

Michael wanted a cookie before lunch. Mom said, "First wash your hands." Michael ran to the sink. He got his fingers wet and turned to go. "Wait," said Mom. "Soap too. Count to twenty." Twenty felt like a long time. Michael rubbed the soap on his fingers. It felt smooth and slippery. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he stopped. "This is too slow," he said. His big sister came in. She was watering the little plant on the windowsill. "Sing the birthday song," she said. "One song is almost twenty seconds." Michael sang, "Happy birthday to you." He scrubbed while he sang. The soap made white bubbles. He rinsed his hands under warm water. His fingers smelled like clean soap now. "The song made twenty seconds fast," said Michael. Mom smiled and handed him a cookie. Michael took a big happy bite.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a new puzzle with her. It was a puzzle of a red fire truck. She tried to fit a piece. It did not go in. She tried again. It still did not go in.

"Please help me, Daddy," said Sadie. Daddy reached back his hand. He held the piece the cool way, flat and slow. The piece went in. "Thank you, Daddy," said Sadie. She clapped her hands.

Then Sadie dropped the box. Pieces fell on the floor. "Sorry, box," said Sadie. She waited for the car to stop. The car stopped at a red light. Daddy helped pick up the pieces. One by one, they went back in the box. "The light was red, so the car stopped," said Sadie. Daddy smiled. Then the light turned green, and off they went.

Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to draw a rabbit. She drew one ear, but it flopped down. "My rabbit looks like a pancake," she said.

Her friend Tomo slid over a block. "Try this," he said. The block had four flat sides. Gabriella put it on her paper and traced around it. A square! She turned the square sideways. Now it looked like a body. She traced a small square for the head.

Next she found a block with three sides. She traced it twice. Two triangles stood up like ears. "Triangles have pointy tops," she said. "That is why my rabbit ears stand up now."

She traced a long block too. The rectangle made a good door for the rabbit house. Then she found a round cup. She traced the bottom. A circle made the rabbit's tail, round like a ball.

A ladybug began to crawl across her paper. Gabriella watched its round little body. She drew a tiny circle for it too.

"Look, Teacher Mia," she said. Teacher Mia smiled. "Your rabbit has square parts, triangle ears, and a circle tail. Nice work."

Gabriella held up her paper. "My rabbit can hop into his rectangle house now," she said.

Everett ran to the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint a picture of his cute rabbit toy. The rabbit was green, his very favorite color. But there was no green paint! The pots were red, blue and yellow only. Everett looked and looked. He felt like crying.

Then he saw his friend Mia. She dipped her brush in blue paint. Then she dipped it in yellow paint too. Her paper turned green! Everett gasped. Blue and yellow made green! He grabbed his brush fast. He put blue on his paper. He put yellow on top. Green! It spread like magic.

He painted his rabbit green with big happy strokes. Then he made white snow at the bottom, like the paint was snow falling. Mia clapped. "It's so cute!" she said. Everett held up his paper and shouted, "Blue and yellow make green!"

Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big red ball. Avery wanted the ball. Another girl was there too. The girl looked at the ball.

"Me first," said the girl. She hugged the ball. Avery waited. She held Mama's hand and counted. One, two, three, four, five.

The girl rolled the ball on the floor. Then she gave it to Avery. "Your turn," she said. Avery hugged the ball. It was soft like her pillow at home. It had a bright red color.

Avery rolled the ball too. Then she gave it back. "Your turn," said Avery. They took turns. Back and forth, back and forth. A worker came by. "Time to hold the ball now," she said. "No rolling in the store." So both girls held the ball.

Avery looked at Mama. "She waited, so she got a turn," Avery said. Mama smiled and nodded. The other girl waved goodbye. Avery waved back. "Bye, ball," said Avery.

Mia was ready for bed. She looked out the window. It was snowing. Soft white bits fell down, down, down. Mia felt happy. She loved snow.

Then she reached for her toy horse. It was not on the bed. Her horse was missing. Mia felt sad. She looked under the pillow. She looked under the blanket. No horse. Mia stomped her foot. She felt angry. She wanted her horse now.

Then the room went dark. A big shadow sat on the wall. Mia felt scared. She hid under the covers. "Who is there?" she asked. Daddy came in and turned on the little lamp. The shadow was just her coat. "It was my coat," Mia said. "The dark made it look big." She felt calm again.

Daddy found the horse. It was in the toy box. Mia hugged her horse tight. She felt so excited. "The snow made me look for you!" she told her horse. She snuggled down and closed her eyes. The snow kept falling outside. "Goodnight, horse," Mia said.

Grandpa came to stay at Harrison's house. He put a big suitcase in the guest room. Grandpa unzipped it, and Harrison looked inside.

"Grandpa, why so many shirts?" Harrison asked.

"One shirt for each day," said Grandpa. "I am staying one whole week."

Harrison counted the shirts with his finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." There were seven shirts. Harrison felt a little worried. When the shirts were gone, Grandpa would go home. Each morning Grandpa put on one shirt. Each night it went in the wash basket. The pile got smaller and smaller.

Harrison had an idea. He ran to the laundry room. "Mama, help!" he said. "We wash Grandpa's shirt fast!"

Mama smiled. She washed the blue shirt. She hung it up by the window. It flapped in the air from the fan.

The next morning Grandpa picked a clean shirt from the pile. It was the blue one. "Look," said Harrison. "It came back! Washing makes it come back."

Grandpa laughed a big laugh. "Yes, it does," he said. "So I can stay my whole week."

Grandpa pulled Harrison onto his lap. His feet touched the floor on both sides, because Grandpa was so big. Harrison snuggled into the soft shirt.

"Seven days," said Grandpa. "And this is day three."

"Four more shirts," said Harrison, and he hugged him tight.

Benjamin ran to the playground. His friend Mia was on the bench. She was crying. A big dog had run by. It was too fast. It was scary for her. Now the dog was gone. But Mia was still sad.

Benjamin sat next to her. He had his toy farm in his pocket. He put the little cow in her hand. Mia stopped crying. She made the cow jump. Then she laughed.

"You are happy now," Benjamin said. "The cow made you happy." Mia nodded. They watched the little cow hop on the bench. Soon they ran to the slide together. Benjamin slid down first. Then Mia slid down too. She held the cow up high and shouted, "Whee!"

Sarah sat with her family at a big table. A huge screen hung on the wall. A big game was on. Everyone looked up and watched.

But the screen had no sound. The players ran and ran. Nobody could hear the crowd. Grandpa leaned far forward. He cupped his hand by his ear. Sarah looked at the screen. Then she looked at the little box under it. A red light glowed there.

"The sound is off," Sarah said. "That is why we can't hear!" Dad smiled and pressed the button on the box. The crowd cheered loud. Everyone clapped and laughed.

A waiter came by. Dad said, "Please buy Sarah a juice. She fixed our game." The waiter brought a cold cup. Next to Sarah, a little boy dropped his spoon. "Sorry," he said. Sarah picked it up and gave it back. Then they all looked up at the screen. The players ran fast, and the crowd roared.

Henry ran down the hall. He was going to meet the new baby. In his pocket was a little sand from his sandbox at home. Dad stopped him at the door. "We wash our hands first," said Dad. "Sand has germs. Germs can make the baby sick." Henry looked at his hands. The sand was there, small and bumpy. Henry washed his hands at the sink. He washed slow. He washed each finger. Then Dad sat down and put a pillow on Henry's lap. "Babies are young," said Dad. "Her head is wobbly. So we hold very still." Henry held very still. Dad laid the baby on the pillow. Henry kissed her soft little head. "Hello, baby," said Henry. "My hands are clean now. That is why."

Penelope wanted to make soup for dinner. Her apron would not stay on. So she took it down from the hook where it liked to hang. Then she put it on all by herself.

"Can I help?" asked her brother Tom. He was a big boy, almost six. "Yes," said Penelope. "You can stir." Daddy put the pot on the stove. Penelope chopped an onion. Then her eyes began to water. Big tears ran down her face. She felt scared. "Why am I crying?" she asked.

Daddy gave her a hug. "The onion did that," he said. "It makes little smelly bits fly up to your eyes." Penelope sniffled. So that was it. The onion made her cry. Tom stirred and stirred, and the soup got hot. Soon the whole kitchen smelled good. "Dinner time!" called Penelope.

Felix woke up sleepy. Today was the candle party at Grandma's house. Felix wanted to hold a candle like the big kids.

The candles were in a small box. Felix tried to lift the box. It was too heavy. "Not yet," said Grandma. "Little candles need big hands."

Grandma gave Felix one candle. She lit the wick. Felix held it very still. The flame danced up high. Felix laughed. "The candle is waving at me!"

Then Felix saw it. Grandma lit her candle from Grandpa's candle. Then Dad lit his from Grandma's. The light went from one flame to the next.

"I know why," said Felix. "One fire makes many fires. Sharing makes more light!"

Grandma blew a kiss at him. Felix held his candle up high. The little flame waved back.

Grandma took Iris to the salon. Iris got a big chair. It went up and down. Her legs were too short, so she let them kick in the air. Grandma held a little card. It said "Iris, first haircut."

The hair lady came with a spray bottle. Psshh, psshh. Water fell on Iris's hair. Why water? Iris touched her hair. It was wet now. The wet hair lay flat and smooth. Dry hair had bounced up. Now the hair lady could cut it straight.

Snip, snip. Little pieces fell down. They stuck to Iris's cheek. She laughed. When the chair went down, Iris looked in the mirror. She saw short hair and a happy face. "Does wet hair cut better?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Wet hair lies flat." Iris touched her soft new hair one more time.

Levi stood at the running track. He held a red beanbag. A hoop lay on the ground far away. He wanted to get it in. Levi threw the beanbag high. It went past the hoop. Thump. It hit the real track floor. Why did it fly too far? Then Levi tried again. This time he swung his arm low and slow. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed right in the hoop. "A slow throw goes in," said Levi. Next, his friend Mia tossed him a big ball. Levi held out one arm. The ball bounced off. Then he made a basket with both hands. The ball went right in. "Two hands catch the ball," said Levi. The kids marched around the track. Levi marched with his beanbag. What would he try next?

Alexis visited Grandma on a rainy day. Rain went tap, tap on the window. Grandma said, "Let's find your socks. Your feet look cold."

They looked under the big chair. "One sock!" said Alexis. He held it up. It was red and soft like a bunny.

"Now we need one more," said Grandma. Alexis looked under the table. "Two socks!" he said. He counted them. "One, two, four, nine, ten!"

Grandma smiled. She touched each sock with her finger. "One, two," she said slowly. Alexis watched her fingers. He tried again. "One, two!" He put the socks on his feet. They were warm.

"It works when I touch each one," said Alexis. Grandma laughed and hugged him.

"Ten toes next," she said. "Let's count them in the tub."

Abigail could not find her bunny. She looked in the toy box. Bunny was not there. She looked behind the big chair. Bunny was not there either.

"Where are you, Bunny?" she called. Her tummy felt tight. Bunny was her real bedtime friend. She needed him for sleep.

Then Abigail had an idea. Last night she had bunny in the bed. She went to her bed. She bent down low. She looked under the bed. It was dark under there. She could not see well.

"Let me help," said Dad. He got the flashlight. He shined it under the bed. Abigail peeked again. There was bunny! "My blanket pushed him," she said. "He slid under the bed." The blanket had made bunny slide down. That is why he was hiding.

Abigail reached in and pulled bunny out. He was dusty. So she helped Dad clean him with a soft cloth. She hugged bunny close.

"Goodnight, Bunny," she whispered. She tucked him in tight. Then she slid down under her own blanket too. "Stay by me this time," she said.

Colton ran into daycare. It was snack time soon. But today the snack was a surprise!

"I want to find the snack!" said Colton.

He used his eyes to look. He looked in the toy box. He looked under the table. No snack there. Then he used his nose to smell. He sniffed and sniffed. Something sweet! His nose smelled cookies!

Miss Maya laughed. "Good nose, Colton. Now cover your nose and try."

Colton put his hand on his nose. He could not smell the cookies anymore! He took his hand off. The sweet smell came back. His nose did the smelling. His hand made the smell stop!

"The cookies make my nose happy!" he said.

Then the cookies came out. They were warm. Colton touched one with his fingers. It was soft and a little messy on top. He took a bite. His tongue tasted sugar and chocolate.

Just then baby Ben woke up. Baby Ben heard the happy singing. His ears heard the song. He bounced in his seat.

Colton clapped. "Baby Ben hears us! I see him bounce!"

Miss Maya gave baby Ben a cookie too. He made a big messy smile.

"More cookies, more noses!" said Colton. Everyone laughed.

Billie wanted to help Mama cook. The pot on the stove was hot. It made a small puff puff sound. Billie stood close to Mama, just like always. The kitchen light was bright above the counter.

Billie saw a shiny knife on the counter. "Can I hold that?" she asked. "Not that one," said Mama. "Knives are for grown-ups." Billie nodded and put her hands behind her back.

Then she saw steam rise from the pot. "What is that?" she asked. "That means it is hot," said Mama. Billie touched the cold fridge door instead. The fridge felt cool on her fingers.

"Hot pot, cold fridge," said Billie. "Steam tells me it is hot!" Mama smiled. "That's right," she said. Billie stirred the bowl Mama gave her. Then she gave Mama a big swing of her arm, and the spoon went round and round.

Hayden wants to wash his hands. His toy lion is dirty too. He carries lion to the bathroom. Mama comes with him.

Hayden sees two taps. He points to the red one. "That one is hot," says Mama. "Hot can hurt you." Hayden touches the cold tap instead. Cold water runs out. It feels nice on his fingers.

He rubs soap on lion. The water turns gray. "Lion is getting clean," says Hayden. He waits. He rinses and rinses. Slowly the soap goes away.

Then Hayden sees the little hole in the wall. Something shiny sits inside it. He wants to touch it. Mama holds his hand. "That is not for Hayden," she says. Hayden looks at the shiny thing. He looks at his clean lion.

Hayden hugs Mama's leg. "Stay close," he says. "Hot tap red. Cold tap blue." He waves the shiny hole goodbye. "Bye bye," says Hayden, and lion gets one more rinse.

Aaron rode down the big slide. He held his toy car in his hand. Then it was time for snack. Later, Aaron looked in his pocket. His car was gone.

"My car is lost!" said Aaron. His friend Mia came to help. They looked by the swings. They looked in the sand. No car. Aaron sat down on the slide steps. "I had it here," he said. "I went down the slide. Then I walked to the bench." Mia smiled. "Let me ride down the slide!" she said. Mia went down, slowly, looking left and right. At the bottom, in the green grass, something red was peeking out.

"Because you rode the same way, you found it!" said Aaron. He held his car up high. The cloudy sky turned sunny, and the two friends ran to play in the little forest of bushes by the fence, car zooming ahead.

Asher loved summer camp. His team was going to have lunch outside. But first, the camp teacher said, "Wash your hands with soap." Asher looked at the soap. He did not want to wait.

He got his bread and took a big bite. A tiny bit of dirt was on his hand. It went right onto his bread. Asher looked down. "Yuck," he said. "My bread has dirt."

The teacher smiled. "Let's try again." Asher put soap on his hands. He rubbed them while he counted. "One, two, three." He counted all the way to twenty. The bubbles felt cozy and warm.

Then he got new bread. He looked at his hands. They were clean. No dirt on the bread this time.

"Dirt gets on my food because my hands were dirty," Asher said. "So I count to twenty. Bubbles, count to twenty. Bubbles, count to twenty."

After that, Asher did not skip the sink. He washed after the toilet too. He rubbed the bubbles and counted. Then he ran to his team, holding his clean hands up high.

Mya went to the library storytime room. She sat on a striped cushion. The librarian read a book about a red bird. Mya clapped when the story was done.

Then the librarian said, "Mya, here is your first library card." Mya held it with both hands. It had her name on it. She picked a book about paint. It had a blue cat on the front.

"I want to keep this book forever," Mya said. "It can live in my room."

The librarian shook her head. "The book goes home with you. Then you bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Mya looked at the book. She looked at her card. She counted on her fingers. "One day, two days, three days, four days. Then I bring it back?"

"Yes," said the librarian. "You can borrow it again too."

Mya carried the book to the desk. She gave her card. The librarian stamped the book.

At home, Mya read the book to her teddy bear. She read it to her socks. She read it to her mom.

When the four days were done, Mya took the book back. A boy was waiting there. He took the blue cat book and smiled.

"The book came back," he said. "Because I brought it back," said Mya.

She picked a new book about a striped fish. "This one can come home too. Then it comes back too."

Weston sat at the dinner table. He wanted the yummy bread. It sat far, far away. The bread basket was on the other side of the salt storm, where Daddy shook white salt like snow.

"Milk, please," said Mommy to Daddy. Daddy passed the milk. Weston watched with big eyes.

Weston reached for the bread. His arm was too short. He stretched and stretched. Oops. His cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table like a river.

"Sorry, Mommy," said Weston. Mommy wiped the milk. Weston thought hard. When Mommy said please, Daddy passed things. So the magic word made hands move.

"Bread, please," said Weston. Daddy smiled and passed the basket. The bread was warm and soft. Weston took a big bite. Crumbs tickled his chin.

"Thank you, Daddy," said Weston. Weston clapped his hands. The magic words worked. "Please gets bread," he said. "Thank you makes Daddy smile." Daddy gave him one more piece, just because.

Iris went to Papa's office. She saw a big tablet on his desk. She wanted to draw a monkey on it.

The screen was dark. Iris tapped it, but nothing happened. Then she found the small round button on the side. She held it down. The screen lit up. "The button makes it go on," she said.

Iris found the drawing app. It had a little paint pot on it. She tapped the paint pot. It opened. She picked a sharp pencil tool and drew a curly tail, big ears and a happy face. Then Papa said it was time for lunch.

Iris pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in its soft cover. She put it on the shelf, just like Papa showed her.

Papa printed her monkey. He gave her the page. Iris was careful, but one corner started to rip. She held the page with both hands. "Now the monkey is safe," she said. Papa smiled and pinned him up by his desk.

Isabelle went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. There were lanterns everywhere. There was a long table with little candles. The candles were for the festival of lights.

Isabelle wanted to see the candles up close. She stood on a chair. She reached out her hand. "Look, Mama," she said. "This candle is little now. It was big before!" The flame had burned the wax. The candle got short because the fire ate it. "The fire makes it small," said Isabelle. "It goes fast!"

Mama smiled. She lit a new candle. It was tall. Isabelle watched the flame. It danced and shone. The wax began to drip, drip, drip. A little drop fell onto the plate. "Another one is getting small," said Isabelle. She held Papa's hand and watched the light.

Emmett went to the store with Dad. Emmett wanted to make pizza for dinner. He picked a red apple, but Dad said, "We need cheese and bread." Emmett put cheese in the cart. He put round flat bread in the cart, too. At home, Emmett began to build his pizza. First the sauce. Then the cheese on top. Mom put the pizza in the hot oven. Emmett waited. He watched the little window. The cheese was hard and cold before. Now it went soft and bubbly. "The hot oven melts the cheese," said Emmett. Water dripped off the lettuce and made a puddle on the floor. Emmett wiped it up slowly with a towel. Ding! The pizza was ready. Emmett took a big bite. "Tasty!" he said. "More cheese, please, Emmett," said Mom, holding out her plate.

Gabriel wanted the big red truck. His sister Mia had it. She held it tight in her hands.

"One more minute," said Mom. "Then it is your turn." Mom set the timer. It went tick, tick, tick. Gabriel watched it. How did the timer know? At school, his teacher used a timer too. The timer said beep! Mia gave him the truck.

"Your turn," she said. "Thank you, Mia," said Gabriel. He pushed the truck. Vroom, vroom. Mia waited and waited. She did not grab it. The timer went tick, tick, tick again. Beep! Now it was Mia's turn.

"Can we share?" asked Gabriel. He put blocks in the truck. "You put them in. I dump them out," said Mia. They both laughed. Then Gabriel had an idea. He tickled the truck like a baby? No! He tickled Mia's toes instead. She laughed so big.

"The timer helped us," said Gabriel. "We both got turns." Mia hugged the truck tight, then she hugged Gabriel too. "Tick, tick, beep!" she shouted.

Norah wants to bake a cake. The cake's name is Big Sun Cake. Norah mixes eggs, milk and flour in a shiny silver bowl. She stirs and stirs. The batter is smooth and wet.

Norah pours the batter into a pan. She puts the pan in the oven. Then she waits. She waits some more. Nothing happens. The batter stays wet and cold.

Mom smiles. "The oven is not on yet," she says. Mom turns the dial. A little light glows. The oven gets hot. Hot, hot, hot.

"Now watch," says Mom. The batter puffs up. It gets big and round like a real sun. Norah claps her hands.

"The oven was cold," says Norah. "Cold ovens do not bake. Hot ovens bake cakes!"

Dad comes in. "Stop, my tummy is growling," he says with a grin.

Norah cuts him the first big piece.

Iris sat at the dinner table. She had ten little peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two, three," said Iris. She pushed one pea with her finger each time. "Four, five, six." Then she stopped. The next word was hiding from her. "Eight?" she said. Dad shook his head and smiled.

Dad held up seven fingers, no, just some fingers, near her plate. "Sss," he said, like a soft snake. "Seven!" said Iris. She poked the next pea. "Seven! Then eight, nine, ten." All the peas had a number. The clock on the wall gave a little tick. Iris ate one pea. "Now nine!" she said. Dad laughed and ate one too.

Penelope went to the store with Mama. She held her toy monkey, Mo. Mo had a low bump on his head. "Mo is hungry," said Penelope. "What do monkeys eat?" Mama smiled. "What do you think?" Penelope thought hard. "Bananas! Monkeys eat bananas!"

First they walked down the toy aisle. There were balls and blocks and a big red truck. Penelope looked high. She looked low. No bananas here. "This is the toy aisle," she said. "Toys are for playing. Bananas are food!"

So they walked to the food part of the store. There were apples and bread and milk. And there, on a low shelf, sat a big yellow bunch of bananas. Penelope reached up. She picked one out. "Mo, look! A banana for you!" She held it near Mo's mouth. "Mmm," she said, in her best monkey voice. "Yum, yum, yum."

Mama laughed. "Mo likes it here." Penelope hugged the banana and Mo together. At home, Penelope ate the banana herself. Mo watched from the table. "Monkeys share," Penelope told him. Then she took a crayon and tried to write the word banana, but she only made a wiggly line. "That says banana," she said. Mo seemed happy. "Mmm," said Penelope, in her best monkey voice again.

Jacob ran to the big slide at the playground. He touched it. "Ouch! Why is it so hot?" he asked. The sun was shining on it all day. That was why.

So Jacob ran to the small slide. It sat under a tree, in the shade. He touched it. It felt cold. "Ha! The sun makes the big slide hot," Jacob said. "The shade keeps the small slide cold."

Jacob slid down the small slide. He went slow. Then he slid down the big, hot slide very fast. "Whee!" Fast and slow. Hot and cold. Big and small.

A boy named Tom laughed. "You went down the smelly slide," he teased. "A dog sat on it!" Jacob giggled and held his nose. "Yuck!"

Then Jacob got to ride the twisty merry-go-round. Round and round he went, fast, then slow, then fast. "This is my best gift ever," he said. "A sunny day at the playground!"

Jake put on his clean blue shirt. Grandma made it for him. It smelled like warm soap.

At school, Jake built a tall block tower. It was very tall. Ben bumped the table. The tower fell down. Crash. Jake felt sad. His eyes got wet.

"Ben, you bumped the table," said Jake. "The tower fell because of the bump." Ben felt bad. "I am sorry," he said. "I will help you."

Then Ms. Kim rang the little bell. "Story time!" she said. Jake felt excited. He loved stories. He jumped up and down. Ben laughed.

Ms. Kim read a book about a bear. "Can you spell bear?" she asked. "B, E, A, R," said Jake. He felt happy.

Ben and Jake built the tower again. It was even taller. "This tower is so big!" said Jake. He gave Ben a big hug.

The bookmobile came to Edouard's street. It was a little truck full of books. Edouard climbed the steps with his mom.

The library lady smiled at him. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Edouard nodded. He got a card with his name on it. He picked a book about a big red truck.

He held the book tight. "Can I keep it forever?" he begged.

"Not forever," said the lady. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back by a certain day. Other people want to read it too."

Edouard looked at the book. Other kids liked trucks too. Maybe someone else was waiting for this one.

"Can I read it tonight?" he asked. "And bring it back next time?"

"Yes," said the lady.

That night, mom read the book to him twice. Edouard fell asleep with the truck book under his pillow.

The next morning he asked, "Is it the bring-back day yet?"

Mom laughed. "Not yet, little one. First we read it some more."

Edouard smiled and turned the page.

Sara ran to the park with Daddy. Her bunny was gone! Bunny was lost somewhere.

"Where did you play last?" asked Daddy. Sara thought hard. "The sand!" she said. "Bunny was in the sand!" They ran to the sand box. Not here. Look again! They ran past the water cup fountain. Not here. Look again! A big dog began to bark, bark, bark at a thin green bush.

Sara peeked in the bush. No bunny. Then she remembered. She had sat on the bench for a snack. They ran to the bench. Sara bent down low. She looked under it. There was bunny, soft and sandy, waiting by her shoe!

"I found you!" Sara hugged bunny tight. The dog barked one happy bark, as if to say hello.

Lucy sat at her big table. She wanted to paint her doll's dress green. She looked and looked. "Where is the green paint?" she asked. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. No green.

"Cat, do you see green?" she asked. The cat said, "Meow." Lucy laughed. "Silly cat. You see naps."

Lucy had an idea. She put one drop of blue in a cup. She put one drop of yellow in the cup. She stirred it round and round. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said. "The blue did it. The yellow helped."

Outside, it began to snow. The snow fell on the grass. "Look, Cat!" said Lucy. "The deep snow hides the green grass." She painted the doll's dress. It was green, green, green.

"Now you have a green dress," Lucy told the doll. The cat said, "Meow."

Logan had a little drum. He wanted to play a song. He hit the drum very fast. The sounds came out all jumbled. The cat ran under the chair.

"This is hard," said Logan.

Mama sat down next to him. She showed him the drum. "Try it slow," she said. "Slow and steady."

Logan hit the drum. Bump. Bump. Bump. He went slow. The bumps sounded nice. The cat came back and sat by his feet.

Logan went slow, one, two, three. Then he went slow some more. Then he tried a little faster. Bump-bump-bump! The song came out just right.

"I did it!" said Logan. "Slow made it work. Fast made it messy."

Mama clapped her hands. Logan patted the cat. The cat purred very soft.

"Play it again," said Mama. So Logan read his drum book, found a new song, and began to play. Bump. Bump. Bump.

Aurora went to the dentist with her mama. The chair was big. It had a wheel on one side. "Can I spin it?" she asked. "Yes, but only once," said Dr. Kim.

Dr. Kim had a little mirror. "Open your mouth wide," she said. Aurora opened it very wide. She was a young girl, but she could open like a lion. "Roar," said Dr. Kim, and Aurora giggled.

Then Aurora closed her lips. The mirror could not see her teeth. "Oh no," said Dr. Kim. "My mirror is sad." Aurora opened again. The mirror went in. "I see the problem. A spot is hiding." Dr. Kim let the water squirt wash it away. "The spot went away because I opened my mouth!" said Aurora. "That's right," said Dr. Kim. "Now let me spin the chair wheel once."

Isabella put on her red shoes. Today was a school day. At school, Mr. Tom had a chart. "Ben feeds the fish today," said Mr. Tom. Isabella wanted to feed the fish too. "When can I feed them?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Mr. Tom. Isabella made a sad face. Tomorrow felt very far away.

Then Isabella watched the day. Now it was story time. Later it was snack time. Then the sun went low in the sky. Mom came to pick her up. "Sleep first," said Mom. "Then tomorrow comes."

Isabella slept in her high bed. She woke up. The sun was high again. She put on her red shoes. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom, smiling.

At school, Isabella got the little cup of food. She fed the fish. The fish ate fast. "Yesterday Ben fed you," she said. "Today I feed you!"

It was Saturday morning at Charles's house. Everyone came to watch the big game. Papa sat on the couch. Aunt Jo sat on the floor. Uncle Ben sat by the door. Charles counted the people. "One, two, three, four, and me makes five!"

The red team ran with the ball. Then the red team scored. Everyone jumped up and shouted. The shout was loud. It felt scary to Charles. He hid behind Papa's leg. "It is okay," said Papa. "I am right here."

Charles watched again. The blue team ran with the ball. The blue team did not score. Nobody shouted. Charles looked around. He saw why the shouting happened. "They shouted because the red team scored," he said. Papa smiled and nodded. Aunt Jo dropped some chips. She had to sweep them up with her hand. Then the red team scored one more time. Everyone shouted again. This time Charles shouted too. "Go red team!" said Charles. Papa gave him a big hug.

The lights went out. The whole room went dark. Leo's mama lit some candles. The candles made little flames. The flames made big shadows on the wall.

"Look!" said Leo. He moved his hand near a candle. His shadow moved too. He wiggled his fingers. The shadow fingers wiggled. "It moves because of the light!" he said.

The flashlight was on the table. Leo grabbed it. He clicked it on. But the light was small and dim. He clicked it again. Still dim. "The battery is low," said Mama. "We are a team. You hold the candle. I will hold this one."

The flame tickled the air above it. Leo giggled. "The candle is tickling!" he said. The wax began to drip down the side. Mama said bedtime would come early tonight.

Leo held his candle all the way to his room. His shadow walked with him, big on the wall. "Come on, shadow," said Leo. "Sleep time."

Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Grandma waved from the porch. "Come see, Gabriel," she said. Gabriel ran to the big table. Grandma had paper and paints. "We will make a map," she said. "A map for a treasure walk."

Gabriel drew a tree on the map. But he wanted green paint for the leaves. There was no green pot on the table. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. Gabriel frowned. "No green," he said.

He dipped his brush in the yellow pot. He made a yellow leaf. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue pot. The yellow leaf turned green. Gabriel opened his eyes wide. "Yellow and blue make green!" he said. He painted more green leaves, one by one.

Then they walked the map to the treasure. It was a jar of salty crackers by the red door. A blue bird sat on top. "Crunch," said Gabriel. Grandma laughed and waved to the bird.

Luca sat in the car with his blanket. It was soft and white. Mama was in the front seat. They were going to get the new baby.

Luca held up his blanket. "This is for the baby," he said. "Babies like big kid things."

Mama smiled. "Babies are very small," she said. "They cannot hold a big blanket yet."

At the house, Daddy put the baby in Luca's arms. Luca gave the blanket. The baby's hands did not grab it. The blanket fell down. Luca picked it up.

Then Luca tried a little sock. The baby grabbed the sock! One little hand held on tight.

Luca counted, "One sock, two hands, three little fingers." The baby held the sock all the way home.

Luca whispered, "Babies like little things. I will bring little things." The baby squeezed the sock again.
